Court, after notice to parties in interest, to approve purchase of decedent's real estate at private sale by his executor. 

Page 55, Sec. 36. New. Act of June 11th, 1941, P.L. 117 

amending Act of July 2nd, 1935, P.L. 540, authorizes fiduciaries subject to the jurisdiction of common pleas courts with the approval of said court, to accept deeds of mortgaged property in lieu of foreclosure of mortgage, but requires deed to recite that it is so accepted to save foreclosure costs. 

Act of August 5th, 1941, P.L. 819, amending Act of May 

5th, 1935, P.L. 99, gives similar authority with like requirement to fiduciaries subject to the jurisdiction of orphans' courts but does not require approval of such courts. 

Page 95, Sec. 45 (a). The rule discussed in Sec. 45 (a) held not to apply to sale by Secretary of Banking as Receiver, Central Trust Company, 41 D. & C. 304. 

Page 95, also Page 516. The Act of July 2d, 1941, P.L. 227, preserves brokers' rights to commissions where sales procured by them are rescinded because of a fiduciary's receipt of a higher offer.

Page 147. Sec. 55 (b). New. Act of July 28th, 1941, P.L. 

539, now authorizes Counties and Municipalities of the State to give "special warranty deeds" upon re-sale of unredeemed property acquired at tax or municipal claim sale.

Page 165. Secs. 67 to 70. Note in connection with these sections that the Uniform Acknowledgment Act has been enacted in Pennsylvania by the Act of July 24th, 1941, P.L. 490. 

The new act authorizes alternate forms of acknowledging instruments of conveyancing but the prior law has not been repealed and the older forms set forth in the book may and probably will still be used.

Page 174. Act of June 18th, 1941, P.L. 136, authorizes certain other officers of the armed forces (this includes naval officers) of the United States to take acknowledgments. 

Page 249. Add at the end of Sec. 97 (c) the following. 

There is another method of satisfaction provided by the old 

Act of Apr. 11, 1856, P.L. 304 (21 P.S. 685) which authorizes the satisfaction of mortgages and judgments upon production of the instruments with payment endorsed thereon by the legal holder in presence of two witnesses, and upon certificate of the president judge or the "district judge" of the proper county allowing the same. The instruments are then filed with the recorder of deeds or, in the case of judgments, with the prothonotary. This act, while apparently obsolete provides a method which the author is informed is still in use in some of the counties.

Page 253. Add to the end of Sec. 98, new Act of July 24th, 

1941, P.L. 466. By this act mortgages due the Commonwealth are presumed paid where no demand or payment of interest or on account of principal has been made for fifty years. 

The Department of Justice is authorized to satisfy such mortgages on application of the property owner. 

Pages 269-274. Note at end of Sec. 100 (D) that a new

PREFACE TO SECOND AND REVISED EDITION. 

More than a quarter century has passed since the first edition of this work was written. It was a period that included three business depressions, one of them the most severe and prolonged in our history. The terrific decline in real estate values which followed, tested severely all laws regulating real property and its transfer. Much litigation ensued, culminating in many decisions by which the law relating to real estate has been virtually re-examined. 

During the period referred to many important statutory revisions and codes, bearing upon the transfer of real estate titles, were enacted. Among these may be mentioned the Intestate Laws, the Wills Act; the Fiduciaries' Act; the Partition 

Act and the Revised Price Act-all of. 1917; the Uniform 

Fraudulent Conveyance Act of 1921; the Municipal Claims and Tax Lien Act of 1923; the Real Estate Brokers License Act of 1929; the Act Regulating Discharge of Liens, 1929; and the

Corporation Laws and the Building and Loan Laws of 1933. 

These have necessitated a re-writing of the portions of the original book relating thereto.

The style, presentation and arrangement of the first edition received such universal approbation by the bar, the law students and the real estate profession that it has been thought well to continue the same form. Therefore the section numbers and headings of the original text have been preserved and where deemed practical, new matter has been added thereto by "sub-sections" (indicated by lower case letters) and by "divisions" of sub-sections (indicated by numbers). When new sections were found necessary, they have been inserted after the sections to which they relate, but the numerical order has been maintained by adding a capital letter to the prior section number for the new section. Though this method may appear, at first glance, to be somewhat clumsy, it does iii

iv 

PREFACE TO SECOND AND REVISED EDITION 

have the advantage of permitting sections of the first edition (that have been cited in court decisions) to be readily located in this book, together with any added new matter or new cases supporting the same.

This revision has added some sixty new sections to the original work, and as many more new sub-sections and subdivisions. Case citations have been brought down to date, and the practice of carrying them in the text itself has been continued. Footnotes, which at the best are an annoyance to the reader, have been used sparingly, and only when and where they might be helpful.

The chapter on "Searches" has been revised in collaboration with Peirce Mecutchen, Esq., of the Philadelphia Bar, formerly Vice-President and Title officer of the Land Title 

Bank and Trust Company; and the chapter on "Settlements" with James R. Wilson, Esq., also of the Philadelphia Bar, whose knowledge and experience in this subject is well-known. 

The author also acknowledges his indebtedness to other able members of the bar whose researches embraced in papers read to the Pennsylvania Title Association and the different bar associations, were found helpful. Due credit to each has been given in an appropriate footnote where their respective papers have been referred to.

The chapter on Real Estate Brokers has been thoroughly revised. The Real Estate Brokers' License Act has been analyzed, re-arranged and presented in what is thought to be a more logical order than that of the statute. Its effect upon the rights, liabilities and duties of the broker have been noted, and a sincere effort made to present the principles of the many cases on brokers' commissions in a natural classification. 

The novel feature of using forms to illustrate the text, and adding an appendix of others, to a book on Conveyancing, employed for the first time in the original edition, proved so popular that it has been continued with many new forms inserted. For the particular convenience of the bench and bar, the statutes cited in the text include a reference to the section where they may be found in Purdon's Pennsylvania

PREFACE TO SECOND AND REVISED EDITION 

Digest, and a chronological table of statutes as well as a table of the cases cited, have been appended. 

All of this has produced a book which is over twice the size of the original work. It is hoped it will be found to be twice as useful. 

Philadelphia, June 1, 1941. 

GROVER C. LADNER

To 

MY FATHER HON. ALBERT H. LADNER, SR.

PREFACE TO FIRST EDITION. 

Being appointed some time ago to conduct a course in Conveyancing, the author had occasion to seek for a book suitable for use as a guide for those taking the course. While excellent works have been written on Conveyancing, no book has been written which covers the modern practice or forms. The author therefore was compelled to write out his own lectures and while doing so conceived the idea of enlarging them so as to make a compact and practical book for the use of all persons transacting a real estate business. 

The modern conveyancer, whether lawyer or layman, not only wants to know the law of conveyancing but what to do and how to do it. With this thought in mind the author has endeavored to set forth the law of conveyancing as clearly and concisely as possible and with ample citation of authorities. Everything obsolete has been omitted. Little space has been used discussing doubtful propositions of law. The dangerous shoals have been pointed out and the method to avoid them set forth. Liberal use has been made of forms to illustrate the text and many more have been added in an appendix so that it is hoped every form used in modern conveyancing will be found included; a convenience which will probably be appreciated by the busy lawyer, conveyancer and beginner alike.

The methods of carrying on a real estate business have changed radically within the last score of years. The custom of insuring title and making settlements through Title Insurance Companies, especially in the larger cities has developed marvelously. A chapter has therefore been added on Title 

Insurance Companies, including their mode of transacting business and stating settlements. At the same time a chapter on Title Searching and instructions how to search has also vii

viii PREFACE TO FIRST EDITION 

been included for the use of those who still prefer to do their own searching. 

The author desires to acknowledge his indebtedness to 

Albert H. Ladner, Jr., Esq., of the Philadelphia Bar, for many valuable suggestions and forms embodied in this book. 

GROVER CLEVELAND LADNER Philadelphia, Pa., October 1, 1912.

$12. Definitions of Title. 

By Descent, Purchase, Adverse Possession 

I. 

1. Definition of Terms. Conveyancing, Land, Title. 

23 23 Conveyancing has been defined as the science of transferring title to land (Mitchell on Conveyancing in Pa. 258).

To properly understand this definition we must first understand the meaning of the words, "land" and "title".

Land is defined by Blackstone as comprehending all things of a permanent substantial nature (2 Blk. 16). In the earliest days a very sound and natural distinction was made between things movable and things immovable. The former became known as personal property and the latter became known as real property. If, then, real property is something immovable, land is real property. So also anything that is substantially annexed or fastened to the land, such as a house, becomes immovable. Hence it becomes real property. Properties movable and immovable are from the very nature of their distinction so essentially different that it is not difficult to see why different methods of transferring ownership in them should have arisen in the law. Ownership of a horse can be transferred by a physical delivery of the animal, but land cannot be delivered in the same way. Hence a totally different method was evolved to transfer land.

§3 

The other word of our definition to be explained is title. 

What is title? Title is best defined as the evidence of ownership of land. Conveyancing, therefore means the science or method of transferring the evidence of ownership of a permanent, fixed, immovable thing. As intimated this method is so totally different from the method of transferring ownership of personal property that it has been well termed a science. 

We will, therefore, later consider title, what it is, how acquired and how transferred.

II. 

ESTATES IN LAND. 

2. Definition of Kinds of Estates. 

Before proceeding to consider the evidence of the ownership in land we must first understand the quantity of a person's ownership in land, i.e., estates in land. The term estate is doubtless familiar to the reader and the question is often heard, "What estate does such and such a person have in a certain piece of land," meaning of course what is the quantity of his interest. Does he own it absolutely, does he merely lease it or does he hold it for life? Estate means quantity of Ownership in land and is to be distinguished from title which is the evidence of ownership of that quantity, be the quantity great as a fee, or small as an estate for years. 

In brief, estate means quantity; title means quality. 

Blackstone (2 Blacks. 104) divides estates into two general divisions, each of which is subdivided as follows: 

[Fee Simple. 

Life Estate 

For one's own life. 

For the life of another. 

Estates of freehold 

Estates by the curtesy. Dower.

$3 

Estate for years.

Estates less than freehold Estate at will. 

Estate at sufferance.

From the table it will be seen that an Estate of Freehold is any estate of uncertain duration other than an Estate at Will. The only freehold estates at the present time which still persist in the law are these above set forth. At common law there were many others such as e.g. Estates Tail; but in order not to confuse the mind with terms that are obsolete, we will confine ourselves to those that are still in use. Those interested in the historical side of the development of estates in land we refer to the second book of the Blackstone's Commentaries and the case of Fisher v. Morris, 5 Whart. 3581839. 

3. Freehold Estates. 

(a) A Fee Simple Estate is the largest estate that a man can have in lands. It is the pure, simple, unconditional and absolute estate (Mitchell on Real Estate and Conveyancing 91). It is commonly called an estate in fee. It is the estate with which we are most usually brought in contact and represents absolute ownership of land. (b) A Life Estate as the name indicates is an estate for life. It may be granted for the grantee's own life or for the life of another; in any event to be a life estate it must cease with the life of the person for the length of whose life it was granted. (c) Estates of Dower and Curtesy were formerly life estates and treated as subdivision thereof. However, as they arise differently and have been greatly modified by Statute in 

Pennsylvania, we have set them apart. (1) An Estate of Dower is an estate created by mere operation of the law. It was the one-third interest which a married

$5 

woman had for life in all land owned in fee which the husband had at the time of and after his marriage. The 

Intestate Act of Penna. as revised in 1917 (Act of June 7, 

1917, P.L. 429; 20 P.S. 1, 2. See $134 of this book), now gives to the wife of an intestate in lieu of dower one-third of the whole estate, real and personal, if there are two children or more, and one-half if deceased leaves but one child or none. Further, this share is now absolute and in fee, whereas formerly and at common law dower was merely a life estate. 

Before this revision of 1917 the old common law dower still prevailed where a husband conveyed away his real estate without his wife joining in the deed, but now §3 of the Intestate Act of 1917 (20 P.S. 31) for the first time gives the wife the same share in lands aliened by her husband in his life time, without her joining in the conveyance as those of which he died seised. This statute applies only prospectively, i.e., to conveyances made after the statute, so that the old common law dower may still exist in cases of lands conveyed without a wife's joinder before the date of the statute (Merrick v. DuPont, 285 Pa. 368-1926). (2) An Estate of Curtesy is also an estate which arises by operation of law. At common law it was the right which vested in the husband upon marriage to enjoy upon his wife's death and during the term of his natural life all of the real estate which she owned in fee. Here, again, there has been a change by the Intestate Act (June 7, 1917, P.L. 429, §4, 20

P.S. 32) in that the old curtesy estate of a surviving husband is taken away and he is given in lieu thereof the same share as that of a surviving widow, viz: One-third absolutely of the whole estate, real and personal, if two children or more, and one-half if one child or none.

As will be seen hereafter (§§165, 166 of this book), the husband and wife under the Intestate Act have not only the right to take the share granted in lieu of dower in cases of actual intestacy, but each now has the right to claim the same against their spouse's Will. Also in cases of actual.

§ 

intestacy where no children survive an additional allowance of $5000. See (§134 of this book [20 P.S. 11, §2(a)]). 

4. Estates Less than Freehold. (a) An Estate of Years is an estate which is let unto another to enjoy for a stipulated time. It is an estate granted for a limited, definite period of time. Whether given for one month or for one year or for ten years, it is nevertheless an estate for years. The distinguishing feature about it is that it comes to an end at a known certain definite time. An estate for years whether for one month or 2,000 years is but personal property and no more (Townsend v. Boyd, 217 Pa. 

386-1907), and therefore not subject to the lien of a judg ment (Bismark B. & L. v. Bolster, 92 Pa. 123—1879). 

(b) Estate at Will is where lands are let by one man to another to hold at the will of the owner who is known as the lessor¹ or it may be created to continue at the will of the lessee, i.e., the party receiving the estate. It has been said, that in Pennsylvania by reason of the Act of March 21, 1772, (I Sm. L. 370 §12, 68 P.S. 361), requiring a reasonable notice to quit to be given a tenant at will such tenancy is in this State merely nominal (Clark v. Smith, 25 Pa. 137—1855) and that such tenancy has become in effect one from year to year. Since the more recent act however, Act of March 

31, 1905 P.L. 87 §1 (68 P.S. 366), permitting actions of possession to be brought against a tenant holding "either by license or lease whether oral or written ** for an indeterminate time", after thirty days' notice in writing to quit has been served; it would now seem more accurate to now say that a tenancy at will has virtually become one from month to month (McHenry v. Shaffer, 58 Pa. Super. Ct. 171-1914) and see (Morgan v. Williams, 39 Pa. Super. Ct. 580-1909). 

1 The reader is probably familiar with the significance of the termination or and ee in legal terminology, viz: that or denotes the doer of the act, ee the one to whom the act is done. A lessor, he who leases; lessee, he who receives the lease. Vendor, he who sells; vendee, he who buys.

$7 

(c) An Estate at Sufferance is where one comes into possession of the land by lawful means, but keeps it afterwards without any title at all. E.g., a tenant in possession after the tenant at sufferance so long as the owner "suffers", or permits him to remain (Sutmeyer v. 

Thornton, 63 Pa. Super. Ct. 607—1916). lease has expired, is a 

5. Joint Estates. 

By joint estates are meant such estates as are vested in more than one person at the same time, in the same land. 

At common law there were four kinds: Estates in Joint 

Tenancies, Coparcenary Estates; Tenancy in Common and 

Estates by Entireties. The first two are virtually obsolete as to real estate and no longer require much consideration; the other two survive to the present day, the last one especially being frequently met with in modern conveyancing. (a) An Estate in Joint Tenancy. At common law a joint tenancy in land existed whenever two or more persons acquired land by one and the same instrument (Mitchell on Real 

Estate and Conveyancing in Pa. 245). Each party to such an estate was considered in law as having vested in him the undivided share of the whole estate. Thus it followed that if one of two joint tenants died his right survived to the other. This effect could not be avoided nor could either compel a division of the estate.

In Pennsylvania this estate has been rendered largely obsolete as to real estate by the Act of March 31, 1812 (5 Sm. 

L. 395, 20 P.S. 121), which took away from joint tenancy the incident of survivorship unless expressly preserved and in effect converted it into a tenancy in common. This Act has been interpreted to be an Act of construction, that is to say, it does not forbid the creation of a joint estate with the attribute of survivorship if the language creating the joint estate clearly expresses such an intent (Redemptionist Fathers v. 

Lawler, 205 Pa. 24-1903; McCallum's Estate, 211 Pa. 2051905). Before this Act a transfer of an estate to two persons

§ 

was presumed to be joint and to carry with it the incident of survivorship. If this were not intended, there had to be in the grant or devise some appropriate words to indicate that survivorship was not intended. The Act now reverses the situation and requires the use of appropriate words to impose the incident of survivorship. Trust Estates alone are excepted and between joint trustees the right of survivorship still exists. (b) Estate in Coparcenary. This is an estate defined by 

Blackstone (2 Blackstone Com. 187) to be one where lands of inheritance descend from the ancestor to two or more persons. 

This estate is obsolete; it no longer exists in Pennsylvania because the intestate laws of this commonwealth provide that where lands descend to several persons under its provisions they shall take and hold as tenants in common. (See $134, of this book, §19 of intestate laws infra, 20 P.S. 132). (c) Tenancy in Common. Is where two or more persons not husband and wife have an undivided interest in the same land. As the name implies, it means land held in common. 

Each co-tenant is considered in law as being possessed of the whole of an undivided part not of an undivided part of the whole. It, therefore, follows there is no survivorship in this species of joint estate and any one of the co-tenants may compel partition of the whole or devise his portion to his heirs. Tenants in common have no authority to bind their co-tenants by an agreement concerning the use or control or affecting the title of the joint property (McCullough's Petition, 275 Pa. 456-1923). Consequently agreements of sale, leases, deeds, mortgages, must be executed by all the co-tenants in order to bind all. But it has been held when repairs are absolutely necessary or an expenditure made at the instance of the municipality such as for a sidewalk or curb, or taxes, water rents or for insurance, the consent of the co-tenants will be implied and he is liable to contribute to the reasonable cost of whatever is essential to meet the requirements of the municipality. (Sharp v. Keiser,

$9 

95 Pa. Super. Ct. 174-1928). The rule as to improvements voluntarily made, is otherwise (Cobbett v. Gallagher, 339 Pa. 231-1940).

By the Act of May 24, 1917 P.L. 270 §1 (72 P.S. §5968) 

the undivided interest of a tenant in common or co-parcener who has paid his proportionate share of taxes assessed against the land, may not be sold or title thereto divested by any treasurer's or sheriff's sale for failure of the other tenant or tenants in common to pay their share of taxes. (Lohr's Estate, 132 Pa. Super. Ct. 125-1938). The same act authorizes any tenant in common or co-parcener whose land is about to be sold for non-payment of taxes to pay his proportionate share of such taxes whereupon his interest will not be sold.

A tenant in common may also under the Act of June 24, 1895 P.L. 237 §1 (68 P.S. 101) sue in assumpsit to recover from his co-tenant who was in exclusive possession, a proportionate part of its rental value (Duggan v. Duggan 291 Pa. 

556-1928). But since this right is purely statutory (Calvano's Estate 35 D & C 395-1939) he must aver that the defendant was in possession and that he (the plaintiff) was excluded from possession (Hoog v. Diehl 134 Pa. Super. Ct. 

14, 19-1938).

Since the Act of 1812 all estates except estates by entireties (See §5(d) 1) and trust estates held in Pennsylvania by a plurality of persons are to be regarded as tenancies in common, unless the language of the instrument creating the tenancy expressly provides otherwise. (§5(a) Supra). (d) Estate by Entireties. 

1 Definition and Construction. In our definition of the 

Estate of Tenancy in Common it will be observed we excepted husband and wife. This, because an estate vested jointly in husband and wife would be an estate by entireties. 

It differs from a tenancy in common in that the incident of survivorship is present, and as Blackstone explains "if an

§5  

estate in fee be given to a man and his wife they are neither properly joint tenants or tenants in common, for husband and wife being considered one person in the law they cannot take the estate by moieties (halves) but both are seised by the entirety." Even clearer is the explanation of Chief Justice 

Lewis in Stuckey v. Keefe's Excrs., 26 Pa. 397, 399-1856, viz.: “A conveyance to a husband and wife is neither a tenancy in common nor a joint tenancy. The estate of joint tenants is a unit made up of divisible parts; that of the husband and wife is also a unit; but it is made up of indivisible parts. In the first case they are several holders of different moieties or portions and upon the death of either, the survivor takes a new estate. He acquires by survivorship the moiety of his deceased co-tenant. In the last case, although there are two natural persons, they are but one person in law, and upon the death of either the survivor takes no new estate. It is a mere change in the properties of the legal person holding, and not an alteration in the estate holden. The loss of an adjunct merely reduces the legal personage holding the estate to an individuality identical with the natural person. The whole estate continues in the survivor the same as it would continue in a corporation after the death of one of the corporators. 

A tenancy by entireties therefore arises whenever an estate vests in two persons who at the time when the estate vests are husband and wife (Klenke Estate, 210 Pa. 572-1904; 

Myers Estate, 232 Pa., 89-1911). If they are not in fact husband and wife a deed to them as such is ineffective to create a tenancy by entireties; they receive and hold title as joint tenants or tenants in common, whichever be appropriate; (Thornton et al. v. Pierce, 328 Pa. 11-1937). Nor can a tenancy by entireties be created, by a husband having sole title to real estate, conveying an undivided one half interest therein to his wife, even though the deed recites an intention to create an estate by entireties. This for the reason that it is necessary for the interests of the husband

$11 

and wife to be acquired by the same conveyance. (Walker 

Estate, 340 Pa. 13-1940).

Where a married woman and others held land in common and all joined in partition and her share was conveyed to her and her husband, the law looks at the character of the transaction rather than the form of the conveyance in order to define her interest and considers the share as still hers, a divided share being substituted for an undivided one; (Stoffal v. Jarvis, 235 Pa. 50-1912, following Stehman v. Huber, 21 

Pa. 260-1853).

In Stuckey v. Keefe's Excrs., lands were conveyed to a husband and his wife, "their heirs and assigns to hold as tenants in common and not as joint tenants." But the Court there held that this clearly expressed intention to make the husband and wife tenants in common rather than by the entireties, could not be regarded. Whether this rule prevailed after the Married Womens Property Acts was doubted in 

Merrit v. Whitlock, 200 Pa. 50-1901, though not decided.

The Superior Court, however, in Hoover v. Potter, 42 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 21, 1910, held there was nothing in the Married 

Womens Property Acts of 1848, 1887 and 1893 which changed the common law rule that a devise or a grant of real estate to a husband and wife gave a title by entireties. Nevertheless, title companies continued in doubt and for many years ere they insured such a title as one by entireties, required the habendum of the deed to contain the words, "to hold as tenants by entireties and not as tenants in common." Finally in Bleese v. Anderson, 241 Pa. 198-1913 it was held that while the Married Women's Properties Acts do not abolish or affect estates by entireties, where the grant, expressly or in effect creates such estate, yet.said the Court, "at no time since the recent legislation conferring full competency upon married women to take and hold real estate as their individual property, have we ruled that a conveyance to the husband and wife granting distinctly defined undivided parts of individual estates to each, must be construed to create an estate by entireties notwithstanding the expressed

§5  

intention of the grantor to the contrary." While this case does not mention Hoover v. Potter, it nevertheless in effect overruled it. Thus the proposition of Stuckey v. Keefe's 

Excrs., 26 Pa. 397-1856 buttressed by Hoover v. Potter, 42 Pa.

Super. Ct. 21, 1907, but doubted in Merritt v. Whitlock, 200 

Pa. 50, 1901, that a husband and wife could not hold title together in any other way than by entireties, was at an end. 

There still remained the question of construction to be given to a deed to a husband and wife as grantees without indicating the tenure. This was effectually, and logically settled in the Estate of Mary Vandergrift, 105 Pa. Super. Ct. 

293 at page 296–1932, where Judge Gawthrop laid down the governing rule as follows: "While recent cases decided since the passage of Married Women's Property acts have held that a conveyance to the husband and wife granting distinctly undivided parts or individual estates to each, will not be construed to create an estate by entireties against an express intention of the parties that they shall take otherwise (Blease v. Anderson, 241 Pa. 198-1913; Merritt v. Whitlock (supra.) and Young's Estate, 166 Pa. 645-1895), and that a husband and wife may take and hold as tenants in common, as individuals and not as a common law unity, if that be the actual intent, it is still the law that where a deed to a husband and wife discloses no intention to create any estate but one by entireties, such an estate is created in the grantees.” 

2 Effect of Estate by Entireties. Judgments against either husband or wife. Upon the death of either husband or wife, the survivor takes the whole estate and his estate dates not from the time of the death of the other but from the date of the deed. So, if a judgment lien is entered against а husband who holds real estate by entireties and the husband dies, the judgment lien does not bind his wife's estate because her estate relates back to the date of the deed and so antedates the judgment; (Hetzel v. Lincoln, 216 Pa. 601906). Nor would such a judgment bind the joint estate of the husband and wife. During the lifetime of the husband, only his expectant interest is bound. Consequently it has

$13 

been held that the husband and wife together could, despite a judgment, against either, convey a clear and unencumbered marketable title free from its lien, (Beihl v. Martin, 236 Pa. 

519, 528—1912), where it was said, "the owner of such a lien must hold it subject to possible extinction in either of two events, the predecease of the debtor or the alienation of the estate by the joint acts of the parties. The efficiency of the lien depends on the non-happening of either." 

Where, however, the debtor survives, the judgment remains a valid lien against his estate, and would be prior in lien even to a mortgage dated after its entry executed by both husband and wife (Fleek v. Zillhaver, 117 Pa. 213—1887).

Partition of an estate by entireties cannot be compelled and the incident of survivorship cannot be divested unless both husband and wife join in the deed. This is so even after divorce A. V. M. as to property acquired before the Act of 

May 10, 1927 P.L. 884 (68 P.S., 501), (Mertz v. Mertz 139 

Pa. Super. Ct. 299-1937). Neither husband nor wife in whom property has jointly vested by entirety can sell or assign their individual rights therein without joining the other, or dispose even of the expectancy of survivorship, and creditors of either acquire no enforcible lien by obtaining judgment, or title by sale in execution: (Gassner v. Pierce, 286 Pa. 529-1926.)

One exception is to be noted, which results from the Act of June 11, 1913, P.L. 468 (48 P.S., 133,) and May 24, 1923

P.L. 446 (48 P.S., 137), authorizing a sale of real estate so held, upon an execution issued on a judgment recovered by the wife for her and her children's support either in the Quarter Sessions or in the Common Pleas or other courts, or any action brought upon articles of separation or other contract with the husband stipulating for the wife's support. 

The purchaser at such a sale acquires the title theretofore held by both to the same effect as though they had joined in the conveyance of the same. (See Commonwealth v. Rutkowski, 23 Schuyl. Co. 243-1927; Hurley v. Hurley, 10 D. & 

C. 278-1928).

$5 

3 Effect of Divorce on Entireties. Rent. Even a divorce from the bonds of matrimony does not convert an estate by entireties to one of tenancy in common. (Alles v. Lyon, 216 

Pa. 604-1907). But partition may now be compelled after a divorce A. V. M. as to property acquired by entireties after the Act of May 10, 1927 P.L. 884 (68 P.S., 501).

Rents. As to income from the property after divorce, it has been held, that while the marriage subsists, it is a matter of indifference which of the parties leases the property or which of them obtain the rent; presumptively the moneys received will be expended for the benefit of both of them. The unity of the relation of the parties results in a unity of the estate. Leasing by either is for the benefit of both of them in that relation. Therefore it must follow that after a divorce, if the parties cannot agree between themselves as to a division of such income, the court upon application, will divide it equally between them. If one of the parties collects from the tenant more than an equal share of the income, the law implies a promise to pay to the other, his or her fair share; (O'Malley v. O'Malley, 272 Pa. 528-1922). And where one of the divorcees remains in sole possession, the other, it was held, might recover one-half of the fair rental value of the property, (Cornelius v. Cornelius, 104 Pa. Super. 

Ct. 455-1932). But where a tenant paid the whole rent to one of the two divorcees who held title by entireties, it was held, in Gassner v. Pierce, 286 Pa. 529-1926, that a payment to either was a good satisfaction of the rent and the tenant could not be compelled to pay a second time. 

4 Estates by the Entireties in Personal Property. Hus band and wife may hold not only real estate, but personal property and choses in action as well, as tenants by the entirety (Gillan v. Dixon 65 Pa. 395-1870; Bramberry's 

Estate 156 Pa. 628-1893; Sloan's Estate 254 Pa. 346-1916).

It most frequently appears in bank accounts of husband and wife, (Madden v. Gosztonyi S. & T. Co. 331 Pa. 476-1938). 

In McCarter's Estate 36 D. & C. 625—1939, it was held that

$15 

where household furniture is in the joint possession of husband and wife living together at the time of the husband's death, a fair presumption arises, in absence of proof to the contrary that the title was in both by entireties. 

5 Neither Spouse May Exclude the Other From the En joyment of Entireties Property. Neither adultery of the wife nor conduct which provides ground for divorce, will destroy her equity in land held by entireties. (Hornak v. 

Hornak 309 Pa. 281-1932.) In that case it was also held that where the husband by concealment and constructive fraud, procures from his wife a deed to another person, from whom he takes back a deed to himself in severalty, the deed will be set aside by decree in equity. No presumption flows from the marital relationship alone, that one spouse in conveying the estate held by entireties acted as agent for the other (Thees v. Prudential Ins. Co. 325 Pa. 465—1937). 

The respective rights of spouses who hold property by entireties has been excellently summed up recently in the case of Madden v. Gosztonyi S. & T. Co. 331 Pa. 476–1938 where the former Chief Justice (Kephart) said at page 489, "The authorities * ✦✦✦ show that either spouse presumptively has the power to act for both so long as the marriage subsists, in matters of entireties, without any specific authorization, provided the fruit or the proceeds of such action inures to the benefit of both and the estate is not terminated. 

But neither may by such action destroy the true purposes of the estate by attempting to convert it, or a part of it, in bad faith, into one of severalty. "As stated where the estate stands in the name of husband and wife, there is no implication of agency to conclude the estate. Thus, where a husband and wife hold a mortgage, the husband has no authority to take a deed to himself and in that way destroy the wife's interest in the mortgage. 

Sparrow v. Mowers 315 Pa. 460-1934. Nor is there a presumption of agency in the wife to convey real estate held by entireties without the husband's joinder: Thees v. Prudential 

Insurance Company, 325 Pa. 465-1937. See Schroeder v.

$6

Gulf Refining Co. (No. 1), 300 Pa. 397-1930, where a release was given by the husband to the wrong-doer without the joinder of his wife. "Where a deposit is made payable to either spouse, agency or authority exists by implication and the husband or wife may from that authority withdraw the entire account, but the money thus withdrawn is impressed with the entirety provision that it is the property of both, and any one dealing with such specific property as severalty, knowing it belongs to both, must submit to the consequences. However, the bank acting in good faith is protected when funds are withdrawn by either. Berhalter v. Berhalter 315 Pa. 225—1934.' 

6 Taxation. Estates by entireties are benignly viewed by the legislature. They are not subject to the Pennsylvania 

Transfer or Inheritance Tax and are expressly exempt from the tax imposed by the Act of July 14, 1936, First Ex. Sess. 

P.L. 44 (72 P.S. 2301) on the accrual to a surviving joint tenant of a deceased's interest in property held jointly. This exemption was held constitutional in Kelly's Estate, 336 Pa. 

305-1939; and Stone's Estate, 35 D. & C. 615-1939. But it has been held where a husband conveyed a one half interest in real estate of which he held the sole title, his wife could not escape taxation on her deceased husband's interest, because such a conveyance did not create a tenancy by en tireties. (Walker Est. 340 Pa. 13, 1940). Estates by en tireties are subject to the Federal Estate Tax (Tyler et. al.

v. United States 281 U.S. 497-1930). 

III. 

6. Title. What it is. 

TITLE, KINDS OF. 

Title is the evidence of ownership in land. Land cannot be moved; hence if the owner should go on a long journey he must leave it behind. Suppose on his return he finds a stranger in possession. The rightful owner to eject him must rely on his evidence of ownership, in other words, his

§

17 

title. Hence can be seen the necessity of having the title in a convenient permanent form. For this reason have arisen the various methods of preserving this evidence of ownership of land as reflected in the modern recording systems of which we will treat later (See Chapter VIII, page 310). Title may be good or bad or occupy an intermediary position such as weak. Let us begin at the bottom of the ladder and work up. 

Of course an absolutely bad title is no title at all, but the lowest form of title is

Naked Possession or Actual Occupation of land without any right or pretense of right to hold and continue possession. 

This one would say at the first blush is practically no title. 

True to a degree, but the mere possession with no right is something more than no possession with no right, for as we shall presently see, a continuance of such possession adverse to the owner may ripen into an absolutely good title. Then, again, if A should occupy a certain piece of land without any shadow of right and B also having no right, should seek to eject him, B cannot argue A's lack of title, for the settled rule of the law is that the plaintiff seeking to eject another must rely solely on the strength of his own title; he cannot recover on the weakness of his adversary's (Lane v. Reynard 2 S. & R. 65-1815). 

7. Right to Possession. 

The next higher grade of title is the right to possession. 

The right to possession springs out of a good title, it belongs to him who has a right to the property. It passes with the right of property. Suppose A purchases a piece of land and when he visits the property he finds a stranger in possession who refuses to move. Here it will be seen the stranger has the actual possession while A has the right to possession. Suppose A without commencing suit to eject the stranger should transfer his title to B. B immediately has the right to possession although he actually never entered into possession. As against the stranger his right would

$8

prevail. Even as to "unseated" or wild land a sufficient title gives to the owner constructive possession so that he can maintain trespass if there were not a title by actual adverse possession made out on the part of the defendants. 

(Darrah v. Kadison 51 Pa. Super. Ct. 133-1912; Kossell v. 

Rhoades 272 Pa. 75-1922). 

8. Perfect or Good Title. 

Finally the perfect title exists where the person who has the possession has also the right to possession and right of property. He has, what we might call a good and complete title. Possession, actual or constructive, is necessary or the title is not complete. To give an example: Suppose A has a complete paper title by which we mean that the evidence of his right forms a perfect chain whether by deed or will.

Suppose now, X enters possession of the premises during A's absence and refuses to vacate on A's return. A is the record owner and has a complete chain of title. Should he proceed against X he will prevail. But suppose A does nothing for twenty-one years and then sells his right to B. B gets the same complete paper title, but X can no longer be ousted. 

X's title now prevails. He has gained what is termed a title by adverse possession. The paper title is still the same but now it is worthless. (See Chapter II p. 26). 

9. Marketable Title. 

Insurable Title. 

This leads us to consider what is termed a marketable title. 

A marketable title is not to be confounded with a good title. 

Strange as it may sound a good title may not be marketable.

Speaking strictly from a legal standpoint there is no such a thing as a doubtful title. A title is either good or bad as far as the court is concerned, but this situation is conceivable, A has a perfect title to some land. B enters into an agreement to purchase it. Then he learns that a stranger has been in possession for ten years. The title of A is undoubted; he 

1 See Definition of unseated Land, page 259. Infra.

§19 

can eject the stranger and so can his successor, but to do so requires the expense, annoyance and hazard of a law suit. 

Legally A's title is good, perfect, but from a practical standpoint it is doubtful, therefore, unmarketable. So also, the placing on record of a deed for that which another owns and which therefore assumes to convey something when it in reality conveys nothing at all puts what is called a "cloud" on the title which requires legal action to remove (Octararo 

Water Co. v. Garrison 271 Pa. 421-1921). No one buys the hazard of a law suit unless at a greatly reduced figure. An unmarketable title has been well defined by the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania, as a title which exposes the party holding it to the hazard of litigation (Reighard's Estate, 192 

Pa. 108-1899; Dohnert's Appeal, 64 Pa. 311-1870; Christ 

Church v. Clark, 47 Pa. Superior Ct. 286-1911; Stone v. 

Carter, 48 Pa. Superior Ct. 236—1911).

Insurable Title. 

It must, however, be remembered that not all objections render a good title unmarketable and the question as to what is and is not marketable title is too large a subject to develop in this book, but in practice the difficulty is avoided by defining in the agreement of sale what the parties mean by a marketable title and it is usually done by inserting the following clause: "The title to be good and marketable, such as will be insured at regular rates by any reputable title insurance or trust company in Philadelphia"-or specify the city where settlement is to be made. (Srolovitz v. Margulis, 35 

Pa. Superior Ct. 252-1908; McGlynn v. London and Risen, 26 D. R. 561—1917). In this way it will be observed that an objection raised by a title company makes the title unmarketable as agreed to between the parties.¹ 

10. Equitable Title. Equity. 

To properly understand the difference between a legal title and an equitable title we must understand the meaning of 

1 For further discussion of this subject see §45(i), Infra.

§10  

the word equity. Equity is a difficult word to define. Blackstone (Blacks, Introduction, §2, page 61) adopts the definition of Grotius, who says that "Equity is the correction of that wherein the law (by reason of its universality) is deficient." 

But this definition like all others requires explanation. Bispham, in his admirable book on Equity Jurisprudence, explains the meaning of equity by setting forth its history rather than by attempting to define it, and we cannot do better than to adopt his method. 

Historically the fountainhead of English justice was the sovereign, the King. At the time of the Norman Conquest and immediately thereafter the law was administered by the King and a certain council which he convened from among the lords of the realm. From this council there developed the courts later known as the Court of King's Bench, the Court of Common Pleas, etc. In all of these courts there was administered justice according to the rules and precedents of the common law. Under these rules and precedents the party injured was only entitled to a judgment of money damages to compensate him for his injuries. As time passed it became evident that money damages awarded after an injury was not always a sufficient compensation for the injury suffered. 

E.g., suppose a man had a beautiful grove of shade trees and his neighbor, out of pure wantonness cuts down a shade tree, the next day cuts down another and announces his intention of continuing to do so until all are gone. The injured man can, of course, sue and recover damages. But money damages, while they may punish the wrongdoer does not replace the trees. The court of law could not prevent the trespasser from continuing his wanton trespasses. It could only give damages to the aggrieved party. Again, suppose A agreed to sell a certain valuable painting to B and later refused to carry out his agreement, B could sue him, but money damages would not give him that certain painting and if it were the only one of its kind manifestly no amount of damages could redress the injured party.

Again, X has a stream of water running through his place

$21 

which he uses to run his mill, Y who is up stream diverts the water, leaving X's mill high and dry. The common law court could give X damages, but his stream was gone forever.

Thus, examples could be multiplied where the common law by reason of its inflexibility (universality) afforded no proper relief to the injured party. Now, as the King was the Supreme Judge, or head of Justice, it became natural for the injured subject to whom money damages afforded no relief to petition his sovereign for redress. The King had the power to grant extraordinary relief if the case warranted it. 

Usually the King would refer the petition to his chancellor, the official who acted at that time in the capacity of Secretary to the King. These petitions for relief became so frequent that later in the reign of King Edward I, an ordinance (Bispham's Principles of Equity (6th Ed. 10) was issued for the purpose of relieving the King from the business of attending petitions addressed directly to him, whereby it was provided that "All petitions touching the Seal do come first before the chancellor" and further "if the demands be so great and so much of grace that the chancellor and those others cannot do without the King, then they shall bring them before the King to know his will." Soon the practice of presenting the petition to the chancellor in the first instance became firmly established.

As applications increased it became necessary for vice chancellors to be provided and so arose a separate court of justice known as the Court of Chancery or Court of Equity, in which court, a suitor who had no adequate remedy in the common law court could get relief. This, therefore, is what is meant by Grotius in the definition above given that equity is the correction of that wherein the law is deficient. The 

Equity Court has power by injunction to restrain a trespass such as set forth in the example on page 20, and to compel A to pass over the specific painting which he agreed to sell B, and compel Y to return the stream to its original bed. 

But to the present day consistent to the cause which gives it

§10  

its origin, the equity court will take jurisdiction of a matter only when the suitor has no adequate remedy at law. 

As America was colonized by the English people who brought with them their native customs and laws, America inherited both the common law and equity of the Mother Country and retained them after the revolution. Pennsylvania, to be sure, administered her equity under common law forms during the early part of the 19th century, but later the legislature conferred upon the courts of law, equity powers of the English Court of Chancery. And now, while the same judge may sit either as a law judge or equity judge, when he sits as equity judge or chancellor, the practice of the court of equity is strictly adhered to. In some States, New Jersey, and Delaware e.g., separate courts of law and equity are still maintained, although most of the States as well as England have abolished separate equity courts and like Pennsylvania have conferred equity powers upon the judges of law courts who at certain times sit as chancellors and administer equity according to the equity practice, forms and rules. 

Returning now to the question of the difference between a legal title and equitable title, we find that according to the common law the person who had the title to land was the only one recognized. The common law courts would not recognize the right to the title as being in any other person. 

Equity, on the other hand, being unfettered by the precedents of the common law, recognized rights which the common law would not entertain. E.g. suppose A agreed to sell his land to B, and then subsequently refused to do so. The legal title of course remained in A, but the right to the title was really in B. B in all fairness should have the land upon payment of the purchase price because A agreed to give it to him. Yet 

B's right to title was not recognized in the common law court. B might recover damages for A's breach of contract, but he could not recover the land. Equity, however, stepped in to correct this deficiency of the law. It recognized the fact that B, although he had no title to the land in the legal sense of the term, nevertheless had a right to have that title

§23 

transferred to him. So the chancellor compels A to give title to B and accept the money. 

An equitable title, therefore, is such a title as is recognized by a court of equity while a legal title is such as is recognized by a court of law. Another example of equitable title is a trust. A trust is created by giving title of property to one person to hold for the use of another. In a trust, therefore, the legal title is in one person and the beneficial use or ownership of the property is vested in another. The person who has the legal title is called the trustee. The person for whose benefit the trust exists is called the Cestui que trust. 

The Cestui que trust has no standing in a court of law, but in a court of equity his right prevails. His title is, therefore, an equitable title.

IV. 

HOW TITLE MAY BE ACQUIRED. 

11. May be Acquired in Three Ways.

We have thus considered what title is, and the kinds that exist. We will now consider how title may be acquired and transferred. Blackstone divided the methods of acquiring title to land into two general classes, viz. 1st: Title acquired by Purchase, and, 2d: Title acquired by Descent. For the sake of convenience we will take a subdivision of his first class which he called Title by Prescription and constitute it a third class, which will be called Title by Adverse Possession and consider with it Title by Accretion. 

12. Definitions of Title by Descent, Purchase, Adverse Pos session. 

1. Title by Descent is title acquired by hereditary succession. That is to say, such title that is acquired by the heirs of the prior owners. 

2. Title by Purchase we will define as any other method of acquiring title other than by descent or by adverse possession as e.g., by the owner's act, agreement, will or gift.

§12  

3. Title by Adverse Possession is such title as is acquired by holding possession of the property adversely to the owner for twenty-one years.

In order to logically present this book we shall first briefly consider Title by Adverse Possession and with it Title by 

Accretion and in Waterways, then Title by Purchase with the exception of title acquired by will and finally Title by Descent, including title by will.

DEFINITION AND ORIGIN OF TITLE BY ADVERSE POSSESSION. 

13. Origin of Title by Adverse Possession. 

The method of acquiring title by adverse possession results from the policy of the law to limit the time for bringing actions to recover property, to a reasonable time. As said by the Supreme Court, "No person ought to be permitted to lie by whilst transactions can be fairly investigated and justly determined until time has involved them in uncertainty and obscurity and then ask for an inquiry" (Foulk v. Brown, 2 

Watts 209, 215-1834). Accordingly all jurisdictions have fixed a time limit in which actions to determine rights must be begun. In Pennsylvania the time limit is prescribed by a statute commonly called "Statute of Limitations". 

14. Statute of Limitations in Pennsylvania.

The statute of limitations in Pennsylvania relating to land, as amended by later Acts, now provides in substance that actions to determine rights in land must be commenced within 21 years after the cause of action accrues, otherwise such rights are forever barred: (Act of March 26, 1785, 2 Sm. L., 299, §2; 12 P.S. 72). But persons who are under disability, such as insane, under age, or in prison, are given ten years longer to bring their action from the time the disability was removed by the Act of March 26, 1785, 2 Sm. L., 299, §4; (12 P.S., 73). 

A further act, April 22, 1856, P.L. 532; (12 P.S., 82), modifies the last quoted Act by providing a positive bar even

§14A 



to persons under disability after a lapse of 30 years; (Hunt v. Wall, 75 Pa. 413-1874). An insane person, therefore, and all persons claiming under him are barred after 30 years, even though the disability continues: (McCall v. Webb, 88 

Pa. 150-1878).

Before that Act, a special law applying to the City and County of Philadelphia also provided that actions to recover rights in real estate are forever barred against the whole world after 40 years from the time the cause of action accrued, whether the owners are under disability or not: Act of April 14, 1851, P.L. 612, §16; (12 P.S., 377).

Title acquired by adverse possession may be recorded: See 

Act of May 31, 1901, P.L. 352, (68 P.S. 81) of which we will treat hereinafter (§23). 

14-A. Necessary Factors to Gain Title by Adverse Pos session.

In order to gain a title by adverse possession the possession must be adverse and hostile to the owner for the period of twenty-one years or thirty years if the owner is under disability as above set forth. What constitutes adverse possession depends, of course, more or less upon the general circumstances of each case. The general rule is laid down by the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania in Hawk v. Senseman, 6 S. & R. 21, 24-1820, wherein it is said that the kind of possession necessary to obtain title against the real owner is, an "actual, continued, visible, notorious, distinct and hostile posession. The owner does not forfeit his title to the first straggler who sets himself down on his land; but the policy of the law for the sake of quieting men's possessions, confers the possession right itself upon him who has entered under an adverse claim and held a notorious possession and occupation for twenty-one years. By analyzing this definition it will be seen that four requisites are essential to gain a title by adverse possession: 

1. The possession must be actual. 

2. It must be continuous.

§15  

3. It must be visible and notorious. 

4. It must be distinct and hostile.

II. 

REQUISITES TO ACQUIRE SUCH TITLE. 

15. Possession Must be Actual.

We have seen that the rightful owner has by virtue of his title, constructive possession of the land. Therefore, the stranger must take actual possession of the property to oust this constructive possession. If one takes possession under color of title, such title, while unavailing against the real owner, may nevertheless serve to define the extent and limits of the claim by the party so taking possession (Phila. Electric 

Co. v. Philadelphia, 303 Pa. 422—1931).

Actual possession sufficient to ultimately vest title in the stranger may arise from the following acts: residence on the land, erecting buildings, enclosing it with a fence (Hughs v. 

Pickering, 14 Pa. 297-1850). No particular acts, however, are necessary to establish actual possession but there must be some positive act inconsistent with the right of the real owner. Thus to maintain an actual possession to woodland as such, it has been held necessary that the person entering, take actual possession by residence or cultivation of part of the tract to which the woodland belonged. Such actual possession may be taken by enclosing or cultivating without residence or by residence without cultivation, under a bona fide claim, where there is a designation of boundaries with the ordinary use of the land (Darrah v. Kadison, 55 Pa. Super. 

Ct. 335-1912). The same rule applies to any unimproved land (Kossell v. Rhoades, 272 Pa. 75–1922). So, also, the occupation of land up to a fence on each side by adjoining property owners for more than 21 years, where each party claims the land on his side as his own, gives each party an incontestable right up to the fence, whether the fence is on the line established by the original survey or not. (Miles v. Pa. Coal Co., 245 Pa. 94-1914; Caputo v. Mariatti 113 Pa.

$29 

Super. Ct., 314-1934). But contrary to common belief, neither assessment nor payment of taxes is an element of adverse possession. (Green v. Schrack, 16 Pa. Super. Ct. 

26-1901; Daniels v. Adolf, 89 Pa. Super. Ct., 69–1926), although it may be shown as a circumstance to support a claim of possession (James v. Bream, 263 Pa. 305-1919). For an excellent case reviewing the essentials of the possession required, see Parks v. Penna. R. R. Co. 301 Pa. 475-1930. 

16. Possession Must be Continuous.

In order to ripen into a legal title the possession must be continuous and uninterrupted (Pederick v. Searle, 5 S. & R. 

236-1819; Duffy v. Duffy, 20 Super. Ct. 25-1902). No single act of trespass or a series of occasional journeys to the land are sufficient, the occupation must be continuous. In 

Stephens v. Leach, (19 Pa. 262-1852), it was said, "A man endeavoring to gain a title by adverse possession is bound to continue a positive appearance of ownership by treating the property as his own and holding it within his exclusive control." 

17. Tacking Interests. 

The continuous possession for twenty-one years need not necessarily be by one person. It may be by several persons provided the one derives his actual possession from the other. 

Thus, when A entered upon land, improved it and after staying a few years gave up his improvements and possession to B who stayed nineteen years before an action was commenced by the owner to eject him, it was held that the twenty-one years must be counted from A's occupation (Hughs v. Pickering, 14 Pa. 297-1850). This is called technically "tacking interests." But it must be remembered that for the interests of such trespassers to be "tacked" the one must derive his possession from the other (Moore v. Collishaw, 10 Pa. 2241849).

§18  18. Possession Must be Visible and Notorious. 

Of course a secret occupation or claim of right could not be guarded against. Hence the law requires that the possession must be visible and notorious (Schrack v. Zubler, 34 

Pa. 38-1859). No particular Act or series of Acts is necessary to demonstrate an intention to claim ownership. Such a purpose is sufficiently shown where one goes upon land and uses it openly and notoriously, as owners of similar lands use their property to the exclusion of the true owner. The owner is chargeable with knowledge of what is openly done on his land, and therefore calculated to attract attention; but a mere passive possession without intending to claim the property is insufficient regardless of the time it continues. (Robin v. Brown 308 Pa. 123–124—1932). 

19. Possession Must be Hostile and Exclusive. "The possession which tolls the right of entry must not only be notorious but adverse, hostile and exclusive against the owner. The occupant must claim against all persons and in subservience to none. In other words he must claim and act as though the land belonged to him." (Green v. Simpson, 49 Pa. Super. Ct. 334-1912). This means the possession must be adverse to the owner. The stranger's title must be hostile to the owner's and not subordinate to it, e.g.: If the owner should permit a friend to occupy the premises without fixing a term for such occupation even though such occupation were continued for fifty years, no title could be acquired against the owner, for the occupant claims his possession not adverse or hostile to, but subordinate to the owner. 

Otherwise, anyone whom the owner let into possession might obtain title upon mere failure of the owner to eject him in twenty-one years. Therefore, the hostility is an important essential. He who is in possession must claim against the whole world continuously and aggressively (Stephens v. 

Leach, 19 Pa. 262-1852). As long as one claims under the owner, title by adverse possession can never be acquired.

$31 

The possession must also be exclusive, i.e., it must not be in common with others (Parks v. Penna. R. R. Co., 301 Pa. 475-1930). 

20. Against Whom Such Title May be Acquired. 

Title by adverse possession cannot be acquired against the 

Commonwealth or a municipality (McGuire v. Wilkes-Barre, 36 Pa. Super. Ct. 418-1908), nor against a railroad company for a portion of its right of way, because it holds its title for a public use (Western N. Y. & P. Ry. Co. v. Vulcan Foundry, &c., 251 Pa. 383-1916), nor against anyone with whom the claimant occupies in privity, as for example: Tenant and 

Landlord, Vendor and Vendee (Connor v. Bell, 152 Pa. 444 

-1893; Hads v. Tiernan, 213 Pa. 44-1905; McMinn v. Cummings, 56 Pa. Super. Ct. 77-1914), Tenants in Common (Hayes' Appeal, 123 Pa. 110-1889; Reap v. Dougher, 261 

Pa. 23-1918), unless one tenant in common ousts his cotenant (Smith v. Kingsley 331 Pa. 10-1938); Trustee and cestu que trust (Scott v. Gallagher 14 S. & R. 332-1826); Husband and Wife (Reap v. Dougher, 261 Pa. 23—1918; Collins v. Lynch, 157 Pa. 246-1893). As against the Commonwealth, title by adverse possession can never be acquired; as against the others, it can only be acquired by the party in possession under the relation expressly, openly and notoriously avowing that he holds possession not by virtue of the relation but adversely to it. The twenty-one years will not run until the respective relation is broken by such open hostile and notorious avowal of breach of the relation. 

20-A. Against What Estate Such Title May be Acquired. 

Such title may be acquired not only against a fee simple estate, but against lesser interests in, or parts of or incorporeal rights to lands. Thus, an easement in land, such as a right of way, may be so acquired (Becker v. Rittenhouse, 297 Pa. 317-1929), and barred' (Whitney v. Welshaus, 50 

1 Mere non-user however does not bar an easement, e.g. right to use an alley. 

Nothing less than an absolute denial of right followed by an enjoyment inconsistent with its use for 21 years or more can amount to an extinguishment of it: 

(Nickels v. Hand Band, No. 1, 52 Super. Ct. 145—1912).

§21 

 Pa. Super. Ct. 422-1912), Water rights (Consolidated Water Supply Co. v. State Hospital, 66 Pa. Super. Ct. 610-1917). 

Title thus acquired to such rights in land is more usually referred to as a right acquired by prescription. A ground rent may be barred (See $118 of this book infra.) Where the original entry is under claim of ownership, however, the Statute of Limitations commences to run from the date of entry (Monroe Supply Co. v. Starner, 242 Pa. 18—1913). 

21. How Adverse Possession May be Averted. 

In general the statute may be said to run from the time an action in ejectment might have been begun. The best way to defeat the running of the statute is to commence an action of ejectment against the occupant. Mere notice of title by the one out of possession to the person in possession will not prevent the running of the statute (McCombs v. Rowan, 59 

Pa. 414-1868).

Neither will a clandestine re-entry (id.); but actual expulsion of the occupant and a physical resumption of possession will arrest the statute; but care must be taken in pursuing this remedy lest the owner make himself liable for indictment for forcible entry (Comm. v. Schaffer, 32 Pa. Super. Ct. 382 -1907).

III. 

NATURE OF TITLE BY ADVERSE POSSESSION. ACT OF 1901. 

22. Title So Acquired Is Perfect and Good. 

Up until the expiration of the twenty-one years the inchoate title which the claimant may have can be lost by abandonment of the title; (Parks et al. v. Penna. R.R. 301 Pa. 475-1930); but after the expiration of twenty-one years there is vested in the claimant an indefeasible title in fee simple and free of easements not recognized by the claimant (Phila. Elect. 

Co. v. Phila. 303 Pa. 422-1931). Subsequent neglect to keep up possession cannot confer any equity upon the purchaser of the outstanding paper title which the statute barred (Schall

§

33 

v. Williams Valley R.R. Co. 35 Pa. 191-1860), but this rule has been modified as to certain parties by the Act of May 31, 1901, P.L. 352 (68 P.S. 81), as noted in the next paragraph. 

23. But Must be Recorded If Owner Remove. Form of Deed. 

By the Act of May 31, 1901, P.L. 352, §1, 5, (68 P.S. 81, 85) it is now provided that the title acquired by adverse possession may be recorded and where the claimant leaves possession he must record it within six months after his removal; else it will not be good as against a bona fide purchaser from, or mortgagee of the holder of the paper title, without notice. 

This Act prescribes the form and method of recording. The form of deed for recording title by adverse possession is as follows:- FORM OF CLAIM OF TITLE ACQUIRED BY ADVERSE POSSESSION TO BE RECORDED. 

I, John Roberts, of Ivyland, in the County of Bucks, State of Pennsylvania, do hereby affirm and declare that I have acquired title in fee by twenty-one years adverse possession to the following described land, situate in Rockhill Township, County of Bucks, State of Pennsylvania, to wit: 

BEGINNING at a heap of stones at the corner of Frank Peterson's land; thence along the same north forty-six degrees, west six perches to stones for a corner of William Thompson's land; thence along the same south forty-two degrees, west 12 perches to a post, a corner in the line of Samuel Andrew's land; thence by the same south thirty-seven degrees, east forty-eight perches to a stone for a corner; thence north seven degrees, east seventy-three and five-tenths perches to the place of beginning, containing five acres and sixty-two perches of land, more or less.

Adverse entry was made upon said land by me on or about the 21st day of March, Anno Domini 1886, and continued until about the first day of June, Anno Domini 1912.¹ 

1 If the possession of the claimant is tacked on to that of others who have preceded him (See Par. 17), it should be stated as follows: "Adverse Entry was made upon said lands by Thomas Jones on or about the 21st day of March, Anno Domini 1886, who continued in possession until about the first day of December, Anno Domini 1896, and was succeeded therein by William Smith, who continued in possession until about the ninth day of January, Anno Domini 1905, and was succeeded therein by me, who continued in possession until about the first day of June, Anno Domini 1912.

At the time of said entry, Isaac Brown (Naming some person or persons in the line of existing title or legal title, as nearly as the same may be, the real owner of said lands at the time of such entry) was owner or reputed owner of said land and I claim adversely to him.

24. Title to Lesser Estates. 

Where the holder of a life estate is disseised, that is put out of possession by his failure to oust one who is in actual possession for twenty-one years, the disseisor gets only the title to the life estate, which ends with the death of the life tenant. It will be remembered that the statute only runs from the time the right of action accrues. In such a case as the right of action of the remainderman accrues only on the death of the life tenant, his interests are not barred until twenty-one years thereafter. 

25. Title by Adverse Possession is Marketable. 

The title by adverse possession is purely legal and is as perfect a title as though the holder of it had a deed of record. 

Since the Act of 1901 he may record it and so have a record of it. It is good and marketable and as such recognized and

§25A  

35 enforced by the Courts (Stroud v. Prager, 130 Pa. 401-1889; 

Bell v. Moredock, 54 Pitts. L.J. 379—1907). If he prefers, the party who has gained title by adverse possession may cite the holder (or his heirs) of the former or "paper" title, into court and so definitely establish his right by having his title by adverse possession confirmed by the Court. See Acts of June 10, 1893 P.L. 415 §2 (12 P.S. 1545) and Apr. 16, 1903 

P.L. 212 (12 P.S. 1543). (See also Mildren v. Nye 240 Pa. 72—1913).

IV. 

ACCRETION. RIPARIAN OWNER'S TITLE IN WATERWAYS. 

25-A. Title by Accretion. 

Title by accretion or alluvion is the title which the owner of land on the border of a stream (usually called a riparian owner) acquires to the addition made to his land due to the imperceptible action of the water. (Jeffries v. East Omaha 

Land Co., 134 U.S. 178, 33 L. ed. 872). The reasons usually given for the rule, that the riparian owner is entitled to accretions in front of his land are, either that it falls within the maxim "De minimus lex non curat" ("the law takes no concern of trifles"), or that, because a riparian owner is liable to lose soil by the action of the water he should have the benefit of any land gained by the action. But whatever the reason is, it is an ancient principle of the common law and as such universally recognized. 

25-B. When Such Title May be Asserted. 

It is only the gradual, imperceptible accretions or deposits of alluvion that vest title to the additions thus built up, in the riparian owner of a navigable waterway. (Black v. American International Corporation, 264 Pa. 260-1919; Houseman v. International Nav. Co., 214 Pa. 552-1906). So where land has been made by human agency, by depositing material on a river bottom, the principle does not apply.

§25C  

(Poor v. McClure, 77 Pa. 214-1873; Allegheny v. Moorhead, 80 Pa. 118-1875). 

25-C. Riparian Owner's Title in Navigable Waters. 

In Pennsylvania the extent of the title of a riparian owner to the bed of a waterway depends upon whether a stream is navigable or non-navigable. "In navigable waters the original grants of land bordering thereon are bounded by the low water mark, and the Commonwealth retained as eminent domain for the use of all citizens, the soil and water found between the lines that describe the low water." (Flanagan v. Phila. 42 Pa. 219-1862). The absolute title of the riparian properties extends to the high water mark only. Between the ordinary high and ordinary low water mark his title to the soil is qualified, it being subject to the public rights of navigation and fishery over it, and of improvement of the stream as a highway. He can neither occupy to the prejudice of navigation nor cause obstructions to be placed upon the shore between these lines without express authority of the Commonwealth. (Wainwright v. McCullough, 63 Pa. 66 -1869; Freeland v. Pa. R.R. Co. 197 Pa. 529-1901). In 

U. S. v. Pa. Salt Mfg. Co., 16 Fed. (2d) 476, the late Judge

Dickinson of the U. S. District Court (E. D. of Pa.) in a learned opinion defines what is meant by high and low water mark, and reviews the Pennsylvania Law in relation to navigable streams.

The title to stream beds of navigable waters is in the Commonwealth. It is the owner of the land, over which the water flows (Public Service Lines Across Rivers, 24 D. & C. 3321935. Citing Coovert v. O'Conner 8 Watts 470-477-1839; 

Carson v. Blazer, 2 Binn. 475–1810) and see Cleveland and 

Pittsburgh R.R. Co. v. Pittsburgh Coal Co. 317 Pa. 3951935). Navigable Lakes are governed by the same rule of law, (Conneaut Lake Ice Co. v. Quigley 225 Pa. 605—1909). 

25-D. Riparian Owner's Title in Non-Navigable Waters. 

In the case of non-navigable streams it was the settled practice of the land office, whether under the proprietaries or the

§25D 



Commonwealth to include in warrants and surveys from which all title is derived, such streams falling within the lines of a survey covered by it. The title to the stream bed, therefore, belongs to the owner of the land through which it flows. (Barclay R.R. Co. v. Ingram, 36 Pa. 194-1860). If a nonnavigable stream formed the boundary of a tract of land, the owner thereof owns to the middle of the stream bed. (Coovert v. O'Conner, 8 Watts 477-1839).

Water. But the ownership of the bed of such a stream is not to be considered as including the ownership of the water which flows over it. Riparian owners have no ownership of running water nor have they the right to divert or sell it for general use. They are limited in their own use of it to ordinary purposes incident to the enjoyment of riparian land, and in exceptional cases to extraordinary uses upon the land itself, provided such extraordinary use does not diminish the flow or impair the quality of the water (Scranton Gas & W. 

Co. v. Del. Lack. & W. R.R. Co. 240 Pa. 604-1913; Palmer Water Co. v. Lehighton Water Supply Co. 280 Pa, 4921924). The water itself, subject to such reasonable riparian use which the land owner may make of it is in reality the property of the Commonwealth.

The stream bed is subject to the easement of waters flow and the use of the water for navigation so far as it may be capable of it and for flood control, stream improvement, water supply, etc. See Act of April 8, 1937, P.L. 258. Supplied by 

Act of June 24, 1939 P.L. 842 (32 P.S. (ann.) 631 et. seq.).

Indeed it has been held that when a tributary stream is rendered navigable by the damming of the river into which it flows such action operates to divest the title of the bed thereof and revest it in the Commonwealth. (Cleveland etc. R.R. 

Co. v. Pittsburgh Coal Co. 317 Pa. 395—1935).

The fish in a non-navigable stream are the property of the Commonwealth. It may regulate the catching thereof. (Commonwealth v. Bender, 7 Pa. C. C. 620-1887). Though the owner of the stream bed does not own the fish that live in the water flowing over his land, yet no one may fish by

$25E 

wading between the banks in the stream without being liable for trespass on the stream bed. (Commonwealth v. Foster, 36 Pa. Super. Ct. 433-1908). Such owner may neither erect a dam over three feet in height thereon, or build encroachments or change the cross-section thereof without permit of the Water and Power Resources Board of the Commonwealth, Act of June 13, 1913, P.L. 555, §4 (32 P.S. 684) as amended by Act of May 6, 1937, P.L. 559 (32 P.S. 682 ann.). The

Board of Fish Commissioners is vested with power to require provision to be made in such dams and constructions for fish ways or such devices to enable the fish to ascend or descend as their nature may require (§185 of the Fish Law as amended by Act of April 22, 1929 P.L. 621 §8; 30 P.S. 185).

For review of the law governing public fishing rights in navigable and non navigable waters, see Informal Opinion #600 of the Attorney Generals Office (1935), published in the "Pennsylvania Angler" September 1935, reprints of which can be had on application to the Commissioner of Fisheries of Pennsylvania. 

25-E. Test of Navigability of Streams. 

In Pennsylvania we follow the civil law definition of navigable rivers, rather than that of the common law and we hold navigable not only those streams which are subject to tides, but all rivers capable of being navigated, that is, navigable in the common sense of the term (Flanagan v. Phila. 42 Pa. 

219-230-1862). Nor can the legislature by act of assembly make navigable by law, a stream which is not navigable in fact (Commonwealth v. Foster, 36 Super. Ct. 433—1908).
