26. Introduction. 

INTRODUCTION. 

Definition of Term Alienation. 

Title by purchase we have seen includes all methods of acquiring title except by title by descent, by adverse possession and by accretion. It is therefore the most common method of acquiring title. Before considering in detail the method of acquiring, we must first consider what persons or bodies have the power or right to hold, acquire or convey title to real estate. The capacity to take, to hold and to convey title to real estate, as Professor Mitchell in his excellent lectures on conveyancing says, depends upon a variety of circumstances. "Some persons can take title but cannot hold it. Others can take and hold but cannot convey it." This capacity to take, hold and convey lands is called the capacity to alien or to alienate land and the method of transferring land is technically called the alienation of land which means substantially what we now understand by the term Conveyancing.

$41 

ALIENATION. 

I. 

INDIVIDUALS. 

27. Who May Take, Hold and Convey. In General. 

Any person who has the legal capacity to bind himself by contract, may convey his real estate. The same disabilities which incapacitate him from making a legal contract, incapacitate him from making a valid deed. Keeping in mind the general rule, therefore, that any individual not under a legal disability may freely alienate land, it becomes important to see and understand what these disabilities are. Classified under their respective disabilities, we have: Aliens, Persons of Unsound Mind, Drunkards, Persons Under Duress, Fraudu lent Debtors, Infants, Married Women, Feme Sole Traders, Fiduciaries. Since not all of these individuals are absolutely prevented from alienating, it becomes necessary to consider each one separately. 

28. Aliens.

At common law, it was deemed for the welfare of England that aliens, i.e., foreign-born residents should be forbidden to hold land or inherit land. Blackstone, however, points out they could purchase land but the moment they did so it was liable to be forfeited to the sovereign (2 Blacks. 293). The harshness of this rule has been greatly relaxed and in most states the alien friend is now under no disability. In Pennsylvania, by statute (Act Feb. 23, 1791, 3 Sm. L. 4, 68 P.S. 

22), alien friends may take by descent without limit. But under the Act of May 1, 1861, P.L. 433, 68 P.S. 32), they are permitted to hold by purchase only 5,000 acres and not exceeding $20,000 in net annual value. Up to this limit they may take, hold and convey as freely as a native born or a naturalized citizen. The right to take lands from an alien who thus violates this limitation is the exclusive prerogative of the state, so the state can and frequently does forgive or

$29

waive its right to declare a forfeiture of the land. Especially is this done where the land has been conveyed to others. Such waiver is done by confirmatory statutes which the legislature has passed from time to time. See numerous acts gathered together in Title 68 Purdons Pa. Statutes $51 to 60 inclusive. 

29. Persons of Unsound Mind.

This heading should be taken to include not only lunatics but idiots and all persons of unsound mind. The law presumes every one sane and the burden is upon him who seeks to establish the want of sufficient mental capacity to execute a deed (Youngwood B. & L. Assn. v. Henry 137 Pa. Super. 

Ct. 124-1939) and such incapacity must be established by clear evidence (In re Gangwere's Estate, 14 Pa. 417-1850).

In most jurisdictions, laws have been enacted providing for methods by which a person may be legally adjudged insane, and such a decree when made is conclusive and binding upon all the world and renders deeds of the lunatic absolutely void. 

By Pennsylvania statutes the appointment of a committee after inquisition or a guardian by the court, is a decree which establishes the lunacy of the party absolutely and from that time all capacity to contract is gone and his deed is absolutely void (Imhoff v. Witmer, 31 Pa. 243-1858). The inquisition and decree are recorded and this is notice to all the world of the party's insanity and incapacity to contract. The law also provides that it is the duty of the commissioner and jury, sitting to determine the lunacy, to find how long the party has been insane and if he has lucid intervals. During the period from the time of the commencement of insanity so found to the time of the decree, there is a presumption that the party was without capacity to contract, but this presumption may be overcome by proof that the contract or deed was made in a lucid interval. "But the Act of May 

28, 1913 P.L. 358 (50 P.S. 734) now provides that whenever thereafter Commissioners find a person a lunatic from a date prior to the finding, neither the findings nor the record shall

§

43 

ALIENATION. 

be competent evidence in an action affecting title to land, except in the following instances: (a) Where ten days' written notice of the time and place of the meeting of the Commissioners was served on the party or parties claiming title at the time commission issued. (b) Where claim of title adverse to a lunatic originates subsequent to the date said lunatic was found to be non compos and (c) Where the Commissioners find that the lunatic was insane at the time the adverse claim originated, expressly identifying it." •

Where the party has never been legally declared insane, the question of whether he was, or was not insane at the time of the execution of the deed is, of course, a question of fact to be decided by the jury; the burden being upon him who seeks to set the deed aside. The several acts of assembly give to the committee of the lunatic all the powers necessary to manage his estate, but the real estate cannot be sold or mortgaged without authority from the court. 

30. Habitual Drunkards. 

Drunkenness is really a species of temporary mental derangement. To relieve himself from a contract or deed made while intoxicated, a party must prove that he was so drunk as not to know what he was doing. The deed of a person executed while drunk is not void but voidable, i.e., it may be confirmed or made good when the grantor becomes sober. To set the deed aside he must disavow it promptly; otherwise the law presumes he means to ratify it. Where, however, a person is habitually intoxicated and is declared an habitual drunkard by decree of court, then he is in the same position as a person adjudged a lunatic, and all his deeds are void. 

30-A. Procedure to Alienate Real Estate of Mental Incompe tents and Habitual Drunkards. 

Real estate of a lunatic or an habitual drunkard may be alienated, sold or mortgaged by leave of court under the

44. 

§ 

statutes providing for the same. The Act of June 13, 1836 

P.L. 589 (50 P.S. 691 et seq.) provides that such real estate may be sold or mortgaged only with leave of court and only where the personal estate is insufficient for the payment of the lunatic's or drunkard's debt, the support and maintenance of himself and his family or for the education of his minor children. The procedure is prescribed in §§22 to 33 of that act (June 13, 1836, P.L. 589; 50 P.S. 781, 792). Private sales are authorized by the Act of April 27, 1903, P.L. 325 (50 P.S. 793). In the case of a weak-minded person whose guardian has been appointed under the Act of 1907 and its supplements, public or private sale, mortgages, leases, etc. of the weak-minded person's property may be made, not only for the purposes above mentioned in the case of a lunatic or an habitual drunkard but also whenever such sale, mortgage, leasing, etc. is, in the opinion of the court, for the interest and advantage of the ward. (See Act of May 28, 1907, P.L. 

292, as amended by Act of April 15, 1915, P.L. 124 (No. 59) 

50 P.S., 961, 962). In addition to the above powers to make sales, committees of lunatics and habitual drunkards, as well as guardians of weak-minded persons may make application for the sale of their wards' real estate in accordance with the provisions of the Price Act, Act of June 7, 1917, P.L. 388 (20 P.S. 1561, et seq.). 

31. Weakness of Mind, Senility and Undue Influence.

Mere weakness of mind due to old age, accident or disease is not of itself sufficient to set aside a deed (Nace v. Boyer, 30 Pa. 99-1858; Kleckner v. Kleckner, 212 Pa. 515, 5181905; Hamilton v. Fay, 283, Pa. 175–1925). There must be some fraud or mistake before a formal instrument such as a deed can be set aside. However, the court is alert to protect the aged or weak-minded and the chancellor will usually seize on slight circumstances of fraud to set aside a deed so secured (Hettrick's Appeal, 58 Pa. 477-1868). Where one advanced in years, and thus enfeebled conveys all her means of subsistence to another who occupies a confidential relation

$45 

ALIENATION. 

toward her, and a claim of ownership is subsequently made by the grantee, the burden is upon the grantee to show that the transaction in question was fair. (Palmer v. Foley, 305 

Pa. 169-1931). 

In Pennsylvania, by the Act of May 28, 1907, P.L. 292, as amended by the Act of April 1, 1925, P.L. 101 (50 P.S. 941, et seq.) a method of protecting the property of the aged and weak-minded is now provided. Upon proper application made to the court, by petition filed setting forth that the party is unable, by reason of insanity, feeble-mindedness or other mental defectiveness, of taking care of his property, the court will fix a time for a hearing, and if convinced that the allegations of the petition are correct will appoint a guardian to protect and conserve the estate of such person. Such guardian has the same powers and is subject to the same duties as a committee on lunacy. 

32. Infants.

An infant in a legal sense is a person under twenty-one years of age. The law provides that an infant cannot make a contract, the theory being that he is too immature and must be protected against his own folly. There is a certain exception, viz: He may contract for necessaries. But for our purpose we may disregard this. Remembering that his disability results from his incapacity to contract, it follows he can neither contract to acquire title by deed nor convey it by deed. He may, however, acquire title by deed of gift or by devise or by descent since in such cases no capacity to contract is required.

The deed of an infant is not void but voidable and he has it in his power when he reaches the age of twenty-one years to either ratify¹ his deed, in which event it becomes good, or disaffirm it in which event it becomes void absolutely; but he must do one or the other within a reasonable time after he arrives at the age of twenty-one years, else the law presumes his failure to act to be a ratification (Dolph v. Hand, 1 For a form of such ratification see (214 of this book.

$33 

156 Pa. 91-1893). The contract, however, is voidable only on the part of the infant. An adult party with whom the contract is made is bound. Upon disaffirmance an infant should return the purchase money received for the property, but if he has spent or lost it, his action in disaffirming is nevertheless effectual even though no return can be made for the consideration (Shaw v. Boyd, 5 S. & R. 309—1819; 

Ruchezky v. DeHaven, 97 Pa. 202-1881). A minor cannot ratify the beneficial part of the transaction and avoid the burdens. Thus in Oransky v. Stephanovich (304 Pa. 841931) where an infant had given a purchase money judgment for land it was held on reaching majority the minor might affirm or disaffirm the transaction in its entirety but could not elect to retain the property free of the purchase money obligation.

Altho we have seen that a minor cannot convey or mortgage land in his own right, curiously enough it has been held if he is a trustee for others, he may do so in the execution of his trust, since a minor may be a trustee (Hlawaty v. Zoeck 253 

Pa. 311-1916). In Brunner v. Ringe (57 Pa. Super. Ct. 237 

-1914) where a wife of full age and her husband, a minor executed a deed to the wife's property, it was held the deed was not void but merely voidable and could not be set aside as to either, where no action of disaffirmance was taken until 

15 years after the date of the deed. 

33. Persons Under Duress. 

Deeds made by persons under duress are voidable and may be set aside by action of the party constrained, if done within a reasonable time after the removal of the constraint. By duress is meant some undue compulsion such as threats, actual violence, imprisonment, which prevents the free exercise of the will power of a person and makes him execute the deed or contract through fear alone. A person, however, is supposed to possess ordinary firmness unless it is shown by reason of age or other sufficient cause he is weak or infirm (See $31). The constraint that takes away free agency

§33A 



ALIENATION. 

must be one that is imminent and without immediate means of protection, and such as would operate upon the mind of a person of reasonable firmness (Sulzner v. Cappeau Lemly, Etc., Co., 234 Pa. 162–1912; Ortt v. Schwartz 62 Super. Ct. 70-1916). 

33-A. Fraud and Fraudulent Debtors. 

Fraud which renders a deed void may be roughly divided into two kinds or classes: (a) Where the grantor is an innocent party and has been beguiled, defrauded and overreached by the grantee, and (b) where the grantor is, himself, a party to the fraud, as for example, where he conveys away his property to put it beyond the reach of his creditors. In both classes of fraud it must be understood that a deed once duly acknowledged and recorded can only be set aside as against the fraudulent grantee or his heirs, executors or assigns, who are volunteers, i.e., who have paid no value for the transfer to them. If the fraudulent grantee, before any action to set aside the deed is commenced, sells or conveys the property in turn to an innocent purchaser for value without notice, the deed can no longer be set aside. The only action that remains then to the defrauded party is to sue the fraudulent grantee for damages. 

Considering the two classes separately, we find: (a) Fraud on Grantor.

That where the grantor is an innocent party he must move promptly upon the discovery of the fraud. A solemn act, such as the execution of a deed, is not to be lightly set aside. 

Fraud is never presumed and must be established by clear and satisfactory evidence either direct or circumstantial, or both. The witnesses must be credible and the facts distinctly remembered and accurately stated (Pusick v. Salak, 261 Pa. 

512-1918). The same case holds that want of consideration does not of itself prove fraud, but is a circumstance to be considered in connection with other evidence. Nor is mere inadequacy of consideration sufficient even though the grantor

§33A  

is of advanced age if mentally competent (Walters Execrs. v. 

Martin 274 Pa. 529-1922). However, where there is a confidential relationship existing between the grantor and grantee, such as Trustee and cestui que trust, Guardian and Ward, partner and copartner, principal and agent, master and servant, physician and client, or in general all persons who are associated by any relation of trust and confidence, the party in whom the confidence is placed is held to the strictest accountability and the burden is placed upon him to show that the transaction by which he obtained the benefit from the other was fair, conscientious and beyond the reach of suspicion, and to establish its perfect fairness and adequacy and equity; and if no such proof is established courts of equity treat the case as one of constructive fraud (McCown et. al. v. Fraser 327 Pa. 561-1937; Conway v. Conway, 27 

D. R. 701-1918). 

(b) Fraud on Creditors. Fraudulent Conveyances Acts. 

The other class of frauds are largely statutory in origin and usually result from an attempt by a man insolvent or about to become so, to prevent his creditors from satisfying their claims out of his property. This is declared by statute to be a fraud on creditors. There are two applicable statutes in Pennsylvania, the one is the old English Statute of 13 Eliz. 

Chap. 5, Roberts Digest 295, which is in force in Pennsylvania, and which declares all conveyances "to hinder, delay and defraud creditors" to be void against a fraudulent grantee, his executors and assigns. This Act is set forth in full in Purdon's Pa. Digest, 39 P.S., p. 262, and appended to it is a note containing an exhaustive review of the Pennsylvania decisions interpreting this Act, and the remedies thereunder. It should be noted that the statute not only applies where a debtor conveys away his property absolutely, but whenever he encumbers it or conveys it in some trust so that his creditors are hindered and delayed (Miles v. Harris, 1 

D. & C. 347-1921; Handel etc. B & L Asso. v. Elleford 258 

Pa. 143-1917).

§33A 



ALIENATION. 

The other statute, the one now most usually invoked, is cited as the Uniform Fraudulent Conveyance Act, which was adopted in Pennsylvania in 1921, (Act of May 21, P.L. 1045, 39 P.S., 351). This Act is one of the uniform laws which most all of the states have adopted at the instance of the American Bar Association in order to bring about uniformity of statutory law of the several states. This Act applies to property of all kinds, personal as well as real, and not only to transfers but encumbrances placed on property as well. It provides, "Every conveyance made and every obligation incurred by a person who is or will be thereby rendered insolvent is fraudulent as to creditors without regard to his actual intent if the conveyance is made or the obligation is incurred without a fair consideration." (Act of May 25, 1921, P.L. 1045, §4, 39, P.S. 354; See Fidelity Trust Co. v. Union 

Nat. Bk. 313 Pa. 467-1934). Prima facie any voluntary conveyance by one in debt is fraudulent as to creditors and the burden is on the grantee to prove solvency of the grantor 

(Farmers Tr. Co. v. Bevis 331 Pa. 89–1938). This Section does not prevent a person, even if insolvent, from selling his property for a fair price. The test is the consideration and not the solvency (Jarvis v. Bell, 296 Pa. 568—1929).

The Act defines "insolvency" to mean "when the present, fair, saleable value of his assets is less than the amount that will be required to pay his probable liability on his existing debts as they become absolute and matured" (§2 of the above Act 39 P.S. 352). Such conveyance may be set aside by any creditor having a matured claim (i.e., one presently due) as against any person except a purchaser for fair consideration without knowledge of the fraud at the time of the purchase, or one who has derived title immediately or mediately from such purchaser (§9 of the above Act, 39 P.S. 359). §7 of the same Act (39 P.S., $357) also makes every conveyance and every obligation incurred with actual intent to hinder, delay and defraud either present or future creditors fraudulent as to both present and future creditors. The purpose of this Section is to cover a case where a man, while perfectly

$34 

solvent, deliberately sets about to defraud his creditors by first putting all of his property beyond their reach and then purchasing goods and incurring debts which he has no intention of ever paying. In such case, however, actual intent must be proved (Schline v. Kine, 301 Pa. 586-1930). But a conveyance by a husband to his wife for a nominal consideration is prima facie proof of such actual intent and places the burden of proving the fairness of the transaction on the wife (Ferguson v. Jack 339 Pa. 166-1940). Where the transaction is between a husband and wife, "actual intent" has been held to appear from proof that the deed was given for a nominal consideration (Ferguson v. Jack, 339 Pa. 166-1940).

The most usual cases which come before the Court are those where the conveyances are made to the wife. It should be noted that if the husband is solvent when he makes the transfer, it is valid regardless of consideration (Buckwalter 

Stove Co. v. Edmonds, 283 Pa. 237-1925). But only a solvent husband can thus make a gift of his real estate to his wife and she must show that at the time of the transfer his liabilities were not out of proportion to his assets. If he is insolvent, the wife must prove a fair consideration and the burden is on the wife to establish the validity of her title by clear and satisfactory evidence beyond that required of other creditors (Peoples Savings and Dime Bank & Trust Co. v. 

Scott, 303 Pa. 294-1931; Morrison v. Marks 125 Pa. Super. 

Ct. 177-1937). Deeds conveying away property in fraud of creditors can only be set aside at the instance of the creditors; the fraudulent grantor is bound by his deed and the law will, as a general rule, never aid him to recover back his property (Palmer v. Foley 305 Pa. 169—1931). 

34. Married Women. 

At common law a married women was under many disabilities for, as said by Mitchell (Real Estate & Conveyancing in Penna. 372), "at common law the husband and wife were one person and that one was the husband." In Penn-

$51 

ALIENATION. 

sylvania, step by step married women's rights were increased until the Act of June 8, 1893 P.L. 344, 48 P.S. 31, 32, completed her emancipation. That act provided, "Hereafter a married woman shall have the same right and power as an unmarried person to acquire, own, possess, control, use, lease, sell or otherwise dispose of any property of any kind, real, personal or mixed and either in possession or expectancy and may exercise the said right and power in the same manner and to the same extent as an unmarried person, but she may not mortgage or convey her real property unless her husband joins in such mortgage or conveyance. The second section of the act provides, "Hereafter a married woman may in the same manner and to the same extent as an unmarried person make any contract in writing or otherwise which is necessary, appropriate, convenient or advantageous to the exercise and enjoyment of the rights and powers granted by the foregoing section, but she may not become accommodation indorser, maker, guarantor or surety for another, and she may not execute or acknowledge a deed or other written instrument conveying or mortgaging her real property unless her husband joins her in such mortgage or conveyance. This act is so clear as to require little or no explanation. With the exception of her inability to convey or mortgage her property without joinder of her husband and her inability to become accommodation indorser, maker of a note, guarantor or surety for another, she may do whatever an unmarried woman may do. As Chief Justice Paxson said in Milligan v. Phipps, (153 Pa. 208-1893), "It (the Act of June 8, 1893) has emancipated her from the shackles of the common law so far as her separate property is concerned, and permits her to stand alone and exercise her own judgment." The deed of a married woman made without the joinder of her husband it seems is not void but voidable for after discoverture it may be ratified. Simons Est. 20 Pa. Super. Ct. 450, 468-1902; and such ratification may even be implied. (Jourdan v. Dean 

175 Pa. 599-1896). A deed of a married woman joined in

§34A  

by a minor husband is only voidable as to the minor husband 

(Brunner v. Ringe 57 Super. Ct. 237—1914). 

34-A. Conveyance by One Spouse Direct to the Other. By 

Wife to Husband, etc. (a) After the passage of these married women's property acts, it was a question in doubt as to whether a wife could convey direct to her husband if made bona fide and without seeking to defraud creditors. The matter is now settled that she can. Although it was necessary for the legislature to pass an act (Act of June 3, 1911, P.L. 631, 48 P.S. 71) so declaring in order to overrule the case of Alexander v. Shalala (228 

Pa. 297-1910), which had held she could not. The Act of 

1911 provides "That it shall be lawful for a married woman to make conveyances of real estate to her husband as if she were a feme sole" and also that "all conveyances of real estate heretofore made by any married woman to her husband, which had been duly signed, acknowledged and delivered by her are hereby validated and made good in law.” 

The Superior Court, however, has declared the last clause of this act to be inoperative, on the ground that the attempt of the legislature to validate deeds made by married women direct to the husband before the passage of the act, disturbed vested titles and was, therefore, unconstitutional 

(Buchanan v. Corson, 51 Pa. Super. Ct. 558-1912). This decision only renders the last clause of the act ineffective, the first clause permitting such conveyances in the future, still stands. (Luther v. Luther 22 D. R. 548—1913). In Vander grifts Est. (105 Pa. Super. Ct. 293—1932), it was held that a conveyance by a married woman direct to her husband and herself was valid both under the Act of 1911 (supra) and the Uniform Interparty Agreement Act of May 13, 1927 P.L. 

984 (21 P.S. 551) and created an estate by entireties (See $5(d) 1). But see Walkers Estate (340 Pa. 13-1940) holding a husband could not create an estate by entireties by conveying a one half interest in his property, direct to his wife.

§34B 



ALIENATION. 

(b) While the right of a wife to convey to her husband direct had been a vexed question until settled as above, it had been long settled on the other hand that a husband might not only convey directly to his wife for a valuable consideration but he might also convey to her as a gift when not prejudicial to his creditors (Reagle v. Reagle, 179 Pa. 89-1897; Mitchell v. Phillips, 236 Pa. 311-1912). It has always been considered the better practice in either case to have the married person convey to a third party who in turn conveys to the husband or wife. The title companies and the profession still prefer conveyances to be made to a third party and by him to the spouse intended to receive the title. 

34-B. Sole and Separate Use Trusts. 

Regardless of the Married Women's Property Acts, how ever, a married woman could be given the same power over real estate as that of an unmarried person, by means of what is called a sole and separate use trust. This is done by conveying the real estate to a trustee (Lancaster v. Dolan, 1 Rawle 231-1829), or even to the wife direct (Wright v. 

Brown, 44 Pa. 224-1863) by deed or will expressly declaring the property to be for her sole and separate use and benefit, and granting to her power to alienate it by deed. The instrument creating this sole and separate use trust must always be looked to as defining and limiting her power. She possesses no right of disposition of such property unless so provided in the instrument creating the trust. She may, therefore, neither convey nor mortgage it during the life of her husband unless that power is expressly given by the instrument under which she acquired title (Wright v. Brown, 44 Pa. 224-1863; Holliday v. Hively, 198 Pa. 335-1901).

Such trusts may still be established and the cases last cited hold that the Married Women's Property Acts have no application to them because they are equitable estates.

§35 35. Feme Sole Traders. 

Divorce A. M. et T. 

A feme sole trader is a married woman authorized by statute under certain conditions to carry on business and trade as though she were sole or unmarried. In Pennsylvania, the Act of May 4, 1855, P.L. 430, §2, (48 P.S. 42) provides "that whenever her husband from drunkenness, profligacy or other cause shall neglect or refuse to provide for her or shall desert her, her property real and personal howsoever acquired, shall be subject to her free and absolute disposal during her life or by will, without any liability to be interfered with or obtained by her husband, and in case of her intestacy shall go to her next of kin as if he were previously dead." See also Acts of May 28, 1915 P.L. 639; May 

11, 1927 P.L. 971 (48 P.S. 44). See discussion of these Acts in Walsh Appeal, (330 Pa. 502—1930).

For some time there was considerable doubt as to whether Act of 1855 gave a feme sole trader the right to convey a clear title without joinder of her husband, but it has now been settled that she can (Elsey v. McDaniel, 95 Pa. 4721880 Simons' Estate, 20 Pa. Super. Ct. 450-1902). Not only can she make a deed as though unmarried, but she can also mortgage (Heddens' Appeal, 17 Atlan. Rep. 29) her property without joinder of her husband. It is not necessary for her to be actually declared by decree of court to be a feme sole trader, (Thornton v. Pierce 328 Pa. 14—1937) but the better practice and safer plan is to have her so decreed and then to recite that fact in the deed of conveyance (Ellison v. 

Anderson, 110 Pa. 486-1885). If never declared a feme sole trader, the facts that bring her within the provisions of the Act of May 4, 1855, should be recited in the instrument of conveyance, although failure to do so will not invalidate the instrument (Forman v. Hosler, 94 Pa. 418-1880). When a married woman was deemed a feme sole trader because of drunkenness of her husband the certificate was held to be conclusive evidence of authority so to act until revoked by the Court issuing it, (Browarsky's Estate 252 Pa. 35-1916). 

It seems however that a certificate issued because of deser-

ALIENATION. 

tion may be overcome in the Orphans Court and a husband allowed to take against his wife's will upon proof of a bona fide reconciliation before the wife's death (Hannagan's Estate 

59 Pa. Super. Ct. 61-1915; Hellwig's Estate 59 Pa. Super. 

Ct. 233-1915). (a) Divorce a Mensa et Thoro. Such a divorce (literally from bed and board) does not enable the parties to remarry and is hence not a complete severance of the marital tie, but by the Act of April 11, 1927, P.L. 181 Act No. 151, (48 P.S. 

117a) a wife so divorced is put in the same category of a feme sole and given complete power to encumber, sell or convey her real estate without her husband's joinder. The act applies to marriages contracted and real estate acquired by a married woman before the date of the act as well as thereafter and such interpretation does not render it unconstitutional, (Scaife v. McKee 298 Pa. 33-1929). 

36. Fiduciaries.

By a fiduciary we mean one who occupies a relation of trust and confidence with another. The fiduciaries which we will briefly consider are: Trustee, Executor, Administrator and Guardian. Mr. Fallon, in his book on conveyancing (Pennsylvania Conveyancing, by Christopher Fallon, 91) says: "Generally speaking, trustees, including guardians, executors and assignees, have no power to sell or convey land unless authorized and empowered by the instrument of appointment or under the direction of the court having jurisdiction over the trust.' As stated by the Supreme Court "A trustee has no power to sell trust property unless such power is conferred upon him by the instrument creating the trust either by express words or necessary implication, (Seif v. Krebs 239 Pa. 423-1913). If there is more than one trustee or guardian all must join in the deed, (Nesbitt v. 

Tarbrake, 30 Pa. Super. Ct. 460—1906). 

Where the instrument which creates the trust defines and prescribes the manner in which it is to be executed that

§36  

method must be strictly followed. Before accepting a deed from a fiduciary a purchaser must, at his peril, ascertain the extent of the trustee's power. As Fallon further says, “A deed simply to A B, trustee, without stating for whom or for what, does not afford such an opportunity and is to be considered bad conveyancing." The Golden Rule to be followed is: Look to the instrument defining the powers of the trustee. 

In Bayard v. Farmers' and Mechanics' Nat. Bank, (52 Pa. 

232-237-1866), the court said: "No purchaser either of land or personalty would be safe in buying from a known trustee without looking at the nature and extent of his trust. It is true a trustee may have power to sell, but the power is not a necessary incident to his trust, as it is to the office of an executor. He may have the legal title yet no authority to sell. His sale may be entirely authorized by the instrument which created the trust; it may have been forbidden." 

In Pennsylvania, the Fiduciaries Act (June 7, 1917 P.L. 

447) §28(b), 20 P.S. 712) authorizes executors, trustees, etc. to make either public or private sales where not specifically directed. If a public sale is directed, only a public sale can be made and a private one will carry no title (McCreery v. 

Hamlin, 7 Pa. 87—1847).

On the ground of public policy executors and trustees cannot purchase at their own sale. But such a sale, if not avoided by the parties for whose benefit the trust exists, may be made good by their ratification. If a trustee desires to buy or bid at his own sale he should make application to the court (see Fiducaries Act of 1917, June 7, 1917, P.L. 447, §16(k) 20 P.S. 567). Though it is a general rule that if a trustee buys trust property, even at public sale, brought about or in any way controlled by the trustee, such trustee will be presumed to buy and hold for the benefit of the trust, the rule does not apply where the trustee has no control over, or is not instrumental in bringing about the sale. In such case he may bid, for, and become the purchaser of the property free from any trust upon his part (Calvert v. Woods, 246 Pa. 325-1914; Lusk's Appeal, 108 Pa. 152-1885).

So also an administrator has no power or control over real estate unless the personal property is not sufficient to pay debts in which case he may, as in the case of the executor, petition the Orphans' Court for leave to sell the real estate. II ASSOCIATIONS OF INDIVIDUALS. 

37. The Commonwealth or the State. Eminent Domain. 

Turning now to associations of individuals that may acquire, hold and convey title we will consider, first, the Commonwealth or State; second, Corporations; third, Unincorporated Societies; fourth, Partnerships.

The Commonwealth, i.e., the State, may purchase, hold, sell, convey, lease and mortgage land like any person. It can gain title by adverse possession but cannot lose it in that way. 

The Statutes of Limitations do not run against the Commonwealth and no one can gain title by adverse possession against it (Bagley v. Wallace, 16 S. & R. 245-1827; Com. v. Baldwin, 1 Watts 54-1832). The Commonwealth has the further 

1 See $170D, 170E (infra) where this subject is more fully discussed. 

2 By $14 Fiduciaries Act June 7, 1917, P.L. 286 executor or administrator may also petition Orphans' Court to authorize collection of rents of decedent's real estate where personal property is insufficient to pay debts. For other instances in which executors or administrators may sell or convey real estate see §§ 170 D to 170 I of this book.

§37  

power to take land for public purposes except as restricted by the Constitution, and to delegate this right to certain public corporations as provided by law. This power to take land from individuals against their wishes is called the right of eminent domain. (a) Eminent Domain is the sovereign power vested in the Commonwealth to take private property for public use. It is a reservation in the grant of land by the state to a private owner and is paramount to the right of ownership in the individual. The power is not necessarily created either by 

Constitution or statute but is an inherent attribute of sovereignty itself. Under the right of eminent domain private property can only be taken for a public use, and it is not within the power of the legislature to invest either an individual or a corporation with the right to take private property for private use of some other individual or corporation, even if a method is provided for ascertaining damages to pay what shall be deemed just compensation (Philadelphia Clay 

Co. v. York Clay Co., 241 Pa. 305-1913; Stuart v. Gimbel Bros. 

285 Pa. 102-1926). As to what is meant by a public use, see

Pennsylvania Mutual Life Insurance Co. v. Philadelphia, 

(242 Pa. 47-1913).

But when the right of eminent domain can be legitimately exercised, the Constitution ($10 Bill of Rights) provides that just compensation must be made to the owners, and the various statutes which have prescribed the method laid down by law to ascertain such compensation must be carefully followed when the right is exercised. 

It must be noted that the appropriation of land by a Corporation under the right of eminent domain ordinarily does not carry a fee simple title thereto, in the absence of express statutory language to that effect, but only the right to use and occupy the land for the purpose for which it is taken. (Dickel v. Bucks-Falls Electric Co. 306 Pa. 504-505-1932).

Thus e.g. if a railroad corporation condemns land for a right of way and subsequently abandons its use for that purpose, it cannot sell the strip of land so acquired for it does not

$59 

ALIENATION. 

have the fee simple title, that remains in the original owner and would revert to him or his descendents or devisees if the public use is abandoned. There is an exception to this rule, however, in the case where the Commonwealth exercises its right of eminent domain, for it was held in the case of Craig v. Mayor et al., Allegheny Co. 53 Pa. 477-1866 that acquisition of land by the Commonwealth by right of eminent domain is necessarily in fee. Municipalities are bound by the same rule noted with respect to public service corporations, but the legislature of 1937, by the Act of July 2, 1937, P.L. 2793 (53 

P.S. 1331, 1332) has now provided a procedure where by a municipality may secure a title in fee simple to such real estate as it previously held under a limited title. 

Mortgages and liens on the property condemned are discharged and thrown upon the fund paid for the property. 

In the condemnation of lands for public purpose, liens and encumbrances are divested as a matter of public policy, because it would be inconvenient, prejudicial to and destructive of the right of eminent domain to have such liens remain as a charge on the property. Since the lien of a legacy, judgment or mortgage against property so taken is thus divested, it attaches forthwith to the fund realized from the land and the owner is regarded as a trustee for the benefit of others directly interested who are not necessarily parties to the proceedings (Briegel v. Briegel 307 Pa. 93, 99—1931; Sarapin v. Philadelphia 306 Pa. 388-1932). Inchoate dower or curtesy (See $142, 139 infra) are likewise discharged by condemnation but since during the life of the spouse they are neither liens nor encumbrances they do not attach to the fund realized. (Briegel v. Briegel, Supra.) 

38. Corporations. (a) In General.

Corporations have only such right to hold and alien land as is given them by the authority which created them, i.e., the State. In Pennsylvania the policy of the state, while

$38

originally strict, has with the process of time become greatly relaxed. In view of the fact that titles depend to no small degree upon the applicable law affecting the power of the grantor to convey or mortgage at the time of the execution of the instrument, it seems advisable to briefly review the development of the law with regard to the power of corporations to take, hold and convey real estate. 

In Pennsylvania the Preamble of the Act of April 6, 1833, P.L., 167 sets forth that "no corporation either of this state or of any other state, though lawfully incorporated or constituted, can in any case purchase lands within this state either in its corporate name or names of any person or persons whomsoever for its use, directly or indirectly, without incurring the forfeiture of said lands to this Commonwealth unless such purposes to be sanctioned or authorized by an act of legislature.'

The effect of this provision was to render the title of a corporation not authorized to hold land, defeasible to the 

Commonwealth (Leazure v. Hillegas, 7 S. & R. 313-320-1821;

Runyan v. Coster, 14 Pet. (U.S.) 122-1840). Where the 

Commonwealth has not moved by appropriate proceedings to forfeit real estate held and the corporation conveys away real estate to one authorized to hold it, the title so conveyed becomes indefeasible.

A corporation to the extent authorized by law to hold land, could alienate it and dispose of it as fully and freely as an individual (Ardesco v. N.A. Oil Co., 66 Pa. 375-1870). Prior to the Constitution of 1874, Pennsylvania corporations were each incorporated by a special Act of Assembly and their right to hold land was usually provided for in the incorporating act. After the adoption of the Constitution the legislature passed the General Corporation Act of 1874 which divided all corporations into two classes: corporations not for profit, called "corporations of the first class" and corporations for profit, called "corporations of the second class." 

The former were chartered by the courts and the latter by the Governor of the state. Both classes of corporations were

$61 

ALIENATION. 

authorized to hold, purchase and transfer such real estate as the purposes of the corporations required, not exceeding the amount limited by its charter or by law. 

§6 of Article XVI of the Constitution of 1874 by its lan guage, "No corporation shall **** take or hold any real estate except such as may be necessary and proper for its legitimate purposes" adopted what was virtually the original common law rule with respect to corporate real estate. (Blacks. Comm. 478; 2 Kent. Comm. 281.)

In England this common right of corporations to hold real estate was severely restricted by the so called "Mortmain" statutes which, while directed chiefly at ecclesiastical bodies, applied as well to all corporations, since all were prohibited from acquiring land without the permission of the Crown, and (during certain periods) from the Mesne Lord also. (2 

Blacks. Comm. 282.) But the main purpose of these "Mortmain" statutes was to repress the alarming influence of the ecclesiastical corporations which had, as early as the Norman Conquest monopolized much of the valuable land in England (14 A, C.J. 508, §2391).

While these statutes were enacted to remedy a mischief in England, the Judges of the Pennsylvania Supreme Court who in 1807 were requested to report to the legislature which of the English statutes were in force in Pennsylvania and which in their opinion ought to be incorporated into the laws of Pennsylvania by the Act of April 7, 1807, reported that the "Mortmain" statutes were in effect in Pennsylvania to the extent that no corporation can hold land in Pennsylvania except under special authority of the legislature. (Report of Judges, 3 Bin. 595–625—1808.)

Since that time many acts of assembly on the subject have been passed, some fixing the limit of real estate holdings of specific corporations and others regulating holdings by certain classes of corporations. Should it become material for a conveyancer to ascertain the limit fixed by the earlier laws of a particular corporation, these laws will be found gathered

$38 

 together in Purdon's Pennsylvania Statutes, Title 15, Part 2, beginning with page 372, §741. 

(b) Corporation Laws of 1933. 

Fortunately for the modern conveyancer the law has now been much simplified by the General Revision of our corporation laws made in 1933. Two acts of assembly now replace the former General Corporation Act of 1874. These acts may be cited by the short titles of "Business Corporation Law" (Act approved May 5, 1933, P.L. 364, 15 P.S. 

2852 et seq.) replacing the law relating to the so-called "Corporations of the second class" under the Act of 1874 and "Non-Profit Corporation Law," (Act approved May 5, 1933, P.L. 289, 15 P.S. 2851 et seq.) replacing the law relating to the so-called "corporations of the first class" under the act of 1874.

Both of these acts by identical language in their respective $302 sub-divisions 4 and 5, empower corporations to acquire and alienate (including right to mortgage, lease, etc.) real and personal property which may be appropriate to enable it to accomplish fully and properly its corporate purposes. By these acts the common law rule is virtually restored to Pennsylvania and the "Mortmain" restrictions under previous laws removed. Thus, e.g., under prior laws, corporations not for profit were restricted in their real estate holdings to such as had an annual income of $50,000.00, and literary, religious, charitable or beneficial societies and corporations, were restricted in their holdings as to both real and personal estates in the aggregate to the "clear yearly value of $350,000.00 unless authorized by decree of Court to hold more." These limitations have now been removed, for, by §306 of the "Nonprofit Corporation Law" religious, educational, scientific and charitable corporations are now permitted to take and hold real property, without limitation which is conveyed or devised to the corporations in trust for any religious, educational, scientific or charitable purpose set forth in the corporation charter. Those desiring to read a comprehensive

$63 

ALIENATION. 

review of the statutes and decisions under previous laws now superseded, are referred to the State publication entitled "Pennsylvania Corporation Laws, 1933" where a most satisfactory discussion of the subject will be found in the annotations to §306 of the "Non-profit Corporation Law" by Deputy 

Attorney General E. Russell Shockley. 

It remains to be said, that by §3 of the "Business Corporation Law," corporations for profit whose charters are subject to alterations or amendments by the legislature, (as all charters granted since the Constitution of 1874 are), are made subject to the new act and are correspondingly entitled to all its benefits, but other corporations organized prior to 1874 and whose charters are not subject to legislative revocation or amendment, are denied the benefits of the act until they file a formal acceptance of the provisions of the Constitution of 1874 and of the new act. Non-profit corporations are similarly provided for by §3 of the "Non-profit Corporation Law." In short, therefore, the benefits of the new law are given to all corporations organized since the adoption of the Constitution of 1874 as well as to corporations created earlier, which have specifically accepted the provisions of the present constitution and of the acts. All such are entitled to hold real estate to any extent that is "appropriate to the purposes for which the corporation is created." 

But corporations organized before the Constitution of 1874 and who have not accepted its provisions and the new acts, are governed by the restrictions in their charters and by the earlier acts. A careful conveyancer, therefore, in passing upon the right of a corporation to mortgage real estate to which it holds title, should ascertain first the date of the incorporation of the corporation and if he finds it incorporated earlier than 1874, whether a certificate has been filed accepting the Constitution of 1874 and the present Corporation Acts of 1933. If not, the right of the corporation to hold its real estate must be considered in the light of the earlier statutes to which reference has hereinabove been made.

§39  (c) Sale of Corporate Real Estate. 

It is important also to know that the Business Corporation 

Law and the Non-Profit Law has by §§311 and 308 respec tively, clarified the procedure by which such corporations may now sell or otherwise dispose of their assets including real estate. In brief a business corporation may dispose of all, or substantially all of its property without authorization or consent of its stockholders when done in the usual regular course of business; but if not so done, it must be made pursuant to consent and authorization of stockholders as detailed in §311(b).

Non-profit corporation conveyances are governed by $308 of the law which provides that "unless the corporation's articles or by-laws provide for the approval of another body, it shall not borrow money or purchase, sell, lease away, or otherwise dispose of any real estate unless and until a resolution, authorizing the same, shall have been approved by a majority of the members of the corporation at a regular or special meeting duly convened upon proper notice of this purpose. (For a case construing this part of the section see 

Neth v. St. Johns etc. Church 335 Pa. 155-1939.) The same section also provides that every non-profit corporation may mortgage, sell, lease away or otherwise dispose of any of its real estate without application to and authorization or confirmation of any court except in those cases where the Revised Price Act of 1917 confers jurisdiction upon the Orphans' Court or Courts of Common Pleas of a particular county, to authorize or confirm such disposition. See Florence Crittenton Circle Etc. v. Kotuna 32 D. & C. 413-1938 construing this part of $308. 

39. Foreign Corporations. 

By foreign corporations are meant such as are chartered by another State or country, e.g., a corporation chartered under the laws of New Jersey would be a foreign corporation in Pennsylvania. Foreign corporations have no rights out-

$65 

ALIENATION. 

side of the jurisdiction which created them except such as may be given them by the sovereignty in whose domains they seek to carry on business (Van Steuben v. Central R. R. Co., 178 Pa.-1896). In fact, a foreign corporation not engaged exclusively in interstate commerce (See International Text 

Book Co. v. Pigg, 217 U.S. 91-1910) may be excluded from the jurisdiction of a state altogether. They are, however, usually admitted on terms, but they should comply strictly with the general law providing for the conduct of foreign corporations doing business in the state. 

The right of foreign business corporations to hold real estate is now governed by $1012 of the Business Corporation Law (1933) which provides, "Every foreign business corporation authorized to transact business within the Commonwealth may acquire, hold, mortgage, lease and transfer real property within this Commonwealth in the same manner and subject to the same limitations as domestic business corporations."

In order to be authorized to transact business here a foreign corporation must procure a certificate of authority in accordance with §§1001-2-3-4-5-6 of the Act. 

Similar authorization to non-profit foreign corporations to hold and acquire real estate is given in similar language by $914 of the Non-Profit Corporation Act (1933) and the admission of such corporations to do business here is governed by §§901-2-3-4-5-6 of that Act. 

Here again the law has been greatly simplified. Formerly the policy of the State has been to grant the right to hold real estate very sparingly to foreign corporations, but gradually specific kinds of foreign corporations were given privilege. All such acts prior to 1913 are gathered together in $39 (pages 45 to 48) of the first edition of this Book. 

In 1919 the distinction between foreign and domestic corporations in this regard was swept away (See Act of June 

12, 1919 P.L. 441 Repealed and Supplied by Acts of May 

24, 1923 P.L. 438, Act of Apr. 7, 1925 P.L. 184, May 5, 1927 P.L. 813, 15 P.S. 3161) and the liberal principle of that act has now been incorporated in §1012 of the Business Cor-

poration Law (1933), above quoted and $914 of the Non- 

Profit Corporation Law (1933) above cited. 

40. Unincorporated Societies and Churches. 

Unincorporated associations in general cannot own or alien land in the society name but the title will be treated as being in the individual members just as in a partnership. There is however an exception in the case of charitable and religious societies and churches which may hold title in the society or church name. (Phipps v. Jones, 20 Pa. 260-263-1853; Bur ton's Appeal 57 Pa. 213, 217-1868). Such organizations may take and hold title to land and even gain it by adverse possession (Beech v. Trustees of Trinity Episcopal of Connes ville 3 D. & C. 395-1922).

Where there is a split in the congregation the title of the property is adjudged to be in that part of the congregation which is in harmony with the laws and customs accepted by the whole body before the division took place (Landis' Appeal 

102 Pa. 467-1883, Krecker v. Shirey 163 Pa. 534-1894), and this whether that faction be a majority or a minority (Nagel v. Miller 275 Pa. 157-1922).

Though as a matter of custom and practice the title of religious and charitable organizations is usually held by trustees appointed either by the court or by the association in accordance with its by-laws, the title is nevertheless considered as vested in the association as such (Brendle v. German Reformed Congregation, 33 Pa. 414, 425—1859).

Where trustees are designated to hold title, conveyances have sometimes been made to their successors, though this would appear as unnecessary. (See Liederkranz Society v.

Turn-Verein 163 Pa. 265-1894; Krauczunas v. Hoban 221 

Pa. 213-221-1908).

It has even been held that where land is devised to such an unincorporated society which later incorporates, the title is regarded as vesting in the successor congregation without formal deed of conveyance (Congregation Shaarai Shomayim v. Moss 22 Pa. Super. Ct. 356—1903).

§41(a) 

67 

ALIENATION. 

Until the Act of June 20, 1935, P.L. 353, (10 P.S. 81), under the prior law of Pennsylvania (Act of April 26, 1855 P.L. 

328 §7 and supplements) the church laity was vested with absolute control and disposition of church property subject to the uses for which it was lawfully dedicated. Because this policy was at variance with the cannons, customs and regulations of some of the church denominations and sects, it was a fruitful source of litigation which has now been ended by the Act of 1935. That act now provides that whenever any property has heretofore been or shall hereafter be conveyed for the use of any church congregation or religious society or in trust for religious worship or sepulture, it shall be taken and held subject to the control and disposition of such officers or authorities of such church congregation or religious society having a controlling power according to the rules of such church congregation or religious society, which control shall be exercised in accordance with and subject to the rules, regulations, usages, cannons, discipline and requirements of the religious body denomination or organization to which such church congregation or religious society shall belong. 

This act it has been held covers all property however acquired, and applies to property acquired before as well as after the effective date of the act, and is constitutional. 

(Conavaro v. Brothers of the Order of Hermits of St. 

Augustine, 326 Pa. 76–1936). 

41. Partnerships. 

(a) General Partnership. 

Real estate held by partners for the purpose of the business, is regarded in law as forming part of the assets, or partnership stock, as it is sometimes called, and hence, treated as personal property (West Hickory Association v. Reed, 80 

Pa. 38-1875). In 1915 the legislature adopted the Uniform 

Partnership Act, being act approved March 26, 1915 P.L. 18, 

(59 P.S. 1) and §§25 and 26 (59 P.S. 72, 73), thereof re-enacts the principle that the real estate of a partnership is to be

§41(a)  

regarded as personalty so that the interest of a deceased partner in such real estate held by the firm for partnership purposes, is personal property, and the proceeds of the sale of such interest so treated upon distribution of his estate (Hall's Estate, 28 D. R. 311, 266 Pa. 312-1920).

The question often arises whether real property purchased jointly was intended to be firm property. Even before the 

Uniform Partnership Act it was held that the mere fact of taking property in the joint names will not make it partnership property (Stover v. Stover 180 Pa. 425-1897; Cundy v. Hall, 208 Pa. 335-1904), and in Kreise v. Cartledge, (262

Pa. 55-1918), it was said that in the absence of evidence that real estate owned by the partners jointly was held by them for partnership purposes, the presumption is that such real estate was not partnership property. This is still the rule under the partnership Act (Bell v. Johnston 281 Pa. 57 -1924). But if acquired with partnership funds the reverse is true for The Uniform Partnership Act of 1915, by $8, clause 2, provides "unless the contrary intention appears property acquired with partnership funds is partnership property." But it seems if an innocent purchaser later acquires an interest therein, he has a right to rely on the record, which if it indicates that the partners hold as tenants in common, gives him a superior right unless he had actual notice of the firm's ownership (Magen v. Neiman 301 Pa. 165-1930).

The same section also lays down other governing rules viz: Clause 1 provides: "All property originally brought into the partnership stock or subsequently acquired by the purchaser or otherwise on account of the partnership is partnership property." And Clause 3: "Any estate in real property may be acquired in the partnership name" but when so acquired "can be conveyed only in the partnership name." 

Clause 4: "A conveyance to a partnership in the partnership name though without words of inheritance, (See $54-c infra.) passes the entire estate of the grantor unless a contrary intention appears. 99

§41(a) 

69 

ALIENATION. 

To avoid the difficulties that may arise, it is good conveyancing practice to set out in the deed by which the title to the land is acquired by the partnership, the fact that it is acquired for partnership purposes in order that the individual creditors of each partner be not deceived (Gunnison v. Dime Savings Bank, 157 Pa. 303—1893). 

In Rosenberger v. Kuesel, (292 Pa. 184–1928) it was held "real estate standing in the names of partners as tenants in common, may as between them, be shown to be partnership property; but the rights of the bona fide purchasers and lien creditors of the individual partners must be determined solely by the record title to the realty. It is more than doubtful whether anything short of a conveyance or a duly indexed proceeding showing that a court of record has been asked to reform the deed or an actual decree or reformation will affect the rights of a bona fide purchaser or a lien creditor of such tenant in common." 

§§9 and 10 of the Uniform Partnership Act of 1915 (59 

P.S. 31, 32), lay down with meticulous detail the rules governing conveyances of partnership real estate. They provide in brief that where the title is in the partnership name any partner can convey it in that name provided he is expressly authorized to do so or even impliedly if §9(1) of the act is conformed to. Where the title is held in the names of less than all the partners they may convey unless they be without authority express or implied. If title is in the name of all partners then all must sign the deed. A deed executed by a partner without requisite authority entitles the partnership to sue to set it aside unless it has been in the meanwhile conveyed in turn by the grantee to an innocent purchaser for value without notice. In a recent case (Wilson v. McKee, 110 Pa. Super. 544-549-1933), the Superior Court without referring to the partnership act stated the general rule to be "A partner cannot sell more than his undivided interest in real estate held as partnership stock unless he has sufficient special authority for the purpose. 

A careful conveyancer ought as a matter of good practice

§41(b)  

see that all partners sign the deed and if this is not practical see that the written authorization of the absent partner is produced, and the fact of authority recited in the deed when executed by less than all. (b) Limited Partnerships.

A limited partnership is a partnership in which one or more partners are general partners with unlimited liability and one or more are limited partners who are not liable to creditors of the partnership beyond the respective capital contribution subscribed by them. This is a statutory partnership formed under the Act of April 12, 1917 P.L. 55 (59

P.S. 171 et. seq.). It is sometimes referred to as the "Uniform Limited Partnership Act". It is formed by two or more persons desiring to form such limited partnership, signing and swearing to a certificate which shall state, among other things, the name of the partnership, the character of its business, the location of the principal place of business, the names, the place of residence of each member, general and limited, the term of existence, etc. See Limited Partnership Act, $2, (59 P.S. 172). The certificate of organization must be recorded in the office of the Recorder of Deeds of the County in which the principal place of business of the limited partnership shall be located. The general control and conduct of the partnership is vested in the general partners.

The Act contains no express provision regulating the conveyance of the real estate of the partnership but it may be said that if any provision exists in the certificate of organization, it must be followed. If there be no such provision, then the conveyance of the partnership real estate would be governed by the ordinary or general partnership rules. This in view of $9 (59 P.S. 193) which provides that a general partner shall have all of the rights and powers and be subject to all restrictions and liabilities of a partner in a partnership without limited partners, except that without written consent or ratification of the specific act by all the limited partners,

§41(c) 

71 

ALIENATION. 

the general partner or all of the general partners have no authority (a) to do any act in contravention of the certificate, (b) do any act which would make it impossible to carry on the ordinary business of the partnership, (c) confess judgment against the partnership, (d) possess partnership property or assign their rights in specific partnership property for other than a partnership purpose, (e) admit a person as a general partner, (f) admit a person as a limited partner unless the right to do so is given in the certificate, (g) continue the business with partnership property on the death of, retirement, or insanity of a general partner, unless the right to do so is given in the certificate. The Act should be carefully read before passing upon a conveyance from or to a limited partnership. 

(c) Registered Partnerships. 

A registered partnership is in a sense a quasi corporation. 

It may be formed by two or more persons under the provisions of the Act of May 9th, 1899 P.L. 261 and its supplements (59 P.S. 241). It differs from the limited partnership in that the liability of all of the members for the debts of the partnership is limited to the amount of capital subscribed by the partners respectively. The Act requires the recording of the Articles of Partnership and that the words "Registered" be added to the partnership name. The Act authorizes a registered partnership to adopt by-laws, rules and regulations by a majority in number and interest of the partners, and to adopt and use a common seal. 

A registered partnership may be formed for the purpose of conducting any trade, business or occupation except construction and operation of electric light and power companies, banking or trust companies, water, railroad, street railway or traction companies. §1 of Act (59 P.S. 241). 

As to a "registered partnership's" real estate, it is provided by $9 of the Act (59 P.S. 273) that "the partnership may take, hold, mortgage, encumber, lease or convey, in fee simple, or for any less estate, real estate or interest therein,

§41(d)  

in the firm name. The place of record of the Articles of 

Partnership shall be stated in all instruments of writing relating to real estate, but failure so to state shall not invalidate the instrument. Any instrument relating to real estate, may be signed or sealed by one or more of the partners, for the partnership and in the name of the partnership, if the by-laws, rules or regulations shall so provide, but in case less than all the partners are vested with this power the fact shall be stated in the original articles of partnership, or in amendments thereto, or in a statement duly signed and acknowledged by the partners and recorded in the office of the said Recorder of Deeds". This Section is clear and in passing upon the conveyance of real estate to or from a "registered partnership," its terms should be carefully followed. 

(d) Partnership Associations. 

Even more like a corporation is a "Partnership Association" which under the law of Pennsylvania, Act of June 2, 1874 P.L. 271 §1 and its supplements (59 P.S. 341), may be formed for the purpose of conducting "any lawful business or occupation" by subscribing and contributing capital thereto, which capital shall alone be liable for the debts of the association. It is formed by making a statement in writing to be signed and acknowledged, which will show among other things, the full names of the persons concerned, the amount of the capital subscribed by each, the character of business to be conducted and the name of the Association, etc. 

The name of the Association must have added to it the words "limited" as part of the name. The statement must fix the term of existence and must be recorded in the office for recording of deeds. Provision is made for the election by the members of "managers" and officers to conduct the affairs of the association, also for the adoption of by-laws, rules and regulations and authorizes the adoption of a common seal though the use of the same is not made compulsory. (Stevens v. Philadelphia Ball Club, 142 Pa. 52-1891). The Act also expressly gives the partnership association the right to adopt

and use a common seal and to acknowledge instruments of conveyance, mortgages etc. or writings by their chairman and secretary. (Act of Feb. 18, 1875 P.L. 3, 59 P.S. 362).

As to real estate, the Act of May 1, 1876 P.L. 89 §3, (59 

P.S. 361), supplements the Act of 1874 and provides that all real estate owned or purchased by such an association shall be held and owned, and conveyance thereof shall be made, in the Association name; the same Act provides the Association shall sue and be sued in the Association name. As in cases of other partnerships the interest of the partners in the partnership association is deemed personal property, $4 as amended (59 P.S. 383).
