INTRODUCTION. 

We will now consider the modern methods of conveying title. It is generally known that the actual transfer or conveyance of title to land is made by an instrument called a deed. But before we come to the deed there must have been an agreement between the buyer and seller as to the price to be paid and other terms. This agreement which for reasons to be hereinafter explained must be in writing will be, therefore, our first consideration.

In order to present the subject logically we will consider instruments of conveyancing in the following order:— 

1. Agreements of Sale and Options. 

2. Deeds. 

3. Mortgages. 

4. Ground Rents. 

42. What it is.

AGREEMENTS OF SALE. 

Definition. 

Suppose A. desires to buy B's property. After much negotiation both arrive at a mutual understanding and desire to close out the transaction. This understanding embodies the terms and conditions of the sale and must be in writing and signed by the parties. Agreement of sale 

Agreement of sale may, therefore, be defined as an agreement or contract in writing wherein one party agrees to sell and another agrees to buy real estate under such terms and conditions as are therein set forth. 

42-A. Options.

The distinction between an option and an agreement or contract of sale is broad and plain. An option is an unaccepted offer. It states the terms and conditions under which the owner is willing to sell or lease the land if the holder of the option elects to accept them within the time limited. If the holder does so elect he must give notice to the other party and the accepted offer thereupon becomes a valid and binding contract. If an acceptance is not made

§42A  

within the time fixed, the owner is no longer bound by his offer and the option is at an end. (Uhlman v. Sullivan, 242 

Pa. 436-1913; McMillan v. Phila. Co. 159 Pa. 142–1893.)

Where an option is exercised the title of the optionee relates back to the date of the option and his interest is regarded as real estate as of that time (Kelly's Est. 6 D & C 770-1925 and see $48 infra.)

Options to sell real estate are usually incorporated in leases although they may be entirely separate therefrom. Appropriate forms will be found in Chapter XV. For the reason discussed in the next section (43) options, like agreements of sale, must be in writing to be valid. They must also have an actual or legal consideration, but a valuable consideration, however small or nominal, if given or stipulated in good faith is, in absence of fraud, sufficient. Thus in the case of Real 

Estate Co. of Pittsburgh v. Rudolph (301 Pa. 502-1930), the sum of one dollar was held sufficient. If the option is made under seal (see §§ 51 and 61) the seal imports a consideration and makes the option valid (Schaefer v. Herman, 237 Pa. 86-1912; Real Estate Co. of Pittsburgh v. Rudolph 

301 Pa. 502-1930). When contained in a lease, it requires no consideration separate and apart from that of the lease itself. But nevertheless an option clause in a lease is independent of and forms no part of the demise, hence "the privilege of renewing the lease" does not, when exercised, extend the life of the option for the renewed term (Petit v. 

Tourison 283 Pa. 529-1925; Signor v. Consistory etc. 277 

Pa. 504-1923).

An option must be definite and certain or be capable of being rendered certain. An option to purchase land at a price to be agreed on by the parties is too vague or indefinite to be enforced, but where a lease provided in addition to such a clause "that in the event lessor receives any other bona fide offer to purchase during the term of this option, in such event the lessees must exercise their option to purchase at or in excess of the sum named or agreed upon under such bona fide offer within 15 days", it was held that this vagueness is

$77 

removed by the agreement upon a method making certain the price at which the lessor must allow his lessees fifteen days in which to accept the offer. (Driebe v. Fort Penn 

Realty Co. 331 Pa. 314—1938.) 

If an option be accepted in writing incorporating additional terms, the optionor may reject the acceptance, but if he fail to do so, he is bound by the acceptance as written (Atlas Portland Cement Co. v. American Brick Co. 280 Pa. 449-1924). 

43. Must Be in Writing. Pa. Statute of Frauds. 

It has been considered sound public policy in all states that certain contracts should be required to be made in writing. 

And in all common law jurisdictions the one kind of contract most universally required to be in writing is the contract relating to sale and creation of interests in land. The first statute requiring contracts concerning the sale and creation of interests in lands to be in writing was passed in England in 1676. As recited in its preamble, its purpose was to prevent frauds, it has ever since been known as the Statute of Frauds, and statutes of frauds similar to a greater or lesser extent have been enacted in most every state of the United States. 

(a) Pennsylvania Statute of Frauds-The Pennsylvania Statute of Frauds is the Act of March 21, 1772 (I Sm. Laws 

389; 33 P.S. 1), which provides that "all leases, estates, interest of freehold or term of years or any uncertain interest of in or out of any messuages, manors, lands, tenements or hereditaments, made or created by livery of seisin only, or parol and not put in writing and signed by the parties so making or creating the same or their agents thereunto lawfully authorized by writing, shall have the force and effect of leases or estates at will only, and shall not either in law or equity, be deemed or taken to have any other or greater force or effect, any consideration for making any such parol leases or estates or any former law or usage to the contrary not-

§43  

withstanding, except nevertheless all leases not exceeding the term of three years from the making thereof." 

This part of the statute deals with making of leases and in plainer words provides in substance that leases for a greater term than three years must be in writing. It does not however invalidate a lease to which it applies, it merely shortens its term and the tenancy at will created by application of the statute is changed to one from year to year when possession has been taken and held for more than a year under the lease and the rent paid and accepted in accordance with the terms. (Ferri v. Liberatoscioli 338 Pa. 454-1940).

The other part of the statute which concerns us now continues; "and moreover no leases, estates or interests either of freehold or terms of years or any uncertain interest of, in, to or out of any messuages, manors, lands, tenements or hereditaments shall at any time be assigned, granted or surrendered unless it be by deed or note in writing signed by the party so assigning, granting or surrendering the same or their agents thereto lawfully authorized by writing or by act or operation of law."

This in brief means that no land or interest in land shall be assigned, granted or surrendered unless in writing signed by the party or his agent whose authority to do so must also be in writing. Note however, the provision of the Statute of Frauds providing that a parol agreement for the sale of land shall be unenforceable was made for the protection of the vendor. He only can invoke it. He may waive it. The statute requires no written evidence of the engagement of the vendee, and the latter is bound by his parol contract. If the vendor confesses and abides by his contract it will be good as against the vendee (Dieffenderfer v. Kremp, 25 D.R. 

1011-1916). Nor is an oral contract by which a defendant agrees to sell certain boilers, radiators and valves located in buildings which were to be demolished within the statute 

(Braverman et al. v. Langhorne, 100 Pa. Super. Ct. 4661930).

But an interest in a gas well is real estate and is

$79 

´ within the Statute of Frauds (Stockdale v. Sellers 102-Pa. 

Super. Ct. 447—1931).

While failure to put in writing a contract to sell or lease land prevents the specific performance of it, yet the vendee can recover in a suit at law for breach of contract his actual damages, that is, hand money paid or actual expense incurred as for example, searching title, etc. (Swayne v. Swayne, 19 Pa. 

Super. Ct. 160-1901; Seidlek v. Bradley 293 Pa. 379-1928).

But if the plaintiff can prove fraud he may recover substantial damages also, though in absence of fraud he may not recover damages equivalent to the value of the land or for the loss of his bargain, for this would amount to specific performance of the contract and so circumvent the statute (McClowry v. Croghans' Administrator, 31 Pa. 22-1854; 

Dumars v. Miller, 34 Pa. 319-1859). Failure or refusal to convey is of itself not such fraud (Seidlek v. Bradley 293 

Pa. 379-1928).

Also it should be noted that there are some exceptions to the general rule of the statute's application, such as part performance of the contract, or possession given under an oral contract¹ (Richardson et al. v. Savage, 129 Pa. Super. Ct. 

235-1937). But for the purposes of this book we will disregard the exceptions and consider the general rule to be unbending. The best interests of clients can only be served by reducing all such agreements concerning real estate into writing. 

(b) Written Agreement Cannot be Reformed by Oral 

Testimony.

In order to give a vendor the full protection intended by the requirement of the Statute of Frauds, the court will not permit the vendee to change its terms by oral evidence or to thus supply other terms alleged to have been omitted. 

So in Safe Deposit etc. Co. v. Diamond Coal Co. (234 Pa. 100, 111-1912), the court said "when a party to an executory agreement of sale of lands succeeds in reforming it by oral testimony he reduces the whole agreement to a parol contract 1 For proofs essential to enable a vendee to have specific performance of a parol contract see Tetlow's Estate 321 Pa. 305, 313-1936.

§44  

and deprives himself of the right to have it specifically performed. He pulls down the house on his head. When he converts the writing into an oral agreement the statute declares it to be void. The true contract as declared to the chancellor cannot be enforced."

But when a vendor is willing and does tender a deed conveying all that was actually agreed upon, though mistakenly described in the written agreement, the vendee cannot refuse the deed and sue to recover the purchase price because the description in the written agreement was shown to have been erroneously set forth by mutual mistake, because the Statute of Frauds operates to protect the vendor and not the vendee. (Brown v. Aiken 329 Pa. 566-Note to page 579-1938; 

Roberts v. Roesch 306 Pa. 435-1932). 

44. What the Writing Must Contain: Form. 

The statute requires no particular form (Cadwallader v. 

App 81 Pa. 194-1876), but the memorandum should disclose (a) the interest of the parties, (b) the terms of the sale, (c) a definite enough description to identify the land, and (d) the consideration or the price to be paid. Any agreement which contains these essentials would be sufficient. The agreement need not be under seal (Colt v. Selden, 5 Watts 525-1836). "But with or without the Statute of Frauds, an agreement with unknown terms is void a contract is as much void when the consideration, as when the subject is undefined" (Llewellyn v. Sunnyside Coal Co., 242 Pa. 517–1914).

It has been held that a receipt on account of purchase price, if it contains these particulars, is sufficient (Evans v. Evans, 29 Pa. 277-1857; Schermer v. Wilmart, 282 Pa. 55-1925).

The requisite facts may also appear in two or more papers if from any of them, or from any other writing it is shown they together form the contract of sale (Weisenberger v. 

Huebner, 264 Pa. 316, 317–1919). It has even been held where one corporation agrees to sell real estate to another, the minutes of the corporation, containing the resolution, duly attested by the respective secretaries, are a sufficient signing

$81 

to satisfy the statute as well as a sufficient memorandum 

(Peoples Trust Co. v. Consumers Ice & Coal Co., 283 Pa. 761925). But a check which did not identify the subject matter of the sale was held not to be a sufficient memorandum to satisfy the statute (Stockdale v. Sellers 102 Pa. Super. Ct. 

447-1931). When however an agreement is partly in writing and partly oral it must be held to be only an oral agreement, when determining whether the Statute of Frauds is applicable to it and an agreement which is partly oral will not operate to pass title to realty mentioned in it (Hill v. Houpt, 292 Pa. 339-1928). The agreement need only be signed by the vendor, that is, the man who agrees to sell the land, although it is customary and the better practice to have the vendee sign also. Where the vendor is married the husband or wife should sign also (See §46A infra.)

While it is true that no set form is required, it has become customary to use a form such as the following:- 

This Agreement,¹ made the 12th day of June, A. D. 1908, between 

Andrew Black, of the City of Philadelphia, State of Pennsylvania, and Charles Dolan, also of the City of Philadelphia, State of Pennsylvania. Italics indicate the part which the conveyancer writes in.

party of the second part in the performance of the terms of this agreement) and the balance of the purchase money at the time of the settlement. All perpetual policies of fire insurance to be paid for at withdrawal value and term policy at proportionate value for unexpired term. The members of the Philadelphia Real Estate Board use a form somewhat differently arranged which has been compiled for their members, a form of which is set forth in §50-A and its terms there discussed. 

45. Meaning of the Various Parts. 

(a) The Introduction, to wit:- 

"This Agreement made the 12th day of June, A.D. 1908, between

A. B., of the City of Philadelphia, State of Pennsylvania, of the first part, and C. D., also of said City and State, of the second part. 

Witnesseth that the said party of the first part agrees to sell and convey to the said party of the second part, and the said party of the second part agrees to purchase. 

This part of the agreement may be called the introduction, and its purpose is to recite the names, identify the parties and to state what the agreement is about. 

(b) Description:-Then follows the description, to wit:- 

"All that certain lot or piece of ground with the buildings and improvements thereon erected, known as N.2214 Y. Street, in the 

City and County of Philadelphia, State of Pennsylvania.' 

The description should be definite enough to identify the property, (Howard & Co. v. Innes 253 Pa. 593-1916), but if it names a definite object it satisfies the Statute of Frauds for parol evidence is then admissible to identify the premises. 

(Feld v. Shapiro 87 Pa. Super. Ct. 557-1926). A contract to sell land cannot be specifically enforced unless it identifies the land in terms sufficient for a surveyor to determine its location and size by metes and bounds or adjoiners. So a description such as: "Receive $100.00 earnest money, being part payment on a tract of wood land situate in Tuscarora Township, Perry County, Pa.", was held to be entirely too indefinite to be enforced (Minich's Estate, 21 D.R. 605-1912). Within the city limits the word "property situate No. 2214 Y. Street, in the City of Philadelphia, State of Pennsylvania," is definite enough (McDermott v. Reiter 279 Pa. 545-1924). Where there is no street and number then the description should be

§45 (c) 

by metes and bounds and copied from the vendor's deed, e.g.

as follows:- 

All that certain lot or piece of ground within the three-story brick messuage or tenement thereon erected, situate on the west side of "Y" Street, at the distance of 337 feet northward from the north side of "X" Street, in the Fiftieth Ward of the City of Philadelphia, containing in front or breadth on the said "Y" Street, 18 feet and extending of that width in length or depth westward between two parallel lines at right angles with said "X" Street one hundred feet to a three feet wide alley leading northward from "X" Street to "Z" Street. 

(c) Terms and Conditions. 

"The said party of the second part agrees to pay therefor the sum of sixty-five hundred ($65000) dollars as follows: Two hundred ($200) dollars on the signing of this agreement (which deposit it is hereby agreed may at the option of the said party of the first part, be retained by said party as liquidated damages in case of default by the said party of the second part in the performance of this agreement) and the balance of the purchase money at the time of settlement.' 

The clause in brackets is the liquidated damage clause which while it may be omitted is of great advantage to the vendor. It is recommended however when representing the vendor that it be always inserted for the following reasons:

Under the law if a vendee fails to make settlement, the vendor ordinarily has the choice of these remedies: tender the deed and sue for the whole purchase price (Tripp v. Bishop, 56 

Pa. 424-1867, Keily v. Saunders, 236 Pa. 593-1912), or make a bona fide private or public re-sale and sue the vendee for the difference between the original purchase price and that of the re-sale. (Ashcom v. Smith, 2 P. & W. 211—1830).

The terms of the re-sale must however be as favorable as those of the original sale (Goodritz v. McMahon, 64 Pa. 

Super. Ct. 479-1916). Sometimes, however, the vendor would prefer to invoke neither of these remedies and would rather retain the deposit money and call the sale off, especially when he thinks he can sell it for a better price later on. In such a case after he does re-sell he might be faced

§(c) 

85 

by a suit against him for the deposit money unless he first puts the vendee in default by tendering a deed and good title; (see Eberz v. Heisler, 12 Pa. Super. Ct. 388-1900, Lowenstein v. Armstrong, 27 Pa. Super. Ct. 543-1904). If he makes such a tender he might be embarrassed by the vendee accepting, though of course if the vendee puts himself in default by refusing the tender it is clear that he as a party in default cannot recover back the deposit money paid by him, (Dluge v. Whiteson, 292 Pa. 334-1928, Riling v. Idell, 291 

Pa. 472-1928, Sanders v. Brock, 230 Pa. 609-1911). To avoid being impailed on a technicality, a proper liquidated damage clause as here suggested is highly desirable. 

When such a clause is present in the agreement the law takes the view that the parties have agreed on the deposit money as being liquidated, i.e., determined damages, which the vendor has suffered by reason of the failure of the vendee to keep his agreement. The damages thus agreed upon unless unconscionable or greatly disproportionate are enforceable; (Ellis v. Roberts 98 Pa. Super. Ct. 49-1929, Artzerounian v. Demetriades 276 Pa. 303-1923). The inclusion of such a clause gives the vendor therefore three remedies (a) to tender deed and sue for the balance of the purchase price, (b) to re-sell the property and sue for the loss, if any, and (c) to call the sale off and keep the deposit money as liquidated damages. The words "at the option of the said party of the first part," must not be omitted else the Court may take the view that the vendor has specifically agreed to restrict his remedy to the forfeiture of the deposit money and thereby substituted it for all other remedies. So interpreted he might lose his right to obtain damages for a larger loss upon re-sale (Addesso v. Gargalli, 26 D.R. 169—1916; 

Lichetti v. Conway, 44 Pa. Super. Ct. 71-1910; Riling v. 

Idell, 291 Pa. 472—1928); but see Boyd v. Hoffman, (241 Pa. 

421-1913), apparently holding to the contrary. Unless the agreement by clear and unequivocal language provides that a purchaser may terminate it for his own default, such effect will not be given to it so as to permit him to escape by merely

§45 (d) 

forfeiting the deposit money (see Korman v.

Trainer, 258 

Pa. 362-1917, following Cape May Real Estate Co. v. Hen derson, 231 Pa. 82-1911; Shermet v. Embick, 90 Pa. Super. 

Ct. 269-1926). Because these cases are in apparent confusion it is all the more necessary that the liquidated damage clause be drawn in the form as here suggested. 

The rest of this part of the agreement relates to the terms under which the consideration should be paid. The methods of paying the consideration may be as many and varied as the parties may see fit to agree upon. For example, if it desired to purchase subject to an existing mortgage it may be stated as follows: 

The said party of the second part agrees to purchase said property under and subject to an existing first mortgage of $4,000.00 now against the property and pay therefore the sum of $2,500.00 as follows: $200.00 at the time of the execution of this agreement and the balance at the time of settlement. 

Again, the property may be clear of encumbrance and the vendor agree to take a first mortgage as part consideration, in which event the clause may read as follows:

The said party of the second part agrees to pay and the party of the first part agrees to accept therefor the sum of $6,500 in the following manner: $200.00 at the time of the signing of this agreement and the remainder as follows, by executing to the vendor a first mortgage to the amount of $4,000 on said property and the balance of $2,300 to be paid in cash at the time of settlement. 

(d) Fire Insurance Policies. 

"All perpetual policies of fire insurance to be paid for at withdrawal value, and term policies at proportionate value for the unexpired term.

Fire insurance policies are generally of two kinds, perpetual and term. A perpetual policy is one which remains in force forever without payment of additional premium. It is issued on the payment of one premium based on a charge of 2 per cent. of the amount insured for. Thus the premium of $1,500.00 policy would be $30.00. This policy may be

§45(e) 

surrendered and cancelled at any time and the holder thereof receive a rebate or return of the whole premium paid less 10 per cent. This is what is known as the cancellation or withdrawal value.

A term policy is a policy which, as the name signifies, is issued for a limited term such as one, three or five years. The premium varies according to the risk and the length of the term. The cancellation value of this kind of a policy is the proportion of the unexpired term less the brokers' commission assumed to be 15 per cent. of the premium. Very often, if its value be small, the vendor will throw a term policy in without charge, in which event this clause should read: "All fire insurance policies now on said property are included in the sale.' 

(e) Encumbrance Clause. 

"The premises are to be conveyed free and clear of all liens and encumbrances." 

An encumbrance (sometimes written incumbrance) has been defined to be a right to an interest in land which may subsist in third persons to the diminution of the value of the land, but consistent with the passing of a fee by a conveyance (Nimlets Estate, 299 Pa. 359-1930; Perkinpine v. Hogan, 47 Pa. Super. Ct. 22—1911.)

The clause as above quoted means that the vendor undertakes to pass an absolutely clear title. It has been held that when a person protects himself against an encumbrance by a positive covenant that the property is to be conveyed to him clear of all encumbrance, he is entitled to the benefit of his contract whether he had knowledge of the existence of the encumbrance or not (Strong v. Brinton, 63 Pa. Super Ct. 

267—1916; McDermott v. Reiter, 279 Pa. 545—1924; Nauman v. Treen Box Co. 280 Pa. 97-1924.)

The following have been held to be encumbrances which gave the purchaser a right to rescind the contract and to a return of his deposit money. Right of way released to a railway company, (Strong v. Brinton, 63 Pa. Super. Ct. 267—

§45(e) 

1916). Plotting of a proposed street (Ritter v. Hill, 282 Pa. 

115-1925). Possibility of public benefit being assessed against the property by reason of the vacation of the street, (Shoub v. Dunbar, 256 Pa. 311-1917). Outstanding right to mine coal, (Rayman v. Klare, 242 Pa. 448—1913).

The foregoing types of encumbrance mostly effect the physical condition of the property. Encumbrances may also effect the title as, e.g., mortgages or other liens of record; claims for taxes (Taylor v. Allen, 60 Pa. Super. Ct. 5031915); inheritance taxes (Large v. McClain 4 Sadler 2401886; 7 A. 101-1886); outstanding articles of agreement to sell (Seitzinger v. Weaver, 1 Rawle 377-1829); or inchoate rights of dower, (Withers v. Baird, 7 Watts 227-1838; 

Lafferty v. Milligan 165 Pa. 534-1895). Easements, such as right of way for a railroad (Nauman v. Treen Box Co., 280 Pa. 97), or for private use, (McDermott v. Reitter, 279 Pa. 

545-1924; Patterson v. Freihoffer, 215 Pa. 47-1906). Restrictions against specified uses of a property (Batley v. 

Foerderer, 162 Pa. 460-1894; Coues v. Hallahan, 209 Pa. 

224-1904). But an existing claim that works no injury to the value of the land as, e.g., the right of the City to demand payment for the cost of laying waterpipes from anyone who may in the future use the pipes. Such possible claim was held not to be an encumbrance in Gilham v. Real Estate T. Ins. & Trust Co. (203 Pa. 24—1902), the same was held with regard to sewer claims in Perkinpine v. Hogan (47 Pa. Super. Ct. 22-1911).

Frequently a vendee is perfectly willing to take title subject to certain encumbrance, e.g., mortgages, judgment liens, or building restrictions, and when this is made part of the bargain it should be so stated in appropriate language as follows: "The premises are to be conveyed clear of all encumbrance, except the first mortgage of $4000." (or as the case may be) 

It has been quite customary to protect the vendor by adding also, "and excepting existing restrictions and easements, if any." Note however that while easements and restric-

§45(e) 

89 

tions are encumbrances, all encumbrances are not necessarily either easements or restrictions. In Ritter v. Hill, (282 Pa. 

115-1925), it was ruled that a street which had been plotted but unopened was neither an easement or a restriction within the meaning of the phrase last quoted.

In practice usually when an encumbrance is discovered before conveyance of title the vendee may either refuse to take title, rescind the agreement and receive back his deposit money, or make take title subject to the encumbrance upon the vendor reducing the consideration to be made for the property commensurate with the diminution of the value. (Andrien v. Heffernan 299 Pa. 284-1930). But even in cases where the existence of the encumbrance is not discovered until after settlement and conveyance of the property the vendee still has his remedy, e.g., Lehman v. Paxton, (7 Pa. Super. Ct. 259, 262-1898), where the grantee was held entitled to recover the amount he was compelled to pay to discharge a lien filed by the Commonwealth for unpaid purchase money due it; and it has been stated as a general rule that where a grantee accepts a deed with "special warranty" (See $55(c) for meaning of special and general warranty), the covenant of an agreement of sale to convey clear of encumbrance survives so that an action may be maintained for the breach thereof by the grantee; (Wazonek v. Saul, 3 D. & C. 293—1923). This because the general rule of law, that the acceptance of a deed in pursuance of a contract of sale is presumably in satisfaction of all previous covenants of the agreement of sale, does not apply to this particular covenant; (Lehman v. Paxton, 7 Pa. Super. Ct. 259, 262-1898; Close v. Zell, 141 Pa. 390-1891). And see Dintenfass v. Greenberg, (318 Pa. 20-1935).

But where a vendee elects to accept conveyance with full knowledge of the existing defect, he cannot thereafter make claim for the loss sustained (Hannan v. Carroll 277 Pa. 321923; Bricker v. Kline 86 Pa. Super. Ct. 594-1925); unless the parties have expressly reserved their rights by agree-

§45 (f) 

ment or an express covenant to protect is inserted in the deed (Andrien v. Heffernan 299 Pa. 284-288-1930). 

(f) Fixture Clause. 

"The gas and electric fixtures, heaters, ranges, plumbing and heating systems, laundry tubs, etc., annexed to said building are included in sale."

Fixtures here considered, are generally such articles as are annexed to freehold. In Pennsylvania the question whether a given article is a fixture or not depends not on the way it is fastened, but upon the intention of the person who attached it (National Bank of Catasauqua v. North, 160 

Pa. 303-1894; McKay v. Meyer Co., 44 Pa. Super. Ct. 2931910; Central Lithograph Co. v. Eatmor Choc. Co. 316 Pa. 

300-1934). Thus gas fixtures, heaters, ranges, ornamental wall mirrors, may or may not be fixtures according to the intention, and it has already been held under certain circumstances that they are not (Heysham v. Dettre, 89 Pa. 5061879; Waltman v. Mayer, 97 Pa. Super. Ct. 236-1929; Kopp v. Bashline, 1 D. & C. 131–1922). Consequently it is good practice to always insert a clause to the effect that gas fixtures, heaters, ranges, etc., are included in sale. Indeed, it is best to specify all articles about which there may be a controversy as suggested hereafter (See $50, suggestion 5). 

(g) Possession Clause. 

"Possession is to be given at the date of settlement." 

The clause as herein set forth means that at the date of settlement the house will be vacant and possession given to 

1 In Clayton v. Lienhard, 312 Pa. 433-1933, Mr. Justice Drew classifies socalled fixtures as (1) Chattels which are distinctly furniture as distinguished from improvements and not peculiarly fitted to the property with which they are used; these always remain personalty. (2) Chattels which although physically connected with the real estate, are so affixed as to be removable without destroying or materially injuring the property or the chattels themselves. Such become part of the realty or remain personalty depending on the intention of the parties at the time of the annexation. (3) Chattels which are so annexed that they cannot be removed without material injury to the real estate or to themselves. These are regarded as realty even in face of an expressed intention that they shall be considered personalty.

§(g) 91 

the vendee. If there should be a tenant whose lease does not expire before the settlement a mere assignment of the lease would not satisfy this clause unless the vendee agrees to waive it. If it is desired to take the property subject to an existing lease, it is usually specified as follows: "Possession to given by assignment of lease.” 

When such a clause is present in the agreement the vendor is not required to deliver absolute possession, but only to assign the lease (Goldstein v. Markovitz, 276 Pa. 46—1923).

But where an agreement provided for possession to be given by "existing" lease and after the agreement the lessor permitted his lessee to assign it to another it was held such assigned lease did not satisfy the terms of this provision 

(Goldberg v. Grossman 105 Pa. Super. Ct. 50—1932). 

(h) Apportionment of Taxes, Etc. Interest and Rents. "Taxes, water rent, rent and interest on encumbrance (if any) to be apportioned for the current term at the date of the settlement." 

Unless this clause be inserted, taxes levied before settlement are an encumbrance and as such must be paid by the vendor (Densmore v. Haggerty, 59 Pa. 189—1868; King v. 

Association, 106 Pa. 165-1884). This is the rule throughout the State, but in Philadelphia, by local custom, taxes and water rents, are apportioned without special stipulation 

(Moore v. Taylor, 29 W. N. C. 495-1892; Schermer v. Wil mart, 282 Pa. 55-1925). Good practice, however, requires the insertion of the clause even in Philadelphia, and certainly outside of that city.

As the mode of apportioning taxes, water rent, rent, etc., will be discussed and explained fully hereinafter when we treat with the subject of settlements (See Chapter XIV, Settlements, $205), it will suffice now to say that under this clause, taxes and water rent and interest on mortgages, if any as well as rent (if the property is occupied by tenant) are apportioned to the date of settlement. That is, if the settlement takes place in June and the vendor has already

§45 (i) 

paid his taxes for the whole year, it is, of course, plain that he is entitled to a rebate or a return of six months' taxes, from the vendee. In Philadelphia it has become customary to apportion the rent also, to the date of settlement (Singer v. Solomon, 56 Leg. Int. 315, 8 D.R. 402-1899), although strictly speaking rent does not accrue day by day, but comes into existence the day on which it is due and belongs to the holder of the legal title on the day it is due. It may be necessary outside of Philadelphia and it is good practice even in Philadelphia that it be provided in the agreement that the rent is to be apportioned, as above set forth. 

(i) Kind of Title Agreed on, Time of Performance, etc. 

"The title is to be good and marketable and such as will be insured by any reputable title insurance or trust company of Philadelphia at regular rates. And the said parties hereby bind themselves, their heirs, executors and administrators, for the faithful performance of the above agreement within thirty days from the date hereof, said time to be the essence of this agreement, unless extended by mutual consent in writing endorsed hereon."

As has been said heretofore (see Marketable Title, §9), in order to clear up any question that may arise respecting the title without maintaining an action of law, it is well to insert the above clause, for by it a safe easy test is specified. It should be noted the language here used relieves the vendee upon proof that a single reputable title insurance company refused to insure (LaTorre v. Edelsman, 22 D.R. 845-1913; 

Srolovitz v. Margulis, 35 Pa. Super. Ct. 252-1908). But when the agreement of sale reads the title shall be "such as will be insurable at regular rates by title insurance companies", such provision will not justify the purchaser from refusing to take a deed for the land because a single title insurance company refused to insure the land (Perkinpine v. 

Hogan, 47 Pa. Super. Ct., 27—1911).

To justify a refusal to take title on the ground that it was not insurable, it is not enough to show that objections were raised on the settlement certificate when first issued by the company, for experience shows that a vendor if given the

§(i) 93 

opportunity can frequently have objections removed by explaining them or otherwise satisfying the doubt raised by the title company. It must be shown that at the time of the settlement the title was not insurable and that the vendor had been given the opportunity to satisfy the company's objection. Thus where a vendee did not furnish a copy of the settlement certificate and notify a vendor of the objections raised therein until the day before the settlement, notwithstanding he had received duplicate settlement certificates from the title company a long time before it was held, he was not allowed to recover his deposit money upon the mere proof of the objections (Groskin v. Knight, Jr., 290 Pa. 274-1927; 

Riling v. Idell, 291 Pa. 472).

In sections of the State where there are no title companies the clause need only read, "The title is to be good and marketable, etc." and the test then is as set forth hereinbefore in the paragraph on Marketable Title (§9) viz. that any title which exposes the holder thereof to the hazard of a law suit, is not marketable. Where the agreement of sale provided that the title shall be made "clear and satisfactory to the purchaser" within a period of time named, a failure to so satisfy the vendor within the time fixed, was held to be good ground for recision of the contract by the vendor (Meyers v. 

Catawissa Coal Co., 219 Pa. 1-1907).

As an agreement of sale is a contract, like any other contract it might end on the death of a party, hence the necessity for that part of the clause which specifies that the parties bind themselves, their heirs, executors and administrators to the faithful performance of the agreement. This prevents any argument that a particular agreement was so far personal as to be performed only during the life of either party. 

Performance. Time of the Essence Clause. 

The last clause of this portion of the agreement which binds "the parties to the performance of the agreement within thirty days ** said time to be of the essence of this agreement unless extended by mutual consent in writing

§45 (i) 

endorsed hereon", is of great importance. This because when no time is fixed for performance it will be presumed to be performed within a reasonable time (Frechie v. Boyd, 100 

Pa. Super. Ct. 553-1930). What is a reasonable time may vary under the circumstances and almost certainly result in litigation. But even when time is specified, it is not of the "essence" of a contract to convey real estate unless expressly made so (Fenimore v. Howard, 29 D.R. 177-1920). Therefore not only should the time for the performance be fixed but it should be declared to be of the "essence" of the agreement, for without the phrase italicized above, the law would not regard the failure to perform by the day fixed as so material a departure from the terms of the contract as to justify rescission by the other party, since delay may be fully compensated by the payment of interest (Morrel v. Broadbent, 291 Pa. 503-1928). The great significance of the "time of the essence clause" was brought to the attention of the profession by the case of Doughty v. Cooney, (266 Pa. 3371920), where a vendee after he had let the time of settlement go by, sought to compel the vendor to convey. The vendor's defense that the purchaser had not performed within the time fixed which by the express language of the contract was made of the "essence" was upheld (See also Moser v. Jacob Brown 

B. & L. Ass'n., 320 Pa. 371-1936). And where an agreement for the sale of real estate makes time of settlement "of the essence of the contract" it remains so even though the time is extended to a later definite date (Mansfield v. Redding, 269 Pa. 357-1921; Wasserman v. Steinman, 304 Pa. 1501931).

Extension of Time for Performance. 

Whether or not the requirement that "the extension of the time of settlement must be made in writing," precludes oral extensions is at present a question of doubt. Piancentino v. 

Young, (272 Pa. 556-1922) indicates that the right to demand strict compliance may be waived by the conduct of the parties. Wasserman v. Steinman, (304 Pa. 154–1931),

§45A 



points to the contrary and strongly intimates that a provision precluding an oral extension cannot be waived by parol but does not expressly decide that question because a waiver was there not sufficiently pleaded. Upon principle it would seem that the parties having once solemnly engaged that no extension should be made except in the manner prescribed, the courts ought not to allow the protection which the parties thought they had achieved, to be frittered away by the doctrine of waiver, thereby opening the door to oral testimony by which a new contract can be substituted for that which the parties had made and which the statute of frauds ordains must be in writing.

If the last day fixed for settlement falls on a Sunday, that day being "dies non" carries the time for performance over to the next day (Troopin v. Cohen, 85 Pa. Super. Ct. 1-1925). 

45-A. Fiduciary Agreements of Sale.

An agreement of sale with a fiduciary who is subject to the supervision of the Orphans' Court as, e.g., an executor or trustee, must be regarded as conditional because the Supreme Court has declared it to be the duty of such fiduciary even after the agreement of sale has been executed to accept a substantially higher offer if made before actual settlement. (Orr's Estate, 283 Pa. 476-1925). This rule applies as well to agreements made under testamentary power as to sales requiring formal application for confirmation by the Orphans' 

Court (McCullough's Estate, 292 Pa. 177-1928). One dealing with a person known to be a fiduciary is held bound by the knowledge of this limtation on the fiduciary's power to contract. (Clark v. Provident Trust Co. 329 Pa. 421-426— 

1938). So there can be no recovery by the disappointed purchaser for the loss of his bargain (Kargiatly v. Provident 

Trust Co., 338 Pa. 358-1940). For this reason it has been suggested that as a matter of fair dealing, information, as well as avoidance of fruitless litigation, that in drawing an agreement of sale where a fiduciary is selling, there should be

$46 

incorporated in the agreement a clause substantially as follows: "Inasmuch as the vendor is acting in a fiduciary capacity, vendor shall have the option at his election to rescind this agreement and return the deposit money without interest if, prior to settlement, vendor shall receive an offer for said property at a higher price or on more favorable terms, and upon the return of the deposit money without interest, as aforesaid, vendor shall be under no further liability to the vendee."1 

46. Execution of Agreement of Sale; Signature by Agent. 

An agreement of sale should be executed, that is, signed by both parties or their agents. But when executed by an agent, of the vendor, such agent must be authorized in writing to do so, otherwise the agreement is not binding on his principal (Parrish v. Koons, 1 Pars. 79—1844), unless his principal subsequently in writing ratifies this act of the agent (Llewellyn v. Sunnyside Coal Co. 242 Pa. 517-1914; Moll v. Dickson, 129 Pa. Super. Ct. 383-1937). A principal may likewise ratify by signing and delivering a deed (Mahon et al. v. Buckley, 24 D.R. 735-1915). This point is an important one and should be kept in mind by all real estate agents and brokers, that they cannot execute a binding agreement of sale nor a lease over three years unless they have authority in writing so to do. Only the authority of the agent for the vendor need be in writing; the authority of the agent for the purchaser need not be in writing (Levy v. Parkway Baking Co., 331 Pa. 360-1938), it may be oral. (See $43.)

When however a signature is made by direction of a party and in his presence to a contract for sale of land the signature is the signature by the party and not by the agent. No question under the statute of frauds arises in such a case (Fitzpatrick v. Engard et al. 175 Pa. 393-1896). A writing 

1 This suggested clause and desirability of its insertion is the suggestion of 

Robert Brigham, Esq., of the Philadelphia bar. See his comments on the subject in the Legal Intelligencer, November 16, 1940, Page 7.

§46A 



under seal appointing brokers sole and exclusive agents for the sale of real estate does not of itself authorize such agents to execute an agreement for the sale thereof, especially where the right to approve the price and terms is reserved by the owner (Gorsuch v. Berman, 270 Pa. 8-1921). But where a written appointment as agent to sell conferred on the agent the power "to lease, rent or dispose of the real estate in any on such terms as to him seem meet and proper", the agent was held sufficiently authorized to execute a binding lease containing an option to sell (Cardon's Estate, 278 Pa. 153-1923). manner Where a principal accepts the deposit money paid on an agreement of sale procured by his agent, he cannot in an action by the purchaser to rescind the contract because of false representations made by the agent defend on the ground that the misrepresentations were unauthorized (Oldbaum v. 

Mayer, 285 Pa. 260-1926).

Where an agreement for sale of real estate is executed by the purchaser and agent of the owner conditioned upon approval of the owner within a specified time, it is regarded as constituting merely an offer which will ripen into a contract only if accepted by the owner giving his approval in writing (Groskin v. Bookmyer, 310 Pa. 588-1933). 46-A. 

Execution Where Vendors are Married. 

If the vendor be married, care should be taken to have the husband or wife sign, else the spouse who has not signed cannot be compelled to join in the deed (Schwoerdfeger v. 

Kelly, 223 Pa. 631-1909). If she sign, then she may be compelled to execute the deed even though her name does not appear in the body of the agreement of sale (Bailey v. Cooney, 284 Pa. 508-1925). Where a wife has not signed the agreement of sale and the purchaser is willing to waive the signature of the wife who refuses to sign the deed, he may take title from the husband subject to the wife's dower, but without abatement of the purchase price (Corson v. Mulvaney, 49 Pa. 88-1865; Hughes v. Antill, 23 Pa. Super. Ct. 290-

$47 

1903). And where a purchaser is willing to take such title as the husband can give, the refusal of the wife to join in the deed is no defense to an action for specific performance to compel the husband to convey (Stratford v. Lukens, 52 Pa. 

Super. Ct. 355-1913; but see Saler v. Lessy, 76 Super. Ct. 

15-1921). But the converse of this proposition does not follow, that is to say, where a husband has refused to sign an agreement of sale for the wife's property though the agreement is signed by the wife, a deed from her would be ineffective to convey any title, because under the Act of June 8, 1893, P.L. 344, (48 P.S. §31), a conveyance by her without the husband's joinder is prima facie void and not merely voidable at the husband's election (Simons' Estate, 20 Pa. 

Super. Ct. 450, 468–1902). Though she could ratify it on becoming discovert (Jourdan v. Dean, 175 Pa. 599-1896). 

A wife who has signed a contract without joinder of her husband will not be allowed to keep the deposit money if her husband refuses to execute the deed (McCoy v. Niblick, 228 

Pa. 342-1910); nor have any affirmative relief where she endeavors to take advantage of her position (Irvin v. Blacka, 305 Pa. 191-1931). Where the title is in both husband and wife as tenants by entireties neither spouse can sell or convey the property without the consent of the other (Newhard v. 

Newhard, 303 Pa. 299, 301-1931). Of course an agreement of sale containing the signature of but one spouse where title is so held is therefore wholly ineffective. 

It must also be remembered that an agent who signs for both husband and wife must have written authority to do so, executed by both. 

47. Acknowledgment of Agreements of Sale: Recording. 

Prior to the Act of April 4, 1901, P.L. 67, (21 P.S. 82) to enforce an agreement of sale against a married woman it was necessary for her not only to sign but to acknowledge it separate and apart from her husband in accordance with the 

Act of Feb. 24, 1770 (1 Sm. L. 307, §2, 21 P.S. 82 note; See 

Bingler v. Bowman, 194 Pa. 210-1899). Though the Su-

$99 

perior Court in Saler v. Lessy, (76 Pa. Super. Ct. 15, 18, 1921) intimated to the contrary, the Supreme Court in Bailey v. Cooney, (284 Pa. 508-1925) has definitely settled that such acknowledgment is no longer necessary. 

It is not necessary therefore for an agreement of sale to be acknowledged by any of the parties before a notary public and is rarely done, although it has this very important advantage which is overlooked by many real estate agents and brokers, to wit, when acknowledged it may be recorded. An agreement of sale may, under the recording acts, if properly acknowledged by the vendor, be recorded (Gans v. Drum, 24 

Pa. C. C. 481-1900). By recording an agreement constructive notice is given to the world of the agreement to sell and should the vendor thereafter refuse to carry out his agreement and deliver a deed, the vendee's agreement becomes a cloud on the title which prevents the vendor from selling to any one else; thus practically enabling the vendee to compel the vendor to keep his agreement, without commencing action at law. However an agreement executed and acknowledged by a vendor's agent must be accompanied by a power of attorney showing the agent's authority to sign, otherwise it will not be accepted by the recorder of deeds for record. 

48. Legal Effect of Agreement of Sale. 

The moment an agreement of sale is signed it has the effect of vesting in the vendee what is known as an equitable title to the land. As was said in Kerr v. Day, (14 Pa. 112-1850), "when an agreement is made for the sale of an estate, the vendor is considered as a trustee for the purchaser of the estate sold, and the purchaser as a trustee of the purchase money, for the vendor." So it is that the vendee has a right to go to a court of equity to enforce the terms if violated by the vendor and compel the execution of a deed to him (Borie v. Satterthwaite, 180 Pa. 542-1897). The vendor has a similar right to so enforce his equitable title to the purchase money (Hess v. Vinton Colliery Co., 255 Pa. 78-1917), though the vendee may waive this right and sue for damages

$48 

in a court of law (See $45c). So also it follows that when an option is exercised, the optionee's interest is deemed real estate from the date of the option (Kelly's Estate 6 

Many are the consequences which follow this interpretation of an agreement of sale. Thus in Leafgreen v. Drakes 

Excrs., (300 Pa. 369-1930), it is pointed out, that the result in equity of a contract of sale of land is, that the land sold becomes the property of the purchaser, and the purchase money the property of the vendor, whence it follows that the purchaser is entitled to the rents of the estate from the time fixed for the completion of the transaction and the vendor is entitled to interest on the purchase money from the same time. The estate and the money are mutually exclusive and neither party can at the same time be entitled to both. Another consequence of this principle is illustrated by the case of Spratt v. Greenfield, (279 Pa. 437-1924), where it was held that the vendee must bear any loss by fire occasioned to the property occurring after execution of the contract and before delivery of the deed because unless provided to the contrary, the purchaser to all intents and purposes becomes the owner of the land, the vendor retaining title merely as trustee to secure the payment of the unpaid purchase money. 

The same case holds that though in such a case the vendee may have a right to demand that insurance money be transferred to him when collected, if he fails to demand such an assignment he cannot allege a neglect to make such assignment a ground for refusing to carry out the contract to purchase the real estate.

It follows also from this doctrine that after the agreement of sale is executed, the interest in real estate so under contract, descends as real estate at the purchaser's death (Longwell v. Bentley, 23 Pa. 99, 103-1854; Kelly's Estate 6 D. & C. 

770-1925), and a judgment against such purchaser binds the interest and can be seized and sold by the Sheriff (Auwerter v. Mathiot, 9 S. & R. 397-1823). A judgment entered against the purchaser after the agreement of sale is signed and before

§48A 

101 

the deed is delivered takes precedence over other liens which arise after the delivery of the deed (Stephen's Appeal, 8 

W. & S. 186-1884; Guthrie v. Watson 33 L. I. 444)—And this, even though the agreement is not recorded. But not over purchase money mortgages given for the property under contract (Brumbach v. Pearson 13 D. & C. 762-1929). Nor is any revival of such a judgment required to continue the lien after the deed is executed because as to it the property when conveyed to the purchaser is not after acquired property (Gordon v. Gordon, 45 Pa. Super. Ct. 95-1911). Conversely it follows also that upon the signing of the agreement of sale the vendor's interest has become personal property to be administered as such upon his death (Foster v. 

Harris, 10 Pa. 457-1849), though he is regarded as still holding the legal title to the real estate as security for the payment of the purchase price (Spratt v. Greenfield, 279 Pa. 

437-1924). A judgment entered against the vendor becomes a lien only to the extent of the unpaid purchase price due the vendor (McMullen v. Wenner, 16 S. & R. 18-1827; 

McCleery v. Stoup, 32 Pa. Super. Ct. 42-1906). If the purchaser defaults, the vendor may enforce his security by bringing ejectment (Thompson v. Carpenter, 4 Pa. 132-1846).

This equitable lien of the vendor ends with the delivery of the deed (Kauffelt v. Bower, 7 S. & R. 64—1821). It has been held however that this doctrine does not extend so far as to render the unpaid purchase money of real estate located outside of Pennsylvania, taxable under our inheritance tax laws, where the property was not conveyed until after the death of the vendor (Paul's Estate, 303 Pa. 330—1931). 

48-A. Assignability of Agreement of Sale. 

An agreement of sale, unless otherwise provided by its terms, is as freely assignable by the vendee as any other contract. When however the vendee agrees to give a purchase money mortgage as part of the consideration, such obligation renders the agreement of sale unassignable unless the vendor agrees to accept the bond and mortgage of the assignee

§49 

(Golden v. Tentzer 92 Pa. Super. Ct. 202-1927). So also it would seem that where a vendee buys subject to an "existing" mortgage, the vendor cannot be compelled to convey to the assignee since he is entitled to have as part consideration the personal indemnity of the vendee with regard to the mortgage that follows a conveyance "under and subject to the 'existing' mortgage". (Dobkin v. Landsberg 273 Pa. 174, 179-1922; and see $54 (g) infra.)

In the Dobkin case, however, it was pointed out that the obligation on the part of one who agrees to purchase a property "under and subject" to an existing mortgage-to indemnify the vendor against personal liability, might arise out of the original agreement of sale itself, and if the liability thus created is not merged in the deed conveying title, it would be a matter of no consequence whether the vendee executed the deed or not. If, therefore, the obligation under the agreement survived the deed, the agreement might be assignable. Whether a particular agreement of sale becomes so merged into the deed made pursuant thereto, as to extinguish every obligation therein was said to be a nice question. The presumption in the absence of fraud or mistake (see infra. 49(a) is that the acceptance of a deed in pursuance of articles of an agreement is satisfaction of all previous covenants but this presumption may be rebutted by clear evidence showing an intention to the contrary. Fineman v. 

Cutler, et ux, 273 Pa. 189–1922; Dobkin v. Landsberg, (supra) but see next §49 (a). 

49. Extinction of Agreement. 

(a) Merger-An agreement of sale may be extinguished first by deed being made and delivered by the vendor to the vendee in which event it is said to be "merged" into the deed. That is the deed supersedes or takes the place of the agreement of sale (Stoever v. Gowen et al., 280 Pa. 424-1924).

The general rule is that the deed executed, delivered and accepted is taken to be the ultimate intent of the parties and prevails over inconsistent provisions of a prior agreement.

$103 

But there is a well recognized exception to this general rule in the case of independent covenants or provisions in agreements of sale not intended to be incorporated in the deed (Caveny v. Curtis 257 Pa. 575, 581-1917; Shawnee Lake 

Assn. v. Uhler 131 Pa. Super. Ct. 146, 152-1938). The presumption of law is that the acceptance of a deed in pursuance of an agreement of sale of land is satisfaction of all previous covenants. This presumption it is true may be rebutted and by parol evidence but the intention to the contrary must be clear and manifest (Dobkin v. Landsberg 273 Pa. 174–1922).

For further consideration of this subject, the reader is referred to the comprehensive review of the cases on the subject by the late former Chief Justice Von Moschizisker in the case last cited. 

(b) Cancellation or Recision by Parties-If the parties to the agreement mutually agree that it be cancelled, abrogated or avoided, this of course extinguishes the agreement of sale. 

The agreement to rescind an agreement of sale need not be in writing but for the sake of safety and convenience of proof it is much better to have it done in writing (McClure v. Jones, 121 Pa. 550-1888). An offer to cancel must be accepted before it is effective (Shamlian v. Waxman 80 Pa. Super. Ct. 73-1922). 

(c) By Vendee for False Representation. 

An agreement of sale may also be rescinded by the purchaser without the consent of the vendor where it was brought about by false representations on the part of the vendor (Zettlemoyer v. Bloch, 329 Pa. 205–1938), or by his agent (Oldbaum v. Mayer, 286 Pa. 260—1926). 

(d) By Right Reserved in The Agreement. 

It may also be cancelled or come to an end by reason of its own terms as where it contains a provision that "if for any reason, including the fault of the seller, settlement is not effected, the buyer shall be entitled to no more than repayment of his deposit money and this agreement shall be

$50 

null and void and surrendered for cancellation" (Pollock v. 

Silon 34 D. & C. 131-1938). 

50. Suggestions in Drawing Agreements of Sale. 

The condition of the property purchased will of course suggest additional clauses which may be inserted for the better protection of either of the parties. The following are some suggestions as to points to observe in drawing agreements of sale: 

1. If the property about to be purchased is not vacant, specify when and how possession is to be given. 

2. If the vendee is to have possession before settlement have him sign a lease containing the usual ejectment clause (see form §256), for the period to the time of settlement. This will protect the vendor in case the settlement is not completed and the vendee refuses to move out. The ejectment clause in a lease provides a speedy method of ejecting a recalcitrant occupant and saves delay and expense of the ordinary proceeding at law. 

3. See that the agreement provides that taxes, water rent and house rent are to be apportioned at the settlement. By local custom (Moore v. Taylor, 29 W. N. C. 495—1892; Schermer v. Wilmart, 282 Pa. 55—1925, and see §45 (h), in Philadelphia, this is always done, but outside of Philadelphia not unless specified. Taxes levied and unpaid are really an encumbrance and must be removed by the grantor unless the agreement provides that they should be apportioned (King v. 

Association, 106 Pa. 165—1884). Rent is held not to accrue day by day but to spring into existence the day it is due, hence, when a month's rent is paid in advance to the grantor he would be entitled to the whole of it even if the settlement be the next day, unless the agreement provides that it is to be apportioned (Singer v. Solomon, 8 D. R. 402-1899, but see 

Johnson v. Smith, 3 P. & W. 496—1832). 

4. It is well to provide also that municipal improvements or work done in or about the property by the city which might

$105 

be a lien on the property, made between the date of the agreement of sale and settlement must be paid for by the vendee, otherwise the vendor would be forced to bear the expense. 

This because it would be an encumbrance which he would be bound to discharge (Summer's Est. 23 D. R. 983–1914). For this suggestion the author is indebted to a prominent member of the bar who related a circumstance in which a rather shrewd vendee, after the purchase of a property, filed a complaint through a third party with the city where premises in question were not under-drained, the city caused the work to be done and at the settlement the vendee maintained that the city claim was an encumbrance which the grantor was bound to remove. 

5. Fixtures attached pass with the freehold. Not the manner of annexation but the intention determines the question whether a given chattel has or has not become a fixture (National Bank of Catasauqua v. North, 160 Pa. 303—1894). It is a vexed question which can and should be avoided in the agreement of sale. Specify therefore in the agreement of sale that all gas fixtures, heater, range, &c are included in the sale. Much litigation can be avoided by taking the little additional time required to enumerate what fixtures, ornamental or otherwise, intended to be included (§45-f). 

6. When purchasing a property occupied by a tenant, examine the property and determine what fixtures the tenant placed in the property and what he claims the right to remove (McKay v. Meyer Co., 44 Pa. Super. Ct. 293-1910). Do this especially where the premises about to be purchased is a store, for great liberality is shown the tenant in the matter of trade fixtures (Lindsay v. Curtis 236 Pa. 229-1912; McClintock &

Irvine Co. v. Aetna Explosives Co. 260 Pa. 191-1918). 

7. See whether the vendor has the property adequately insured and loss payable is extended to vendee; if not, the vendee ought to insure the premises himself from the date of the agreement of sale. This because under the doctrine of 

Kerr v. Day, 14 Pa. 112-1850 (see $48) he has become the

$50 

equitable owner of the property and the loss for its destruction by fire before settlement would fall on him (Spratt v. 

Greenfield, 279 Pa. 437-1924). Sometimes where the unexpired term of a fire policy is of small value the vendor can be induced to throw it in the sale without charge. 

8. There is an advantage in having the agreement of sale acknowledged before a Notary Public by the vendor. If this is done the agreement can be recorded if the vendor refuses to make settlement, thus making it impossible for him to convey a marketable title to anyone else, until the cloud which the recorded agreement puts on his title, has been removed. 

Note however that an acknowledgment by the vendee does not entitle it to be recorded (Gans v. Drum, 24 Pa. C. C. 4811900). (See also suggestion No. 14 for additional advantage of having the agreement acknowledged by the vendor). 

9. Where a vendor is married see that the wife signs the agreement also. But if she has not signed the purchaser can nevertheless elect to take a deed without the joinder of the wife but subject to her rights. A vendor cannot legally refuse to convey on the ground that his wife refuses to sign the deed (Real Estate Co. of Pittsburgh v. Rudolph, 301 Pa. 5021930). If the vendor is a married woman see that the husband joins or the agreement will be unenforceable, (See discussion under §46-A). 

10. While the settled custom in Philadelphia is that the cost of preparation of the deed and conveyancing expenses as well as the cost of insuring title falls on the vendee, in other parts of the state the custom is for the vendor to prepare the deed and pay the conveyancing expenses. (See discussion and cases cited in §204). In many sections of the state title is not usually insured, searches are used instead, and these just as in the case of title insurance are at the expense of the vendee (See $204). If it be desired to change the custom prevailing in the county where the land is located the agreement should specify accordingly.

$107 

11. In absence of any provision in the agreement of sale to the contrary, a vendor must pay for the internal revenue stamps or other documentary stamps required to be affixed to his deed (Schermer v. Wilmart, 282 Pa. 55—1925). 

12. When specifying an insurable title the vendee should insist on the insertion "at regular rates". Otherwise if the title insurance company is willing to insure for a special or additional premium to protect itself against what is conceived to be a possible defect or a cloud on the title, a controversy is bound to arise over whether the vendor or the purchaser should pay the additional premium. By insertion of the suggested phrase the burden of paying any special or additional premium is on the vendor. 

13. If it is intended to have the purchaser assume an existing mortgage as part of the consideration the agreement should expressly so state, as the presumption is, in absence of such provision, that the vendor will discharge any encumbrance against the property out of the consideration mentioned (Schermer v. Wilmart, 282 Pa. 55-1925). 

14. Unless the agreement of sale is recorded, a vendee's right may be extinguished by the vendor conveying title to an innocent purchaser for value who had no notice of the prior agreement of sale. (Filby v. Miller, 25 Pa. 264-1855). This results from the recording acts discussed hereinafter, in Chapter VIII, where the effect of recording instruments is fully considered. If an agreement is not recorded, but the grantee nevertheless has had other notice of the existence of the prior agreement of sale before settling for the property, the grantee takes title subject to the prior agreement of sale, for that is all that the grantor could convey (Dillinger v. 

Ogden, 244 Pa. 20-1914). In addition to actual notice to a subsequent grantee, possession of the property by a vendee under a prior agreement of sale is regarded as the equivalent of notice, because, "it is the duty of a purchaser of real estate to make inquiry respecting the rights of the party in possession, and failing to do so, they are affected with con-

§50A  

structive notice of such facts as would have come to their knowledge in the proper discharge of their duty (Lazarus v. 

Lehigh etc. Coal Co., 246 Pa. 178—1914; see also Stonecipher v. Keane, 268 Pa. 540-1920; Kinch v. Fluke, 311 Pa. 4051933; and see also further discussion under $188 infra.). 

15. When dealing with fiduciaries subject to the control of the Orphans' Court, it should be remembered that they are in duty bound to accept any substantially better offer for the property embraced in an agreement of sale, if made before actual settlement. See the discussion of this subject and form of clause to be incorporated in agreements in such cases, set forth in $45-A this book (supra.).

§50A  

This agreement it will be seen, though somewhat differently worded from that hereinbefore discussed, is substantially the same in effect and covers the main requirements emphasized as important in this Chapter. It contains several new provisions which require a word of comment. (a) It contains a clause protecting the agent from possible personal liability to either purchaser or vendor, for the performance or non-performance of any of the terms of the agreement. This is of course desirable and proper. (b) Formal tender of the deed and tender of the purchase money is waived. This is a most wise provision. The circumstances under which a vendor or a vendee must prepare and tender a deed or offer the purchase money before the contract can be enforced or rescinded, differ according to the remedy sought (see Eberz v. Heisler, 12 Pa. Super. Ct. 3881900), the local custom of the county where the transaction takes place or the land lies (Berman v. Simpson, 12 Del. 

167-1912; Sweitzer v. Hummel, 3 S. & R. 228-1817; Frowert's Estate, 12 Phila. 148-1878; Callaghan v. McCredy, 48

Pa. 463-1865), or whether either of the parties have indicated an intention not to carry out the agreement (Shrut v. 

Huselton, 272 Pa. 113-1922; Martin v. Cybulski, 282 Pa. 

297-1925). This difficulty as well as the danger of having litigation decided upon the technicality of tender, is avoided by the express waiver of the tender by both parties in the Real Estate Board's form. See for general discussion of the importance of the matter of tender as dependent upon the remedy invoked (§45-c supra.). (c) It forbids the recording of the agreement. In this aspect it is only fair to say the Real Estate Board's form is designed primarily for the use of brokers and agents representing the vendor, hence looks principally to the vendor's protection. We have seen (§50, suggestion 14) that a vendee cannot be fully protected except by recording the agreement. 

However, this is as it should be, a vendor who pays the sale's commission is entitled to the primary consideration of his broker and agent and to any advantage the broker can secure

$50A 

for his protection. One representing the vendee however is in a different position and should if fullest protection to the vendee is desired see that the provision in question is stricken out. (d) The approval of the vendor is also provided for and a limited time for such approval fixed. This has the advantage of doing away with the necessity of checking up on the vendor's agent's written authority to sign. It also serves to warn the vendee that the agreement cannot become binding unless approved by the vendor's signature (see discussion of execution by agent in §46 supra.).

DRAWING OF DEEDS. 

Having executed the agreement of sale, the next step to bring about the transfer of title is the preparation and execution of a deed. The instrument known as deed is therefore our next consideration. 

51. What Is A Deed; Seal. 

A deed, technically speaking, is any writing sealed and delivered by the parties (Mitchell on Real Estate and Conveyancing, 402). Because "deeds" are commonly used in conveying title to real estate, it is quite a popular error to suppose that a deed is an instrument limited to that use only.

$115 

DEEDS. 

The distinguishing feature about a deed is that the writing is under seal. The seal imports solemnity. In the early days a wax seal was required and everyone had his own peculiar device or mark for a seal. Nowadays, the old time wax seal has been dispensed with and is no longer required. Any mark placed after the signature of a person intended to be a seal is so considered (Hacker's Appeal 121 Pa. 192-1888).

Usually a seal is now represented by the word (seal) in brackets or the Letters, (L.S.), which letters, it was held in Hazelton Bank v. Kintz, 24 Pa. Super. Ct. 456-1904, may be used to import a seal. In most legal documents it is printed at the end of the line. Anyone signing opposite the printed seal is presumed in law to have adopted the printed seal as his own 

(Lorah v. Nissley, 156 Pa. 329-1893). 

If therefore any instrument in writing under seal is a deed, it follows legally speaking that bonds, leases, mortgages, &c., which are usually under seal are deeds, and therefore to be exact, deeds to convey property should be termed Deeds of Conveyance. The word deed however has been so consistently used, not only by laymen, but even by the bar, that it has come to have a fixed meaning in the minds of the public and we will therefore not hesitate to refer to a deed of conveyance simply as a deed. 

52. Kinds of Deeds. Deed Poll. Indenture. 

That fountain head of legal definitions, Blackstone (2

Blacks. page 296) very clearly explains the difference between a deed poll and an indenture. An indenture is the appropriate name of a deed to which there are two or more parties as distinguished from a deed poll which is made by one person. 

An indenture derives its name from the indentation which once always appeared on a deed made between two or more parties. Formerly deeds between two parties were written as two copies or counterparts on the same sheet of paper or parchment signed by both grantor and grantee; between the two counterparts some words or letters of the alphabet were written. The copies were then separated by a waive like or

$53 

indented line cut through these words or letters. Each party to the deed received one copy. In case of dispute arising as to the authenticity of either of the counterparts they could be fitted together and the question of genuineness definitely settled. From the indented cut came the name indenture and to this day every deed still begins with the words "This Indenture," although now only the grantor signs.

A deed "poll" differed from the old time indenture in that it was not executed in counterpart and its top was "polled", that is to say, shaved or cut straight, not indented. Its present day survival is to be found in Sheriff's deeds which are deeds poll and are customarily so called. Both indentures and deeds poll are deeds of conveyance of property, and as such are to be distinguished from a "quit claim deed." 

A "quit claim deed" is used when a party wishes to sell or release an interest he may think he has in land but does not warrant the title. Its distinguishing characteristic is that it is a conveyance of the interest or title of the grantor in and to the property described rather than the property itself 

(Greek Catholic Congregation etc. v. Plummer, 338 Pa. 3731940). The deeds about to be considered are deeds of conveyances of property. For form of quit claim deed see $247, 248.
