DEEDS. 

There is much inserted in a deed which could easily be omitted and in fact most of the States including Pennsylvania have adopted by statute a short form of deed of which we will treat hereinafter (§57). But there is this to be said in favor of the old form; every clause and word has had years of legal interpretation and has acquired an exact known meaning to the profession. Furthermore short forms vary in different states, but the common law form of deed is universal. 

An examination of the preceding form of deed discloses that it may be divided into three principal parts:- 

1. The Premises which extends from the beginning of the deed to the words, "To have and to hold." 

2. The Habendum Clause, which extends from the words, "To have and to hold" to the words "In witness hereof." 

3. The Conclusion which embraces the rest of the deed. 

These three principal parts of deeds may be subdivided as follows:- Date. 

Names of Parties. 

Consideration.

Granting Clause. 

Premises includes Description. 

Habendum includes 

Exceptions (if any).

Recital. 

Under and Subject Clause (?) Appurtenance Clause. 

To have and to hold Clause. 

Exceptions (if any).

Under and Subject Clause (?) Covenants and Warranty. 

Execution Clause. 

Conclusion includes Receipt. 

Acknowledgment Clause.

$54 

 54. Meaning of Parts. Premises: 

(a) Date. While the date should in all cases be inserted it is not essential to the validity of the deed. Anciently deeds were not dated. But a date inserted saves the party the trouble and expense of proving the actual date should the question ever arise. A date inserted in the deed, however, is not proof absolute that the deed was executed on that date. 

The date can be contradicted, but it is, of course, prima facie evidence of the time of the deed's execution (Finney's Appeal, 59 Pa. 398–1868; Park v. Neely, 90 Pa. 52-1879; Cutter v. Pierson, 26 Pa. Super. Ct. 10, 13—1904). (b) Names of Parties. Following the date comes the names of the parties, their professions and city in which they live. Care should be taken to insert the correct names of the parties and if they have middle initials insert them. In this way may be avoided the possible expense of correcting the deed or establishing identity. It is good practice to insert the profession or trade following the names. It is to be regretted that this old custom has lately fallen in disuse. It had many advantages, chief among them being its aid in fixing the identity of the individual against whom a title search was being made. E.g.: John Smith, Blacksmith, distinguished him from the hosts of other John Smiths appearing of record, in a way that would leave no doubt in the mind of the person making the title search that he was the one sought. Of like advantage is the adding the name of the city and state in which the grantor or grantee resides, and this is usually done. (c) Consideration. 

That the said grantor, Andrew Black, for and in consideration of one ($1.00) Dollar lawful money of the United States unto him well and truly paid by the said grantee at or before the sealing or delivery hereof, the receipt whereof is hereby acknowledged.

At common law a bargain and sale conveyance (such as the form herein set forth), required an expressed consideration

§54(c) 

121 

DEEDS. 

to make it valid. The amount of the consideration was of no moment so long as it was expressed, hence arose the custom of inserting one dollar as a consideration, a form which has persisted to the present day. The nature and origin and purpose of such a consideration, which is called a nominal consideration, is well stated in Dohan v. Yearicks, 253 Pa. 403-1916, as follows: "The expression 'nominal consideration' in a deed is resorted to by conveyancers to avoid the inconvenience of setting forth the real consideration when that is difficult to set forth briefly, or of a private nature, and to comply with a usage that arose because a deed of bargain and sale, under the statute of uses, originally operated to create a resulting trust for the grantor unless supported by a valuable consideration, which it was formerly held must be a pecuniary one. It is well known that the nominal consideration of one dollar is regarded by all as having served its purpose by its mere mention in the instrument and that it almost never changes hands, although as in this case solemnly receipted for.' 

Before documentary stamp taxes based on the amount of actual consideration were imposed, the nominal consideration was much favored by those desiring to keep from the public the purchase price of the property. Since the purchase price can now be fairly closely calculated from the documentary stamps affixed, that advantage no longer exists. Yet the custom of using the nominal consideration still persists though under our Act of May 28, 1715, §5—1 Sm. L. 126, when a deed is once recorded it may be regarded as valid without a con sideration (Eckman v. Eckman, 68 Pa. 460-1871). More over, as the seal itself imports consideration and against it a plea of want of consideration will not be heard (Piper v. 

Queeney, 282 Pa. 135-1925; Conrad's Estate, 333 Pa. 5611938). But a difference is to be noted between "want of consideration" and "failure of consideration." Thus where no consideration was ever intended as e.g. in a deed executed and delivered as a gift or by a trustee to a successor trustee, such a deed cannot be cancelled or set aside merely because

§54(d)  

of "want of consideration". When, however, a valuable consideration was intended to be given but in fact never paid, this is not "want" of consideration but is called "failure of consideration" and in such case the seal does not prevent the grantor from showing the fact that the consideration bargained for was never in fact paid. This is a general rule relating to all sealed instruments and has been recently most satisfactorily reviewed and explained in Conrad's Estate, 333 

Pa. 561-1938, and see Edmunson's Estate, 259 Pa. 429—1918, which holds the consideration expressed in the deed is not conclusive. Thus it follows that the consideration expressed in modern deeds may be contradicted and the real consideration proved (Alexander v. Bush, 46 Pa. 62—1863). 

(d) Granting Clause. 

"Hath granted, bargained and sold, released and confirmed and by these presents doth grant, bargain and sell, release and confirm, unto the said grantee, his heirs and assigns." 

These words are sometimes called the "operative words" and in the printed form of deeds, usually precede the description, but may be inserted anywhere. While these words are always printed in the deed the strict necessity of these words is no longer required, they may be dispensed with, provided words indicating an intention to convey are used (Auman v. 

Auman, 21 Pa. 343-1853). In Pennsylvania the Act of 1909 

(see infra $58, Act of April 1, 1909, P.L. 91, §2, 3, 21 P.S. 2, 3) provides that the words "grant and convey," or either one of them, shall import, "grant, bargain and sell, release and confirm," etc. The Act of May 28, 1715, §6, 1 Sm. L. 94 (21 

P.S. 8) provides that "the words grant, bargain and sell be adjudged to express a covenant to the grantee, his heirs and assigns, that the grantor was seized of an indefeasible estate in fee simple, freed from incumbrances done or suffered from the grantor, as also quiet enjoyment against the grantor and his heirs, unless limited by express words contained in such deed." Thus where land subject to unpaid taxes was conveyed by deed containing the words "grant, bargain and

§54(d) 123 

DEEDS. 

sell", a breach of covenant of warranty was held to occur immediately upon delivery of the deed, inasmuch as the lien of taxes is an incumbrance within the meaning of the above act (Taylor v. Allen, 60 Pa. Super. Ct. 503—1915). 

Words "Heirs" Important.-The last three words, "his heirs and assigns" are known as words of limitation because they limit or denote the quantity of the estate intended to be conveyed. To pass a fee simple estate the word heirs is essential, and at common law without the addition of such word the grantee took but a life estate (Brown v. Mattocks, 103 Pa. 16-1883; Klingler v. Wick, 266 Pa. 1-1920). These words when not printed in the deed form must be added by the conveyancer. If the grantee is an individual the apt words are "his heirs and assigns". If a corporation the apt words are its successors and assigns. The word assigns, while usually added, is superlative. The word heirs is the important word. The word "heirs" ought, therefore, as a matter of good practice, be always inserted, although since the Act of 1909 ($58 infra.) it is no longer necessary where the words "grant and convey" are used or the intent to convey a fee simple title is otherwise clear (Hess v. Jones 

335 Pa. 569-1939). But even before this act there were five instances as set forth by Fallon (Conveyancing in Pennsylvania, Fallon, 155) in which the word heirs might be dispensed with. (1) In executory contracts or agreements for the sale of land, inasmuch as they are regarded as conveyances in equity, which will permit the passing of a fee upon payment of the consideration, without words of inheritance. (2) A conveyance to a corporation does not require the words "successors and assigns", as it is supposed to have perpetual existence.¹ (3) A fee simple may be created by reference to another instrument in which the necessary words are used, by an 1 Although not all corporations are perpetual, some corporations may limit themselves by their Charter to a term of years. Better use the words successors and assigns, even though superlative.

§54(e)  

indorsement granting "all right, title and interest in the within deed," indicating an intention to pass a fee. (4) A sale by an officer of the law under an order of court may operate to pass an estate in fee without the use of the word "heirs". This is especially so in the case of a sheriff's sale. (5) A conveyance to a trustee which requires the vesting of a fee in the trustee in order to carry out the trust does not require words of inheritance. 

(e) Description. 

"All that certain lot or piece of ground with the messuage or tenement thereon erected, situate on the west side of Y Street at the distance of three hundred and thirty-seven (337') feet northward from the north side of X Street in the Fiftieth Ward of the City of Philadelphia, containing in front or breadth on said Y Street eighteen (18') feet and extending of that width in length or depth westward between two parallel lines at right angles with said X Street one hundred (100') feet to a certain three feet wide alley extending north from X Street to Z Street." 

This part of the deed is called the description and is, of course, to be inserted into the deed by the conveyancer. The object of the description in a deed is to identify the land to be conveyed, and no deed will be operative which does not contain a description sufficient for such identification (Negley v. Lindsay, 67 Pa. 217-225-1870). The description, while it must be clear, need not necessarily be technically accurate, but must be sufficiently precise to enable the surveyor to locate it. Should the deed contain a reference to some other paper which describes the property it will be sufficient (Armstrong v. Boyd, 3 P. & W. 458-1832). For this reason the recital is always placed in a deed. The reference therein to the prior deed insures against any possible mistake in the description. A reference to a survey by a surveyor named but containing no reference to any plan of lots whatever was held not sufficient to impart into the deed a plan of lots containing the name of the survey or mentioned in the deed (Stoever v. Gowen 280 Pa. 424-425-1924).

§54(e)125 

DEEDS. 

(e)1 Description bounded by street or road. 

A conveyance of land bounded by a road or street gives the grantee title of the soil to the middle of the road or street if the grantor owned thereto, but subject of course to the easement of public use of the surface thereof. Such ownership extends from the heavens above to the center of the earth beneath and gives to the owner the right to make any use thereof which does not interfere with the easement of passage. (Stuart v. Gimbel Bros., 285 Pa. 102-1926). So in absence of title papers showing a contrary restriction, the presumption is that a lot bounded by a street extends to the middle thereof and it is the burden of the person asserting the contrary to overcome this presumption (Socket v. Norris town Transit Co., 62 Pa. Super. Ct. 542-1916). In Paul v. 

Carver, 26 Pa. 223—1856, it was held that it would require an express exception in the deed, or some clear unequivocal declaration or certain and immemorial usage to limit the title of the grantee to the edge of the street, and this is so although the measurement of the distance set forth in the conveyance brings the line only to the side of the street, for that fact alone is not sufficient to control the rule of law which carries title to the center of it. 

The same rule prevails where the boundary is a private alley (Saccone v. West End Trust Co., 224 Pa. 554—1909; 

Oliver v. Ormsby, 224 Pa. 564-1909). But where a grantor conveyed to and including an alley it was held that the grantee took title to the soil of the whole alley (Wilson v. Peerless Co., 240 Pa. 473-1913).

The rule is also the same where the description calls for a non-navigable stream, as a boundary, in which case the conveyance carries the title of the grantee to the center of the stream (Leaf v. Pennsylvania Co., 268 Pa. 579-1920). The rule is different however as to navigable streams; these belong to the Commonwealth, and a grantor takes title only to the low water mark thereof (id.). Whether a given stream is navigable or not depends on the fact of it being capable of navigation and not upon any act of assembly so declaring

§54(e)2 

it (Commonwealth v. Foster, 36 Pa. Super. Ct. 433—1908).

Those desiring to pursue further the rights of riparian owners in navigable and non-navigable streams will find the cases reviewed in two opinions by the Pennsylvania Department of 

Justice in re "Public Service Lines Across Rivers", 24 D. & 

C. 332–1935 and "Fishing Rights in Pennsylvania Streams" published in the Pennsylvania Angler, September, 1925. See also §25D. 

Description Designating Unopened Street. Another conse quence of designating a street or alley, as a boundary, is illustrated by the case of Maier et al. v. Walborn et al. 84 Pa. 

Super. Ct. 522-1925, where it was said "The designation of a street as a boundary in a conveyance of land, whether opened or not, if it be on ground of the grantor, is an implied covenant by the grantor that it shall be open for the use of the grantee as a public way, and is also a dedication of the street to public use."

Distances. Adjoinders. 

Outside of the municipalities it is customary to convey lands by description of a survey made thereof as follows: 

"ALL THAT CERTAIN messuage or tract of land being and lying in

Erdley, North Thirty and one-fourth degrees, East forty-three and eight-tenth perches to a stone; thence South Eighty and three-fourth degrees West Ten perches and four-tenths to a stone; thence North Ten and one-fourth degrees, West Seventy-three perches and two-tenths to a stone adjoining land of Philip Gemberling, Jr., of the said Township of Penns, thence North Seventy-nine and three-fourth degrees, East One hundred seventy-two perches and seven-tenths to a stone on the line of other land of said Philip Gemberling, Deceased; thence South Fifteen degrees West One hundred ninety-seven perches to the line stone at the place of beginning. CONTAINING 130 acres and 118 perches neat measure, be the same more or less."'

§54(e)127 

DEEDS. 

It will be noted that these descriptions usually check the land conveyed in three ways. (1) By courses and distances, (2) by monuments, and (3) by adjoining lands. This custom has resulted in many decisions which lay down rules of construction where a conflict arises.

Monuments. Where there is a conflict between the courses and distances and permanent monuments such as a "run", a creek, or a township road, the courses and distances must give way to the monuments (Donaldson v. Fellabaum, 68 Pa. 

Super. Ct. 348-1917). This rule being termed in Pringle v. 

Rogers, (193 Pa. 94, 98-1899), to be a very ancient one, and so recognized as early as Hall v. Powel, (4 S. & R. 456-1818); see also Over v. Lindsay, (255 Pa. 283-1916). So where a purchaser who had an opportunity to see the visible boundaries on the ground and to measure the property, accepts a deed and takes possession, he cannot thereafter refuse to pay the full amount of the purchase money because the quantity of the land was less than he bargained for (Smith v. Donahue, 60 Pa. Super. Ct. 424-1915). A mere stake or post in the ground long since gone, is not such a monument as is con trolling (Allison v. Oligher et al. 141 Pa. Super. Ct. 201—1940). 

But the rule that monuments are of the highest value cannot prevail where there is uncertainty concerning the location of the monument itself, where the monuments are doubtful, resort will be had to courses and distances (Post v. Wilkes- 

Barre Connecting R.R. Co., 286 Pa. 273–1926). Nor where maps, plats or field notes are referred to in the description, these are under such circumstances regarded as incorporated into the description and stand on equal footing with monuments (Harper v. Coleman, 94 Pa. Super. Ct. 62-1928). The rule has been termed to be one of necessity adopted to ascertain the expressed intention of the parties (Fleming v. Klein, 100 Pa. Super. Ct. 40—1930).

Adjoinders. Where a tract of ground is described by calls for adjoinders as well as by courses and distances, and there is a discrepancy between these and the "calls", the grantee

§54(f)  

takes title to all the land within the "calls" (Myer v. 

291 Pa. 145-1927). Curry,

Quantity, is generally regarded as the least certain and yields to other description (Large v. Penn 6 S. & R. 488—1821). 

A description of the property by courses and distances prevails over quantity (Bosler v. Sun Oil Co., 325 Pa. 411—1937).

So also the calls for adjoinders also take precedence over a recital of the quantity of the land conveyed (Miller v. Cramer, 190 Pa. 315-1899), and this is especially so where the acreage recited is followed by the words "more or less" (Dawson v. 

Coulter, 262 Pa. 566-1919). But here again it should be noted that where the actual location of a boundary is in doubt and the writing contains no words to definitely fix the line by either metes and bounds or monuments on the ground, evidence of the acreage becomes a material factor in the determination of the intention of the parties (id). In such case even the words "more or less" are only regarded as words of safety and precaution intended to cover some slight or unintentional inaccuracy (Marino v. Moffa, 68 Pa. Super. Ct. 621-1918). 

(f) The Recital. 

"Being the same premises which Edward France and wife by indenture bearing date the fifth day of July, A.D. 1906, and recorded in the office for the recording of deeds in and for the City and County of Philadelphia in Deed Book W. S. V. 1196, page 213, etc., granted and conveyed unto Andrew Black in fee."

This clause, known as the recital, is not a necessary part of the deed, although it is of value in indicating the source and chain of the title as well as aiding in identifying the land described. It ought, therefore, always be inserted in the deed. Its usual place is immediately following the description. Anything recited in the recital as intended to be done is treated in law thereafter as being done (Penn v. Preston, 2 Rawle 14-1829; Waslee v. Rossman, 231 Pa. 219-1911).

Where the recital and operative part of the deed conflict the operative part prevails if certain and definite (Ontelaunee

$54(g) 129 

DEEDS. 

Orchard's Inc. v. Rothermel 139 Pa. Super. Ct. 44-1939). 

If indefinite the recital may be used to explain it. But recitals in deeds are also to be considered in determining the true intent and meaning of the parties and will restrict general words to a narrower meaning if the intent is clear 

(Penna. Horticultural Society v. Craig, 240 Pa. 137—1913). 

But it cannot be interpreted so as to operate to incorporate into a deed, conveying a lot, a separate and distinct, though adjoining lot the grantors had not included in the description, nor a part of the lot described (Fidelity Mortgage Guarantee Co. v. Bobb et ux, 306 Pa. 411, 418—1932). 

(1) Effect of Recital as to Third Persons. 

The general rule is that recitals in deeds are mere heresay and inadmissible as against third persons who claim by para mount title. (Dougherty v. Welshans 233 Pa. 121-1911.) 

But there is an exception to the rule in the case of ancient deeds accompanied by possession, which are admissible as prima facie evidence of the facts recited even as against third persons (Brock v. Atlantic Refining Co. 273 Pa. 76–1922). 

(g) Encumbrance Clause. Under and Subject. Restric tions. "Under and subject nevertheless to the payment of a certain mortgage debt or principal sum of thirty-five hundred ($3500.00) Dollars with interest thereon as the same may become due and payable.' 

This under and subject clause may be placed either in the premises immediately following the recital or in the habendum, immediately after the "to have and to hold clause". In the deed form set forth on page 116 we have placed it in the premises and referred to it again in the habendum, which is quite a common method.¹

Since the Act of 1878 however, the grantee cannot be held personally liable to the mortgagee for the payment of the mortgage principal unless "he shall by agreement in writing have expressly assumed a personal liability therefor or there shall be express words in the deed of conveyance stating that the grant is made on condition of the grantee assuming personal liability; provided that the use of the words under and subject to the payment of such ground rent, mortgage or other encumbrance shall not alone be construed as to make such grantee personally liable as aforesaid."

Though the Act of June 12, 1878, P.L. 205, §12, (21 P.S.

In Britton v. Roth, 313 Pa. 352, 356—1933, the Supreme

Court summarizes the present law governing the liability of a grantee to pay a mortgage on land of which he accepts conveyance under and subject thereto, as follows: "The grantee of mortgaged premises takes them with a contingent liability to reimburse his grantor for any loss arising through nonpayment of the mortgage debt where the deed recites that the conveyance is "under and subject" to the mortgage on the property. 

May's Estate, 218 Pa., 64-1907; Lowry v. Hensal, 281 Pa. 5721924. A fortiori, the liability of the grantee to his grantor is no less where the grantee personally assumes and agrees to pay the mortgage. In the latter situation, however, the liability of the grantee also extends to the mortgagee who may recover the mortgage debt upon default by an action in the name of the grantor to the use of the mortgagee. Blood v. Crew Levick Co., 177 Pa. 606-1896. Since the Act of June 12, 1878, P.L. 205, no personal liability exists in the grantee to the mortgagee unless the deed contains express words stating the grant is made on the condition of the grantee assuming personal liability or unless the mortgage is personally assumed by an agreement in writing. The act did not affect the rights of the parties as between grantor and his grantee. Lennox v. Brower, 160 

Pa. 191-1894, May's Estate, Supra.' 

It should be noted, however, that such liability of a grantee to his grantor is predicated upon actual payment¹ in good faith by the grantor in relief of the mortgaged debt, (Britton v. Roth supra.; Faulkner v. McHenry 235 Pa. 298-1912), though payment need not be in cash, see Borowsky v. 

Margulis, 310 Pa. 420-1933, where the grantor paid the mortgagee by giving him a new bond and mortgage on a different property not covered by the conveyance, which bond and mortgage was accepted in good faith by the mortgage creditor as full payment and satisfaction.

Ruzyc v. Brown, 327 Pa. 61–1937.

In a suit by a grantor for reimbursement for the amount paid on a mortgage which the grantee took "under and subject" to, it is no defence by a grantee to say that he took title merely as "Strawman" or nominee of the real purchaser (Dintenfass v. Greenberg, 318 Pa. 20—1935).

The purchaser at a sheriff's sale on a second mortgage does not, however, by his purchase from the sheriff become an indemnitor against an existing undischarged first mortgage, for all that he purchases is the defendant's equity in the property being sold. (Ryon Est. 318 Pa. 171-1935; Fair

How Liability May be Avoided. While an owner who has taken title from a "strawman" cannot be sued by the Strawman's grantor (O'Donnell v. Neely, 66 Pa. Super. Ct. 351-354 -1917) it is obvious from these decisions, that even purchasing a property by having a so-called "strawman" execute the bond and mortgage (See §81 B, infra.), affords no protection, for if the "strawman" should become a real man as he did in Aronson v. Heymann 56 Pa. Super. Ct. 501-1914. the liability for the mortgage sought to be avoided may, nevertheless remain. The only way to safeguard against such a possibility is for the grantee when taking title to take from the grantor also, a separate release in writing of any

Such a release could be included in the deed itself and in fact would be better practice since separate writings unless recorded are liable to be lost. The following, or words of similar character, would cover the situation. "Under and subject nevertheless to the payment of a certain mortgage debt or principal sum of thirty-five hundred dollars ($3500) with interest thereon as the same may become due and payable. But it is expressly agreed that the grantee herein shall not be held liable to indemnify or reimburse the grantor for any loss which the grantor may sustain by being required to pay the mortgagee or his successors in interest or to his (grantors') predecessor in title in satisfaction of the debt for which said mortgage was given and that any such liability which may arise by operation of law is hereby expressly released." (g)2 Restrictions. Form of.

Of course, should there be no mortgage to take under and subject to the clause is omitted unless there be certain building restrictions, in which case the clause would read: "Under and subject nevertheless to certain express conditions and restrictions as appear of record in Deed Book W. M. G. 322, Page 

34, etc."

This is the usual method of drawing this clause, although the far better practice is to actually recite the restrictions if not too bulky, e.g. "Under and subject nevertheless to the express conditions and restrictions that said premises shall not at any time hereafter be used as an Undertaking Establishment, nor for the manufacture, bottling or sale of malt, vinous or spirituous liquors nor for the carrying on of any business requiring the use of machinery run otherwise than by human power, and that the porches upon said structure erected on the said lot shall be maintained free of any enclosure or obstruction which might prevent the free and common enjoyment of air, light and view by all of the owners, tenants and occupiers of structures upon any of the lots which may front on the said Y Street between X Street and Z Street.' 

The owner of a tract of land divided into lots, sometimes imposes restrictions on some of the lots as sold. Such re-

§54(g)3 

strictions are not to be defeated merely because similar restrictions are not imposed on the rest of the lots. (Neff v. 

Gorman, 303 Pa. 186-1931). But where it is shown that the restrictions imposed in conveyances of part of a tract which were intended to be applicable to all of the land under a general scheme of development, the restrictions imposed on the part conveyed may, nevertheless, be held to apply equally to the rest. (Neff v. Gorman, supra. citing Ladner v. Siegel, 294 Pa. 360–366—1928 and see Finley v. Glenn, 303 Pa. 1311931.) 

(g)3 Rules Governing Restrictions. 

While it is not the province of a book on conveyancing to go into the subject of the nature, character and enforceability of restrictions very exhaustively, still the mention of a few cardinal rules of construction will be helpful to the conveyancer or lawyer called upon to draft restrictions. 

First, it should be noted that the language of a restriction must be so clear as to raise no doubt of its meaning, this because of the settled rule of law that "restraining covenants are strictly construed against persons seeking to enforce them, and all doubts resolved in favor of natural rights and the privileges of the owner to exercise untrammelled control of his own land; nothing will be regarded as a violation of a restriction that is not in plain disregard of its express words." (Henry v. Eves, 306 Pa. 250-1932.) Because of this principle a motion picture theatre was held not to violate a restriction against any building for "offensive occupation" (Burk v. Kahn, 22 D.R. 691-692-1913). Nor was a liquor license regarded as an "offensive occupation" (Dennis v. 

Burke & Beirn, 26 D.R. 535—1917). Though where the sale or manufacture of intoxicating liquors is expressly forbidden by the deed, such prohibiting was held both legal and enforceable (Cheris Liquor License Case, 127 Pa. Super. Ct. 

355-1937). So where a restriction limited the owner to one dwelling house upon a lot, the erection of a "duplex apartment" being merely one building was held not to be a viola-

§54(g)135 

DEEDS. 

tion of the restriction. The court holding that since the restrictions are not to be extended by implication, the test was whether the building was a single structure and not whether it was intended to house more than one family (Rohrer v. Trafford, R. E. Co., 259 Pa. 297-1918). A "dwelling house in the sense which it is ordinarily used means a house occupied as a residence in distinction from a store, office or other building, therefore a restriction forbidding the erection of buildings other than dwellings is not violated by the erection of apartment houses or housekeeping flats (Johnson v. Jones 244 Pa. 386–1914). On the other hand, where in clear language the restriction forbade the use of land for any other purpose than a private dwelling house an apartment house was held to be a violation of the prohibition (Taylor v. Lambert, 279 Pa. 514-1924). So also a clause which provided that lots "shall be used only for the erection and maintenance thereon of buildings for 'cottage' residences" etc. this was held to exclude apartments (Pocono 

Manor Assn. v. Allen 337 Pa. 442–1940).

Second, note that restrictions are of two kinds, those inserted for the personal benefit or protection of the grantor only, and those intended for the protection of others in the neighborhood and the grantor's successors in title. The latter class of restrictions are called "covenants running with the land". The first class are enforceable only by the grantor, the others continue indefinitely, not only for the grantor's benefit but for his heirs and successors in title, and frequently for the benefit of adjoining lot owners as well (Wimer v. Yellin, 286 Pa. 33-1926). The test in determining whether a particular covenant runs with the land is the intention of the parties, and to ascertain such intent, resort may be had to the words of the covenant read in the light of the surroundings of the parties and the subject of the grant (DeSanno v. Earle, 273 Pa. 265-1922). A conveyancer can set this question at rest by providing in the restriction the following:

§54(g)3 

"And the grantee for himself, his heirs and assigns, agrees to and with the grantor, his heirs and assigns, that said restrictions and conditions shall be covenants running with the land and that in any deed of conveyance of said premises or any part thereof, to any person or persons, said restrictions or conditions shall be incorporated in such deed or deeds of conveyance as full as the same are contained in this indenture.”

Third; while restrictions not limited as to time are strictly speaking considered perpetual, yet since a court in equity may refuse to enforce them when they become obsolete or cease to be of any advantage to those for whose benefit they were imposed, they may become ineffective due to "the resistless evolution of time" (Henry v. Eves, 306 Pa. 250, 255—1932). 

Fourth; Finally, care should be taken in ascertaining how the restriction is to operate. If the restriction prohibits merely the erection of a certain type of building as, e.g., a store, then a building which conforms to the restrictions may nevertheless be used as a store because a restriction against erection is not the same as a restriction against the use. 

Thus in Hoffman v. Parker, 239 Pa. 398—1913, a restriction prohibiting the erection of any building other than dwellings did not prevent the use of a dwelling as a store for the sale of food stuffs where the exterior of the building remained unaltered. Conversely if a restriction is only against the use of a building for a certain purpose but not against the erection, the construction of a building cannot be enjoined even though the use for which it is designed may be prohibited (Peniman v. Hoffman et al. 262 Pa. 100-1918). To guard against such situations¹ the restrictions should be couched in language substantially as follows: "UNDER AND SUBJECT nevertheless, that the hereby granted lot or piece of ground and the building now thereon erected and any which may hereafter be erected, shall be and remain subject to the following conditions and restrictions: 

1. That no building on said lot, or any hereafter erected, shall be erected for or used or occupied as a public garage, manufacturing 1 For a recent case where the restriction was held broad enough to prohibit both erection and use see Pocono Manor Assn. v. Allen, 337 Pa. 442-1940.

$(h) 137 

DEEDS. 

establishment or for any offensive or malodorous occupation, or be used for any purpose than that of a private dwelling house with private garage. 

2. That for the purpose of affording light and air and for the purpose of preserving uniformity of appearance of the entire tract of which the hereby granted lot and building is a part, no building or part of building or porch or piazza or any other addition or appendage thereto shall ever be erected within thirteen feet of the present building line of F Street nor within eighteen feet of the present building line of O Street; nor shall any building or part of building, porch, piazza or additions or projections, other than bay windows, steps and stoops, be erected nearer than ten feet to the division line of the lot or the piece of ground immediately adjoining the hereby granted premises to the east." 

To this should be added as a 3rd clause the clause making the restrictions a covenant running with the land (Supra. Rule Three). (h) Appurtenance Clause. Easements. Exceptions and

Reservations. End of Premises. 

"Together with all and singular the buildings, improvements, ways, streets, alleys, passages, waters, water-courses, rights, liberties, privileges, hereditaments and appurtenances whatsoever unto the hereby granted premises belonging, or, in any wise appertaining and the reversions and remainders, rents, issues and profits thereof, and all the estate, right, title, interest, property, claim, and demand whatsoever of him, the said grantor, as well at law as in equity of, in and to the same. 

If there be any exceptions or reservations they should be inserted immediately following the above clause (see (h)2 infra).

As a matter of law, all easements, rights and incidents which belong to the property conveyed and are necessary to its full enjoyment, pass as appurtenances without mention of them in the deed (Murphy v. Campbell, 4 Pa. 480-1846; 

Casey v. Canning, 43 Superior 31-1910). But only those things that are necessary to the enjoyment of the land conveyed pass without mention; things that are merely convenient do not (Messer v. Rhodes, 3 Brewst. 180-1870).

§54 (h)1-I  

Thus, e.g., alley-ways,' water-courses, light and air are usually merely convenient and hence would not pass as an appur tenance (Hollenbach v. Tiffany, 50 Pa. Super. Ct. 297—1912). 

For this reason the appurtenance clause which is so broadly drawn as to cover every conceivable right, usually always appears in the printed form of deeds. The legal maxim "that what is appurtenant to a piece of land is appurtenant to every part thereof" is well to be remembered, for if a right of way be granted as appurtenant to a tract of land, later if that tract be divided into smaller lots, each of the grantees of the sub-divisions will be entitled to the same right of way (Ermentrout v. Stitzel, 170 Pa. 540-1895), which may have been intended only for the convenience of the single owner of the undivided tract. (h)1 Easements, Kinds of.

Easements are of two kinds; easements appurtenant and easements in gross. It is customary to refer to the former merely as easements and to the latter as easements in gross. 

I. Easement Appurtenant, is a liberty privilege or advantage without profit which the owner of one parcel of land may have in the lands of another; or from the opposite point of view it is a service which one estate owes to another (Perkinpine v. Hogan, 47 Pa. Super. Ct. 22, 25-1911); see also Kieffer v. Imhoff, 26 Pa. 438-1856, for historical discussion. The parcel of land enjoying the privilege or for whose benefit it is created is called the "dominant tenement", while the one which suffers the service is called the "servient tenement". While the most usual illustration of easements is found in a right of way or alley (Kieffer v. Imhoff, 26 Pa. 

1 But see Rhoads v. Walter, 70 Pa. Super. Ct. 25—1918; Tursi v. Parry, 135 Pa.

Super. Ct. 285-1938; holding that where land is sold bounded by a private alley; which alley is in fact opened and used at the time the conveyance is made, and the alley is convenient or necessary to the premises sold, unless there is something in the conveyance restricting the use solely to the grantor or expressly excepting the alley from the grant, the right to use it passes with the conveyance and becomes appurtenant to the property.

§(h)1-II 

139 

DEEDS. 

438-1856), they assume many and varied aspects, e.g., right to water supply (Geissel v. Supplee, 95 Pa. Super. Ct. 3581928; Zimmerman v. Union Paving Co., 134 Pa. Super. Ct. 

373-1938), right to drain through a sewer (Dzmura v. 

Gyurik, 41 Pa. Super. Ct. 398-1909); right to lay a pipe line (Collison v. Phila. Co., 233 Pa. 350-1912), a projecting cornice over another's land (Grace Church v. Dobbins, 153 

Pa. 294-1893). But the occupancy of land by telephone company without a deed of grant, under a parol license merely was held to lack the essential qualities of an easement 

(Bradley v. American T. & T. Co. of Pa., 54 Pa. Super. Ct. 

388-1913).

In a learned discussion of the subject Mr. Justice Maxey in Lindenmuth v. Safe Harbor Water Power Corp., 309 Pa. 

58-1932, points out the modern rule to be that while an easement appurtenant must be attached to a dominant estate it is not necessary for the dominant estate to be contiguous or adjoining the servient estate or that the dominant estate or thing to be benefited by the easement was even in existence at the time of the creation of the parties if the intent of the parties was that the dominant tenement should be thereafter acquired or created. Thus it was there held that an easement to overflow F's land by a dam thereafter to be constructed was nevertheless to be considered an easement appurtenant. 

II. Easement in Gross. An easement in gross is a mere personal right in the real estate of another. It is personal to the grantee because it is not appurtenant to other premises and is not assignable and it has been said it cannot be made assignable by the terms of the grant. This latter statement however was doubted in Lindenmuth v. Safe Harbor W. P. 

Co., 309 Pa. 58-1932, but not expressly decided. But in

Miller v. Lutheran Ass'n., 331 Pa. 241-1938, it was squarely held that whether an easement in gross, such as the right to boat, fish and bathe, may be subdivided by assignments or sublicenses to others, depends upon the nature of the easement and the terms of its creation.

§54(h)2 

 (h)2 Easements How Created. Exceptions and Reserva tions.

Easements are most usually created by what is termed a reservation or exception in a grantor's deed of conveyance. 

The exception or reservation is customarily inserted twice; once immediately following the appurtenance clause (see (h) supra), and again immediately after the habendum (to have and to hold clause) see $55 infra. A customary form thereof being as follows: "Excepting and reserving unto the grantor, his heirs and assigns, the full, free liberty and right at all times hereafter and forever, to have and use a passage way extending along the south end of the lot hereby granted for any and all purpose connected with the use and occupation of the grantor's other land adjoining the lot hereby granted."

Though easements are customarily reserved by language such as above used, there is a real fundamental distinction between a "reservation" and an "exception". A reservation in a deed is the creation of a right or interest which had no prior existence as such in a thing or part of a thing granted. 

It is distinguished from an exception in that it is a new right or interest. An exception is always a part of the thing granted. It is the whole of the part excepted. It thus follows that a reservation is a mere easement while an exception is a part of the fee (Bicking v. Florey, Brick Works, 53 Pa. 

Super. Ct. 358-1913; Lauderbach-Zerby Co., v. Lewis, 283

Pa. 250-1925). If the particular clause be construed as an exception from the grant, no words of inheritance (i.e., heirs and assigns) are necessary because the title to the excepted part remains in the grantor and never passes to the grantee, but if construed as a reservation words of inheritance are necessary, otherwise the right ceases at the death of the grantor, he having created some new right or thing out of the property granted which was not in existence at the time of the granting (Mandle v. Gharing, 256 Pa. 121-1917).

The important words therefore to be included are the words "heirs and assigns" and "forever". Such words ordinarily

§54(h)141 DEEDS. indicate a perpetual easement (Strycker v. Richardson, et al., 77 Pa. Super. Ct. 252-1921). In Hobaugh to the use v. Phila. 

Co., 67 Pa. Super. Ct. 407-1917, where a grantor specified in the grant of a pipe line easement "that so long as oil is carried in such pipe line" the grantor may have therefrom gas sufficient for fuel, it was held that in absence of words of inheritance it created but a personal privilege which died with him.

Of equal importance are words to indicate the character, extent and use of the easement. To avoid litigation the following rules of construction which the Court applies in disputes over easements should be borne in mind by the draftsman of the deed (see Witman v. Stichter, 299 Pa. 484—1930). (a) Courts will in the first instance look only at the document itself to discover the extent and nature of the terms of the easement. If on the face of the document, no doubt arises that the words are used in their primary sense and, if read in that sense they are plain and unambiguous, the matter is concluded. The terms of the grant as they can be learned by words clearly expressed, will regulate and measure the rights of the grantee. (b) Next, where the words are ambiguous or equivocal, then it being impossible to determine the intent of the parties from the language used, evidence of extraneous facts or circumstances will be received in evidence to enable the court to find what the parties meant by the language used, a situation which the careful conveyancer will want to avoid. 

The following cases illustrate the importance of the use of clear, unequivocal language. In Bowers v. Myer, 237 Pa. 533 -1912, where the extent of the use of an alley between two buildings was not defined, limited or restricted, it was held to include the right to use the alley as a passage-way for horses and vehicles as well as pedestrians. On the other hand, where instead of the word "alley" the term "court" was employed it was held not to include the right of passage for automobiles or vehicles, because the term "court" was an apt word connoting an inclosed space or courtyard communicating with

$54(h)3 

a street, but in no sense part of it, a term used where the right of passage is limited to pedestrians (Green v. J. G. Duncan, Jr., & Co., 30 D.R. 794-1921). A right of way "for teams and wagons" was held to include automobiles for an automobile is in a general sense a wagon (Strycher v. Richardson, 77, Pa. Super. Ct. 252-1921). So also a reservation of mineral and mining rights was held not to include petroleum and natural gas (Preston v. South Penn Oil Co., 238 Pa. 

301-1913; Schmidt v. Lieberum, 54 Pa. Super. Ct. 5001913). Nor can a grant of water power be construed as a grant of water itself (Eastern Penna. Power Co. v. Lehigh 

Coal and Nav. Co., 23 D. R. 279-1914). Nor does an easement of a right of way for passage include the right to construct a line of gas pipes therein (Allen v. Scheib, 257 Pa. 61917). 

(h)3 Easements by Separate Deed of Grant. 

While easements are most generally created by exception or reservation in the deed by which a part of the grantor's land is conveyed, nevertheless an easement may be and frequently is created by a separate deed usually called a deed of grant, expressly granting the same to the grantee. A form of such a deed of grant is to be found in §250 herein. In 

Graham v. Safe Harbor Water Power Corp., 315 Pa. 5721934, it was held the owner of land who grants an easement reserves the right to make any use of the servient tenement which does not interfere with the easement. So one who has only the easement of a right of way over the soil of an alley, cannot enjoin the owner of the soil from constructing a balcony above the level of the alley, if it in no way interferes with the enjoyment of the easement of the right of way (Stuart v. Gimbel Bros. 290 Pa. 210-1927).

Where land out of which the easement is granted is owned in common, all the co-owners must join, for one tenant in common cannot by his sole act create an easement in the lands held in common, and his grant passes no right which can be

§(h)4 143 

DEEDS. 

enforced against the other tenants in common (Griswold 

Worsted Co. v. Harrigan, 28 D. R. 342-1919). What was said concerning the care to be used by a conveyancer in drafting exceptions and reservations, applies with equal force to separate deeds granting easements. 

(h)4 Easements by Prescription or Adverse User. 

Just as title in fee to land may be acquired by adverse possession for twenty-one years so easements can be acquired by adverse user for twenty-one years. Such acquisition of an easement is usually called an easement by prescription. In general, it may be said the same requisite to the acquisition of title in fee simple by adverse possession fully discussed in Chap. II, §15 et. seq. of this work, apply to the acquisition of the lesser interests in land known as easements by prescription or adverse user. The theory of the law is that a continuous notorious and adverse user of an easement for more than twenty-one years gives rise to a presumption that a grant of such easement had at sometime in the remote past been expressly made.

In Deeb v. Ferris, 127 Pa. Super. Ct. 489-1937, it was said that the adverse user must be continuous and notorious and adverse. Therefore permissive use is not adverse and does not create an easement by prescription, no matter how long it may be continued; a mere lapse of time in such circumstances raising no presumption of a grant (Demuth v. Amweg, 90 Pa. 181-1879; Woodbury v. Allan, 215 Pa. 390—1906).

But testimony that the owner had not given permission to use a lane has been held sufficient to show the user was adverse and not permissive, Fister v. Reitz, 103 Pa. Super. Ct. 6011938. (h)5 Easements by Implication and Ways of Necessity.

Where an owner of land subjects part of it to an open, visible, permanent, continuous servitude or easement in favor of another part, and then conveys either, the purchaser takes

§54(h)5 

subject to the burden or benefit as the case may be (Grace 

Church v. Dobbins, 153 Pa. 294-1893; Liquid Carbonic Co. v. 

Wallace, 219 Pa. 457-1908; Eshleman v. Parkesburg Iron

Co. 235 Pa. 439-1912), and this is so even though the easement is not expressly mentioned in the deed (Blauser v. Carson, 74 Pa. Super. Ct. 223-1920). The grant or reservation thereof being implied from the conveyance. This is an ancient principle and extends back to common law (Seibert v. 

Levan, 8 Pa. 383-1848; Kieffer v. Imhoff, 26 Pa. 438-1856).

If the easement be of an open notorious character the purchasee is charged with notice of it and imputes to him knowledge of the facts which he could have acquired by exercise of ordinary diligence, Anania v. Serenta, 275 Pa. 474-1923.

The sine qua non of the application of this doctrine is that the easement which thus becomes attached to the grant must be open, visible, permanent and continuous (Green v. J. G. Duncan Co. 30 D.R. 794-1921; Stein v. Bell Tel. Co., 301 Pa. 107 -1930). There can however be no ambulatory location of an easement (Becker v. Rittenhouse 297 Pa. 317-1929).

Some what akin to easements by implication is the principle that when a grantor in a conveyance designates an unopened street or alley as a boundary, if it be on his ground it is regarded as an implied covenant by him that it shall be open for the use of the grantee as a public way as well as a dedication of the street to public use. (Maier et al. v. Walborn et al., 84 Pa. Super. Ct. 522-1925).

Ways of Necessity. Upon the same principle is the "way of necessity", recognized by law though a deed be silent concerning the same. Thus where a parcel of land conveyed, is so situated that access to it from the highway cannot be had except by passing over the remaining land of the grantor then the grantee is entitled to a "way of necessity" over the lands of the grantor (Borstnar v. Allegheny County, 332 Pa. 1561938). But the way must be one of actual necessity and not merely one of convenience (Stein v. Bell Tel. Co., 301 Pa. 107-1930).

DEEDS. 

(h)6 Extinguishment of Easements. 

(I) By Release. An easement however acquired, unless its duration is limited by express terms of the grant, continues until formally surrendered by deed of release or unless extinguished by operation of law as hereinafter explained. 

It is not lost by mere non-user (Nickels v. Hand Band, 

(No. 1), 52 Pa. Super. Ct. 145—1912). 

(II) By Operation of Law. Denial of right for twenty one years. Just as an easement can be acquired by adverse user for twenty-one years so it can also be lost if there be an absolute denial of the right followed by an enjoyment inconsistent with its existence for twenty-one years. Thus where an easement consisting of a roadway across the land of A is closed by A's building a fence across it or building over it or otherwise blocking the road, such action if acquiesced in for twenty-one years extinguishes the easement. But where the fence built across the road is pierced by a gate such act was held not sufficiently hostile as to amount to a denial of the easements owner's right (Nickels v. Cornet Band (No. 1), 52 Pa. Super. Ct. 145-1912).

Merger. An easement may also be extinguished by merger of title, as where the owner of the servient tenement (the land subject to the easement) acquires title to the dominant tenement for whose benefit the easement was created, because as said in Witman v. Stichter, 299 Pa. 484–1930, "where there is a union of an absolute title to and possession of the dominant and servient estates in the same person, it operates to extinguish an easement absolutely and forever, for the single reason that no man can have an easement in his own land; and of course it ceases to be appurtenant, and can only be made so again by express grant. The merger must however result in a unity of both title and possession, else the easement will not be extinguished (Green v. J. G. Duncan Co., 30 D.R. 794-1921).

Revival upon Severance. If during the period of merger the owner of both dominant and servient tenements does not

$55(a) 

physically alter the easement or discontinue the use thereof, upon a subsequent severance of the estate the alienee becomes entitled to all continuous and apparent easements which have been used by the owner during the unity of the estate and which were necessary for the enjoyment of the several parts (Kiefer v. Imhoff, 26 Pa. 438-1856). The necessity required, is only a reasonable one not an absolute one (Frick v. Wirt Co. 2 D. & C. 405—1922). Intertwined with the principle of revival of an easement lost by merger is of course the other principle which implies an easement from the fact where the owner separates the land, having left part of it subject to an open, visible, permanent, continuous servitude in favor of the other part, when he aliens it, the purchaser takes subject to the burden or benefit as the case may be. 

(Drum v. Dinkelacker, 79 Pa. Super. Ct. 91-1922 and see 

$54-h 5 Supra.) 

(III) Extinguishment by Condemnation under Power of Eminent Domain. 

As we have seen before, (§37 (a), all property is held subject to the right of the Government, State or Federal, to take private property for public use directly or through authorized public service corporations upon the condition however that just compensation for the property so taken is made. 

An easement can be condemned and therefore so extinguished under this power of eminent domain (Borstnar v. Allegheny 

County, 332 Pa. 154—1938).

Habendum Part. 

(a) To Have and To Hold Clause. 

"To have and to hold the said lots or pieces of ground above described with the messuage or tenement thereon erected; hereditaments and premises hereby granted or mentioned and intended so to be, with the appurtenances, unto said grantee, his heirs and assigns, to and for the only proper use and behoof of the said grantee, his heirs and assigns forever."

$(b) 147 

DEEDS. 

If there be any exceptions or reservations they are repeated immediately after the word "forever."

The purpose of this clause is to determine what estate passes. In the clause above set forth it provides that the grantee shall have and hold an estate in fee. The habendum and tenendum clause may be used to explain the premises of the deed and perhaps qualify it (Bedford Lodge v. Lentz, 194 

Pa. 399; 1900 Rhodes' Estate, 232 Pa. 489-493-1911). It may enlarge, expound, qualify or vary the estate granted in the premises of the deed (Ontelaunee Orchards, Inc. v. Rothermel et ux, 139 Pa. Super. Ct. 44-1939). But if it be repugnant or hopelessly contradictory to the premises, it will be rejected (Karcher v. Hoy, 151 Pa. 391-1892). The office of the habendum and tenendum may be and sometimes is performed in the premises in which case the habendum is not really necessary; however, it usually appears as a printed part in all forms of deeds. 

(b) Covenants of Warranty. 

"And the said grantor, Andrew Black, for himself, his heirs, executors and administrators, doth covenant, promise and agree to and with the said grantee, his heirs and assigns, by these presents that he the said grantor, Andrew Black, and his heirs, all and singular the hereditaments and premises hereby granted or mentioned and intended so to be with appurtenances unto the said grantee, his heirs and assigns, against him the said grantor, Andrew Black, and his heirs and against all and every person and persons whosoever lawfully claim or to claim the same or any part thereof by, from or under him, them or any of them shall and will under and subject as aforesaid warrant and forever defend."

This clause is the covenant of warranty. A covenant is any writing under seal wherein either party may stipulate the truth of certain facts or may bind himself to perform or give something to the other (Mitchell on Real Estate Conveyancing 437). The words "it is hereby agreed" make the words that follow a covenant (Blood v. Crew Levick Co., 171 

Pa. 328-1895). The most usual covenant found in a deed is the covenant of warranty. It had its origin, as Mr. Fallon

$55(c) 

(Pa. Law of Conveyancing 190) points out, in the fact that in the early history of England, conveyances were chiefly made from a superior to an inferior as from a baron to his retainer or from father to daughter upon her marriage. No examination of the grantor's title was deemed necessary for the grantee relied solely upon his grantor's covenant of warrant or promise to defend his (the grantee's) title. In modern conveyancing the ancient warranty or guarantee has lost its importance because owing to our recording system a purchaser is in the position to examine the title of the land purchased and to ascertain its validity (Whitehead v. Carr, 5 

Watts 369-1836). Of the five ancient covenants formerly appearing in old-time deeds in Pennsylvania only the covenant of warranty has survived and is the only one necessary to treat of here.

A married woman who joins her husband in conveying his real estate is not liable with him for breach of warranty, for the purpose of her joinder in the deed is to bar her dower and to hold her liable would in effect make her surety for payment of her husband's debts in violation of the Act of 

June 8, 1893 P.L. 344-(48 P.S. 32; Crain v. Warner, 87 Pa.

Super. Ct. 605-1926). A grantee cannot recover on his warranty because of a mortgage which he took expressly under and subject to (Grange Trust Co. v. Shade et al. 102 Pa. 

Super. Ct. 122-1931).

The covenants of warranty are of two kinds: Special and 

General. 

(c) Meaning of Special and General Warranty. Special 

Warranty is such as is set forth above and is the one most generally used. It is a promise or covenant on the part of the grantor to defend the grantee against all actions, for the land conveyed which may be brought by the grantor or his heirs, assigns or anyone claiming under the grantor. A general warranty, however, is a covenant on the part of the grantor to defend the grantee's title against all mankind, the whole world. This, of course, is an unusual covenant and so harsh in its terms that it is never presumed to have been intended

§(d) 149 

DEEDS. 

unless expressly stipulated for. It amounts practically to an insurance of title. A purchaser has no right to expect a general warranty in his deed unless he expressly bargains for it (Whitehead v. Carr, 5 Watts, 368–1836), and it has been held that the words, in an agreement of sale that the words "Vendor will well and sufficiently grant, convey and assure the said tract of land to the vendee, his heirs and assigns", entitled the vendee to only a special warranty (Lloyd v. Farrel, 48 Pa. 78—1864). A general warranty would be created by the following words: "And the said grantor Andrew Black, for himself, his heirs, executors and administrators doth covenant, promise and agree to and with the said grantee, his heirs and assigns, by these presents that he, the said grantor, Andrew Black, will forever warrant and defend the said property and every part thereof unto the grantee, his heirs, executors and administrators against the lawful claims and demands of all persons whomsoever.” 

In Hopkins v. Phillips, 76 Pa. Super. Ct. 243–245—1921, it was held, where a vendee contracts with a vendor he is not bound to accept a deed from a grantor other than his vendor, for he has a right to have the personal responsibility of his vendor behind the covenants of warranty contained in the deed, whether general or special.

By the Act of 1909 and its amendment of 1925, (Act of 

April 1, 1909, P.L. 91, §5, amended by Act of Apr. 30, P.L. 

404 21 P.S. §6), providing for a short form of deed, the words "the grantor will warrant generally" shall have the effect and mean the same as the general warranty above set forth, and the words, the grantor will warrant specially, shall have the same meaning and effect as the words set forth in the special warranty on page 147. This act will be considered more fully later (§58). (d) Trustees and Fiduciary Covenants.

From fiduciary grantors the grantee is entitled to no covenants except that the grantor has done no act to encumber the

$56 

estate (Little v. Thorpp, 245 Pa. 539-1914); (for a form of this warranty see form of Executor's Deed, $236, infra). 

56. Meaning of Parts (Concluded). Conclusion of Deed. 

(a) Execution Clause or Testimonium. 

"In witness whereof the parties have hereunto interchangeably set their hands and seals. Dated the day and year first above written. 

Sealed and delivered in the presence of us: (Seal.) (Seal.)" 

It will be observed that the Indenture Deed from which the above clause is an extract retains the word interchangeably from the old form of indenture when it was customary for the grantee to sign. This the grantee no longer does, although the form persists. A deed poll omits, of course, the word interchangeably and is dated at the end instead of at the top. (See form $241.)

In Keller v. Donkin, (31 D. & C., 636—1938), it was held, a deed is violative of the Statute of Frauds (Act of Mar. 21, 1772, 1 Sm. L. 389), and ineffective to pass title if not signed at the end thereof, even though the grantors signed the purchase money receipt and the acknowledgment was executed by a notary public. (b) Receipt. Following the testimonium or execution clause is usually found a receipt in the following form:- "Received on the day of date of the above indenture of the abovenamed grantee the full consideration money hereinbefore mentioned." 

This is signed by the grantor also, although it is of little value where the consideration is only nominal. Even where the consideration mentioned in the receipt in the deed is actual, the receipt may be contradicted (McPherran's Estate,

$151 DEEDS. (No. 1) 212 Pa. 425-1905). And it has been held that while the evidence offered to alter or modify the terms of a written instrument under seal must ordinarily be clear and satisfactory, a mere preponderance of evidence is sufficient to contradict the receipt in a deed (Quinter v. Quinter, 261 Pa. 195 -1918). (c) Acknowledgment Clause "On the 7th day of July, Anno Domini one thousand nine hundred and eleven (1911) before me the subscriber, a notary public for the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, residing in the City of Philadelphia, personally appeared the above named B. M., and in due form of law acknowledged the above indenture to be his act and deed and desired the same might be recorded as such. "Witness my hand and notarial seal the day and year aforesaid. 

Notary Public"

This is to be signed by the notary public or officer authorized by law to take acknowledgments. A somewhat similar form is declared to be permissible in the short form of deed
