II. 

SHORT FORM OF DEED. 

57. Short Form of Deed Under Act of April 1, 1909. 

The reader by this time has probably reached the conclusion that there is much in the form of deed just examined and analyzed that could without loss be omitted. And it is doubtless true that much of the verbiage could be eliminated for it is merely a survival of the times when the scrivener or the conveyancer was paid by the number of words written; when mere prolixity had its own reward. It is not to be wondered, therefore, that many jurisdictions have by legislation pro-

$57 

vided for a short form of deed.

In Pennsylvania also by the 

Act of April 1, 1909 (P.L. 91), 21 P.S. §1, was adopted a short form of deed. The title insurance companies and the older conveyancers are, however, loath to abandon the old form and to adopt the new. There is much to be said on both sides. In favor of the short form the best argument probably is that it facilitates the recording and saves time and expense. On the other hand the adherents of the older form point out that this older form has received years of judicial interpretation and every clause has a known definite meaning, not only in this jurisdiction but in most all common law jurisdiction. Which form will finally prevail cannot now be determined, whether art will yield to commercialism or whether the simplified form will meet the fate of simplified spelling is a question beyond us. We will set forth the short form and leave the question of its use to the individual tastes of conveyancers.

ACT OF APRIL 1, 1909. FORM. 

The form of deed provided for by the Act of April 1, 1909, is as follows: 

THIS DEED. 

Made the seventh day of July, in the year nineteen hundred and eleven (1911) between A. B., blacksmith, and C. D., grocer, both of the City and County of Philadelphia, State of Pennsylvania. 

WITNESSETH. That in consideration of one ($1.00) dollar in hand paid, the receipt whereof is hereby acknowledged, the said grantor does hereby grant and convey to the said grantee all that certain lot or piece of ground with the messuage or tenement thereon erected, situate on the west side of "Y" Street at the distance of 337 feet northward from the north side of "X" Street, in the Fiftieth Ward of the City of Philadelphia, containing in front or breadth on the said "Y" Street 18 feet and extending of that width in length or depth westward between two parallel lines at right angles with the said "X" Street to "Z" Street.

And the said grantor does hereby covenant and agree that he will warrant specially the property hereby conveyed.

$153 DEEDS. 

IN WITNESS WHEREOF the said grantor has hereunto set his hand and seal the day and year first above written. 

Andrew Black (Seal.) STATE OF PENNSYLVANIA COUNTY OF PHILADELPHIA 

On the seventh day of July, A.D. 1911, before me, John Smith, came the above named Andrew Black and acknowledged the foregoing deed to be his act and deed and desired the same to be recorded as such. 

WITNESS my hand and notarial seal the day and year aforesaid.

John Smith. (Seal.) Notary Public. 

My commission expires Feb. 13, 1916. 

58. Provisions of Act of April 1, 1909 (P.L. 91; 21 P.S. I). 

The first section of this act provides:

SECTION 1. Be it enacted, etc., That from and after the approval of this act, in any deed hereafter executed, unless expressly limited to a lesser estate, the words "grant and convey", or either one of said words, shall be effective to pass to the grantee or grantees named therein a fee simple title to the premises conveyed, if the grantor or grantors possessed such a title, although there be no words of inheritance or of perpetuity in the deed.

This simply means that unless a lesser estate is expressly specified in the deed, the words grant and convey shall operate to pass a fee simple title, without the word "heirs" (See $54-d.). Before the passage of this section a conveyance of land without the word "heirs" passed a life estate only 

(Klinger v. Wick, 266 Pa. 1—1920). 

SECTION 2. All deeds hereafter executed, granting or conveying lands, unless an exception or reservation be made therein, shall be construed to include all the estate, right, title, interest, property, claim, and demand whatsoever, of the grantor or grantors, in law, equity, or otherwise howsoever, of, in and to the same, and every

$58 

part thereof, together with all and singular the improvements, ways, waters, water-courses, rights, liberties, privileges, hereditaments, and appurtenances whatsoever thereto belonging, or in any wise appertaining, and the reversions and remainders, rents, issue and profits thereof.

This means that the whole of the grantor's estate and all appurtenances and every part of the land conveyed passes without specific mention thereof. And any part or appurtenance not intended to pass must be expressly excepted. 

SECTION 3. That the words "grant and convey", or either one of said words, in any deed hereafter executed, shall be adjudged an express covenant to the grantee, his heirs and assigns; to wit, That the grantor was seized of an indefeasible estate in fee simple in the property conveyed, free from incumbrances done or suffered from the grantor, as also for quiet enjoyment against the grantor, his heirs and assigns, unless limited by express words contained in such deed. 

This means the words "grant and convey" are to be taken to imply a covenant of fee simple title and for quiet enjoyment, unless expressly limited otherwise, and is a reenactment of §6 of the Act of May 28, 1715, 1 Sm. Law, 94 (21 

P.S. 8). See $54-(d). Such limitations if an encumbrance would naturally be inserted in this form of deed immediately after the description, preceded by the words "under and subject." If the limitation be a qualified estate as e.g. a life estate, it should be inserted before the description e.g. "does hereby grant and convey to the said grantee a life estate in all that certain, etc."

SECTION 4. That a covenant by the grantor or grantors, in any deed, that he, they, or it "will warrant generally the property hereby conveyed", shall have the same effect as if the grantor or grantors had covenanted that he or they, his or their heirs and personal representatives or successors, will forever warrant and defend the said property, and every part thereof, unto the grantee, his heirs, personal representatives and assigns, against the lawful claims and demands. of all persons whomsoever. 

This is self-explanatory.

SECTION 5. That a covenant by the grantor or grantors in any deed, that he, they or it "will warrant specially the property hereby

§58A 

155 

DEEDS. 

conveyed" shall have the same effect as if the grantor or grantors had covenanted that he or they, his or their heirs and personal representatives or successors, will forever warrant and defend the said property, and every part thereof, unto the said grantee, his heirs, personal representatives and assigns, against the lawful claims and demands of the grantor or grantors, and all persons claiming or to claim by, through, or under him or them. 

This is also self-explanatory. 

SECTION 6. That whenever in, any deed, there shall be used the words "release and quitclaim", such deed shall be construed as if set forth that the grantor or grantors hath or have remised, released, and quitclaimed, and by these presents doth or do remise, release, and forever quitclaim, unto the grantee, his heirs and assigns, all right, title, interest, property, claim, and demand whatsoever, both in law and in equity, in or to the lands or premises released, or intended so to be, so that neither the grantor or grantors, nor his or their personal representatives, his or their heirs or assigns, shall, at any time thereafter, have, claim, challenge, or demand the said lands and premises, or any part thereof, in any manner whatever. 

This section means that where it is desired to release any claim to land by what is commonly called a quitclaim deed (See form, $248), the words release and quitclaim are to be substituted for the words grant and convey and shall have the same meaning as the old lengthy form of hath remised, released and forever quitclaimed, etc. (see form, §247). 

58-A. Amendment of 1925. 

Each section of the Act of 1909 just analyzed was amended by the Act of April 30, 1925, P.L. 404 (21 P.S. §§1 to 10), by extending it to include "instruments in writing for conveying or releasing land" (sic.), and by adding a new section 9 (21 

P.S. $10) which reads: "All deeds or instruments in writing for conveying or releasing lands made by any natural person, either in his individual capacity or as a fiduciary, duly signed by the grantors in the manner now provided by law, but with no seal affixed thereto, shall be deemed to be executed with the same force and effect in all respects as though a seal was affixed to the signature, and all such instruments in writ-

$59 

ing signed by the grantors, but with no seal affixed thereto, shall be deemed for all purposes within the purview of all acts or parts of acts of assembly relating to or concerning deeds for the conveyance or releasing of lands."

This amendment makes sealing of deeds unnecessary at least as to individual deeds. (See discussion of this amendment, §61 infra.)

III. 

EXECUTION OF DEEDS. DELIVERY. 

59. Meaning of Term Execution. 

By execution of a deed we mean signing and sealing. A deed is considered to be a solemn instrument and it is presumed in law that before a party has put his hand to it he has made himself familiar with its contents, either by reading it carefully himself or if he cannot read by causing it to be read to him. As a Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of 

Pennsylvania said, "If a party who can read will not read a deed put before him for execution, or if, being unable to read, he will not demand to have it read or explained to him, he is guilty of supine negligence, which, I take it, is not the subject of protection either in law or equity" (Greenfield's 

Estate, 14 Pa. 489-496-1850). It does not follow, however, that once a deed is signed, the injured or deceived party has no redress against fraud, misrepresentation or mistake. The court will relieve in a proper case provided it is shown that the suitor exercised reasonable care and diligence (County of Schuylkill v. Copley, 67 Pa. 386-1871; Rambo B. & L. Ass'n. v. Dragone, 311 Pa. 422-1933). Safe practice requires in all cases that a party read over the instrument that he signs and a careful conveyancer will always, where the party is illiterate, read over and explain the instrument to him before execution. To completely execute a deed so as to pass title, it must be signed and sealed, attested and delivered.

$157 

DEEDS. 

60. Signing. 

Historically sealing antedates signing. In the early times the English people generally, noble as well as peasant, could not write, hence at common law the affixing of the seal only was necessary to the execution of the deed. The Statute of 

Frauds, however, it will be remembered, required that instruments concerning real estate be signed. From this time on, the signing became the important part of the execution of a deed. Sealing by itself is no longer sufficient, the deed must be signed. (Keller v. Donkin 31 D. & C. 636-1938). 

A deed is good if actually signed no matter how poorly the signature be written. If the party is unable to write he may sign by mark, in which event the mark must be attested, i.e., witnessed by the one who writes the party's name. This is done as follows:- Witness: 

Jeremiah Stone his 

Jacob X Strong mark.

The name of the grantor is written out by the witness and the grantor then makes his mark between his Christian and surname. The words, his and mark are then written respectively above and below the mark and the witness signs opposite. (Kelly's Estate 306 Pa. 551, 555-1932). 

61. Sealing.

As the world outgrew the necessities of the age when men made seals because they could not write, seals became less elaborate and in some states have been abolished altogether. 

As we have seen (§58-(a)) Pennsylvania followed suit in 

1925 (Act of May 12, 1925, P.L. 582, §1, 21 P.S. §276) vali dating all deeds of conveyance whether executed within or without the Commonwealth which had been duly acknowledged, delivered and recorded to bona fide purchasers for value, were not to be deemed or adjudged "invalid, defective or insufficient in law by reason of the fact that the signature

§61 

of the grantor or grantors were not signed under seal; but that all and every such deed and conveyance shall be good, valid and effectual in law for transferring, passing and conveying the estate title and interest of the grantor or grantors *** as if all the requisites and particulars required by law had been fully complied with * 

Thus unsealed deeds executed prior to May 12, 1925 were validated while any executed after the Act of Apr. 30, 1925, P.L. 404 (21 P.S. 10) are made effective by that act. #99 Even before the acts dispensing with the seal, a writing without it might operate to convey land, yet strictly speaking it would not be a deed. Neither a wafer nor a wax seal nor a distinctive seal was ever required in Pennsylvania. Any mark made opposite the name and intended as a seal was so considered (Hacker's Appeal, 121 Pa. 192-1888).

Necessity of Seal in Corporate Deeds. 

The Act of Apr. 7, 1927, P.L. 138 (No. 110) §1, 21 P.S. 

§277), validates deeds of conveyances, mortgages or other instruments affecting real estate of corporations, joint stock or partnership associations, limited partnerships, and registered partnerships, where "they shall have been erroneously executed by failure to affix the corporate seal or otherwise". 

Cases in litigation at the date of the act not to be affected. 

Prior to $9 of Act of Apr. 30, 1925, P.L. 404 (21 P.S. $10), see $58-A supra, a deed of a corporation was always required to be under seal though not necessarily in any prescribed form (Nicholas v. Machine Co., 7 North 137-1900).

Whether a corporate deed is still required to be under seal is a question. Although the language of $9 of the Act of 1925 is broad enough to include deeds of corporation, yet there is grave danger that it may be held to apply only to deeds of individuals, because the title of the act which by our constitution (Article III, §3) is required to "clearly express the subject of the act." The applicable portion of this title reads: "and abolishing the necessity of personal seal on deeds and instruments in writing for conveying or releasing lands"

§

159 

DEEDS. 

(italics supplied). "Personal" can hardly mean "corporate". Moreover, the validating act of 1927, supra, seems to imply the need of seals in corporate deeds, because it speaks of the "erroneous" omission of seals, etc. Then too, the Act of 1925 may also be held defective as embracing more than one subject matter, which is also forbidden by Article III, §3, of the Constitution, since the act is both an amendment to the short form deed act of 1909 and an abolition of the necessity of seals (See Bogardus v. Yardley Mills, 321 

Pa. 581-1936). Apparently the question has not yet been raised and until the act is held by our Supreme Court to be constitutional and to apply to corporate deeds, it will be wise to insist that all such deeds be sealed.

Even in the case of individual grantors, it is always better to insist on the deed being sealed, whether now necessary or not, because, the value of a seal is to be found in the fact that when a plaintiff sues on a sealed instrument he need only prove the signature and rest, for the consideration and delivery are presumed from the fact that the instrument is under seal. The burden then shifts to the other party 

(Austen v. Marzolf, 307 Pa. 232-1932). Whether the lan guage of the Acts of 1925 (Supra.) will be construed as broad enough to entitle a deed executed without a seal as entitled to the same presumptions of evidence as a sealed instrument is debatable. Until this question is decided by our Supreme 

Court the interest of clients will best be served by insisting that instruments of conveyancing be sealed. 

62. Attestation. Subscribing Witnesses. 

Attestation means witnessing. The witnessing of the execution of a deed by subscribing witness or witnesses was not necessary at common law and is not required in Pennsylvania generally speaking, though it is usually done so that in case of any dispute thereafter it may be known who was present, in order that their testimony may be procured (Long v. 

Ramsey, 1 S. & R. 72-1814), and from this it follows that a deed was held not to be invalidated where it was shown that

$62 

a subscribing witness's name was signed after delivery of the deed (Conway v. Conway, 27 D.R. 701-1918; Barnard v. 

Kell, 271 Pa. 80—1921).

Conveyances to Religious or Charitable Uses. 

Before 1939 there was one important exception to the rule just stated in that the Act of Apr. 26, 1855 P.L. 328, §11 (10 

P.S. 12), forbade the conveyance of real or personal estate to any corporation or person in trust for any religious or charitable use except by a deed or will attested by two credible and at the same time disinterested witnesses, at least one calendar month before the decease of the alienor or testator. 

The requirement of two witnesses was held not to be satisfied where a deed was witnessed by a single witness even though also acknowledged before a notary public (Darr's Estate 39 

D. & C. 210—1940). By a credible witness was meant one who is not disqualified to testify by mental incapacity or crime (Combs & Hankinson App. 105 Pa. 155-1884). And an attesting witness under that act meant a subscribing witness (Paxson's Est. 221 Pa. 98-1908). Disinterested was held to mean disinterested at the time of attestation (Historical So ciety v. Kelker 226 Pa. 16-1909). Section 11 of the Act of 1855 

was amended by the Act of June 1, 1911, P.L. 702 (10 P.S. 12) by defining a disinterested witness to mean one not interested in such religious or charitable use, which seems to have been the interpretation of the original Act (Stinson's Estate No. 

1, 232 Pa. 218-1911).

The need of subscribing witnesses to a will containing a devise or bequest for a religious or charitable use, was removed by the Act of July 2, 1935, 20 P.S. 195 Anno., (see $162 infra.). And by $2 of the Act of May 10, 1939 P.L. 141, (10 P.S. 12 Anno.), §11 of the Act of 1855 was repealed absolutely. Under the present law therefore no subscribing or attesting witness are necessary to the validity of a gift for a religious or charitable use whether by deed or will. 

The only restriction in the law at present affecting a conveyance for a religious or charitable gift by deed is that im-

$161 DEEDS. posed by the first section of the Act of 1939 Supra., which reads "Any gift for religious or charitable uses hereafter made to take effect in possession or enjoyment at or after death of the donor, shall be void unless made at least 30 days before such death, and any promise hereafter made to give real or personal property for religious or charitable uses, shall be unenforceable unless made 30 days before the death of the promisor. The 30 day period provided for in the Act, shall be so computed as to exclude the first and include the last day thereof".

It will be noted this 30 day limitation would not apply to a case where a conveyance is made to take effect immediately upon delivery of the deed but only where the gift is to take effect at death of the grantor. But a promise to give is unenforceable unless the donor survives its making 30 days.

As to what is meant by a religious or charitable use see 

63. Delivery of Deed. 

After signing and sealing of deed but one thing remains to be done in order to vest title in the grantee, that is, the deed must be delivered. A deed signed and sealed or even acknowledged does not take effect until delivered. No ceremony or form whatever is necessary to a valid delivery. The delivery may be consummated by words alone, or acts alone, or by both together. No formality is essential, and the question is to be determined by the intention of the parties as evidenced by their acts and declaration. The actual manual investiture of it need not be proved. When a deed is acknowledged before a proper officer as being signed, sealed and delivered, and the manual possession of the grantee is established, a presumption arises that an absolute and unconditional delivery is intended, unless by act, expression or writing an indication is made of an intention to qualify the formal act (Leiser et al. Executors v. Hartel 315 Pa. 537). See also 

Long v. McHenry, 45 Pa. Super. Ct. 530-1911; Lewis v. 

Merryman et al., 271 Pa. 255-1921). But this presumption

§63A  

may be rebutted by evidence that no delivery was in fact intended and was held to be sufficiently rebutted by proof that the grantor continued long in possession of the land without recognition of the grantee's claim. (Leiser et al. Executors v. Hartel 315 Pa. 537-1934). Delivery is therefore a question of intention (Critchfield v. Critchfield, 24 Pa. 100-1854).

It is plain that if a grantor prepares a deed, signs and seals it and puts it in his desk for safe keeping until settlement and it is stolen by the grantee, this is not a delivery and the deed will be of no effect (Sears v. Scranton Trust Co., 228 

Pa. 126-1910). Transfer of possession of the deed is delivery and delivery will often be presumed from the facts. 

Thus possession of deed by a grantee raises a presumption in absence of evidence to the contrary that the deed was properly delivered (Clauer v. Clauer, 22 Super. Ct. 3951903). And this though unrecorded (Devall v. Glover, 250 

Pa. 417-1915) or not recorded until after the grantor's death (Loughran v. Kummer, 297 Pa. 179-1929). But where the deed though fully executed and acknowledged is retained by the grantor in his possession, recording it after his death cannot operate to effect delivery (Harroun v. Graham, 258 

Pa. 245-1917).

So far as innocent third parties, i.e., purchasers for value without notice, are concerned, the general rule is well settled that where a deed appears to be signed, sealed, delivered, acknowledged and recorded, a purchaser has a right to act on the faith that this was all done as it purports to be in proper form by the proper parties. This because of the re cording acts (Piper v. Queeney, 282 Pa. 135-1925). 

63-A. Acceptance by the Grantee.

The act of delivery is not complete without an acceptance of the deed by the grantee (Security Mutual B. & L. Assn. v. 

Bien 27 Del. 51-1937). Acceptance may be and usually is presumed from the recording thereof, acquiesced in by the grantee and presumably with his consent. But, surreptitiously placing a deed on record without knowledge or con-

$163 

DEEDS. 

sent of the grantee does not prove acceptance nor raise a presumption of acceptance, and the grantee may have it stricken off and the recorded instrument declared null and void upon discovery of the same (Warren-Balderson Co. v. 

Kilian et. al. C.P. 2 (Phila.) Dec. 3, 1927 #4746).

During the recent depression this principle became one of importance because taxes on real estate in Philadelphia are a personal liability of the registered owner. A grantor cannot escape this liability by merely recording a deed for his unproductive real estate to a grantee. Unless such grantee is willing to accept the same the title does not pass for the delivery is not complete.

When, however, a grantee accepts a deed expressly or impliedly, the general rule is, the deed though signed by the grantor alone becomes the mutual act of the parties, the same as if signed by both, and by acceptance the grantee takes the property subject to the burden imposed on the grant, and is bound to perform the conditions therein stipulated though he has not signed the deed (Beedy v. Nypano R.R. Co., 250 Pa. 

51-1915). The same is true even where the acceptance is not expressed, but only implied from the grantee accepting the benefit of the deed (Spencer v. Spencer, 253 Pa. 3151916). 

64. Delivery in Escrow. 

That 

Delivery is not always absolute, it may be in escrow. is where a deed is delivered to a third person as an escrow to take effect upon the performance of same conditions on the part of the grantee. As for example, where a grantor delivers a deed to a real estate broker with instructions to deliver it to the grantee when the grantee pays the purchase price. Here the delivery, as far as the grantor is concerned, is complete, yet the deed does not take effect until the grantee complies with the conditions. If the agent with whom the deed is left as an escrow delivers it to the grantee without the performance of the conditions, the title of the grantee is voidable, that is, it can be avoided if action be taken before

$65 

a bona fide purchaser buys from the grantee without notice (Blight v. Schenck, 10 Pa. 285-1849). A delivery in escrow can only be made through a third party. Delivery direct to grantee to be held in escrow until conditions are performed will not operate as an escrow, and the law regards such delivery as absolute (Gish v. Brown, 171 Pa. 479-1895).

Where a deed contained a declaration of the grantor that it was sealed and delivered by her and it was found in possession of a third person after the death of decedent and recorded by the grantees, delivery was held prima facie established as a valid delivery may be made to a third party for the grantee (Chambley v. Rumbaugh, 132 Pa. Super. Ct. 312 -1938). 

65. Destruction of Deed Does Not Revest the Property. 

Once a deed is delivered title passes to the grantee and can only be gotten back into the grantor by a new deed of conveyance. Mere destruction of the deed does not revest the title in the grantor (Coleman v. Reynolds, 181 Pa. 317–1897; 

Tate v. Clement, 176 Pa. 550-1896). But the surrender by the grantee to the grantor of an unrecorded deed intended as collateral security will divest what was only a lien of the grantee (Harmony Nat. Bank's Appeal, 101 Pa. 428-1883).

IV. 

ACKNOWLEDGMENT AND PROBATE OF DEEDS. 

NOTARY PUBLIC. 

66. Necessity For and Meaning of Acknowledgment. 

We have seen that signing, sealing and delivery of deed without more vests the title in the grantee. Acknowledgment is not necessary to pass the title (Maguire v. Preferred 

Realty Co., 257 Pa. 48-1917), but acknowledgment is necessary in order to record the instrument (Act of May 28, 1715, 1 Sm. L. 94, $2, 21 P.S. §42). This practically makes acknowledgment necessary in every case, for without it there is no

$165 

DEEDS. 

protection against the frauds which the recording system has done away with.

By acknowledgment is meant the appearance of the grantor before an officer qualified by law to take acknowledgments (usually a notary), and formally acknowledging the execution of the instrument as his act and deed. 

(a) Commonwealth's Deeds. 

The Act of Apr. 4, 1919, P.L. 49, (21 P.S. 390), makes deeds of the Commonwealth and patents recordable without acknowledgment and it is unnecessary therefore for the 

Governor to acknowledge deeds by the Commonwealth. 

(Execution of Commonwealth's Deeds 35 D. & C. 609—1939). 

The best practice is to have the acknowledging clause recite the fact that the officer was authorized to do so by resolution of the board of directors. The secretary should attest as witness even where he is the officer making the acknowledgment, (See form of acknowledgment by corporation, $211). 

67. How Made. 

The acknowledgment must be made by the grantor in person and the official taking the acknowledgment while he need not be personally acquainted with the grantor should be satisfied as to his identity (Comm. v. Haines, 97 Pa. 2281881). (a) Acknowledgment by a Corporation. Is made by one of the officers authorized to do so, either by the president or the secretary. For form, see §211. 

"A corporation may acknowledge any deed, conveyance, mortgage or other instrument of writing by an attorney appointed by such corporation, and such appointment may be embodied in said deed, conveyance, mortgage or other instrument of writing in substantially the following form (Act of May 11, 1901, §1, P.L. 171, 21 P.S. §111)." "The (name of corporation) doth hereby constitute and appoint (name of appointee) to be its attorney for it, and in its name and as

§68  

and for its corporate act and deed to acknowledge this (name of instrument), before any person having authority by the laws of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania to take such acknowledgment, to the intent and purpose that the same may be duly recorded.” $2 of the same act also provides that "such acknowledgment may be made before any person or officer now or hereafter to be authorized by the laws of this Commonwealth to take acknowledgments of deeds or other instruments of writing, whose certificate of such acknowledgment shall be in substantially the following form: 

and day of 

I hereby certify that on this in the year of our Lord before me the subscriber (title of officer taking acknowledgment), personally appeared (name of attorney), the attorney named in the foregoing (name of instrument), and by virtue and in pursuance of the authority therein conferred upon him, acknowledged the said (name of instrument) to be the act of the said (corporation's name). 

Witness my hand and seal the day and year aforesaid. ... (Seal). (b) Acknowledgments by trustees are made the same as by individuals except that the clause should recite that he is a trustee. Although the word trustee annexed to his name has been held sufficient without more (Dail v. Moore, 51 Mo. 

589-1873 (See form, $209). (c) Acknowledgments by attorneys in fact should be as the act of their principal as well as their own act (See form, $210). 

68. Separate Acknowledgments of Married Women No 

Longer Necessary in Pennsylvania.

In some of the states, for example New Jersey, it is still necessary for an acknowledgment of the wife to be separate and apart from her husband, but in Pennsylvania, by the 

Act of April 4, 1901 P.L. 67 (21 P.S. 82), this is no longer required, and the acknowledgment of a married woman may now be taken as though she were a feme sole, that is, like

$167 

DEEDS. 

that of any other person. While separate acknowledgments were required prior to the Act of 1901, various validating or curative acts were passed curing such defective acknowledgments where the deed or mortgage was given for a valuable consideration. To make such a void acknowledgment good under these acts the valuable consideration must be shown 

(Colonial Trust Co. v. Foster, 234 Pa. 152-1912). 

69. What a Valid Certificate of Acknowledgment Must 

Contain.

It has been the policy of the State of Pennsylvania to prevent any injustice from arising from any defects that may happen in the certificate of acknowledgment. Hence from time to time the legislature passes acts which validate all acknowledgments taken before its passage, which may be invalid by reason of omission or defects of form. A sample of such an Act is the Act of Apr. 11, 1931, P.L. 28. This the 

Legislature has power to do (Journeay et al. v. Gibson, 56 Pa. 

57-1867). However, by bearing in mind the few essentials that are requisite to a proper acknowledgment there should be no fear of any defective acknowledgments. 

The certificate of acknowledgment to be valid should always contain these things:a. The date. 

b. The venue. 

c. The name of the grantor. d. The signature of the officer taking the acknowledgment. e. His official position. f. His seal. g. If a notary, the date of the expiration of his commission. h. Certification by a notary public taking an acknowledgment of a bank, banking institution, or Trust Company, that he is neither a director, officer or stockholder of the same. (See following form.)

$69

 STATE OF PENNSYLVANIA COUNTY OF PHILADELPHIA 

-SS. 

On the seventh day of July, Anno Domini, 1911, before me the subscriber, a notary public for the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, residing in the City and County of Philadelphia, personally appeared the above named A.B. and in due form of law acknowledged the above indenture to be his act and deed and desired the same might be recorded as such. 

Witness my hand and seal the day and year aforesaid.

John Smith (Seal.) Notary Public. 

Commission expires June 11, 1913.

Since the Act of April 1, 1909, P.L. 91, the venue may possibly be omitted and the form of acknowledgment set forth at the end of short form of deed, §57, may be used for all purposes. a. Date. The date should appear. By this is meant the date when the deed is acknowledged, not when executed, although the best practice is to have the deed acknowledged as soon as it has been executed. The acknowledgment may be made at any time after execution, but the deed cannot be recorded until it is acknowledged. 

b. Venue. By venue is meant the place of residence of the officer taking the acknowledgment. In the form above given it appears in the words, "a notary public of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania residing in the City and County of Philadelphia." Should the officer be a magistrate or justice of the peace, the venue would read: A magistrate or justice of the peace of the County of Philadelphia, etc. c. The name of the grantor who makes the acknowledgment must, of course, appear. d. Signature of the officer taking the acknowledgment is obviously necessary to the validity of the certification. e. Official position of the officer taking the acknowledgment must appear in order that the authority of the officer to take acknowledgment may appear on the face of the certificate.

§69A 

169 DEEDS. f. Seal. The seal completes the act of certification and should appear after the signature. 

g. Expiration of Notary Public's Commission Date. 

Notary publics are required in addition to append the date when their commission expires under Act of April 4, 1901 (P.L. 70). h. Certification that Notary is not an Officer, Director or

Stockholder of the Bank or Trust Company whose Acknowledgment is taken.

In view of the Act of March 24, 1903, P.L. 50, which prohibits a director, officer, or stockholder of any bank, banking institution or trust company from performing duties of notary in his company, an acknowledgment or affidavit taken for any bank, banking institution or trust company should contain a certification by the notary in words such as following: "I am not a stockholder, director or officer of said company.' 99 

69-A. Effect of Certificate of Acknowledgment. 

A certificate of acknowledgment to a deed is prima facie evidence of the due execution of the deed including knowledge of its contents, but is subject to rebuttal where fraud is alleged, especially where there are no intervening rights 

(Pusick v. Salak, 261 Pa. 512—1918).

71. Notary Public. How to Become One. 

Notaries public are, however, the most usual officers before whom acknowledgments and affidavits are taken. Any per-

§71  

son, male or female, of good character, twenty-one years of age, is qualified to be a notary in Pennsylvania. Secure an application form by writing to the Secretary of the Commonwealth, Harrisburg, Pa. This form must be filled out according to the instructions indorsed thereon. The application must then be indorsed by the State senator of the senatorial district in which the applicant resides. It is then forwarded to the private secretary of the governor, together with two letter of reputable citizens recommending the applicant to be a person of good character. The application must also be accompanied by a certified check for $25.00. If the governor of the State approves the application, he appoints the applicant and if such appointment is confirmed by the senate, the commission issues. The commission runs for four years when the appointment is confirmed by the Senate, otherwise the commission reads "until the end of the next session of the Senate." This commission must be recorded at the office of the recorder of deeds of the county in which the notary resides, and a bond filed, and oath of office taken at the prothonotary's office. Should the senate not be in session when the application is made, the governor is authorized by law to issue a commission which expires at the expiration of the next session of the senate. When the senate convenes it may confirm the appointment and a new commission issues for four years from the date of confirmation.

In Harding v. Pinchot, 306 Pa. 139—1932, it was held the governor has absolute discretion in the matter of appointment of notaries and may refuse to appoint any particular person for any reason he may have or for no reason at all, and the Court will not interfere with his discretion. 

The bond which must be filed must be in an amount fixed by the Governor, and must have a duly authorized surety company as surety or two sufficient individual sureties to be approved by the Governor conditioned for the faithful performance of the duties of Notary Public, and for the delivery of his or her register and all other public papers into the office of the recorder of deeds of the proper county in case of

April 14, 1840, P.L. 334, §3, as amended by the Act of June 10, 1931, P.L. 480, §1, 57 P.S. §81). 

(a) Seal. By the Act of May 6, 1931, (P.L. 99, §1, 57 P.S. 

31), a Notary is required to provide a seal with which to authenticate all his acts, instruments and attestations. This seal to have engraved on it the name, surname, the words "Notary Public" and his location of office. This changes the device of the seal which formerly required the Coat of Arms of Pennsylvania and the place of the Notary's residence. 

(b) Residence. By the Act of June 10, 1931, (P.L. 479, 

57 P.S. 61, 62), even though a Notary's commission directs him to reside in a particular city, borough, town or township of any county he is authorized to have a domicile in any part of said county or of any adjoining county provided he shall keep an office in said city, borough, town or township of the county named in the commission: §2 of the Act makes valid all notarial acts theretofore or thereafter performed within the Commonwealth even outside of the place within the county for which he was commissioned but requires thereafter that the notary append to such notarial acts the name of the place for which he was commissioned.

A female notary that marries must, before the performance of any notarial act, return her commission to the governor, giving her married name, whereupon a new commission will issue to her in her new name for the unexpired term without any additional charge, although a new bond must be entered. 

By the Act of May 25, 1893, P.L. 136 (57 P.S. 61), the notarial acts of a notary done in the State outside of the place for which he was commissioned are also legalized. 

71-A. Responsibility and Liability of Notaries Public and 

Their Sureties.

As far back as 1879 a respected Judge of this county (Finletter, J.) in the case of Comm. v. Barrett, (6 W.N.C. 385 -1879), called attention to the importance of responsibility of the office of Notary Public and deplored the ease with which

§71A  

they could secure commissions "resulting in many inefficient persons securing commissions with the consequent possibility of injury to the public and to themselves."

However the public is not entirely without protection because both the Notary and his surety are liable on the bond filed for any injury resulting from official misconduct (Comm. v. Reilly, 16 D. & C. 311—1932). Such action is properly brought in the name of the Commonwealth (the obligee in the bond) to the use of the party aggrieved (Olson v. Goetz, 15 D. & C. 261-1931). In that case it was held that a statement averring that a Notary took the acknowledgment of two illiterate persons to a deed after informing them they were acknowledging a mortgage set forth a good cause of action. 

In Comm. v. Collar, (15 D.R. 317-1906), it was held the injured party could recover where a Notary forged a signature. But a Notary is not liable for an honest mistake in the identity of a person appearing before him; but if he takes the acknowledgment of an impostor not personally known to him, in reliance merely on an introduction by a third party he is responsible for the loss resulting therefrom (Comm. to use of Russell v. Fidelity, etc. Co., 17 D. & C. 416-1933 

M.C. Phila. County). Where a Notary forges the names of parties to a mortgage and then certifies thereto he and his surety are liable (Comm. v. Barrett, 6 W.N.C. 385-1879).

The same is true where a notary fraudulently affixes his 

Notarial Seal to a forged mortgage, (Comm. to use v. Turner et al., 39 D. & C. 252-1940). Where it is charged that a

Notary gave a false certificate of acknowledgment the burden of proof is on the plaintiff to show a clear intentional dereliction of duty, as a Notary's act is regarded as a judicial act and the presumption is, that the Notary acted on reasonable information and discharged his full duty (Comm. v. Haines, 97 Pa. 228-1881). 1 

(a) Notary's Record or Register. A Notary should pro vide himself with a register or record book for without it he will soon find his affairs in a maze of uncertainty and doubt.

When called on by the Court he should not expect to rely on 1 On appeal in this case (see 340 Pa. 468-1941) it was held that before a surety can be held liable, the plaintiff must show that the official misconduct of the notary caused the injury; (see also Shay v. Schrink 335 Pa. 94-1939).

§71B

DEEDS. 

his memory, which is apt to prove treacherous, but rather he should be able to turn to some authentic record of his official acts made at the time. Every act should be set down in ink, if possible, in some permanent form easily accessible, and in such manner as will state the substance of the attestation or acknowledgment clearly. Such record is not only desirable for the Notary, but is necessary by reason of the fact that the Federal and State governments can at any time call for a statement of the official acts of the Notary, which in order to be authentic must be based upon some written record. In this Notary's record should be set down the hour, day, month and year, for these become of vital importance if the correctness of his attestation is questioned. The names of the parties to an acknowledgment, affidavit, etc., should be carefully noted. The Notary's fees should also be set down. 

These Notary record books or registers can be purchased at most any law stationer. 

71-B. Notary Fees in Pennsylvania.

Notary fees are regulated by statute, namely, the Acts of 

March 28, 1814, 6 Sm. L. 228, §16, (57 P.S. 91); July 10, 1919, P.L. 903, §1, (57 P.S. 92); May 9, 1923, P.L. 180, §1; (57 P.S. 

92); May 20, 1865, P.L. 846, §1, (57 P.S. 93); Act of April 8, 1867, P.L. 892, §1, (57 P.S. 94); the last two acts applying to

Philadelphia and Allegheny Counties respectively though the Philadelphia Act of 1865 was afterward extended to Bedford, Fulton, Somerset and Delaware Counties and except for acknowledgment of deeds and mortgages was extended to Lycoming and Centre, Montour, Columbia, Westmoreland, Blair, Wyoming, and Snyder Counties; and see also Act of April 14, 1868, P.L. 1066 (57 P.S. 93 note), relating to York County.

The Act of 1865 required notaries public in Philadelphia to pay each and every year to the Treasury of the Commonwealth five per cent of the gross amount of their receipts, but this tax on fees of notaries was repealed by the Act of 1925, March 

19, P. L. 51, Act No. 32, §1. (57 P.S. 93 note).

§72  72. Probate of Deeds Where Grantor is Dead or Unable to Appear. 

By probate of deeds is meant proof of its execution by means other than acknowledgment. This may be done under the Act of May 28, 1715 (1 Sm. L. 94, §5 21 P.S. 471), which provides that if the grantor is dead or cannot appear, the deed may be proved by the affidavit of the two subscribing wit nesses. By the Act of March 18, 1775 (1 Sm. L. 422, 21 P.S. 

44) the oath of one witness is made sufficient. The usual method of probate is to endorse on the deed the affidavit of the witness that he saw the grantor execute the instrument. This affidavit is signed by the witness and attested by the magistrate or justice of the peace. The affidavit need not be signed by the witnesses although it is customary to have them do so. 

The attestation by the justice of the peace is the necessary thing (see form, §§216, 217). Probate of a deed entitles it to be recorded even though not acknowledged. 

Where the grantor and his witnesses are dead or cannot be found, a Justice of the Supreme Court or of the Court of 

Common Pleas is authorized, by the Act of Mar. 18, 1775 1 Sm. L. 422 §4 (21 P.S. 44) to examine witnesses to prove the handwriting of the grantor. In such a proceeding the judge is not concerned with possible defects in the grantees title but only whether the instrument is proved to have been executed by the grantor and should be recorded as such (Delahanty's 

Petition 29 D. & C. 277-1937).

NATURE OF MORTGAGE. ANALYSIS. 

73. Definition of Mortgage, Bond and Warrant.

A mortgage is a pledge of an estate in land, as collateral security for the repayment of money or performance of some other act. In form it recites the fact that the mortgagor is under obligation to pay a certain sum of money at a certain period and to pay interest at certain intervals. For the purpose of securing the performance of these covenants, certain land (described) is conveyed to the mortgagee which conveyance is defeasible on the performance of the covenants set forth (see form on page 188). Accompanying a mortgage, although not necessary to its validity we usually find an instrument called a bond and warrant which consists of a bond or an undertaking to repay the money set forth at the time fixed, and a warrant of attorney authorizing an attorney-atlaw to appear for and confess judgment for the obligee (see form, pages 199, 201).

The bond and mortgage are separate and distinct instru-

$185 

MORTGAGES. 

ments but are securities for one and the same debt. A mortgage creates a lien, as will be hereinafter explained, on the particular property described therein. The bond and warrant of itself creates no lien until entered of record as a judgment, when it becomes a judgment lien against all of the defendant's real estate from the date of its entry, but as to mortgaged property the lien relates back to the date the mortgage was recorded (Keene Home v. Startzell, 235 Pa. 1101912). In some instances when the mortgaged premises have depreciated in value and the mortgagor has other property the advantages of proceeding on the bond and warrant are obvious. For this reason a bond and warrant is usually demanded and given along with the mortgage. 

74. History and Development of Mortgages. 

A brief résumé of the history and the development of mortgages is interesting as well as instructive. The early English used two forms of mortgages or pledges of land, one known as the "vivum vadium" and the other as the "mortuum vadium." In a vivum vadium the land was conveyed to the creditor to hold until out of the rents, issues and profits the creditor could pay the debt, when the debtor was entitled to receive back the land. In the mortuum vadium the land was conveyed unto the creditor, who took possession and held it until the debt was paid; during this time the rents, etc., were not applied to the reducing of the debt, but were retained by the creditor. Manifestly this was a most rigorous and harsh kind of a pledge, and soon fell into disuse. Later this form was modified so that possession of the land was not given to the creditor unless the debt was not paid upon a certain day fixed. This modification became the modern mortgage (i.e. mort (dead) gage (pledge)) so called, says Littleton, "because if the money was not paid on the day fixed the land was forfeited and became "dead" to the mortgagor. If it was paid then the pledge became "dead" to the mortgagee." It will be observed that this mortgage differed from its forerunners, the vivum vadium and mortuum vadium in this very

§75  

material point. In the latter class of pledges possession of the land was given when the debt was created and the instrument made, in the former the mortgagee or creditor never was given possession of the land unless the mortgage debt was not paid. 

75. Origin of Equity Redemption of a Mortgage. 

The common law form of the mortgage was thus strictly an estate on condition. In other words, if the condition was performed, i.e., if the money was paid at the time stipulated, the interest of the mortgagee was extinguished. If, on the other the condition was broken, that is, if the money was not paid, an absolute fee simple estate vested in the mortgagee and all right of the mortgagor was gone. It frequently happened that land of great value was mortgaged for an amount equal to half the value and very often less than half value. 

The forfeiture in such instances was a very great hardship against which the common law courts could give no relief. In such instances the mortgagors turned to the equity courts (See $10 on Equity, supra.) for relief. The equity courts decided that while it was true, strict interpretation of the common law vested in the mortgagee absolute title upon the breach of the condition at the time fixed, still justice required that the mortgagor be given a further opportunity to redeem the property and if he could pay back to the mortgagee the debt, interest and costs he should have his land back. This right to redeem the property after forfeiture naturally came to be called the "Equity Redemption". And the name still survives in the expression termed a person's "equity" in property by which is meant, of course, the interest a person has in a property over and above the mortgage. At first no time was set within which the right of redemption in equity had to be applied for, and it naturally followed that the mortgagee felt insecure as to his right to the property even though the land was forfeited and the mortgagor had made no move in equity to redeem it. This led to great uncertainty and worked a hardship upon the mortgagee since he feared to

$187 

MORTGAGES. 

improve the land because his occupation might later be disturbed. Consequently the mortgagees in turn began to go to the equity court for relief and filed what was known as a "bill of foreclosure", in which he asked to have the mortgagor's right of equity redemption ended or "foreclosed" as it were. 

The equity court would then fix a certain day at or before which the debtor, that is the mortgagor, was required to pay his debt and if he failed to obey the order of the court the estate became absolutely forfeited to the mortgagee. Of course, this to a certain extent again involved a hardship upon the mortgagor, who often was willing but unable to pay the money to redeem his property. The matter was finally and most justly settled by a statute or act of Parliament which authorized the equity court to sell the property at the request of either party and to pay the balance of the proceeds realized from the sale to the mortgagor. In some states, New Jersey, e.g., foreclosure suits are still brought in equity. 

Remedies in Pennsylvania. In Pennsylvania it has been held (Donley v. Semans 26 D. R. 235-1916) the remedies upon a mortgage after maturity or default are three: First, an action at law: Second, the ancient common law remedy of entry or ejectment whereby the mortgagee gains possession and takes the profits of the estate subject, however, to the equity of redemption in the mortgagor: Third, the scire facias, commonly referred to as sci. fa., given by the old provincial 

Act of 1705 (1 Sm. L. 57 §6, 21 P.S. 791), whereby the equity of redemption can be "foreclosed" and the mortgaged property sold at Sheriff's Sale (Atkinson v. Walton, 162 Pa. 219—1894).

The sci. fa. act was held to be a new proceeding and not a substitute for the common law remedy of ejectment which still exists (Smith v. Shuler, 12 S. & R., 240—1824, Bauer v. Fenn, 90 Pa. 359-1879).

There was no equity jurisdiction in our courts to entertain bills of equity to foreclose a mortgage (Ashurst v. Montour 

Iron Co., 35 Pa. 30-1860); unless the mortgage raises a trust and then a bill of foreclosure may lie only at the instance of the cestui que trust (Bradley v. Chester Val. R.R. Co., 36 Pa.

$76 

141-1860). At present there is still no such equity jurisdiction in Pennsylvania except in the case of corporate mortgages as to which, under the Act of April 11, 1862, P.L. 477 

(see Bruckman L. Co. v. Pittsburg Ins. Co., 307 Pa. 561, 564 

-1932) and Act of May 4, 1893, P.L. 29 (17 P.S. 285; See 

Girard Trust Co. v. Avonmore Land Co., 221 Pa. 52-1908), there is such jurisdiction. 

76. Effect of a Mortgage in Pennsylvania. 

It will therefore be seen that our modern Pennsylvania Mortgage is much different in its nature and effect from that at common law. Though as between the immediate parties thereto it is still a conveyance of land upon condition, so far as third parties are concerned it is to all practical purposes but an encumbrance or a lien against the mortgaged property which cannot be divested by private sale and if subject to no prior judgment lien, even by a sheriff's sale on subsequent liens. The legal nature and effect of our modern mortgage will hereinafter (§81-C) be more fully discussed after we have analyzed the various parts and clauses of the mortgage and bond. See also Bulger v. Wilderman et. al. 101 Pa. Super.

Ct. 168-1931, for a learned discussion of the subject by President Judge Keller.

On behalf of the Mortgagee. 1 By examination thereof it will be seen that it consists of two principal parts; first, a conveyance of the property; and second, a defeasance, i.e., a contemporaneous agreement that the conveyance shall be as security only. 

1 It will be noted that a mortgage instrument is even called an "Indenture.”’

§(a)1 193 

MORTGAGES. 

The conveyance part extends from the beginning of the instrument to the words "Provided Always Nevertheless".

This conveyance part may in turn be divided into two parts consisting of (a) the premises or whereas clause and (b) the conveyance proper or deed part. 

(1) Conveyance Part: (a) Premises: The premises ex tend from the beginning of the mortgage to the words "Now this Indenture Witnesseth" (see form, page 188), and recites the names of the parties, the day, the debt and the terms. 

The premises then recites the accompanying obligation or bond in a summarized form and sets forth the conditions under which the mortgage debt becomes payable. These conditions include (1) to repay the mortgage principal at the stipulated time and to pay interest thereon at the stipulated rate and times; (2) to reduce tax and water rent receipts annually; (3) a requirement to keep the mortgaged premises insured; (4) that foreclosure may be instituted upon default and attorneys fee paid. 

(1) Term of the Mortgage:-Interest. The time fixed in the mortgage at which the mortgage principal becomes payable is known as the term of the mortgage. In the form hereinabove set forth the principal sum is payable "at the expiration of five years from the date hereof". This means it cannot be paid off by the property owner nor demanded by the mortgagee before that time without consent of the other. Where, however, a mortgage reads, "payable within one year from the date hereof", it means the mortgagor can pay it off at any time, but the mortgagee cannot demand it until the year has expired (Schotte v. Meredith, 138 Pa. 165-1890). Where no time is fixed for the payment of the principal sum of the mortgage, the law supplies the omitted element and makes the debt due immediately (Rhone v. Keystone Coal Co., 250 Pa. 3361915).

When a mortgage becomes due and both parties are agreeable the term of the mortgage may be renewed or extended by what is called an agreement of extension (see

§77(a)2 

$103-C infra) which need not be and rarely is recorded (For form see $224). The extension of the time of payment of a mortgage in absence of fraud does not impair its priority or standing as a lien (Beckman v. Altoona Trust Co. 332 Pa. 

545-1938). But even without an extension of mortgage the lien continues until the mortgage debt is paid (Beckman v. 

Altoona Trust Co. Supra.)

Interest is, of course, payable at the times stipulated in the mortgage which may be annually, semi-annually, quarterly or even monthly, and at the rate as agreed to by the parties. 

Customarily it is fixed semi-annually except in building and loan association mortgages. Where a mortgage stipulated interest at the rate of five per cent, but the principal was not demanded when due and the mortgagee continued to accept interest at five per cent, it was held there was an implication that the loan might continue at the five per cent rate (Howes 

Executors v. Milliron, 30 D.R. 405-1921). But where a fragment of the principal sum of the mortgage is withheld after maturity without consent of the mortgagee, the mortgagee is entitled to interest at the legal rate (6%) from the date it should have been paid even though the rate stipulated in the mortgage was but three per cent (Ludwig v. Huntzinger, 5 

W. & S. 51-1842). 

(2) Production of Tax and Water Rent Receipts:-Since taxes become a liens ahead of the mortgage, the mortgage provides that the receipts for the payment thereof must be produced annually on or before the time fixed in the mortgage. 

This enables the mortgagee to assure himself that the taxes and water rent have in fact been paid. It has been held that a condition in a bond and mortgage requiring production of tax and water rent receipts by the mortgagor in order to avoid default does not constitute a promise to pay such taxes or water rents. The obligation of the registered owner to pay the taxes is one which arises by law and entitles the mortgagee to reimbursement if compelled to pay the same because of the registered owner's failure to do so (Germantown Trust Co. v.

Stanley Co. 338 Pa. 533-1940 Penna. Co. v. Bergson 307 Pa. 

44-1932).

§(a)3 195 

MORTGAGES. 

(3) Insurance Clause:-Mortgages on improved property all require the premises to be insured in an amount equal to the mortgage. The fire policy is issued in the name of the owner of the property but has attached thereto what is called a "standard mortgagee fire clause," by the terms of which the loss is payable to the mortgagee. The possession of this policy is given to the mortgagee. If the policy is cancelled by the company or expires before the mortgage debt is paid, the property owner must replace it with a new one else a default occurs. Pursuant to the Act of June 8, 1915 P.L. 919, reenacted by the Act of May 17, 1921, P.L. 682 (40 P.S. 658), a standard of form of mortgagee clause or rider is used by all fire insurance companies which has been frequently construed by our Courts; (See Miners Bank, etc. v. Merchant's Fire Ins. 

Co., 131 Pa. Super. Ct. 21-1938, where these cases will be found collected by Judge Rhodes and where a copy of such standard form of mortgagee clause appears in the footnote to page 22). In general it may be said "a mortgagee clause attached to a fire policy is not an assignment of the policy or a loss clause payable to the mortgagee, but an independent contract of insurance" (Knights of Joseph B. & L. Ass'n. v. 

Mechanics Fire Co., 66 Pa. Super. Ct. 90-1917; Overholt v. 

Reliance Ins. Co., 319 Pa. 340—1935). But, nevertheless, such insurance contract with the mortgagee is composed of the provisions in the mortgage clause and such of those in the policy as are essentially applicable to the mortgagee clause and the mortgagee's interest (Miners Bank, etc. v. Merchants Fire 

Ins. Co., 131 Pa. Super. Ct. 21-1938). So in Abbottsford 

B. & L. Assn. v. William Penn Fire Ins. Co., 130 Pa. Super. Ct. 

422-1938 it was held an Insurance Co. has under the standard mortgagee clause of Pennsylvania, the same option as to the mortgagee to restore the premises as it has against the owner and mortgagee cannot demand payment in cash. 

1 For history and origin of Fire Insurance Mortgage Clause see excellent lec ture to Phila. Bar Assn. entitled, Rights of Mortgagees under Policies of Fire 

Insurance by Horace Michener Schell, Esq. of the Philadelphia Bar, published in Legal Intelligencer of Feb. 26, 1938. See this article also for a clear exposition of the legal rights of the respective parties concerned, arising under the mortgagee clause.

§77 (b) 

It has been held that the insurance clause in a mortgage operates as an equitable assignment of a fire policy so that suit thereon can be maintained even though a policy is issued in the name of the property owner without a mortgagee clause attached (Ruppin v. Perkiomen Valley, etc. Ins. Co., 6 D. & C. 

271-1924). 

(4) Default Clause: Attorneys' Fees:-The failure of the mortgagor or property owner to keep these conditions makes the principal sum of the mortgage immediately demandable at the option of the mortgagee and permits him to invoke the appropriate remedy provided by law or by the mortgage or bond as recited in the so-called sci. fa. clause which follows, though a mortgagee is by no means limited to this remedy alone. Included in the sci. fa. clause is usually found an agreement to pay the mortgagee's attorneys' fee or commission for collection at a rate stipulated, customarily five per cent. 

This attorneys' commission has been held by the Courts to be in the nature of a penalty and subject to the equitable control of the Court, and when excessive, will be reduced to a reasonable compensation. However, such agreement is strictly legal 

(Daly v. Maitland, 88 Pa. 384-1879; Cunningham v. 

McCready, 219 Pa. 594-1908). In Jarvis v. Stoffal, 54 Pa.

Super. Ct. 362-1913, an attorney's fee of fifty dollars was held sufficient where judgment was merely entered on a mortgage bond of $2000. (5) Conveyance Proper:-Then follows what may be called the conveyance proper or deed part. It reads exactly like a deed from the consideration clause to the end of the habendum clause. Only the conclusion and warranty clause is omitted (compare with deed on page 116). In this part of the mortgage is inserted the description of the property mortgaged (see form of mortgage, page 190) and following it the recital, at the conclusion of which is placed, should the mortgage be a second mortgage, the appropriate under and subject clause, which in such case would read as follows:-

$197 

MORTGAGES. 

"Under and subject nevertheless to a certain mortgage debt or principal sum of 

Dollars with interest thereon as the same may become due and payable" (see page 117). 

(II) Defeasance:-The remainder (see form page 191), of the mortgage is the defeasance. This is the contemporaneous agreement which provides that if the mortgagee is paid the principal of the debt on the day set forth and the conditions set forth in the conveyance part of the agreement be faithfully kept, then the indenture and estate thereby granted as well as the recited obligation or bond shall cease, determine and become void. This defeasance clause therefore converts an apparent absolute deed into a pledge. 

78. Where Defeasance Is Not Annexed to the Conveyance. 

As above intimated although usually the conveyance part of a mortgage and defeasance are always found annexed together or in one instrument, the law does not require them to be fastened together, but when separate they must be executed in strict accordance with the terms of the Act of June 8, 1881, P.L. 84, (21 P.S. 951). The requirements of this act are well stated in the words of Justice Gordon delivering an opinion of the Supreme Court where he says:- "There is now but one method left by which a deed absolute on its face can be reduced to a mortgage; the defeasance must not only be in writing and of the same date as that of the deed, but must also be signed, sealed, acknowledged and delivered by the grantee in the deed to the grantor. Furthermore it must be recorded in the recorder of Deeds' office in the county where the land lies within sixty days after the execution thereof" (Sankey v. Hawley, 118 Pa. 30-1888). See also 

Grove v. Kase, 195 Pa. 325-1900; Safe Deposit Co. v. Linton, 213 Pa. 105-1905; O'Donnell v. Vandersaal, 213 Pa. 5511906; McHendry v. Shaffer, 242 Pa. 476-1913.

Under the decisions a defeasance is not receivable in evidence to defeat an absolute deed unless it was made and re-

$78 

corded in accordance with the provisions of this act. The provisions of this act have been modified in two material particulars by the Act of April 23, 1909, P.L. 137 (21 P.S. 951); which while still requiring that the defeasance in order to reduce a deed absolute on its face, to a mortgage, be in writing, signed and delivered by the grantee to the grantor, omits the words made at the same time the deed is made. Further this new act provides "and in so far as it may effect any subsequent grantee or mortgagee of such real estate for value", unless it is also acknowledged and recorded, &c., before the execution and delivery of such subsequent grant or mortgage. 

The words in italics are not contained in the old Act of June 8, 1881, and are manifestly more equitable to both parties since the only one who ought really be protected by enforcing the recording are subsequent grantees and mortgagees who have given value on faith of the absolute deed appearing of record. 

Thus is done away with the hardship which followed where the intended mortgagee claimed the benefit of the omission to comply with the technical requirements of the Act of 1881, and thus secured for himself a fee simple title where he was only meant to have a mortgage.

In Burkhart v. Insurance Company, 11 Pa. Super. Ct. 2801899, it was held that third parties who had no interest, were not in position to raise the question as to the sufficiency of the defeasance.

It should also be noted that the Act of 1881 as modified does not apply to an agreement by a grantee to re-convey property upon the repayment of the sum loaned. The act is regarded as being confined strictly to deeds which operate to defeat the main conveyance and has no application to separate undertakings to re-convey the property even though the whole transaction may, in fact, amount to a mortgage (King's Estate, 215 Pa. 59-1906).

In practice it is best to avoid all questions by adhering to the form wherein the conveyance and defeasance are contained in one instrument.

$199 

MORTGAGES. 

79. Certificate of Residence of Mortgagees. 

By the Act of April 29, 1909, P.L. 289; (21 P.S. 625) all mortgages, assignments or agreements given to secure the payment of money at interest must contain a certificate signed by the mortgagee, assignee, &c., or his or her duly authorized agent setting forth the precise residence of the mortgagee, assignee or party entitled to the interest money. The Recorder is bound under this act to refuse to receive for record any such mortgage assignment or agreement unless it contains such a certificate of residence. The object of this act is to enable the tax assessors to ascertain the names and addresses of all persons who have money at interest in order that they may be properly taxed. The certificate required need not be inserted in the body of the instrument. Nor is it required to be any more formal than a mere statement of 

Residence such as the following:

I hereby certify that my residence is 1321 M. Street, Philadelphia, Pa. 

RICHARD BROWN 

This may be indorsed on the back of the Mortgage or written along the margin. This certificate need not necessarily be made by the mortgagee, his agent or anyone cognizant of his address may certify it.

(Seal) (Seal) The bond and warrant of attorney to confess judgment are really two separate instruments although they are usually spoken of as if but one, and this probably because they are usually fastened together. The bond itself as may be seen from the form set forth above recites the fact that the maker thereof, called the obligor, (who is the mortgagor in the mortgage) holds himself indebted to the obligee (mortgagee) in the sum of seven thousand ($7,000.00) dollars. The amount of the bond is by custom made in double the amount of the sum

$81 

really due, doubtless in order to amply protect the obligee as to interest and costs, should proceedings thereon become necessary. Following the bond proper which is nothing more or less than an acknowledgment of indebtedness, comes the conditions of the bond.

The conditions of the bond are the same as those found in the mortgage, (See §77), viz. to repay at the expiration of the term fixed (here five years) the principal sum due (here $3,500.00), and interest thereon at the times and rate fixed; to produce receipts for taxes and water rents assessed on the mortgaged premises at the time fixed (usually September 1st, every year); to maintain fire insurance as collateral in an amount equal to the sum due (here $3,500.00) upon the buildings on which the mortgage is made. It then recites that if these conditions are performed the obligation or bond is to become void or otherwise to remain in full force, virtue and effect.

It provides further that if default is made in the production of the taxes and water rent receipts or in the payment of interest or maintenance of the insurance, then the whole amount of the bond is to become immediately due and payable and proceedings may be commenced to recover the same, &c. and judgment may be confessed against the obligor on the accompanying warrant of attorney, with an attorney's commission for collection of five per cent, added to the amount due, or that proceedings might be commenced on the accompanying indenture of mortgage. It contains a waiver of the debtors exemption law as well as a waiver of inquisition, as to which see next § (81). 

81. Warrant of Attorney. Proceedings on the Bond and 

Warrant and on a Mortgage Compared.

The warrant of attorney is an instrument which provides the holder with a short cut to obtain judgment. Ordinarily to recover money due, a suit must be instituted which if contested may result in some time, before a judgment can be recovered and even if uncontested it takes about three weeks

§

205 

MORTGAGES. 

before judgment can be entered. Obviously an instrument which enables a judgment to be placed on record instantly without any delay whatsoever is of immense advantage, especially if it is desirable to obtain a prior lien on other property of the mortgagor and beat out some other creditor who is suing to obtain a judgment. A warrant of attorney is therefore a valuable addition to the bond and proceedings thereon afford a complete remedy exclusive of the mortgage proceedings. A judgment so entered becomes a general judgment lien not only against the mortgaged premises but against all real estate owned by the mortgagor at the time the judgment is entered. But while the lien of the judgment so entered relates back to the date of the recording of the mortgage so far as the mortgaged property is concerned (Keene Home v. Startzell, 235 Pa. 110-1912), as to other property of the mortgagor the judgment is a lien only from the date of its entry.

Among the advantages of proceeding on the bond may be mentioned the speed with which the foreclosure can be pursued. Another advantage of proceeding on the bond is that the Act of 1901 (July 9, P.L. 614, §10; 12 P.S. §309), re quiring an affidavit naming the real owner of the mortgaged property to be filed, is restricted in its application to Sci. fa. proceedings on the mortgage only (Keene Home v. Startzell, Supra; West Arch B. & L. Ass'n. v. Nichols, 303 Pa. 4341931). Proceeding on the bond therefore obviates the necessity of ascertaining whether the ownership of the mortgaged property has been conveyed by the mortgagor to another; information sometimes difficult to obtain where the deed of transfer is not promptly recorded. However, in Philadelphia

County this advantage has disappeared by reason of a rule of court, (No. 96) which prohibits execution on such judgment unless an affidavit is first filed setting forth the name, address of the real owner, and that notice of the date of the entry of the judgment has been sent by registered mail to the owner as well as to the obligor in the bond. This rule of court also requires that at or after the issuance of the writ of execution

§81  

ten days written notice by personal service or registered mail of the place, date and hour of the intended sale and the real estate intended to be sold, must be given to the "defendant in the writ" and to the owner and before the sale, and an affidavit must be filed that said notice has been properly given. 

If, however, the name and address of the real owner or defendant is not known and cannot be ascertained, an affidavit to that effect is regarded as sufficient compliance with the rule.' 

On the other hand a judgment cannot be entered by confession on a bond after the death of the mortgagor, because death automatically revokes the warrant of attorney to confess judgment, (Lanning v. Pawson, 38 Pa. 480-1861; Kummerle v. Cain, 82 Pa. Super. Ct. 528-1924); though it can be entered against the survivor of two obligors (Croasdell v. 

Tallant, 83 Pa. 193-1876; Woodward v. Carson, 208 Pa. 

144-1904). The converse however is not true, viz., the death of the obligee does not prevent judgment being entered against a living obligor, but should regularly be entered in the name of the deceased's personal representatives (Aiken v. Mayberry, 128 Pa. Super. Ct. 15-1937). Where a bond and warrant is more than ten years old, a judgment by confession thereon can only be entered by leave of Court and if more than twenty years old only after a rule to show cause on the de fendant (Rule No. 138, Rules of Courts of Common Pleas, 

Philadelphia County; similar rules prevail in most of the other counties of the State).

Where the obligor-mortgagor was admittedly sane when the Bond and Mortgage was executed but becomes insane thereafter, the proper procedure is to apply to the Court for leave to enter judgment by confession against him (Moore's Case 

133 Pa. Super. Ct. 419—1938).

The form of the bond and warrant here set forth entitles the mortgagee to enter judgment even before any default and before maturity, for it contains no restriction or condition requiring maturity or default before confession of the judgment, but execution cannot issue until default has occurred or maturity has arrived (O'Maley v. Pugliese, 272 Pa. 356-1922; 

1 By rule of court #240 (Legal Intel. Mar. 11, 1941; vol. See infra §81-A (c) for discussion of the effect of a "waiver clause'' in this regard.

Integrity Insurance, etc. Co. v. Rau, 153 Pa. 488, 1893), and upon application to the Court, execution if issued, will be restrained (Durso v. Fiorini, 98 Pa. Super. Ct. 111–1929; Mellon v. Ritz, 332 Pa. 97—1938).

It will be seen therefore that by having the loan secured both by a mortgage and bond and warrant, the mortgagee has his choice of remedies and has not only a remedy against the property mortgaged but a personal right against the mortgagor as well. But when a mortgagee proceeds and sells under a judgment entered on the bond, the mortgage is divested and he cannot thereafter proceed by Sci. fa. on the mortgage, (Penna. Co. etc. Trustee v. Emmons et al., 338 Pa. 

81-A. Waiver Clauses of Bond and Warrant. (a) Waiver of Exemption. The form here set forth waives the benefit of the debtor's exemption law which at present exempts from levy and sale (exclusive of wearing apparel of the defendant and his family, bibles and school books, which are also exempt) property to the value of $300.00 (Act of Apr. 

9, 1849; P.L. 533, 12 P.S. §2161). Such waivers have been upheld, being regarded as personal privileges (Billmeyer v. 

Evans, 40 Pa. 324-1861; Front and Huntington B. & L. 

Ass'n. v. Berzinski, 130 Pa. Super. Ct. 297-1938). (b) Waiver of Inquisition. At an early date the legislature took steps to protect land from forced sales for debts. 

The Act of 1705, 1 Sm. L. 57, provided that lands which in seven years would yield sufficient rent to pay debt, interest and costs, could not be sold for debt and a sale of real estate on a writ of fieri facias (fi. fa.) could not issue unless there was first an inquiry or inquisition to determine whether it could in seven years discharge the debt (Levy v. Spitz 297 Pa. 

136-1929). But it was held that such procedure was for the benefit of the debtor and that it could be waived (Levy v. 

Spitz Supra; Overton v. Tozer, 7 Watts, 331-1838). Such

§81A  

a waiver is included in the form of bond and warrant set forth in $80.

The practice prevalent in Philadelphia permitting real estate to be sold without inquisition when a judgment was entered on a note or a bond containing an express waiver of inquisition and condemnation was first recognized by the Act of June 16, 1836 P.L. 769, (12 P.S. 2383), substantially re enacted by the Act of May 10, 1881 P.L. 13 (12 P.S. 2382 and 

2383 note. See Levy v. Spitz, 297 Pa. 136-1929), and confirmed by the Act of Apr. 21, 1921, P.L. 206 (12 P.S. 2384), and which extended the operation of the waiver so as to make it effective not only against the mortgagor but also against any subsequent owner of the liened property (Altoona Trust 

Co. v. Fockler, 311 Pa. 426, 434-1933). Finally by the Act of May 6, 1929, P.L. 1557, sale is now authorized of the mortgaged real estate under a judgment on the bond accompanying such mortgage upon a writ of fi. fa. without inquisition or any other writ. This act was held to be constitutional in West 

Arch B. & L. Ass'n. v. Nichols, 303 Pa. 434—1931, and strictly speaking the need of a waiver of inquisition is no longer necessary if the mortgagor is still the owner of the property. 

It is better however to still use a form of bond and warrant containing the waiver of inquisition clause, because the Act of 1929 applies only to a sale of the mortgaged premises and would not authorize the sale of other property of the debtor without inquisition or without a waiver thereof nor where the mortgagor is no longer the owner of the property sought to be sold. Moreover, if the Act of 1929 were repealed the mortgagee could still pursue the same right under the waiver of inquisition clause. (c) Waiver of Exemption from Civil Process While in Mili tary or Naval Service. 

Since 1861 (see Act of Apr. 18, 1861, P.L. 408), it has become customary for the State and National governments whenever war occurs to protect those called to military or naval service by exempting them from the issuance of or enforce-
