ment against them of civil process while in active service. 

This was done by the Act of Apr. 28, 1899 P.L. 133 §59; 

Act of April 9, 1915, P.L. 80; Act of May 3, 1917, P.L. 113, $50; Act of June 22, 1917, P.L. 628, §34. (51 P.S. 201)

While these acts have now all been repealed it is likely that another war would find similar statutes immediately enacted for they have been held constitutional in Breitenbach v. Bush, 44 Pa. 313—1863.¹ No one can quarrel with the principle that those called to the military or naval services are entitled to both consideration and indulgence from their creditors, but the fact remains that during the last World War there were many abuses of these "stay laws", which were not only too frequently invoked by those who did not need to do so and others from unworthy motives-not to protect the home, but to "milk" the properties of the rents and leave a mortgagee at his wit's end because of the deprivation of his income for the duration of the war.

If it be desired to guard against such a condition arising in some future war, the following exemption clause may be inserted in the bond and warrant: "It is hereby expressly agreed that the obligor, his heirs, executors, administrators and assigns, waives and relinquishes all rights and benefits of any and all acts, Federal or State, passed or which may in the future be passed, exempting from civil process or the enforcement thereof against persons in the military or naval service of the United States or of this State, or granting any stay of execution to such persons." 

As to the propriety of inserting such a provision no opinion is expressed. war occurs. The presence of the clause would enable a mortgagee to differentiate between worthy and unworthy and grant indulgence to a soldier's family when needed or refuse it if not deserved.

That such a waiver would be valid seems to be conceded by the general authority. Thus in Breitenbach v. Bush, 44 Pa. 

313-1863, it was said, "We have often said that stay laws, exemption laws and limitation laws are ordinarily constitutional, though applied to existing and prior contracts, and we have followed the distinction which prevails in the Supreme Court of the United States between the obligation of the contract and the remedies furnished by law for enforcing the obligation. We understand the rule to be that whilst the legislature may not impair the obligation, they may modify the remedy. But it sometimes happens that the parties contract concerning the remedy-that they stipulate in the body of the contract that in case of failure of payment by a certain day there shall be no stay of execution, or that the mortgagee, may enter and sell the mortgaged estate or that exemption rights shall be waived. In such cases the rule is that the remedy becomes part of the obligation of the contract and any subsequent statute which effects the remedy impairs the obligation and is unconstitutional." The validity of a "stay waiver" was as against such an act expressly upheld in 

Snyder v. Ayres, 46 Co. Ct. 60; 65 Pitts, 533-1917, and it seems to be generally so held, 50 C. J., §251, p. 558. 

81-B. How Personal Liability on Bond May Be Avoided: 

Straw Man. Act of 1903. 

(a) Strawman Bond. It is to avoid personal liability on the bond that mortgages are sometimes made by a so-called "straw man". That is, if a responsible person desires to have a mortgage, without personal liability, placed upon a property he is about to buy, he causes the property to be conveyed to some person without financial responsibility-the "straw man❞—-and this "straw man" executes the mortgage and bond and warrant to the mortgagee, then conveys the

§81B 

211 

MORTGAGES. 

premises, subject to the mortgage thus created, to the real owner. In this way the "straw man" only is liable on the bond and warrant and being financially irresponsible, the mortgagee is confined solely to his remedy on the mortgage. 

This method of protecting oneself from personal liability on a mortgage is usually practiced by persons who deal extensively in real estate. Such men from the very nature of their business cannot afford to be personally responsible for the payment of the principal of a mortgage after they have conveyed away the property, yet they would be so long as the mortgage remains if they executed the bond. 

But it should be noted the efficacy of this protection is based on the fact that the "straw man" continues to remain financially irresponsible, for should the "straw man" afterwards become a man of substance, financially speaking, and compelled to pay the amount of the bond, the real party will be liable to the straw man upon the implied covenant of indemnity arising from the under and subject clause in the deed (see $54 (g)1. Thus in Aronson v. Heymann 56 Pa.

Super. Ct. 501-1914, where an agreement of sale provided that the vendor was to receive as part of the purchase money a second mortgage of $5,000 (straw bond) this was held not to refer to the covenants of the bond for the bond is a real bond, but made by a man supposed to be execution proof, and where the "straw man" subsequently became a man of financial responsibility and was compelled to pay the bond he was allowed to recover from the vendee the amount paid. 

To guard against this possibility the real party when taking title from his "straw man" should also take from him a full release of any future liability to indemnify under the "under and subject" clause (See $54 (g)1. 

(b) Release Under Act of 1903. 

Where no straw man is used to create a mortgage the personal liability of the mortgagor continues even after he has parted with the title in fact as long as the mortgage remains. 

This is so even where the purchaser expressly assumes and

§81B  

agrees to pay the mortgage (Martin v. Mathews, 26 D.R. 951917). The Act of 1903 (April 28, P.L. 327; 21 P.S. 735), however, provides a method by which a mortgagor who has parted with the title to the mortgaged premises may call in his bond and warrant after expiration of the term of the mortgage. Under this act he must first tender to the mortgagee (or to his assignee or whoever may be the holder of the mortgage) the full amount of the mortgage principal with interest to day of tender, and demand that the mortgage be assigned to him. Upon refusal of the holder of the mortgage to accept tender and comply with the demand, the mortgagor may petition court for a decree relieving him of all personal liability under the bond and warrant. Thereafter the holder of the mortgage must look solely to the land as his security. 

This act furnishes a full and complete method of procedure but must be strictly followed (Brecht v. Bealis, 19 Pa. D.R. 

664-1910). The decree obtained by the mortgagor may be indexed at the prothonotary's office and noted on the margin of the record of the mortgage at the recorder of deeds office. 

The purpose, effect and scope of this Act of 1903 was fully discussed in Willock's Estate, (58 Pa. Super. Ct. 159—1914), cited and approved by the Supreme Court in Kiedaisch v. 

Elkins Bank, 325 Pa. 241, 249—1937, where it was said, "Attention is called to the fact that this act refers to the bond and mortgage given by the mortgagor according to its terms and conditions, not to a bond and mortgage loaded down with new conditions imposed by others to which the mortgagor is not a party, but the bond and mortgage as they existed at the time he signed them." Thus where the mortgagee signs an extension of mortgage agreement with the subsequent owner or otherwise materially alters the terms and conditions without securing the consent of the mortgagor, the mortgage is entitled to a decree of exoneration if he proceeds under this 

Act. 

(c) Release in Bond or Mortgage.

Of course the collection of the mortgage debt may be restricted to the mortgaged premises by an express provision

$213 

MORTGAGES. 

in the bond or mortgage or separate agreement in writing. 

Thus in Neville v. Kretzchmar 271 Pa. 222-1921 where it was provided "Recourse on bond with mortgage to be had against mortgaged premises only," was held to be effective to exempt the mortgagor from personal liability. 

81-C. Remedy by Rent Seizure or Taking Possession of 

Mortgaged Real Estate. 

(a) Mortgagee's Rights to Seize Rents. 

It frequently happens that a mortgagee would prefer not to foreclose when default is made, yet unless he moves to protect himself the mortgagor or owner will collect rent and keep it for his own use paying neither taxes, interest nor repair charges. This is called in real estate parlance "milking" a mortgaged property. Or some owners will remain in possession and pay neither rent, taxes nor interest. To meet such conditions a mortgagee not willing to acquire the property by foreclosure has an ample remedy. This is to notify the tenant of the default in the terms of the mortgage and require payment of future rents to the mortgagee. The basis of this remedy was stated in Alexander's Estate (No. 2) (34 

D. & C. 170, 172-1938) to be: "A mortgage in Pennsylvania while generally regarded as a mere encumbrance or lien so far as third parties are concerned, is nevertheless between the mortgagor (or his successors in title) and the mortgagee strictly a conveyance on condition-a conveyance which usually includes an express assignment of rents, issues and profits so that upon breach, the mortgagee cannot only take possession and hold the same until the default has been cured or the mortgage repaid, but may make the assignment of the rents, issues and profits effective by merely notifying the tenant to pay the rent thereafter to the mortgagee, his at torney or agent (Miles et al. v. Abe Kolsky Co., Inc., 13 D. & C. 

579-1930, Finletter, P.J.), see also excellent and illuminating 1 營 ​* 1 (See form of mortgage, at page 190) clause that reads "Together with all and singular the buildings * and the Reversions and Remainders, Rents, Issues and Profits thereof.'

§81C  

opinion of President Judge Keller in Bulger v. Wilderman, et al., (101 Pa. Super. Ct., 168-1931), and Harper v. Consolidated Rubber Co., (284 Pa. 444, 451-1925), as well as Randal v. Jersey Mortgage Investment Co., (306 Pa. 1—1932). 

By virtue of the conveyance in a mortgage, of rents, issues and profits, the mortgagee upon default may require rents accruing after notice to be paid him even as against an attaching creditor who attached prior to default and notice but upon a judgment subsequent to the mortgage. This for the reason that an attaching creditor's rights rise no higher than those of his judgment debtor (Miners Savings Bank v. 

Thomas 140 Pa. Super. Ct. 5—1940). 

This right of the mortgagee it was held could not be defeated by an owner previously assigning his right to the rents as lessor to a third party, for the rents were already subject to the prior assignment in the mortgage; Bulger v. Wilderman et al., 101 Pa. Super. Ct. 168-1931-a case which may be read with much profit as it is a clear exposition of the nature and character of a mortgage in Pennsylvania and its legal effect. 

But it has been held that a mortgagee cannot, as against the grantee under a tax sale of seated lands, retain the right to possession previously taken because of the mortgagor's default (Day v. Ostergard, et al. Legal Intel., Sept. 18, 1940, vol. 

CIII p. 496).

If the mortgaged property be vacant a mortgagee whose mortgage is in default may enter and take possession if he can do so peaceably and rent the same to his own tenant or if the owner is in possession or refuses to surrender possession upon demand an action of ejectment will lie to enforce the mortgagee's right (Bulger v. Wilderman, supra, and cases therein cited).

Where a mortgagee takes possession of the mortgaged premises and gives notice to the tenant under a lease executed after the date of the mortgage, any rentals collected by the owner thereafter are payable to the mortgagee and this applies to a deposit made with the owner to secure the payment of future rents. The appropriation of the deposit to rent is for the benefit of the mortgagee and the owner must account

§81C 

215 

MORTGAGES. 

therefor (Real Estate Land Title Co. v. Homer B. & L., 138 Pa. Super. Ct. 563-564-1940). 

Where a mortgage does not contain the usual clause assigning to the mortgagee "all rents, issues and profits", and a tenant holding under a lease executed after the date of the mortgage, refuses to pay the rent to the mortgagee upon demand and notice by him of the mortgage default, such tenant cannot be compelled by an action in equity to do so. This for the reason that the absence of an "assignment clause" in the mortgage prevents the mortgagee from claiming as lessor's assignee. (Peoples-Pittsburgh Trust Co. v. Henshaw, 141 

Pa. Super. Ct. 585-1940); while the fact that the lease was made after the mortgage, operates to vest in the mortgagee no reversion therein, so that there is neither privity of estate nor of contract between the mortgagee and the tenant. Hence the mortgagee cannot proceed by distress or recovery of the rent (Brown v. Aiken, 329 Pa. 566–576–1938). In such case the remedy of the mortgagee would be to proceed by ejectment to oust a tenant who will not voluntarily pay the rent to or recognize the mortgagee's right to possession; or, as pointed out in Peoples-Pittsburgh Trust Co. v. Henshaw case (supra), proceed with foreclosure or issue an attachment execution if the mortgagee holds the lessor's judgment bond. 

A mortgagee who takes possession of the mortgaged premises does not thereby limit or restrict in any way the fundamental right secured to him by law, to foreclose his mortgage and issue execution upon any judgment entered on or under it and become purchaser of the property free and clear of all estates, interests and claims subordinate to the mortgage (Girard Trust Co. v. Dempsey, 129 Pa. Super. Ct. 471-1938). (b) Application of Rents Seized by Mortgagee.

A mortgagee who takes possession, or seizes the rent does not become thereby the real owner, he is rather a quasi trustee for the owner and must account for the rent seized (Provident Trust Co. v. Judicial B. & L. Assn. 112 Pa. Super. Ct. 352,

§81C  

356-1934) and it follows that he does not have the registered owners liability as to taxes (Fassitt v. North Tioga B. & L. 

Assn., 133 Pa. Super. Ct. 146-1938). If the mortgagee in possession agrees that the taxes be paid out of the rents he must do so (Integrity Trust Co. v. St. Rita Bldg. & Loan Assn., 112 Pa. Super. Ct. 343—1934, Aff. 317 Pa. 518–1935) for such an agreement is to be regarded as based on a good consideration. In absence of such agreement, if the mortgagee in possession does not appropriate the rents received either to interest or principal of the mortgage, the owner has a right in a suit against him, after foreclosure, for unpaid taxes, to defend on the ground that it was the duty of the mortgagee to have applied the unappropriated rents to taxes. (Provident Trust Co. v. Judicial B. & L. Assn., Supra.; Real Estate 

Land Title etc., v. Homer B. & L. Assn., 138 Pa. Super. Ct. 

563-564-1940; id. v. id., 124 Pa. Super. Ct. 17-1936).

If the mortgagee in possession appropriates the rents to the mortgage interest or principal as received or at least before judgment in foreclosure proceedings, the rents thereby become his individual property and the owner cannot complain that they were not applied to the payment of taxes (Penna. Co. v. Verlenden, 119 Pa. Super. Ct. 399, 402—1935; 

Integrity Trust Co. v. St. Rita Bldg. & Loan Assn., Supra.;

Robinson v. Home Life Ins. Co. 322 Pa. 284-285-1936). But mere collection of the rents under the terms of the mortgage is not of itself regarded as an appropriation (Provident Trust 

Co. v. Judicial B. & L., 112 Pa. Super. Ct., 352-356-1934;

Securities Guaranty Corp. v. Pacheto, 112 Pa. Super. Ct. 360 —1934).

Suggestion. It is suggested that an owner (who is not also the mortgagor), before surrendering possession or assigning leases to the mortgagee, ought to secure an agreement from him, that the rents collected be applied to payment of taxes after necessary repairs and collection charges. In practice, most mortgagees recognize this to be fair and will agree. If the mortgagee refuses to so agree, there is (in Philadelphia at least) a method by which such application can be compelled,

§217 

MORTGAGES. 

that is to demand that the Receiver of Taxes proceed under the Act of April 19, 1883, P.L. 9, §3 (53 P.S. 4917) which authorizes demand for payment of delinquent taxes on the tenant. This demand, if refused, may be enforced by distress on the tenant's goods. The tenant is fully protected by the 

Act which in effect authorizes the tenant on such demand to pay the rent as it accrues, to Receiver of Taxes, to be applied on account of delinquent taxes until fully paid. The threat of invoking such procedure will usually constrain a stubborn mortgagee to do the fair thing i.e., either agree to apply rents to payment of taxes or foreclose and take title. Of course where the owner is also mortgagor, he is liable on his bond for the deficiency in any event and there is little then to be gained from the order in which the mortgagee applies the rents.¹

II. 

WHO HAS AND WHO HAS NOT POWER TO MAKE A MORTGAGE. 

82. Individuals.

Married Women. 

(a) Individuals. In General. In general anyone having capacity to alienate real property has a right to mortgage it, 

(see ante Chapter III on Alienation, Page 40). A married man can mortgage his real estate without his wife joining in the mortgage even though he cannot sell. And a purchaser at a sheriff's sale upon foreclosure of this mortgage takes it free from the wife's interest or dower (See $145 (g)). Unless of course it is made with the fraudulent intent of barring the wife's dower (McClurg v. Schwartz, 87 Pa. 521-1878). 

(b) Married Women's Mortgages Require Husband's 

Joinder Therein.

While a husband can mortgage without his wife joining, the Act of June 8, 1893 (P.L. 344, §1, 48 P.S. 31), forbids a 

1 For further discussion of other duties, liabilities or obligation arising from mortgagee taking possession, see article of Oscar G. Bender, Esq., of the Phila delphia Bar, entitled, "Recent Developments in the Law of Real Property'' 

Legal Intelligencer, Feb. 26, 1938. See also comprehensive articles by Frank O.

Walter, Esq., also of the Phila. Bar in the Fiduciary Review Dec. 1940 and Jan. 1941.

§82  

wife to make a mortgage without her husband joining. But strictly speaking, under this Act it is only the mortgage which he is required to join in, so that if he joins in the bond also as usually required by mortgagee, he thereby becomes personally liable on the bond and must look to his wife for reim bursement (DeVincentis v. Holden, 306 Pa. 212—1932). 

Even in the case of a Building and Loan mortgage where joinder in both bond and mortgage of a married woman by the husband was expressly required by the Act of Apr. 10, 1879, P.L. 16, §7, the same was held (see Cooke v. Jones, 10 

D.R. 283-1901), it being said "if the husband desired to restrict his liability to the separate estate of the wife he should have had inserted in the bond such a stipulation." (See also 

Regis B. & L. Assn. v. Humphries, et ux 17 D. & C. 53-1931). 

Since the Act of June 4, 1901, P.L. 67, (21 P.S. 82) her acknowledgment of a mortgage need no longer be separate and apart from her husband. Should the wife be divorced, or if she be living separate from her husband under articles of agreement wherein her husband has released all his rights, and interest in her property, then she may convey or encumber or mortgage her estate as though she were a feme sole (see §§34, 35 and Act of June 9, 1897, P.L. 212; 21 P.S. 52). The curative acts passed to make valid mortgages of married women not separately acknowledged before the enabling act, were held in 

Colonial Trust Co. v. Foster, (234 Pa. 152-153-1912) to operate only where the mortgage in question was executed for a valuable consideration.

The purposes for which the wife uses the money obtained by a mortgage does not affect the validity of the instrument, thus she may mortgage the property to raise money for her husband's use (Daubert v. Eckert, 94 Pa. 255-1880; Peoples -Pittsburgh Trust Co. v. McCaffrey et ux, 336 Pa. 5471939). Or she may mortgage her estate to secure a debt due by her husband, (Hagenbuch v. Phillips, 112 Pa. 284-1886;

Jamison v. Jamison, 3 Wh. 456-457-1838; Hanover Trust Co. 

v. Keagy, 335 Pa. 356-1939). A married woman is liable on bond given by her and her husband accompanying a mortgage

$219 

MORTGAGES. 

secured on real estate owned by the husband and wife as tenants by entireties to the extent that the proceeds are used for purchase money and for the improvement of the premises 

(Penna. Co. v. Koller 319 Pa. 249-1935). 

Although a married woman cannot mortgage her estate without the joinder of her husband, curiously enough by statute (Act of May 25, 1878, P.L. 152, §1), she is permitted to satisfy or assign a judgment or mortgage by herself. 

(c) When Husband's Joinder Is Not Required in Wife's 

Mortgage. There are certain exceptions to the general rule that a married woman cannot mortgage her real estate without joinder of her husband. These are: (1) Where a husband has been declared a lunatic by proper proceedings (Act of 

May 25, 1878, P.L. 154; 50 P.S. 799); (2) Where the mortgage is approved by the Court under $2, Revised Price Act of June 7, 1917, P.L. 388, §2, as amended by Act of May 2, 1919, P.L. 

111; (20 P.S. 1563); (3) Where her mortgage is given to secure part of the purchase money for the mortgaged real estate (Hersh's v. Hersh, 22 Lanc. R. 89-1905); (4) Where the husband has released all rights and interest in her property by articles of separation duly recorded (Act of July 9, 1897, P.L. 212; 21 P.S. 52); (5) Where she has been decreed a "Feme sole trader" (Act of May 4, 1855, P.L. 430; §2, 48 

P.S. 42; Act of May 11, 1927, P.L. 971; 48 P.S. 44). 

83. Infants.

Under this term we include all persons under twenty-one years of age. An infant cannot make a deed for reasons herein before set forth (see ante §32). And since he cannot make a valid deed it follows he cannot make a valid mortgage. 

Such a mortgage if made, becomes like an infant's deed, voidable and if not repudiated within a reasonable time after the infant arrives of age it is regarded as having been ratified and becomes binding (Johnson v. Furnior, 69 Pa. 449, 455-1871).

§84 

 84. Other Persons Under Disability. 

With regard to other persons under disability such as lunatics, etc., it may generally be stated that this power to mortgage depends upon their power to alienate or convey property. This has been already covered under the Chapter 

III on alienation (ante § 28 to 33 Inc.). By consulting Chap ter III and applying the rule that whoever cannot make a deed, cannot mortgage, the question as to whether such person has the right to mortgage becomes answered. 

85. Trustees and Fiduciaries.

If a trustee or other fiduciary has the power given him by the instrument under which he acts, to sell, he is regarded as having also the power to mortgage without express mention of it (Lancaster v. Dolan, 1 Rawle 231-1829). This for the reason that a mortgage is but a conditional sale (Zane v. 

Kennedy, 73 Pa. 182-1873; McCreary v. Bomberger, 151 Pa. 

323-1892). But this rule does not apply unless the power to sell is absolute and unrestricted. A careful examination must therefore be made of the trust instrument to determine the nature of the power of sale and whether there is any specific limitation denying the right to mortgage. Conversely if a fiduciary is given no power of sale he has no right to mortgage unless such right is expressly given. Though if a trustee has power to invest in real estate he may make a purchase money mortgage for part of the purchase price (Gernert v. 

Albert, 160 Pa. 95-1894). 

86. Corporations. 

(a) Business or Profit Corporations. As set forth in the chapter on alienation (§§38-39), a corporation in so far as it has power to hold land may alienate as freely as an individual unless restricted by statute. One of the restrictions imposed by statute is the power to mortgage. The power to mortgage has been restricted by law in Pennsylvania to the extent that

$221 

MORTGAGES. 

certain conditions must be complied with in order for the mortgage to be valid; these restrictions have been passed mostly for the benefit of the stockholders. To avoid a reckless incurring of indebtedness, the constitution of the State of Pennsylvania adopted 1874 directed, that "the stock and indebtedness of corporations shall not be increased except in pursuance of a general law nor without the consent of the persons holding the larger amount in value of the stock first obtained, at a meeting to be held after sixty days' notice given in pursuance of law." (Article XVI, $7 Constitution of 

Pennsylvania). In 1889 was passed the Act of May 21, P.L. 

257; (15 P.S., §341), which amended the prior act of April 

18, 1874, and allowed corporations to borrow money by bond and mortgage on their real property to an amount not exceeding one-half of their capital stock paid in and at a rate of interest not to exceed six per cent per annum. By the 

Acts of February 9, 1901, P.L. 3, §1, and April 22, 1905, P.L. 

280, §1; (15 P.S. 241), corporations were authorized with the consent of the holders of the larger amount in value of their capital stock to increase their indebtedness without any limitation and to mortgage all or any of their assets. Though these acts have been repealed so far as corporations organized under, or subject to the Business Corporation Law (Act of 

May 5, 1933, P.L. 364; 15 P.S. 2852), are concerned (See

History of corporation laws, supra, §38), they are cited here because they still apply to existing mortgages executed under these respective acts as well as to corporations organized prior to the constitution of 1874 which have never accepted the constitution and have not acquired the benefits of the 

Business Corporation Law of 1933. 

Today all corporations organized under, or incorporated previously and subject thereto, or who have qualified by accepting the Constitution of 1874 and the provisions of the Business Corporation Law of 1933 (See §3; 15 P.S. 2852-3), may incur indebtedness and mortgage their assets in any manner and in any amount if authorized by the affirmative vote or at least a majority of the outstanding shares entitled to vote

§86 

($409 Business Corporation Law of 1933; (15 P.S. 2852-309),

Constitution of Pa., Article XVI, §7). 

It will be seen, therefore, that a mortgage by a corporation must, in order to be valid, comply with the law. If it operates to increase the indebtedness of the corporation the consent of its stockholders must be obtained as provided in the Constitution of the State. If the mortgage is, however, only to secure an existing indebtedness, then obviously the special consent of the stockholders is not required (Ahl. v. Rhoads, 84 

Pa. 319-1877; Powell v. Blair, 133 Pa. 550-1890). It is to be recommended that a conveyancer who is not a member of the bar should always consult an attorney before attempting to arrange or draw a mortgage for a corporation client. 

(b) Nonprofit Corporations. Religious and Charitable 

Corporations.

As hereinbefore noted (See §§ 38a and 38b) the restrictions formerly imposed on real estate holdings of nonprofit corporations or corporations of the first class as they were formerly known were removed by the Nonprofit Corporation 

Law of 1933, Act of May 5, 1933, P.L. 289, §302, Clauses 5, 6; (15 P.S. 2851-302); and $308 of the same act sets forth the procedure necessary for such corporations to borrow money and to acquire and dispose of real estate. This section provides: "Unless its articles or by-laws provide for the approval of another body, a nonprofit corporation shall not borrow money, or purchase, sell, lease away, or otherwise dispose of any real estate, unless and until a resolution authorizing the same shall have been approved by a majority of the members of the corporation at a regular or special meeting, duly convened upon proper notice of this purpose. The resolution of the members authorizing the borrowing of money need not specify the particular sums, rates of interest, or times of maturity of the loans, but such items may be agreed upon and authorized by the directors of the corporation. Every nonprofit corporation may mortgage, sell, lease away, or otherwise dispose of any of its real estate without application to, and the authorization or confirmation of, any court, except in those cases where the Revised Price Act of 

1917, approved 7th day of May, 1917 (P.L. 388; 20 P. S. 1561 et seq.),

§223 

MORTGAGES. 

and its amendment and supplement, confers jurisdiction upon the orphans' court or the courts of common pleas of a particular county to authorize and confirm the selling, leasing, conveying upon ground rents, or mortgaging of real estate by a corporation. All proceeds derived by a nonprofit corporation from any loan, sale, lease, ground rent or mortgage, shall be faithfully and specifically used for or applied to the lawful activities of the corporation, and in case such proceeds are derived from any real estate subject to a trust the trust shall be impinged upon such proceeds."

This provision of the act changes the previous law under which it was well settled that religious, scientific, educational, or charitable corporations were required to petition the court for permission to sell, lease or mortgage its real property (Burton's Appeal, 57 Pa. 213-1868; Application of Mercer

Home (Fisher's Appeal) 162 Pa. 232-1894; Nauman v. Weid man, 182 Pa. 263–1897; Seif v. Krebs, 239 Pa. 423—1913; St.

Mary's Immaculate Conception Greek Catholic Church's Peti tion, 296 Pa. 307-1929; Revised Price Act, 1917, P.L. 388, 

§§1 and 2 (20 P.S. 1561-3) as amended). 

The quoted section of the Nonprofit Corporation Law of 1933 as pointed out in the annotation by Deputy Attorney 

General Russel Shockly, to the State Publication of the Penn sylvania Corporation Laws, 1933, page 208, "specifically provides that recourse to the court for the sale, leasing or mortgaging of corporate real estate is not necessary except in those cases specifically covered by the Price Act, viz. (1) where the corporation has no capacity to convey, which situation is now rare and will not rise under this act; (2) where the corporation holds property in excess of the amount permitted by its charter or by-laws, which situation will seldom arise under this act, and (3) where the corporation holds property in trust, which situation will arise more than ever under this act." 

Good conveyancing practice requires that the mortgage show on its face the authority by which it is executed and when it does not appear, a certified copy of the resolution or decree of court authorizing the same as the case may be, should be supplied.

87. Corporation Mortgage to Secure Bond Issue. 

If the mortgage of the corporation is made to an individual mortgagee, the form of the mortgage and bond and warrant is similar to an individual's mortgage. See form of Corporation Mortgage in forms appended to this book (§274). Where, however, the mortgage is made by a corporation for the purpose of raising a large amount which no single individual will loan, then the mortgage is made to a trustee for the benefit of bondholders and the amount divided among a number of individuals. E.g., suppose a corporation desires to borrow $100,000.00 and to secure it by a mortgage against its property this amount is divided into 100 bonds of $1,000.00 each. Each individual receives one bond for every $1,000.00 he advances. 

Suppose 100 individuals each put up $1,000.00, obviously the corporation cannot execute a mortgage to each, so it executes one mortgage for $100,000.00 to a trustee who represents all the bondholders (See form $275). If default is made in the payment of the principal or interest, any bondholder may demand that the trustee proceed to foreclose and if the trustee neglects to do so, the bondholder may bring appropriate proceedings in court to compel a foreclosure and sale, provided of course there are no provisions in the mortgage to the contrary, or requirements, as is usually the case, necessitating a certain proportion in amount of bonds to demand foreclosure. 

Unless the deed of trust, corporate mortgage or bond con-

$225 

MORTGAGES. 

tains a further restriction to the contrary, each bondholder may sue in his own name for the interest on default and for the principal of the bond if unpaid at maturity, and recover judgment (Frey v. United Traction Co. of Pgh., 320 Pa. 1961935; Western Pa. Hospital v. Mercantile Library Hall Co., 

189 Pa. 269-1899). If such right is expressly restricted however the limitations on the exercise thereof will be en forced Rittenhouse v. Lukens Steel Co., 116 Pa. Super. Ct. 

303-1935. But the restrictions in the mortgage or bond will not be extended to an independent agreement assuming lia bility thereof (Werner v. Mercantile Co., 39 D. & C. 79—1940). 

A provision to the effect that "no bondholder shall have the right to institute any proceeding for the foreclosure of the mortgage, or the execution of any trust thereof or for the appointment of a receiver, unless the holders of a majority in value of the bonds have first requested the trustee to proceed", was held not to preclude an individual bondholder suing and recovering judgment on his bond. (Livingston v. 

Blue Creek Coal & Land Co., 338 Pa. 473-1940). But these cases also hold that since the mortgage was made for the protection of all bondholders ratably, the plaintiff by the terms of his contract is not entitled to execution against any property, mortgaged or pledged so long as the other bonds secured by the same property are unpaid and entitled to the benefit of the security. (Putnam v. Pittsburgh Rys. Co. 330 Pa. 210 

-1938).

After Acquired Property Clause. 

It is customary to insert in corporate mortgages or deeds of trust to secure bond issues, an after acquired property clause, by which the lien of the mortgage is agreed to extend to and cover after acquired property. Such clause has been held to be valid and enforceable against the mortgagor. 

(Colonial Trust Co. v. Harmon Creek Coal Co., 287 Pa. 2841926; Phila. Wil. & Balt. R.R. Co. v. Woelpper 64 Pa. 3661870).

§87A  87-A. Nature of the Debts for Which a Mortgage May Be Created. 

While as previously mentioned, ($81-c), a mortgage as between the parties thereto, operates as a conveyance of the mortgaged land upon condition, so far as third parties are concerned, a mortgage is for all practical purposes more in the nature of a lien and to be regarded, when duly recorded, as security for a debt. or A mortgage may be security for either (a) a pre-existing debt (b) a debt created at the time the mortgage is given, (c) a debt to be incurred in the future. 

We have also seen that usually a debt is evidenced by a bond which is referred to in the mortgage although it may be evidenced by any other obligation, such as a note. Indeed a mortgage may be given unaccompanied by any bond or any other obligation, though our practice in Pennsylvania has been to always accompany a mortgage by a bond and warrant of attorney in the form previously discussed. (a) Mortgage given for a Pre-existing Debt. 

A mortgage for a pre-existing debt is as effective as when given for a debt incurred at the time of the execution of the mortgage, with the exception of the possibility of being avoided in bankruptcy as a preference, if bankruptcy proceedings are instituted against the mortgagor within four months from the date of the recording thereof. If bankruptcy proceedings are instituted within that period of time, it, of course follows that such a mortgage is voidable as a preference, loses its lien and is reduced to the level of an ordinary debt. 

(b) Mortgage Debt Incurred at the Time of Execution of the Mortgage.

If a mortgage is created in good faith to secure a present loan, that is, a loan made at the time the mortgage is executed

$227 

MORTGAGES. 

and delivered, even though the mortgagee might have reason to believe the borrower to be insolvent at the time, it would not be such a transaction as could be voided as a preference under the bankruptcy law, the theory being of course, that the mortgagor's assets are not depleted, he is simply changing the form of his property. This, of course, operates precisely the same as though he had sold his real estate for a present consideration. (Tiffany v. Boatman's Saving Insti tution, 85 U.S. 368-1874). (c) Mortgage Given for an Indebtedness to be Incurred in the Future. 

Mortgages given for indebtednesses to be incurred in the future are usually called an advance money mortgage and will be hereinafter more fully discussed in §89. 

III. 

KINDS OF MORTGAGES. 

88. Purchase Money Mortgages. 

A purchase money mortgage, as its name indicates, is a mortgage given by the vendee to the vendor as consideration or part consideration for the premises conveyed. It must be executed at the same time that the deed is executed (Cake's 

Appeal, 23 Pa. 186–1854).

An ordinary mortgage becomes a lien from the time of its recording notwithstanding its date (See Section on Recording, $126, infra). A purchase money mortgage is an exception to this rule and becomes a lien from its date, if recorded at any time within thirty days of its date (Act of April 27, 1927, P.L. 440, §1; 21 P.S. 622). Therefore if two mortgages are given for the purchase money, although recorded on different days, but both within the thirty-day limit, one cannot be prior to the other and they are equal liens. A sheriff's sale on either would divest the other (Pease v. Hoag, 11 Phila. 5491875). To avoid this effect, if it is intended to make one purchase money mortgage subject to another, it should recite

§88 

what is called a second mortgage clause (see §92 this section, for form). Such waiver of priority is binding and will be enforced (Klaus v. Majestic Apartment House, 250 Pa. 194 

1915).

It is not necessary that a purchase money mortgage should disclose on its face that it is for purchase money, if in point of fact, it was given for purchase money (Oransky v. Stepan avich, 304 Pa. 84-1931; Commonwealth Title Co., v. Ellis 

192 Pa. 321-1899).

A purchase money mortgage takes priority over a judgment entered against the vendee after the agreement of sale was signed and before delivery of the deed (Cake's Appeal, 23 Pa. 

186-1854), and the same is true as to purchase money obligations or conditions in general (Bridge v. Bridge 32 D. & C. 565 -1938). It has also been held that while a minor vendee who executed a purchase money mortgage may on reaching majority, either affirm or disaffirm the transaction in its entirety, he or she cannot retain the property free and clear of its liability for the purchase money obligation (Oransky v. 

Stepanavich, 304 Pa. 84-1931). 

Before the Act of May 28, 1915 P.L. 631 repealed and supplied by the Act of April 27, 1927 P.L. 440 (21 P.S. 622) it was not necessary that a purchase money mortgage should be given to the seller, it could be executed to any nominee to whom the vendor had by act and deed assigned his right (for form see $227). Good practice required however that such assignment be recited in the mortgage because in Albright v. 

Lafayette Building Assn. (102 Pa. 411-1883) it was held where a purchase money mortgage is given to a third party there is no implied notice of the fact that it was for purchase money as is the case where the mortgage is executed to the seller (for form of such recital see $300 infra.). The Act of 

1915 (Supra) not only reduced the recording period of purchase money mortgages from 60 to 30 days but introduced an apparently new limitation by the phrase "No mortgage given by a purchaser to a seller for any part of the purchase money of land so mortgaged shall be affected etc. if the same

$229 

MORTGAGES. 

be recorded within 30 days from the execution thereof."

This would seem to limit the benefit of a purchase money mortgage to cases where the mortgage is given by purchaser to seller, a limitation which exists by statute in Maryland and 

Ohio (Case's Petition 27 D. & C. 391, 396—1936). 

The same limitation was included in the later Act of 1927 (Supra.) though the clause preserving its priority if recorded in 30 days was worded differently viz. "provided that it be recorded within 30 days from the date of the mortgage"; previously it read "30 days from execution thereof." There is a serious question not yet decided by the Appellate Courts whether these Acts operated to limit the purchase money mortgage privilege to the seller alone and thereby preclude assignment of the right to receive a purchase money mortgage by the seller to a third party (Martin's Estate 135 Pa. Super. Ct. 

136, 142—1939). Upon general principles the right of assignment not being forbidden by express language or necessary implication, it would seem that such right still exists. It was so held by Judge Farr of Bradford County in a well-con sidered opinion in (Case's Petition 27 D. & C. 391-1936). 

However until the Act receives a construction of the Supreme Court on that point wisdom dictates the advisability of having a purchase money mortgage executed to the seller and the mortgage by him assigned to the ultimate holder. 

89. Advance Money Mortgages.

A mortgage may be given for future advances to be made thereafter. Such mortgages are valid securities for such advances as soon as made, whether the advances be made to mortgagor or a third person designated by him. Such mortgages are known as "advance money mortgages," or mortgages for future advances. They are commonly used by builders to raise money for a building operation. Such a mortgage is, however, a prior lien as to subsequent encumbrances only from the time such advances are actually made, unless by the terms of the mortgage, an obligation is imposed upon the mortgagee to make all advances (Dahlem's Estate,

$89 

175 Pa. 444, 453–1896) in which case advances, even though made after the subsequent encumbrance, take priority (Batten v. Jurist et ux 306 Pa. 64, 70—1932). In other words, unless the mortgagee actually binds himself absolutely to make the advances, the mortgage will only be a lien, as to subsequent encumbrance, from the time the money is actually advanced. 

But this rule is only for the benefit of intervening encumbrancers (Moats v. Thompson et al., 283 Pa. 313-1925). If no money is actually advanced, the "advance money mortgage" does not become a binding lien against the mortgagor because of the want of consideration. But if the mortgage is assigned by the mortgagee to an innocent and bona fide purchaser without notice, said mortgage becomes an absolute and valid lien against the mortgagor. Since the recording of the mortgage clothes it with an apparent validity upon which innocent third parties have a right to rely (Johnson v. Mc- 

Curdy, 83 Pa. 282—1877).

The form of an advance money mortgage is precisely the same as an ordinary mortgage, and, indeed, it only differs from the ordinary mortgage in that the latter is given for a past or present consideration, whereas the former is given for à future consideration. Though good conveyancing practice requires the contract governing the advances be in writing and recited in the mortgage, it has been held such a contract may be oral (Wardman v. Iseman, 99 Pa. Super. Ct. 5511930) and need not be recited in the mortgage (Land Title & 

Trust Co. v. Shoemaker, 257 Pa. 213-1917), nor recorded (Batten v. Jurist et ux, 306 Pa. 64, 70—1932). 

Until the decision of Page v. Carr (232 Pa. 371-1911), the

Mechanics' Lien Law (Act of June 4, 1901, P.L. 431, §13) 

gave mechanics' liens a preference over advance money mortgages as far as the newly-erected buildings or improvements were concerned. The Supreme Court, however, in the case just cited held such preference unconstitutional and void, it being in conflict with §7, Article III of the Constitution forbidding special legislation. Mechanics' liens, therefore, are now in no better position than other subsequent liens or

$231 

MORTGAGES. 

encumbrances, and the priority of advance money mortgages covers not only the land but the newly erected buildings and improvements as well. 

90. Equitable Mortgages.

An equitable mortgage, says Fallon (Pennsylvania Law of Conveyancing 383), is a lien of such a nature as will be recognized in equity as a security for the payment of money and will be treated as a mortgage. Like other equitable charges it will only be enforced against the party whose action gives rise to it or those who take the land without giving a valuable consideration therefor. Bona fide purchasers for value without notice and subsequent legal mortgagees for value will not be effected by these equitable liens. In England, an equitable mortgage can be created by merely depositing the title deeds with the mortgagee, but not in Pennsylvania nor generally anywhere in this country (Shitz v. Dieffenbach, 3 Pa. 2331846). Mere deposit of title deeds in Pennsylvania is of no avail to create any lien unless accompanied by a written instrument which must be recorded (Edward's Exec'rs. v. Trumbull, 50 Pa. 509-1865). In fact, the only kinds of equitable mortgages that exist in Pennsylvania are such as may be implied by a court of equity from the nature of the transaction between the parties or where on account of some informality in the execution of the instrument it cannot operate as a legal mortgage nor be enforced as such. As to effect of possession of mortgage papers see $101A (infra.). 

90-A. Mortgage by Equitable Estoppel. 

If a man sells and conveys land to which he has no title and afterwards acquires the title to the same land, he cannot claim it against his grantee (Calder v. Chapman, 52 Pa. 359-1866; 

Clark v. Martin, 49 Pa. 299-1865). This has been called 

'Title by Estoppel', or 'Title by Equitable Estoppel'. The same equitable principle which declares that when a party conveys property to which he has no title, his subsequent

§90A  

acquisition of the title will inure to the benefit of his vendee and estops him from claiming against his vendee, applies to mortgages as well as indefeasible deeds of conveyance (Cleary v. Kennedy, 16 W.N.C. 313-1885; Clark v. Martin, 49 Pa. 299 

It follows, therefore, that a man who mortgages property he does not own and thereafter acquires title thereto, cannot prevent the mortgagee from asserting his lien there against. 

Upon this principle it has been held that where a mortgage subject to a first and second mortgage is sold at sheriff sale under the first mortgage so as to discharge the second mortgage lien, if the mortgagor re-acquires the property from the sheriff's vendee, it restores the second mortgagee's right to proceed by Sci. Fa. against the re-acquired property. (Cleary v. Kennedy, 16 W.N.C. 313-1885). This case, though followed in Elliot v. Holley, 23 D.R. 1034-1914, was limited in its application by the cases of (Rauch v. Dech, 116 Pa. 1571887; Rushton v. Lippincott, 119 Pa. 12-1888, and Kennedy v. Borie, 166 Pa. 360-1895, to situations where the sheriff sale which divested the junior mortgage, was brought about by fraud or collusion between the mortgagor, or owner of the land, and the prior lien, or mortgage holder. It is now settled by the most recent case, viz., Bowen v. Boyd, (326 Pa. 3851937), opinion by Mr. Justice Barnes, that in absence of fraud or collusion the lien of a junior mortgage, discharged by judicial proceeding, is not revived when the mortgagor re-acquires title to the mortgaged premises by conveyance from the purchaser at the sheriff's sale.

It should be noted that the doctrine of mortgage by equitable estoppel applies only between the mortgagor and mortgagee. See Gallagher v. Stern, (250 Pa. 292-1915), holding that where a mortgagor includes in a mortgage, property which he does not own at the time but which he subsequently acquires, the mortgage will bind the after acquired property as between the parties, but not as against subsequent judgment creditors without notice. (See also Gallagher v. Stern 59 Pa. Super. 

Ct. 225-1915.)

$233 

MORTGAGES. 

91. First Mortgages. 

Mortgages are customarily referred to either as "first" or "second", according to their priority. As the name implies, a first mortgage is a first mortgage lien upon the property encumbered. If given at the time of the execution of the deed it becomes a purchase money mortgage as set forth in §88. 

A first mortgage is regarded as the safest and most desirable kind of investment. Trust funds are permitted by law to be invested in them subject to the conditions prescribed by §41-a, Fiduciaries' Act of 1917 as amended by Acts of July 2, 1935, P.L. 545; May 28, 1937, P.L. 1037; June 24, 1939, P.L. 718, (20 P.S. 801). 

92. Second Mortgages. Second Mortgage Clause. 

A second mortgage is precisely the same as a first mortgage except that it is a second lien on the property mortgaged. It, of course, follows that it is not as good a security as a first mortgage unless there is ample margin between the aggregate amount of the mortgages and the market value of the property. 

Ordinarily it is not necessary to recite the fact that the mortgage is under and subject to an existing mortgage if recorded subsequently, but it is customary to insert in the second mortgage directly after the recital a clause similar to the one in the deed form set out in §53 (consult also form, $261) as follows: 

Under and subject nevertheless to the payment of a certain mortgage debt or principal sum of $3,500.00 with interest thereon as the same may become due and payable. 

In Klaus v. Majestic Apt. House, (250 Pa. 194-1915), where both first and second mortgagees attempted to include in their lien the household furnishings of a hotel, the under and subject clause in the second mortgage operated to the disadvantage of the second mortgagee in that the court ruled that having accepted the second mortgage subject to the prior lien of the first mortgage, it could not compete with the first mortgage in the distribution of a fund created by the sale of per-

§92 

sonal property covered by both mortgages even though no valid lien upon such personal property was conferred thereby. 

There is, however, one very important exception to the statement that it is unnecessary to recite the second mortgage as being under and subject to a first, and that is where the second mortgage is given by the vendee at the same time he is taking title and executing a first mortgage, the law may imply both mortgages to be purchase money mortgages, and as such equal liens if recorded at any time within thirty days after execution. (See $88). To guard against this possibility the second mortgage should expressly stipulate that it is not a purchase money mortgage and is to be a second lien. The following clause is generally used for this purpose and is known as the second mortgage clause. "Being the same premises which Andrew Black by indenture dated the 12th day of January, A.D. 1911, and intended to be recorded, granted and conveyed to the said mortgagor in fee. And it is hereby expressly certified and declared that it is not a purchase money mortgage and that it is subject both in lien and payment to a certain mortgage to secure the payment of ($3,500.00) given by said mortgagor to Isaac Thomas, dated January 12, A.D. 1911, and intended to be recorded; and that the lien of said mortgage shall not be affected or impaired by a judicial sale under a judgment recovered upon this present indenture or upon the bond secured hereby; but any such sale shall be expressly advertised and made subject to the lien of the said mortgage.' 2.2 

This clause is inserted as the recital in the conveyance part of the mortgage, see form Building and Loan Association Mortgage, ($268), and following the habendum is inserted this clause: "Under and subject both in lien and payment to a certain mortgage to secure the payment of $3,500.00 given by the mortgagor to Isaac 

Thomas, dated January 12th as above fully set forth."

These clauses must always be inserted in the second mortgage where title is passing and two mortgages are given all at the same time. The second mortgage must then be dated and recorded subsequent to the first mortgage. It will be

$235 

MORTGAGES. 

seen that the effect of this clause is to expressly disavow the implication that it is a purchase money mortgage and to declare it to be subject both in lien and payment to the designated first mortgage. 

93. Building Association Mortgages. Building and Loan Associations. 

Pennsylvania is the home of building and loan associations, and Philadelphia County is the birthplace. The first building and loan association was organized in Frankford, Philadelphia County, now part of the City, in 1831. They have since spread all over the country but have developed differently in different states. However, the Pennsylvania plan is still regarded as the more conservative and successful and will here be briefly explained. 

The fundamental principle upon which this institution rests is co-operation. It was designed to meet the needs of men whose savings were too small to put to any substantial use alone. But by combining the savings of a number of persons into an association, these small individual savings formed an effective bulk sufficient to purchase a home for one member, then another and so until the object for which the association was formed was accomplished. In the beginning these associations actually purchased the land and then erected houses which were divided among the members. Later, this practice fell into disuse and the members bought their own land and built thereon a house, borrowing the money from the association and securing the association by a mortgage. 

Nowadays, when property is built so much more cheaply by an operating builder, the building associations mostly confine themselves to the loaning of money on mortgages to enable the member to purchase a house. But the fundamental purpose remains the same, to wit: the aiding of men of small means to become home owners. 

Prior to the Act of May 5, 1933, P.L. 457; (15 P.S. 1074), building and loan associations were organized and regulated by the Corporation Act of April 29, 1874, P.L. 73, its supple-

$93 

ments and amendments. In 1925 a commission that had been authorized to codify and revise the banking and building and loan association laws, reported a codification and revision which aimed to correct certain evils and to modernize the law. 

It failed, however, to be enacted. The finance collapse of 

1929 which heralded the onset of the great depression proved the need of such building and loan association law revision. 

A new codification, based in part on the previously suggested code and upon the depression experiences which had developed the weaknesses of existing law, was drafted by the Attorney General's Office. This code was enacted in 1933 (Acts of 

May 5th, P.L. 457, 15 P.S. 1074), and is given the short title of 'Building and Loan Code'. It is not within the scope of this work to review the building and loan code but a brief exposition of the theory and the operation of these associations will enable the building and loan mortgages to be better understood.

Under the building and loan code of 1933, the capital of these associations may be without limit, but a limit may be specified in the articles of association. Shares may have a par value of not less than $100 nor more than $200.00. Most associations have a par value of $200.00. These shares are paid in installments of one ($1.00) a month per share, and the money so received is loaned out to the various members at 6 per cent interest. The payment of these dues or installments are continued until the amount of the installments paid in, together with the earnings of the association, equals $200.00 per share. The stock is then said to have matured and the amount of $200.00 per share is then credited to the shareholders by being paid in cash to those shareholders who have not borrowed from the association and by cancelling the debt and satisfying the mortgage of those who have. 

The time in which the stock of a building and loan association will mature depends, of course, upon the economy with which the society is conducted, the security of loans and the absence of losses. The salaries are generally very small and usually only the secretary and treasurer receive salaries out of

$237 

MORTGAGES. 

the association funds. A conservatively managed association should mature its stock in twelve years, i.e., after 144 installments of $1.00 per share have been paid in. The balance between the amount so paid in, viz., $144.00 and $200.00 to wit: $56.00, represents the accumulated earnings of the association during the twelve years; this is at the rate of about 6 per cent compounded. Some associations have matured their stock in nine, ten and eleven years and the earnings in such cases are proportionately larger.

The loans of building associations must be made on written applications signed by the person for whose benefit the loan is to be made. The code specifies the form and contents of the application and makes false statements therein a criminal offence. ($902 of the Building and Loan Code). Printed forms of applications are usually supplied by the Association to the applicants. When a properly signed application for a mortgage loan is received by the association, the premises to be mortgaged are examined and a report, together with an appraisement of the property offered for security, is made to the board of directors. If the board approves the loan, it is granted upon the condition that the applicant, if not already a shareholder of the association, will subscribe to the requisite number of shares the loan requires. In a $200.00 share association, a minimum of one share would be required for every two hundred dollars of the proposed loan. $901 of the Code authorizes associations to charge a "premium" to be paid by the borrower in addition to the interest, provided the borrower agrees in writing to pay such premium. 

Such premiums are expressly declared by the Code not to be usurious. Premiums had their origin in the practice that arose in the earlier days when there were more applications for loans received by building and loan associations than there was money available. Applicants would then bid a "premium" for priority, and the highest bidder would get the loan. 

This practice was recognized by law and held not to be usurious provided there was bona fide competitive bidding (Stiles Appeal, 95 Pa. 122-1880). Though a by-law stipulating a fixed

§94  

premium was held illegal (Roeser v.

German National Building and Loan Association, 32 Pa. Super. Ct. 100-1906; Home 

B. & L. Ass'n. v. Kowatch, 123 Pa. Super. Ct. 218-1936).

Later by the Acts of May 14, 1913 P.L. 205, (15 P.S. 961 note) 

and its amendment, April 8, 1927, P.L. 179, and agreement in writing between the borrower and the association for a specified rate of premium, not to exceed two per cent per annum on the amount of the loan, was authorized and declared valid without competitive bidding. These acts are now supplied by $901 of the Code. 

94. Building Association Mortgages (Continued). 

Kinds Of. 

Restrictions On. 

A building association mortgage differs from an ordinary straight mortgage in that they are given to secure the monthly payments of dues, interest, etc. for such length of time as may be required for the stock to mature. Mr. Justice Fell, in 

Freemansburg B. & L. Ass'n. v. Watts, (199 Pa. 221-1901) said: "In carrying out the plan on which building associations are organized and conducted, it is not intended or required that a stockholder who borrows from the association will discharge the debt he incurs by direct payments on account of it. 

He pays at stated periods dues on his stock, the interest on the money borrowed and when the premium bid for the loan has not been deducted, the installments on it. When by the receipt of dues, interest, premium and fines for non-payment of dues, all of the stock of the association or of the series to which the borrowed stock belongs becomes full paid or matured, the value of his stock equals the amount of his debt and the transaction is ended by the surrender of the stock by him and the cancellation of his obligation to the association." 

By consulting the form of a building and loan association and bond and warrant the explanation of the transaction by Justice Fell becomes exceedingly simple to understand. The borrower may borrow $200.00 for each share of stock he holds. 

Thus, to borrow $1,000.00 he must have five shares of stock, so that at maturity the amount of his stock equals the loan.

$239 

MORTGAGES. 

The stock so subscribed for is assigned as collateral security, together with a mortgage on the property to the association. 

The Building and Loan Code, §903 (15 P.S. 1074—1903) now regulates and limits the form and kind of mortgages that an association may accept as security for loans, as follows: (a) Share Mortgage Loan, which is a loan on "the bond of the borrower secured by the transfer and pledge to the association of installment shares in such association, which belong to the borrower and which have a par value at least equal to the amount of the loan, and further secured by a mortgage upon real property which belongs to the borrower, such mortgage being for at least the full amount of the loan. A loan secured in this manner shall be known as a "share mortgage loan", and the mortgage securing such a loan, as a "share mortgage". (b) Direct Reduction Mortgage Loan, which is a loan on the bond of the borrower secured by the transfer and pledge to the association of direct reduction loan shares in such association which belong to the borrower and which have a par value at least equal to the amount of the loan, and further secured by a mortgage upon real property which belongs to the borrower, such mortgage being for at least the full amount of the loan. A loan secured in this manner shall be known as a direct reduction mortgage loan, and the mortgage securing such loan as a "direct reduction mortgage”. (c) Split Mortgage Loan, which is a loan on the bond of the borrower, secured by a mortgage upon real property which belongs to the borrower, such mortgage being for an amount not to exceed one-half of the amount of the loan, such portion of the loan to be known as the straight-mortgage portion of the loan; on a bond for the remainder of the loan, secured by the transfer and pledge to the association of installment shares in such association, which belong to the borrower and which have a par value at least equal to the amount of such remainder of the loan, and further secured by a mortgage upon such real property for an amount equal to the remainder of such loan,

$94

such remainder of such loan to be known as the share-mortgage portion of the loan. A loan secured by both a straight mortgage and a share mortgage in this manner, shall be known as a split-mortgage loan. A split-mortgage loan may also be in the form of a single bond and mortgage which meets all the requirements of this section. The straight-mortgage portion of a split-mortgage loan shall not be secured by shares, and an association shall not charge fines upon such portion of the loan.

An association shall not demand payment of the straightmortgage portion of a split-mortgage loan, except in case of default by the borrower in the terms of the loan, until the share-mortgage portion of the loan has been repaid in full by the maturing of shares assigned or pledged as a security therefor or by any other method. Upon such payment of the share-mortgage portion of a split-mortgage loan, an association shall either demand and enforce payment of the straightmortgage portion of the loan, or convert such loan to a sharemortgage loan or to a direct reduction mortgage loan upon the transfer and pledge to the association of installment shares or direct reduction loan shares in such association which belong to the borrower and which have a par value at least equal to the amount of such loan. 

(d) Restrictions on Building & Loan Mortgage Loans. 

The rest of this section (§903) of the code imposes the following limitations on its mortgage loans: (1) the mortgage must be a first lien on unencumbered, improved dwellings, housing not more than four families, or in process of construction and situate within this Commonwealth; (2) not to exceed eighty per cent of the fair value of the property; (3) loans may not be granted directly or indirectly to any one person in the corporation to a total amount exceeding five per centum of the amount paid in by its shareholders on account of shares. (4) Mortgage loans are limited to $20,000. on any one piece of real property. (5) The mortgage taken must not have any other mortgage or lien equal in lien to it which is

$241 

MORTGAGES. 

owned by any other corporation or person. These limitations, however, do not apply to purchase money mortgage transactions when taken by an association upon real estate owned by it.

Prior to the code there were no such restrictions upon building and loan associations mortgage loans. As a consequence, unwise practices arose such as accepting as security for a loan, mortgages (frequently second mortgages) upon hotels, office buildings, bowling alleys, garages, theatres, factories, and other industrial and specialty buildings. The depression developed that not only were such loans ruinous but that even second mortgages on dwellings, conservatively placed, put the associations at the mercy of the first mortgagee who called their mortgages, thereby forcing associations to take over first mortgages or lose their own investments. The consequences proved disastrous. The safeguards now imposed result from the experiences learned in the hard school of "depression." 

These limitations may confidently be expected to prevent a repetition of the tragic results which wrecked so many associations during the depression period. Forms of the different types of building and loan association mortgages will be found in the chapter on Forms. (§§268, 269, 270). 

95. Leasehold Mortgages.

We have seen that in general any freehold estate (see §3), of land may be mortgaged; so also a leasehold interest may be mortgaged. This is an important privilege where the lease is for a long term of years. Under Act of April 27th, 1855, P.L. 368, §8, (21 P.S. 838) every lessee for a term of years may mortgage his lease with all buildings, fixtures and machinery thereon with the same effect as in case of freehold interest. But the mortgage must be acknowledged and recorded with the lease or a copy thereof (Ladley v. Creighton, 70 Pa. 490). (See form $278). This Act has been construed to authorize the mortgaging of a lease of any kind of real estate (Hilton Appeal, 116 Pa. 351-1887). Such mortgage, however, does not affect the landlord's rights, priority

§95A  

or remedy for rent. As the right to mortgage leaseholds is a statutory right it is strictly construed, so that where a lease and a mortgage of said lease are duly recorded and both expire on a date named and the lease is extended after the expiration of the original term but the extension of lease is not recorded, the lien of the mortgage is not extended but it lost on the date when the lease had expired, and this applies not only to the lien on the lease, but as to the lien on the fixtures and machinery belonging to the lessee which are considered appurtenant to the lease (Stock v. German Catholic Press 

Co., 230 Pa. 127). 

95-A. Extent of Coverage of Lien of Mortgage. Chattel Mortgages. Industrial Mortgages. 

The general rule is that a real estate mortgage does not cover personal property on, or attached to the mortgaged premises (other than manufacturing or industrial plants), unless it comes within the category of fixtures (see for discussion of what are and what are not fixtures, §45f; and see 

Harmony Building Assn. v. Berger, 99 Pa. 320-1882). This general rule prevails even though the mortgage by express terms seeks to include personal property. Thus in Klaus v. 

Majestic Apt. House Co. (250 Pa. 194-1915), where the mortgage expressly included "furniture fixed and movable and all articles necessary and appurtenant to or now or hereafter to be used in and about the hotel plant", it was held ineffective to establish a lien, as against creditors, upon the furniture and the household furnishings belonging to the mortgaged apartment hotel company. See also Real Estate 

Land T. & T. Co. v. Bankers Trust Co., (104 Pa. Super. Ct. 

493-1931). (a) Chattel Mortgages.

(b) Industrial Mortgages. 

While as has been stated, at common law in Pennsylvania a mortgage lien on personal property could not be created by 1 For a form of this kind of mortgage see that set forth in the Act of 1887 (21 P.S. 862). 

2 See 12 of this act (21 P.S. 922) for form of such mortgage.

§95A  

a real estate mortgage, or a chattel mortgage (except as authorized by the foregoing statutes), unless the personal property has become a fixture of the real estate, nevertheless there is an exception to this general rule in the case of mortgages on manufacturing or industrial plants. The origin and extent of this exception to the rule has most recently been restated by former Chief Justice Kephart in Roos v. Fairy 

Silk Mills, (334 Pa. 305-1939) as follows: "Due to the demands and requirements of our changing economic order, we early developed in this state the principle of an 'industrial mortgage' which included as part of the freehold, personal property in and about a manufactory. This principle became more important as our industrial life expanded so that the necessary credits to sustain and finance manufacturies and other like industries could be obtained with some degree of certainty that the security offered would be continued. 

Therefore it was held that where premises were used in manufacturing or similar industries the real estate and personal property necessary to the plant as a going concern, were subject to the lien of an industrial mortgage. This opened the way for persons interested in such industries to assure investors in a manufactory not only of a stable security for money loaned on the plant, but one that could not be broken down and destroyed by selling it piecemeal.” "The rule removed the unwieldy strict rule of the common law relating to chattels as applied to manufacturing estab lishments. Chief Justice Gibson in Voorhis v. Freeman 2 W. & S. 116 (1841) at 119 *** announced the Pennsylvania rule, in a case which involved soft and chilled rolls lying loosely in an iron mill that 'Whether fast or loose the machinery of a manufactory which is necessary to constitute it, and without which it would not be a manufactory at all, must pass for a part of the freehold' ・ ・ ・ ・ In Commonwealth Trust Co. of Pgh. v. Harkins, 312 Pa. 402-1933, in which we considered all our precedents bearing on the question, we are now reviewing, whether cited or not, we laid down the broad principle that all machinery in a manufacturing plant neces-

$245 

MORTGAGES. 

sary for its operation as a complete going concern, is part of the freehold and bound by the lien of a mortgage thereon." 

That case further held the rule to apply even though the machinery was not expressly mentioned in the mortgage, the description of the mortgaged premises as a "factory building" in conjunction with the appurtenance clause in the customary form (as in §54(h) and mortgage form, §77), being regarded as sufficiently establishing it as an industrial mortgage. 

Illustration of the extent to which this principle is applied may be seen in Commonwealth Trust Co. of Pgh. v. Harkins, (312 Pa. 402-1933), where the lien of an industrial mortgage was held to cover jigs, patterns, and dies; Central Lithograph Co. v. Eatmor Chocolate Co., (316 Pa. 300-1934), where the lien of such mortgage was held to cover all candy making machinery including trucks and trays for the transportation of the materials in the factory. 

In the recent case of McClure v. Atlantic Rock Co. 14 A. 2d 

124; 339 Pa. 296-1940, it was held that a mortgage, upon an operating coal plant, which was afterwards converted into a stone quarry, covered fixtures installed subsequently in the stone quarry since it was the intention of the parties that the mortgage should cover the industrial use of the property. 

96. Recording of Mortgages. 

The Pennsylvania recording system and laws will be considered in a separate chapter hereinafter (Chapter VIII, §121 et seq.) but it is necessary to remember that unlike a deed the mortgage takes priority from the time it is recorded and not from its date. That is, the mortgage first recorded is first lien notwithstanding a prior mortgage has been executed before but not recorded until thereafter. The only exception to this rule is the purchase money mortgage which takes effect from its date if the mortgage is recorded at any time within 30 days thereof (formerly 60 days, sec. 88 at p. 228. But 

Mr. Fallon (Pa. Law Conveyancing by Christopher Fallon, 

Esq., Page 402), doubted whether in Philadelphia County by reason of the Act of May 25th, 1878, P.L. 151, even purchase

§97  

money mortgages are not required to be recorded at once like any other mortgage. But Purdon's Penna. Statutes regards this special Act of 1878 as having been repealed by the Act of May 12, 1925 P.L. 613; (21 P.S. 351) but in view of that fact that the Act of 1925 contains no express repealer, quaere as to the effect of the Act of June 12, 1931 P.L. 558 (§191) (21 

P.S. 351 anno) amending the Act of 1925 by, inter alia, excluding purchase money mortgages from its operation. To be safe, therefore, the immediate recording of all mortgages is recommended. The neglect to record, however, does not defeat the mortgage as to the mortgagor but merely suspends its lien as to any bona fide mortgagee or purchaser of the property without notice of its existence. A mortgage unrecorded in the lifetime of the mortgagor gains no lien by being recorded afterwards. It ranks merely as a debt under seal of the decedent (Nice's Appeal, 54 Pa. 200-1867).
