DISCHARGE OF MORTGAGES. 

97. By Payment and Satisfaction of Record. 

Generally speaking the lien of a mortgage continues until the mortgage debt is paid (Beckman v. Altoona Trust Co. 332 

Pa. 545-1939).

A mortgage paid and satisfied of record is of course discharged. The recorder of deeds will not satisfy the record of a mortgage unless the original instrument is produced. 

Should the original mortgage be lost, mislaid or destroyed, appropriate proceedings are provided by the Act of June 8, 1911, P.L. 717 (21 P.S. 697, 698), whereby on petition to the court, &c., satisfaction will be ordered or whatever relief is necessary, granted. (a) Payment.

Payment may be either actual or presumed. A mortgage is presumed paid if no payment has been made either on account of principal or interest for twenty years, but it re-

§(a) 247 

MORTGAGES. 

mains a lien unless satisfied by court proceedings as explained in $98 of this book. 

. years

Actual payment of mortgage principal cannot be made by the mortgagor, except in building association mortgages until due. But the mortgagee may waive his right to refuse to receive it before it is due. However the mortgagee cannot require payment until due. When payment of principal is due, depends upon the wording of the mortgage. A mortgage payable within a certain time may be paid off at any time; so a mortgage payable within a year from date can be paid off at any time during the year (Patterson v. Judge, 17 

W.N.C. 127–1885; Horstman v. Gerker, 49 Pa. 282-1865).

Therefore in filling in the printed form of mortgages insert the words "payable at the expiration of from the date thereof." (See also 77(a) 1, Supra.) Payment to discharge a mortgage should be made to the mortgagee or to an agent authorized to receive the same. A husband is not by virtue of the marital relation considered agent of a wife mortgagee, nor is an agent appointed to collect the interest regarded as having authority to receive the principal (Shay v. Schrink, 335 Pa. 94-1939). Payment to the mortgagee will discharge the mortgage even though previously assigned by him unless the assignee shall have given notice of the assignment to the mortgagor. Mere recording of the assignment is not sufficient notice (Foster v. Carson, 159 Pa. 

477-1894). Where a dispute arises as to the proper party, entitled to receive the principal of the mortgage, the mortgagor may protect himself by petitioning the court for leave to pay the principal into court. The court will then decide the question of the rights of the disputants and award the money so paid into court to the one legally entitled. 

Where a mortgagor paid a part of the mortgage debt and receipted for the same on the margin of the record and 10 months later paid the balance and took an assignment of the entire amount thereof, it was held as against subsequent lien creditors, and in absence of evidence that owner in making the first payment intended that the mortgage should continue

§97 (b)  

to exist, the mortgage was to be regarded as extinguished (Marshall v. Klein, 96 Pa. Super. Ct. 580-1929). The general rule is that where a debt represented by a senior lien is paid, the lien of a junior creditor advances in legal status whether or not the prior lien is marked formally satisfied, 

(Weir v. Potter Title & Mortgage Guar. Co. 323 Pa. 212—1936, and see §100A on merger infra.). (b) Satisfaction of Mortgage.

By satisfaction of a mortgage is meant a notation on the record of the mortgage that it has been paid and discharged. 

In practice this is done as follows: the mortgagee takes the mortgage and the bond to the recorder of deeds' office. The book in which the mortgage has been transcribed is sent for by the recorder or his deputy, who writes along the margin of the record, "This mortgage is this day satisfied", and the date. The mortgagee signs this written statement and pays the satisfaction fee. The recorder or the deputy then attest the mortgagee's signature. The mortgage itself is then stamped "Satisfied” and so certified by the recorder or his deputy and is delivered to the mortgagor or owner. The mortgagee should then also deliver the accompanying bond to the mortgagor, or the owner of the property, or whoever has paid off the mortgage. same.

A careful mortgagor will also require the mortgagee to write across the face of the accompanying bond, the words "Paid in Full", or words of similar import, and to sign the

The mortgagor should, of course, insist that the bond so cancelled be delivered to him with the satisfied mortgage. 

This should not be omitted because, although a bond and mortgage taken for the same debt are so far one, that the payment of either, discharges both, nevertheless, this is only so if so intended. In Longacre v. Beers, (106 Pa. Super. Ct. 

57-1932) a verdict on a bond, the accompanying mortgage of which has been satisfied, was upheld where the mortgagor proved to the satisfaction of the jury that the mortgagor had agreed that the bond might be retained as security for another

249

debt. See also Winters v. Wolfskill, (126 Pa. Super. Ct. 168 -1937).

Unless the mortgagee appears in person and enters satisfaction upon the margin of the record, there is no way of satisfying a mortgage except by formal letter of attorney duly executed, acknowledged, stamped and recorded. (Satisfaction of Mtgs. 26 D.R. 240). See next (c). 

(c) Satisfaction by Power or Letter of Attorney. 

Where it is impractical for the mortgagee to personally appear before the recorder, satisfaction may be entered by a power or letter of attorney, authorizing the recorder of deeds to enter satisfaction for the mortgagee. (See Form, $265).

Or the power of attorney may designate a third person to enter satisfaction, who must then go to the recorder of deeds' office to satisfy the mortgage. In either case the power of attorney must be recorded. This necessitates the payment of the recording charge for recording the letter of attorney as well as the satisfaction fee. A power of attorney directed to the recorder of deeds of the county where a mortgage is recorded, is effective to authorize his successor in office to satisfy the mortgage described therein (Act of April 28, 1915, P.L. 198, §1; 21 P.S. 701). But where a power of attorney was made out in the name of the recorder of deeds as an individual, without reference to his office or official title, it was held ineffectual to authorize the successor in office to satisfy under this act (Petition of Wedge's 34 D. & C. 11938).

Corporation mortgagees satisfy mortgages by having their board of directors authorize the execution of a power of attorney to a specific individual, agent or officer, or they may, if they choose, authorize the recorder of deeds to satisfy the particular mortgage. Forms of powers or letters of attorney will be found in the Chapter on Forms. They are either special or general. The former authorize the satisfaction only of the particular mortgage mentioned in the power. 3

$97 (d) 

General Powers, grant authority to satisfy all mortgages in the name of the mortgagee.

It should perhaps be mentioned that the Act of May 9, 1929, P.L. 1691, No. 544, (21 P.S. §701), validates satisfactions of mortgages heretofore entered by virtue of an authorization acknowledging the receipt of the amount due or in any other manner than by satisfaction entered by the mortgagee personally, by the recorder of deeds or by any other person acting under letter or power of attorney, duly executed and acknowledged, provided said acknowledgment of receipt of amount due, etc. has been signed and acknowledged by the mortgagee or his assignee, and is recorded. Before that Act however, such authorization was held to be insufficient (Satisfaction of Mortgages 26 D.R. 240-1916). (d) Obligation to Satisfy.

Certain remedies are provided by the statutes of the Commonwealth where a mortgagee refuses to satisfy the record of the mortgage. The Act of May 28th, 1715, 1 Sm. L. 94; 

§§9, 10, (21 P.S. §§681–682), requires the mortgagee to satisfy a mortgage within three months after tender made of reasonable charges after payment of the mortgage principal and interest, otherwise he becomes liable in an action by the parties aggrieved for damages not to exceed the amount of the mortgage. In several cases substantial damages were awarded under this statute. See Crawford v. Simon, (159 Pa. 

585-1894); Steigerwald v. Phila. Brewery Co., (21 Super. Ct. 

540-1902). To recover under this act it is necessary only to show neglect to satisfy the mortgage. It need not be shown that the refusal was wanton or malicious (Graham v. Mt. Airy 

B. & L. Ass'n., 102 Pa. Super. Ct. 116-1930).

Where there is a dispute between the mortgagor and mortgagee as to the amount due, the exclusive remedy to obtain satisfaction of a mortgage is under the Act of April 3, 1851, P.L. 868, §14 (21 P.S. §684), which enables the mortgagor to apply to the Court for leave to pay into the Court the amount claimed by the mortgagee, upon which payment the Court will

$251 

MORTGAGES. 

order satisfaction of the mortgage at once, and then proceed to determine the proper amount due, making decree accordingly. In Green v. Knights of Joseph B. & L. Ass'n., (25 

D.R. 800-1915), it was held that this act furnished a complete and adequate remedy to the mortgagor, and therefore a bill in equity to procure satisfaction of a mortgage, would not lie. Where the aggrieved party is not the mortgagor but the terre tenant, i.e., the owner of the property subject to the mortgage, such a bill in equity would not lie, for it was held in the case of Assurance Co. v. Power, (12 Phila. 377-1877), that a terre tenant had no right to pay the money into Court under the Act of 1851.

Where payment has been made but no satisfaction entered, a further remedy was provided by the Act of June 11, 1879, P.L. 141, as amended by the Act of May 13, 1931, P.L. 123, §1; (21 P.S. 687 anno.), which is made available to the mortgagor, his legal representatives, or the owner of the mortgaged property where the mortgagee, or holder of the mortgage has failed for any reason to satisfy the mortgage for six months by which, a decree of satisfaction can be secured from the Court. 

This act gives either party the right to demand a jury trial to settle any issue of fact (Byer v. Lancaster Lodge, 121 Pa. 

Super. Ct. 435—1936). 

98. Discharge by Order of Court in Proceedings to Satisfy 

Mortgages Presumed Paid. Lost Mortgages, etc.

Whenever a mortgage has been paid and the holder thereof has died (Act of March 31st, 1823, 8 Sm. L. 131, §1, 21 P.S. 

683) or has removed from the state (Act of June 20th, 1883, P.L. 138; 21 P.S. 689), or where it was given for security merely (Act of June 22, 1897, P.L. 184; 21 P.S. 693), and there has been a failure to satisfy it, appropriate proceedings in Court may be taken to compel satisfaction. 

While a mortgage is not a charge upon real estate and consequently is not subject to the conclusive presumption of extinguishment created by the Act of Apr. 27, 1855, P.L. 

368 $7 (12 P.S. 80) since it is a "specialty" (i.e. an instru-

$98 

ment under seal), it is subject to the ordinary rebuttable presumption of payment after 20 years. (McDonough v. Barnes, 30 D.R. 263-1920). The rule that after a lapse of 20 years debts by specialty are presumed to be paid is a rule of convenience and policy resulting from a necessary regard for the peace and security of society, and also for the debtor, who should not be called upon to defend stale claims at a time when witnesses are dead and papers lost or destroyed. This presumption does not bar the debt however. Unlike the

Statute of Limitations, it is merely a rule of evidence affecting the burden of proof, and no new promise is required as the basis of the action. Within 20 years the burden of proving payment is on the debtor, after that time it shifts to the creditor. To rebut the presumption any competent evidence tending to show the debt is not in fact paid will be received. 

Although it need not be of the same quality as required to remove the bar of the Statute of Limitations, it should be clear and convincing, especially where suit is not brought until after the death of the debtor. (Sheafer v. Woodside, 257 Pa. 276-1917).

By the Act of June 10, 1881, P.L. 97, §1, as amended by the 

Act of April 27th, 1927, P.L. 461, §1; (21 P.S. 688), proceedings are provided wherein a mortgage may be satisfied by the Court where no payment on the principal or interest has been made for twenty years. Such lapse of time raises a presumption of payment of the mortgage and the Court is empowered upon petition, duly filed, to make an order to satisfy such mortgage of record.

Where a mortgage has been paid, but never satisfied, the 

Act of June 11, 1879, P.L. 141, §1, (21 P.S. 687), provides for proceedings whereby satisfaction may be had even though the mortgagee cannot be found. The same act provides a like remedy where the mortgagee was a corporation whose existence has been terminated, or become doubtful. 

There is also a special Act of April 10th, 1849, P.L. 619, §12, (21 P.S. 692), providing proceedings to satisfy lost mortgages.

$253 

MORTGAGES. 

This Act, however, applies only to Philadelphia, Montgomery and Lycoming Counties. 

99. Discharge of Mortgage by Release. Form. 

Where a mortgage covers but one property and it is desired to release the lien against that property, the simplest way to do it is of course by satisfaction of the record. But it sometimes happens that one mortgage is drawn to cover several properties and it is desired by the parties to relieve one property from the lien without relieving the rest. This is accomplished by an instrument called a "Release of Mortgage. A release of mortgage is an instrument in writing duly executed by the mortgagee and acknowledged though not necessarily under seal, agreeing not to collect the mortgage debt by sale of the portion of the premises released (Wentz v. De Haven, 1 S. & R. 312-1815). The release should be recorded in order to clear the title of the released premises. The form of a release is as follows:

It must be remembered that a mortgagee is not bound to release any part of the mortgaged premises without the payment of the entire principal (Home Bldg. Ass'n. v. Troth, 3 

Del. Co. 169-1887). In other words, if a mortgage of $1,000.00 covers two properties the mortgagor cannot tender $500.00 and demand the release of one property. The giving of a release is always an act of accommodation on the part of a mortgagee and may or may not be for a consideration. But release taken from a trustee should always be for a valuable consideration lest the trustee be exceeding his trust powers in giving the release in which event the release would be void as to the cestui que trust. (Kirk's Appeal, 87 Pa. 243, 2481878). Sometimes there is given what is called a blanket mortgage or a mortgage which covers a large tract of land consisting of a number of separate lots. If an agreement be made at the time this mortgage is made that the mortgagee will release from time to time separate lots from the lien of his mortgage, as sold, upon the receipt of the proportionate share of the mortgage debt, such an agreement is binding and the mortgagor can compel the release of the lien of the mortgage from the lots sold upon tender of the proportionate share of the mortgage. But unless such agreement is made the mortgagor cannot compel the mortgagee to release any part without tender of the whole mortgage debt. 

Where a bond and mortgage are given to secure the same obligation, a release of one releases both unless a contrary intention is shown (Purman's Estate, 334 Pa. 238-1939).

And where a mortgagor has parted with his title to the mortgaged premises, a release of part thereof by the mortgagee without the knowledge or consent of the mortgagor will discharge the latter from personal liability for any loss to the mortgagee resulting in a deficiency in the proceeds on a subse-

§100 

quent sale under foreclosure proceedings. By such release, the mortgagee assumes the risk of the unreleased portion of the property being of sufficient value to secure his debt (Assigned Est. of James Hunter, 257 Pa. 32-1917). A release to a lessee of the lien of a mortgage on the leased premises was held to be valid in Harp B. & L. Ass'n. v. Davis, (56 Pa. Super. Ct. 282-1914).

There is one other matter of importance to remember in releasing a portion of premises from lien of a mortgage, and that is that if a mortgagor sells a portion of the mortgaged premises without obtaining a release, and thereafter sells another portion sufficient in value to pay off the whole mortgage for which he does obtain a release of mortgage, this last release operates to discharge and release the first portion sold (Schrack v. Shriner, 100 Pa. 451-1882; Meigs v. Tunnicliffe, 214 Pa. 495-1906). This because when pieces of land subject to a common encumbrance are sold successively by the owner, they are liable to the encumbrance in the inverse order of their alienation (Turner v. Flennikin, 164 Pa. 4691894; Higginbotham's Est. 51 Pa. Super. Ct. 458, 459—1920). 

100. Discharge by Judicial Sale. 

(a) Sheriff and Judicial Sales.

The final method by which the lien of a mortgage may be discharged or divested, is by a judicial sale on the instrument itself or on some lien equal or prior thereto except as otherwise provided by the statute hereafter considered. 

First, a word as to what is a judicial sale. Judge Baldridge, in Newcastle v. Whaley's Heirs, (102 Pa. Super. Ct. 492, 496 -1931), says: "What may accurately be denominated a judicial sale is not very well settled. There are certain well defined tests, however, to which it must conform. It must be based on a judicial order as a result of a judicial proceeding, and be subject to the Court's confirmation ・ ・ ・ . The term includes sales by Sheriffs, Marshals, Masters, Commissioners or by Trustees, Executors or Administrators, where

$257 

MORTGAGES. 

Sales by the order 

(Dixcy's Exrs. v. 

Also sales under the latter sell under decree of a court." of the Orphans' Court are judicial sales 

Laning and Sill, 49 Pa. 143, 146-1865). partition proceedings in the same court (Girard Life Ins. Co. v. 

Farmers & Mechanics' Bank, 57 Pa. 388, 394-1868). Also sale by Administrators for payment of debts (Vandever v. 

Baker, 13 Pa. 121, 126). But a sale by a trustee under a mortgage under authority therein given is not a judicial sale (Bruckman Lumber Co. v. Pittsburgh Ins. Co., 307 Pa. 561, 1932; Comm. v. Keystone Graphite Co., 248 Pa. 344, 3451915). Neither is a sale under testamentary power a judicial sale. (Fisher v. Kurtz, 28 Pa. 47-49-1857.)

It is not within the province of this book to enter into an extended discussion of the discharge of liens by judicial sale, but the general rules by which it may be determined when mortgaged real estate may be regarded as divested or discharged from the lien of a mortgage will be noted. Taking the most familiar type of a judicial sale as an example-a sheriff's sale—it may be said that if the mortgaged real estate be sold at such a sale on the mortgage or the accompanying bond, whether for interest or principal, it will discharge the mortgage (Ruth and Stoner's Appeal, 20 W.N.C. 375-1887; 

West Branch Bank v. Chester, 11 Pa. 282—1849). That is to say, the purchaser at the sheriff sale gets title clear of the mortgage which was foreclosed and clear of any liens equal, or subsequent in lien, to the mortgage and also clear of any prior liens, such as judgments, which are not protected from discharge by statute. These are thrown upon the fund produced by the sale, and the fund is distributed, in the order of priority, to the liens discharged.

This rule is simple enough, but what happens when the sale is not pursuant to a mortgage foreclosure? This calls for the application of statutory provisions which are best understood by a brief reference to their history. 

Prior to 1830, a sheriff sale, and in fact, all judicial sales operated to divest all liens on real estate whether prior equal or subsequent to the lien which gave rise to the sale. The

§100  

general rule still is that judicial sales discharge all liens save where express statutory exceptions have been made (Baird v. 

Moshannon Coal Co., 318 Pa. 63, 64-1935). Perhaps the most familiar, if not the most important exceptions to this general rule are the statutes saving mortgages from being divested by judicial sales under certain conditions and circumstances.

Exception was first made to the general rule in sheriff sales by the Act of April 6th, 1830, P.L. 293, (21 P.S. 651 note), which provided under what circumstances mortgage liens would not be discharged. This was the forerunner of a series of acts designed to protect liens of different kinds. The Act of 1830 applied only to sheriff sales but the Act of March 23rd, 1867, P.L. 43 (21 P.S. 651 note) extended its terms to cover all types of judicial sales.¹ (See infra. this book for a review of these acts, in §176 "Encumbrance Search (Mortgages)." 

The several acts restricting the discharge of mortgage liens were codified and revised by the Act of April 20th, 1929, P.L. 

874; (21 P.S. 651), which provides that a mortgage lien will not be discharged or in any wise affected by any judicial sale of the real estate on which it is a lien if it is, at the time of the sale, prior to all other liens on the same property except (1) other mortgages (2) ground rents (3) purchase money due the Commonwealth (4) taxes, municipal claims and assessments not at the date of the mortgage entered as a lien in the prothonotary's office (5) taxes, municipal claims and assessments which though afterwards accruing have by law priority given them. (The word 'priority' refers to priority of payment out of proceeds of sales, and not to priority of lien). 

William H. Hall, Esq., in his excellent book, "Searches and

Titles", page 114, simplifies the language and meaning of this 1 A title searcher must familiarize himself with the step by step development of the statutory law restricting the general rule that a judicial sale discharges all liens. He will find these acts gathered together and discussed in Bushong's Pennsylvania Land Law, Vol. 1, paragraph 330, VIII P. 266 et seq. Also the interesting summary of these acts compiled by Henry R. Robbins, Esq., eminent title expert of Philadelphia as published in 2 Dunlap's Forms (Ed. 1930) 2873, may be read with profit.

Act of 1929, as follows: "By virtue of this Act the lien of a mortgage on 'seated' lands will not be divested or in any wise affected by a sheriff sale on such real estate based on a judicial encumbrance; (a) if it is the very first lien on the property described in the mortgage; (b) if it is second, or subsequent to the lien of other mortgages which are not preceded by other liens; (c) if it is second, or subsequent only to a ground rent; (d) if it is second to any claim of the Commonwealth for purchase money due it; (e) if it is second to taxes, municipal claims and assessments not entered as liens of record in the Prothonotary's office when the mortgage was created."

It is to be noted that Mr. Hall limits the application of the act to 'seated' lands. This is correct. The act contains an express proviso that it shall not apply to cases of mortgages on unseated lands or sales of the same for taxes. 'Unseated lands' is a phrase used in Pennsylvania to designate uncultivated lands subject to taxation, i.e., 'wild lands' as opposed to 'seated lands' which at some time or other have been occupied for residence. Thus in Wallace v. Scott, (7 W. & S. 

248-1844), it was held a tract of land ceases to be 'unseated' as soon as it is actually occupied with a view to permanent use, and that occupation may be said to commence with the moment of entry for the purpose of clearing the land. 

Of course, as noted at the beginning of this section, a sheriff sale on a prior mortgage or ground rent will discharge a mortgage later in lien; and so also will a mortgage on which the sale is held, be discharged.

The title of a purchaser at a sheriff sale relates back to the date of the mortgage and defeats all intervening estates including easements acquired subsequent to the mortgage as e.g. a right of way (Dexter v. Pennsylvania Power Co., 127 

Pa. Super. Ct. 419-1937), a lease (Hostetter's Petition, 57 

Pa. Super. Ct. 601-1914; Roush v. Herbick 269 Pa. 1451920). 

(b) State Tax Lien. Priority. In Comm. v. Lowe Coal 

Co., (296 Pa. 359-1929), it was held that the lien of state

$100

taxes was a first lien and not discharged by a sheriff sale, but this was changed by the Act of June 3rd, 1933, P.L. 1474, and June 11th, 1935, P.L. 303; (72 P.S. 1401), which provides that state tax liens will be divested in any case where the lien of a ground rent, mortgage or other lien created by, or entered against a predecessor in title, will be discharged. (Davis v. Seltzer, 313 Pa. 382-1934). In such case the

State lien is transferred to the fund realized at the sale even though that fund is insufficient to pay all or any part of the Commonwealth's claim. The Seltzer case involved the lien of corporation taxes prior to the above acts. A similar ruling had been previously rendered by the Supreme Court in a case involving an inheritance tax lien, which was held to have no priority over a mortgage created before the decedent acquired title. (Scranton Lackawanna Trust Co. v. Same, guardian, 310 Pa. 125—1933). 

(c) Municipal Tax and Claim Priority. The Act of May 

16, 1923 P.L. 207, (53 P.S. 2021 et seq.) which supplies the earlier Act of June 4, 1901 P.L. 368 and its supplements, now regulates local tax liens (i.e. county, city, borough, incorporated town, township, school, bridge, road and poor taxes) their priority and collection by sale of the real estate upon which these taxes are assessed. Taxes are made a first lien and with all charges, expenses and penalties for failing to pay promptly, are first payable out of the proceeds of any judicial sale after payment of the costs of sale and of the writ on which the sale was made (§2 of Act of 1923 (Supra.), 53 P.S. 

2022). When the sale realizes enough to pay the costs of sale and taxes, the lien of the same is divested (Harrisburg Trust

(d) When Mortgages may be Discharged by Municipal Tax and Claim Sales. 

Mortgages and other liens, ordinarily preserved against discharge, may also be divested if the municipal claimant pro ceeds under §31 of the Act of 1923 (53 P.S. 2051). This sec tion provides that if a property cannot be sold for a sum sufficient to pay all taxes and municipal claims and the upset price fixed is not bid, the sale may be adjourned and a petition filed reciting the facts, upon which the Court shall grant a rule upon all parties in interest to appear and show cause why a decree should not be made directing sale, free and clear of all claims, mortgages, charges and estates. A sale made under such a decree will operate to divest a mortgage, which when so discharged, will be thrown on the fund and subordinated to payment of costs, taxes and other municipal claims. A mortgagee or other party in interest is given the privilege of arresting the proceedings and preventing the sale if he pays the petitioner the whole of the claim with interest and costs. 

This provision of the Act was held to be constitutional and applicable even to mortgages executed prior to its enactment, and despite the contrary provisions of the Act of April 20, 1929, above referred to, protecting mortgages from discharge. 

(City of Erie v. A Piece of Land, Etc., 14A. 2d. 428, 339 Pa. 

321-1940). This decision is further discussed in §176 "En cumbrance Search, (Mortgages" at p. 431 of this book).

Sales by Court orders, and receivers' sales, are judicial sales. Mortgages on property sold thereunder are protected by the Act of Apr. 20, 1929, P.L. 874 (21 P.S. 651) just reviewed. Indeed that Act expressly refers to sales "made by virtue or authority of any order or decree of any Orphans' or

But it seems the informality of a mortgagee's consent cannot be taken advantage of by an heir after a sale was had pursuant to a decree of the Court directing the same free of a mortgage lien, where it was so advertised and the mortgagee accepts payment out of the proceeds. (Mosley's Estate 39 D. & C. 159-1940).

100-A. Discharge by Merger.

A mortgage may sometimes be discharged by what is called a merger. This may occur when the title to the mortgaged property, and the mortgage, become vested in the same person as, e.g., where the property is conveyed to the mortgagee. 

Every conveyance of title of the mortgaged premises to the mortgagee does not necessarily operate as a merger. A merger is a question of intention, and where the intention is to keep the mortgage alive, there will be no merger, but such intention must appear from the surrounding circumstances 

(Landis v. Robacker, 313 Pa. 271, 272-1933). In Golder v. 

Bogash, (325 Pa. 449, 451—1937), it was said; "Discharge of a mortgage obligation by merger of the legal and equitable titles depend upon the intention of the mortgagor and mortgagee at the time of the alleged merger." Merger is never presumed when it is to the mortgagee's interest to keep it alive. (Moats v. Thompson, 283 Pa. 313; Sheehan B. & L. Assn. v. 

Scanlon, 310 Pa. 6-1933).

Intention is a question of fact. "Where it is shown the mortgagee will benefit by keeping the mortgage alive, there is a presumption that he so intended." (See also Moats v. 

Thompson et al. Exrs., 283 Pa. 313—1925).

§100B 

265 

MORTGAGES. 

Where, however, a mortgage is paid off by the property owner who has the mortgage assigned to him, it would seem that presumptively this would extinguish the mortgage by merger (Weir v. Potter Title and Mtg. Co. 323 Pa. 212—1936), though an intent to the contrary may be shown, (Marshall v. 

Klein, 96 Pa. Super. Ct. 580-1929). But the general rule is that when a mortgage has been paid by the mortgagor, the mortgage is extinguished and cannot be kept alive against subsequent lien creditors, (McCartney v. Kipp, 171 Pa. 6441895; Kinley v. Hill, 4 W. & S. 426-1842).

Where a husband and wife owned a mortgage as tenants by the entireties and the husband accepts a deed personally for the mortgaged property, there is no merger. (Sparrow to use, v. Mowers, 315, Pa. 460—1934). Nor will the extinguishment of a mortgage lien by merger resulting from a voluntary conveyance of title, operate as a release on the obligation on a bond or a judgment entered thereon, unless it was agreed by the parties that the conveyance should have that effect. A careful conveyancer will avoid the uncertainty of this rule by reciting in any deed conveying the mortgaged property to the mortgagee a statement to the effect whether or not the deed is intended to discharge the mortgage and its accompanying bond.

A conveyance by owner of real estate to a mortgagee was held to be a sale for purpose of establishing a loss for Federal 

Income Tax purposes in Phillips v. Commissioner of Internal 

Rev. 112 Fed. 2nd 721-1940.

V. 

DEFICIENCY JUDGMENTS. 

100-B. Deficiency Judgment Rule in Pennsylvania.

The aim of a mortgage foreclosure is obviously to enable a mortgagee to recover his loan. When the mortgaged property is sold at sheriff's sale for more than the sum due the mortgagee, together with the costs and expenses, the overplus very properly belongs to the owner unless there be other liens

§100C  

junior to the mortgage. Conversely, if the mortgaged real estate sells for less than the mortgage debt, the mortgagee is naturally entitled to recover the uncollected balance out of other property of mortgagor (Wolfe's Appeal, 110 Pa. 1261885). This right to demand the uncollected balance is in common parlance called a "deficiency judgment", though technically under our law there is no such thing as a deficiency judgment in the sense that a formal judgment of that description is rendered by the court or entered by the Clerk for the amount not made by the sale of the mortgaged property. 

There is in reality only the original judgment for the full amount of the indebtedness upon which a deficiency may exist after the issuance and return of the execution process under which the mortgaged property was sold (See Bank of Douglas v. Neel, 247 Pacific Rep. 132-134).

The doctrine of Wolfe's Appeal, 110 Pa. 126-1885, although not a case in which the mortgagee bid in the mortgaged property for a mere nominal sum has been developed by later decisions into the inequitable Pennsylvania rule that the price at which the mortgaged property is sold by the sheriff, even when purchased by the mortgagee for a nominal bid of $50, is conclusive as to the value of the mortgaged property. The effect of this rule is to enable a mortgagee to keep the penny and the cake. He gets the property and retains the full amount of his judgment. 

100-C. History and Development of the Inequitable Pennsyl vania Rule. 

With the general principle of Wolfe's Appeal, (110 Pa. 126 

1885), there can be no real quarrel. It was the unfortunate extension of that principle eight years later, in Lomison v. 

Faust, (145 Pa. 8-1892), to a case where the mortgagee had bid in for the nominal sum of one hundred dollars a farm he had previously sold to the mortgagor for $1,000 in cash and a mortgage of $6,500, which must be criticized. The extreme hardship of the situation there was commented upon by the

§100C 

267 

MORTGAGES. 

Supreme Court in the following language: "We would gladly relieve the appellant if we could do so consistently with well settled principles of law *** the plaintiff is making an unconscionable use of his power. He has his farm back with one thousand dollars purchase money in his pocket and permanent improvements far more valuable than the three years' rent which he has lost. He also sold the defendant's personal property for $475. In addition he had his judgment in full force and unsatisfied for nearly its whole amount, the result probably of the appellant's ignorance or neglect in not having the farm bid up so as to cover it. The appellee is now proceeding to sell upon this judgment another farm belonging to the appellant after which he still holds a mortgage upon his life and earnings for all time to come. 99 It will be noted that one of the reasons for denying relief was that the mortgagor could have 'bid up' the price at the sheriff's sale. In those days and indeed, up to about sixteen years ago, it was easy for a mortgage debtor to get credit for nearly the real value of the property being sold, by bidding it up at the sheriff sale. Unfortunately, this method of relief in Philadelphia was rendered difficult, if not actually abrogated by a rule or standing order of the local courts, adopted 

November 7, 1924, which changed the deposit required from the bidder at the sale from $50.00 to 10% of the bid. If the bidder is unable to pay 10% of his bid in cash, the property is put up again at the same sale and bidder who failed to pay his deposit is denied the right to bid again. It is obvious that the 10% deposit rule made it impossible for the mortgagor who is without funds, even to pay his taxes or his interest, to successfully bid to protect himself. A mortgagee bidding at such a sale has an unfair advantage in that he need not comply with the 10% deposit rule. Such a deposit also discourages bidding by outsiders, because sheriff sale guarantees no title so that an outside bidder bids at his peril. When, therefore, the deposit required was only $50.00, many bidders would risk that amount which they could forfeit later if an examina-

§100C  

tion of the records disclosed a faulty title. This bidding-call it 'speculative' if you will-had a potent effect stimulating the real estate market by preventing property going for sacrifice prices. But the almost prohibitive deposit called for by this rule resulted in Philadelphia in mortgagees being the only bidders. Instead of the outside bidder going to the sale, he goes to the mortgagee after the sale and buys from him at a sacrifice price, with title guaranteed. So it happens that rarely is there any bidder at Sheriff Sales in Philadelphia now other than the mortgagee who needs only to bid the nominal sum of $50.00. Mortgagees are thus enabled to acquire the mortgaged property without competition for a nominal sum and still hold the unsatisfied judgment for the full amount of the mortgage debt.

It is one of the saddest commentaries upon the rule of "stare decisis" that a harsh, unconscionable rule laid down in a poorly considered opinion founded on a precedent which could easily have been distinguished was accepted without question by the several decisions following it,' until it became embalmed as an inflexible principle of law, that: "The price realized at a foreclosure is conclusive as to the value of the mortgaged premises." (White's Estate, 322 Pa. 85-89- 1936).

It is to be greatly regretted that the Supreme Court, usually alert to correct inequity, has not so far over-ruled Lomison v. 

Faust, 145 Pa. 8. Such action is not without precedent. See 

York's Appeal, (110 Pa. 69, 78–1884), and United Security 

Case, (321 Pa. 276, 282-1939). All that is needed is for the

Court to admit the realities of the situation and concede that where a mortgagee buys in the mortgaged property, as the only bidder, for a nominal sum, that bid ought not to be accepted by a Court of Justice as more than prima facie evidence of the value of the foreclosed property. 

The depression of 1929 intensified public dissatisfaction with 

1 Mollenauer v. Smith, 51 Pa. Super. Ct. 517-1912; Ruetschlin's Estate, 245 

Pa. 473, 478-1914.

§100D 

269 

MORTGAGES. 

the "harsh" rule,' for mortgagors not only lost their property but remained indebted for the full amount of the mortgage and bond as well. Some it worried to death; others it drove into bankruptcy. Relief was demanded of the legislature and the result was a series of Deficiency Judgment Acts which will be considered in the next paragraph. 

100-D. Deficiency Judgment Acts. 

(a) Act of January 17, 1934 (Special Session) P.L. 243. 

The Legislature convened in the Special Session of 1933, strove to remedy the situation by the Mortgage Deficiency Judgment Act of 1934. That Act made it obligatory upon a mortgagee within six months after foreclosure sale to petition the court to fix the fair value of the property sold, and empowered the court to direct credit for the same to be given in reduction of the judgment. Failure on the part of the mortgagee to proceed to have the deficiency judgment so fixed, resulted in its automatic satisfaction.

This act provided a simple and expeditious relief but unfortunately, in October, 1936, it was declared unconstitutional by the case of Beaver B. & L. Assn. v. Winowich, 323 Pa. 

483-1936. In this case, Mr. Justice Stern, who wrote the majority opinion, held the act unconstitutional because it in fringed Article 1, §10 of the United States Constitution, pro viding, "No State shall pass any law impairing the obligation of contracts", as well as under a similar provision, restricting our Legislature; see Article 1, Section 17 of our State Constitution.

The reasoning of the Court, briefly put, was that under the precedents cited, the laws in force at the time and place of the making of a contract enter into the obligation with the same force and effect as if expressly incorporated in the terms. 

1 So termed in White Estate, 322 Pa. 85 at page 90. See as an example justifying this term, Marsh v. Bowen, 335 Pa. 314-1939 where the mortgagee having bought in for a nominal sum, a property mortgaged for $10,000., sold his deficiency judgment for a few hundred dollars; it was held the assignee might recover the full deficiency, approximately $10,000.

§100D  

This being so, it was beyond the power of the Legislature to radically change the remedy with regard to mortgage foreclosure as it existed at the date the mortgage was made. That under the law as it stood before the act, the amount bid at the sheriff's sale was conclusive between the parties as to the amount to be credited on the judgment, hence the mortgagee could not be denied his right to collect the whole deficiency so fixed. Of course, the Act of 1934, and that which followed and extended it, viz., July 1, 1935, P.L. 503, was perfectly valid as to new mortgages, but by its terms the act expired 

June 30, 1937.

In the dissenting opinion Mr. Justice Barnes pointed out that the mortgagor's obligation to pay the full amount of the mortgage debt was in no wise impaired, changed or altered all that the act did was to require the mortgagee to establish and give credit for the fair value of the mortgaged premises before he could proceed against other property of the debtor. That so far as the method or procedure by which this is accomplished is concerned, no person has a vested right in any course of procedure, King v. The Security Co., 241 Pa. 

547-1913, and that a state possesses control over its remedial processes and may make changes in the methods of procedure without violating the contract clause of the Federal Constitution. That Mr. Justice Hughes pointed out in Home B. & L. 

Assn. v. Blaisdell, 290 U.S. 398-433-1934, "In modes of proceeding and forms to enforce the contract the Legislature has the control and may enlarge, limit or alter them provided it does not deny a remedy or so embarrass it with conditions or restrictions as to seriously impair the value thereof." To which might be added that according to Breitenbach v. Bush, 44 Pa. 313—1863, it seems that only what the parties "stipulate in the body of the contract" concerning the remedy, is protected by the Constitution.

Subsequently in Richmond Corp. v. Wachovia Bank, 300 

U.S., page 124-1937, there came before the Supreme Court of the United States practically the same question decided in the Winowich case. It seems in North Carolina there had

§100D 

271 

MORTGAGES. 

existed a procedure sanctioned by the law of that state, if the mortgage so provided, whereby the holder of the mortgage, or the deed of trust as it is there called, could sell the mortgaged property at a trustee's sale. There, as here, it was the law that if the mortgagee bought in the property at the sale, he could recover in an action at law, the difference between the price he had bid and the face of the indebtedness. North 

Carolina, to relieve against this hardship, passed an act requiring the mortgagees in such cases to credit against the amount sought to be recovered, the fair value of the property bid in by him. It will be seen that the statute there was for all practical purposes the same as our Act of 1934. The 

United States Supreme Court, speaking through Mr. Justice 

Roberts, held that the North Carolina statute did not offend the contract clause of the United States Constitution and said: "The loan rendered the appellees debtors to the appellant, for that debt the borrower pledged real estate as security. The contract contemplated the lender should make itself whole, if necessary out of the security, but not that it should be enriched at the expense of the borrower or realize more than would repay the loan with interest". Subsequently in Honey man v. Jacobs (306 U.S. 539-1939) the United States Su preme Court, following the Richmond case on an appeal challenging a somewhat similar deficiency Judgment Statute of 

New York, said: "The question is whether in the instant case, the denial of a deficiency judgment substantially impaired the appellant's contract right. The bond provided for the payment to him of $15,000. with stipulated interest. The mortgage was executed to secure payment of that indebtedness. 

The contract contemplated that the mortgagee should make himself whole, if necessary out of the security, but not that he should be enriched at the expense of the debtor or realize more than what would repay the debt with costs and expenses of the suit. Having a total debt of $15,717.17 with expenses etc. of $1,319.03, the appellant has obtained, through his foreclosure, the property of the debtor found to be worth over $25,000. He has that in hand. We know of no principle

§100D  

which entitles him to receive any more. Assuming that the 

Statute, before its amendment, permitted the recovery of an additional amount through a so-called deficiency judgment, we cannot say there was any constitutional sanction for such a provision which precluded the Legislature from changing it so as to confine the creditor to securing the satisfaction of his entire debt."

But whether or not these cases in effect reverse the Winowich case is now academic for two reasons: first, because the old Mortgage Deficiency Judgment Act has expired by its own limitations, and, second, because even if the majority decision of our Supreme Court was wrong in its interpretation of the U. S. Constitution (as to which it must perforce give way to the United States Supreme Court), its decision, nevertheless, is still final so far as its interpretation of a smiliar contract clause of our own Constitution, (§17, Article 1) is concerned. 

Before leaving the Winowich case, attention must be called to the concurring opinion of Chief Justice Kephart, who pointed out that aside from the Deficiency Judgment Act of 1934, the mortgagor had a remedy by which he might avoid the consequences sought to be relieved against, viz., to move to set aside the sale because of gross inadequacy of price, since gross inadequacy of price in absence of competitive bidding was tantamount to a legal fraud. This view of the Chief Justice was later upheld and adopted by the whole court in Hettler v. Shephard, (326 Pa. 165-1937).

The profession should note, however, that such move must be made before acknowledgment and delivery of the sheriff's deed, otherwise, it is too late (Knox v. Noggle, 328 Pa. 3021938; Beckman v. Altoona Trust Co., 332 Pa. 545-1938).

And the price bid must be grossly inadequate (American State 

Bank v. Mariades, 328 Pa. 428-1938). This remedy is at best unsatisfactory, for the setting aside of such sale is largely a matter of discretion for the Court below which will not be reversed unless there be a clear abuse (id.). So we have a rule uncertain and bound to vary with the locality and disposition of the Court concerned. However, where a lower Court re-

§100D 

273 

MORTGAGES. 

fused to set aside a sale where $1,107.95 was bid for a property, which owner claimed to be worth $30,605 and mortgagee admitted a valuation of $15,000., the Supreme Court reversed the lower Court's refusal to set the sale aside (People's Pittsburgh Trust Co. v. Blickle, 330 Pa. 398-1938). What will happen if a second sale also brings a grossly inadequate price is a question that has not yet arisen. In Philadelphia, at least as long as the 10% deposit rule is in force, there is no assurance that any one other than the mortgagee's attorney would ever bid.¹ 

(b) Deficiency Judgment Act of 1937. 

Disappointed but not disheartened by the Beaver, etc. B. & 

L. v. Winowich case (323 Pa. 483—1936) the people demanded further legislation and the Legislature of 1937, passed a new act, the Act of July 2, 1937, P.L. 2751, which sought to remedy the situation in another way. Briefly stated, this act, unless the mortgagee was willing to release all claim to a deficiency, prohibited foreclosure until the mortgagee had the fair value of the mortgaged property first fixed by court proceedings as therein outlined. After the "fair value" was so fixed, the sheriff sale might be proceeded with, but the property could not be sold unless at least the fair value, as fixed in the previous proceedings, was bid.

If such fair value was not bid, the court was required to postpone sale for not more than six months. A second postponement was also required if the second sale still did not bring the "fair value". This act, in seeking to remedy an injustice to the mortgagor, went to the other extreme and unwisely so hampered the mortgagee that it would have discouraged if not destroyed the mortgage investment market of Pennsylvania. In Pennsylvania Company, etc. v. Scott, 

(329 Pa. 534-1938), and Home Owners Loan Corp. v. Ed- 

1 The reader is referred for further discussion of this subject to a well written paper entitled, "Recent Development in the Law of Mortgage Foreclosure" by 

Edwin C. Emhardt, Esq., of the Philadelphia Bar, Legal Intell. for Friday, July 

19, 1940 (vol. CIII page 105).

§100D  

wards, (329 Pa. 529-1938), this act was also declared unconstitutional not only as to existing mortgages but future mortgages as well-a decision not regretted by the bar or public, as was the Winowich decision.

There is still a strong demand in favor of legislative relief, especially in view of the fact that in many other States, equitable deficiency judgment acts have been held constitutional both by State and U. S. Supreme Courts. 

Several bills were introduced in 1939 but the legislators found difficulty in satisfying the Supreme Court's decisions, and the bills were held over for further study. 

Since the foundation stone on which the injustice of our deficiency judgment rule rests is the "judge made" rule of law that the price bid at the sheriff's sale, even though a nominal sum, is conclusive, the remedy lies with the court responsible for the rule. It is within the power of the court to overrule its former decisions and declare that thereafter the price bid at a sheriff sale will be regarded as prima facie evidence only of the value of the property at the time of sale. By this means the injustice now inflicted on mortgagors would be relieved and the mortgagee's right preserved to recover what he is entitled to but no more. This would be entirely in keeping with the history of the deficiency judgment development, because originally the theory of a mortgage foreclosure was that the mortgagee merely took the property in full satisfaction of the mortgage debt¹ (6 Kent Comm. 182). The right to collect by an action of law on the bond, was a later development arising from the desire to compensate a mortgagee where the land was insufficient in value. Thus a laudable development of the law to correct an inequity to the mortgagee has been made a means of perpetrating a grosser inequity upon a mortgagor, yet one that could be easily corrected by a decision boldly asserting that the "conclusiveness of the sum bid rule" will hereafter no longer be observed. 

1 See Article by Harold C. Vaughan, Esq., in Pennsylvania Law Rev. June 

1940, page 957 at 961.

275 

MORTGAGES. 

100-E. Deficiency Judgment Rule in Insolvent Estates. 

It seems to the writer a queer development of our modern system of jurisprudence that while under the unconscionable deficiency judgment rule, a mortgagor, if solvent, can get no relief from a grasping mortgagee, at a time it is most needed, yet after he becomes insolvent or dies leaving an insolvent estate, his creditors may require the mortgagee do equity by crediting against his claim the actual value of the property acquired at sheriff's sale, (United Security Co. case, 321 Pa. 276-1936).

The forward movement indicated by this decision was not maintained, however, for in Emlen's Estate,2 333 Pa. 238-1939 (where the Court, unfortunately, had only the benefit of an ex parte argument) the application of the United Security rule was restricted to cases where the mortgagor, at the time of his death or insolvency, still owned the mortgaged property. 

2 The Supreme Court by this decision, in effect reversed Alexander's Estate, 31 D. & C. 17-1938, where it was stated "We are urged, however, to limit the rule of the United Security case to those cases where the mortgage collateral remains unconverted at the time of the death; and this because, by the sheriff sale, the mortgagee has acquired the new status of owner; that as such, the mortgagee's title is free and clear of the equity of redemption, and he cannot thereafter be made to account for the value of the property so acquired. True the settled law is that his title is so indefeasible that he could not be compelled to account for the value thereof to the mortgagor: White's Estate, supra.; but so far as the creditors are concerned the collateral has only changed its form. If the mortgage creditor wishes to, he can still surrender it in its changed form and prove his claim for the full amount. (See Section 28 of the Insolvency Act of 1901, supra., quoted in the footnote on page 282 of the United Security Trust Company Case, supra.) Or, if he wishes to, he can retain it and prove the deficiency between the fair market value of his collateral in its changed form, and the amount of his judgment. Or if he has resold it (as in Bugh's Estate, supra) he can prove his claim to the amount of the difference between the price for which he resold the property and the judgment. Under all such circumstances he is getting what is fairly due him. As against creditors of the insolvent debtor, he is entitled to no more.

If we limit the just rule of the United Security Trust Company case by upholding the distinction contended for, we would in effect be penalizing a considerate mortgage creditor who displays forbearance to his unfortunate debtor in time of stress, and be putting a premium on harsh, inconsiderate treatment of a debtor by a creditor who deserves no advantage. The inevitable result would be that mortgage creditors, inclined to be lenient, would feel impelled to foreclose immediately upon default in order to escape such disadvantage. The consequent destruction of real estate values, and adverse effect upon the public in general, needs no comment.'

ASSIGNMENT OF MORTGAGES. EXTENSIONS. 

101. Definition of Assignment. Form. 

A mortgage, like any other chose in action or debt, may be assigned by the mortgagee at his pleasure and indeed after the death of the mortgagee, by his executor or administrator. 

This is done by an instrument called an "assignment of mortgage, " which in form, is a writing under seal, signed, witnessed, acknowledged and recorded. The usual form is as follows: 

ASSIGNMENT OF BOND AND MORTGAGE.1 

Know all Men by these Presents, That I, Richard Black, of the

City of Philadelphia, State of Pennsylvania, Merchant the Mortgagee named in the Indenture of Mortgage hereinafter mentioned, for and in consideration of the sum of Thirty-five Hundred ($3500.00) Dollars lawful money, unto me in hand paid by Robert Johnson, Builder, also of the said City and State at the time of the execution hereof, the receipt whereof is hereby acknowledged, do hereby grant, bargain, sell, assign, transfer and set over unto the said Robert Johnson, his heirs, executors, administrators and assigns, ALL That Certain Indenture of Mortgage given and executed by John Smith to Richard 

Black, bearing date the second day of January, A.D. 1912 and recorded in the Office for the Recording of Deeds in and for the County of Philadelphia in Mortgage Book, W. S. V. No. 1575, page 321, &c.² 

on All that Certain lot or piece of ground with the Messuage or Tenement thereon erected, Situate on the West side of "Y" Street at a distance of Three hundred and thirty-seven feet Northward from the North side of "X" Street in the Fiftieth Ward of the City of Philadelphia. Containing in front or breadth on said "Y" Street Eighteen feet and extending of that width in length or depth Westward between parallel lines at right angles to the said "Y" Street One hundred feet to a certain Three feet wide alley extending Northward from "X" Street to "Z" Street.

Also the Bond or Obligation in the said Indenture of Mortgage recited, and all moneys principal and interest due and to become due thereon with the Warrant of Attorney to the said Obligation annexed. Together with all Rights, Remedies and Incidents thereunto

This assignment when duly executed and acknowledged, should be recorded, (Act of Apr. 9, 1849 P.L. 524, §14; 21 P.S. 

623), and when recorded, all the incidents and force of a public record attach to it and it is notice to a subsequent assignee, (Pepper's Appeal, 77 Pa. 373-1875), but it is not notice to the mortgagor or property owner (see §§102–103).

§101A  

No assignment of mortgage is entitled to be recorded unless in writing and acknowledged by the assignor before an officer authorized to take acknowledgments, and contains a certification of the precise residence of the assignee or assignees (Act of Apr. 21 1937, P.L. 327; 21 P.S. 623 Anno). By the Act of Apr. 6, 1876 P.L. 18, §1 (21 P.S. 624) and the Act of Apr. 21, 1937 P.L. 327 (21 P.S. 623 Anno) the records of deeds is required to note the assignment when recorded, also upon the margin of the record of the mortgage. 

The old Act of May 28, 1715 (1 Sm. L. 90) §8, required assignments of bonds and mortgages to be executed under seal "before two or more credible witnesses" otherwise suit could not be brought on the assigned instruments by the assignee in his own name. This Section (8) of the Act of 1715 was expressly repealed by the Act of Apr. 4, 1929 P.L. 164, but even before its repeal and even though its provisions had not been complied with, the assignee could always bring suit in the name of the assignor, to his, the assignee's use (Phila. v. 

Lockhardt, 73 Pa. 211-1873; Shaub v. Shaub, 29 D.R. 1241919). And since the Act of Apr. 22, 1863 P.L. 567 (12 P.S. 

142), could bring suit in his own name or, at his election, in the assignor's name to his use (Phila. Saving Fund, etc. v. 

Orloff, 37 D. & C. 88-1939). Now by the Rule 2002 of the

Rules of Civil Procedure, effective Sept. 4, 1939, promulgated by the Supreme Court, actions to the use are abandoned and suits are required to be brought in the name of the real parties in interest. (Phila. Savings Fund v. Orloff, supra.). 

101-A. Parol Assignments. 

Assignment of a bond and mortgage may be made by parol and need not be in writing, provided it be accompanied by delivery of the instrument. One who takes a formal assignment of a mortgage without delivery of the mortgage and bond to him, assumes the risk of meeting sooner or later someone able to show an earlier valid title, and when a person appears, claiming the mortgage under a parol assignment, he cannot justly complain of consequences due solely to his failure

§101B 

279 

MORTGAGES. 

to exercise common prudence in an ordinary business transaction (Brumbach v. McLean, 196 P. 321-1900; Brumbach v. 

Johnson, 187 Pa. 602-603-1898). 

101-B. Assignments of Participating or Fractional Interests in a Mortgage.

Instead of assigning the whole mortgage to one assignee, an undivided interest may be assigned to each of several assignees. Trust companies have in recent years made a practice of so dividing, as it were, a mortgage among different trust estates of which they are trustees.¹ This is frequently done in a most informal manner though the far better plan is to assign the mortgage to a trustee by a formal deed of assignment in trust, reciting that the purpose is to hold the same in trust for the various undivided interests to whom participations should be issued, much in the form of bonds issued by a trustee for a corporate mortgage. Such a form was adopted by many trust companies who sold the participations or fractional interests to investors. The trust deed of assignment should specify the powers and duties of a trustee and limit independent remedial actions of the holders to whom the participating interests or certificates are issued, as well as include the power to the trustee to protect the mortgaged property if foreclosed and the income be insufficient to pay taxes or prior liens, by requiring the participants to pay their pro rata shares of such charges and expenses. 

The informal method followed by some trust companies may work satisfactorily so long as the company controls all of the participating interests, but it becomes fraught with grave danger if any of the interests pass beyond the control 1 This practice, originally of doubtful validity, was made legal by a series of acts amending $41 of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917 and by amendments to the Supplement to the General Corporations Act of 1874 under which most trust companies were incorporated (Act of May 9, 1889 P.L. 162). If the reader desires to pursue the question further, he should read Sec. 41 of the Fiduciaries 

Act of 1917-P.L. 447, sub. sec. 7 as amended by Act of June 24, 1939, P.L. 

718, Sec. 1, 20 P.S. 801 Ann., also Adjudication in Abbott Est. (O.C.Phila. County 

July Term, 1909, no. 149), not reported.

§101B 

of the company, as for example, when certain of the trusts end.2 

The fact is, that in absence of any instrument limiting such effect, an assignment of undivided or participating interest makes the assignees joint owners, and as such they would have equal rights to manage the mortgage for the benefit of their own interests and be answerable to each other for nothing but positive misfeasance. (Cronister v. Weise, 8 Watts 215 -1839; Donley v. Hays, 17 S. & R. 400-1828). The payment to one of several mortgagees at maturity will discharge the mortgage. McFarland's Est. 17 D. R. 936-1908). And an owner of one such participating interest might sue separately and recover judgment for his share of interest or principal, issue execution thereon and sell the mortgaged property and such sale would discharge the mortgage (Moyer v. Garrett, 96 Pa. 376, 379-1880; West Branch Bank v. 

Chester, 11 Pa. 282-1849; Clarke v. Stanley, 10 Pa. 4721849; Cronister v. Weise, 8 Watts 215-1839).

Where the assignor retains an interest in the mortgage, his rights are equal with those of his assignee, for the general rule is that where fractional parts of the same obligation are assigned to different persons, all the assignees share pro rata 

(Land Title Bank and Trust Company v. Schenck, 335 Pa. 

419-1939, and see cases cited on page 431). But where the assignor guarantees payment of the fractional or the participating interest, he is postponed to his assignees who have the right to be paid first (Id., Agricultural Trust, etc. Company's 

Mortgage Pool, 329 Pa. 581-1938; North City Trust Company case, 327 Pa. 356-1937). This subordination of the assignor who guarantees the fractional interests assigned, applies only as to the fractional parts retained, or held by the assignor. It does not follow such fractions, originally held by him, which are afterwards bona fide sold to other assignees, or pledged. (Land Title Bank and Trust v. Schenck, 335 Pa. 

419-1939; Hancock's Appeal, 34 Pa. 155-1859).

102. Effect of Assignments and Rights of Assignees. 

The assignment of mortgage carries with it all security which the mortgagee has for the same debt. As soon as the assignment is made, the assignee should immediately notify the mortgagor that the mortgage has been assigned to him, and that in future, payments should be made to him, the assignee. Unless such notice is given, a payment made by the mortgagor after the assignment to the original mortgagee will be binding against the assignee. The mortgagor is entitled to actual notice and he is under no duty to watch the record, for in Foster v. Carson, 159 Pa. 477-1894, it was said, "It would be an intolerable hardship if every time he may wish to make a payment and obtain credit on his debt, he would be compelled to visit the recorders of deeds' office to ascertain whether or not his mortgage had been assigned". (See O'Maley v. Pugliese, 272 Pa. 356-359-1922.)

The assignment of a bond and mortgage is governed by the same rules of law governing assignment and transfer of other non-negotiable instruments, to wit: that the assignee stands strictly in the place of the assignor and is entitled to all the right and remedies¹ of the assignor and subject to all of the equities, which the assignor is subject to, existing at the time of the assignment. Thus if it should happen that before the assignment of the mortgage, the mortgagor has paid the mortgagee a portion of the principal of the mortgage, or has some set-off, his set-off is good against the assignee even though the assignor made no mention of it (Morgan's Appeal, 126 Pa. 500-1889). In order to fully protect himself, therefore, against such possible contingency, it is 

1 In Philadelphia Company v. Viener (C.P. 1 Dec. T. 1937 No. 2278; Leg. Int. 

Sept. 19, 1939), it was held by Judge Lewis that an assignment of a bond and mortgage, carried with it an assignment of an extension agreement previously entered into between the mortgagor and the then holder of the obligation, and this without specific mention of the extension agreement in the assignment. It being held that the words "together with all rights, remedies and incidents thereunto belonging" (See form (101) was sufficiently broad to cover the extension agreement which could be regarded as "an incident" as well as forming one of the "remedies thereunto belonging.' וון

customary for the assignee to have the mortgagor execute what is called a 'certificate' or 'declaration of no set-off' (Ritter v. Thomasky, 70 Pa. Super. Ct. 615-1918), which is set forth and explained in the next paragraph. It is submitted that the assignee should always require a certificate of no setoff and record the assignment and have the mortgage papers delivered to him, for in no other way can he be safe. 

103. Certificate or Declaration of No Set-Off. Form. 

A certificate or declaration of no set-off is an instrument in writing, signed and sealed by the mortgagor, owner or title holder in which he certifies that he acknowledges the receipt of notice of assignment of the mortgage and bond, and declares what amount of the principal of the mortgage debt is that he still owes, and that he has no set-off, charge or other claim against the same. The form is as follows: 

CERTIFICATE OF NO SET-OFF.1 WHEREAS, I, John Smith, of the City of Philadelphia, State of 

Pennsylvania, being the present owner in fee of the premises described in the indenture of mortgage hereinafter recited, do hereby acknowledge that I have received notice of an assignment about to be made of said mortgage and of the bond or obligation therein recited by Richard Black of the City of Philadelphia, State of Pennsylvania, the holder thereof, to Robert Johnson, of the said City and State, and I do hereby declare that the sum of Thirty-five hundred ($3500.00) Dollars being the amount of the mortgage therein is still owing with interest, at the rate of five and four-tenths per cent per annum, from the second day of January, A.D. 1912, and thereafter payable half yearly on the second day of the months of July and January upon the bond and mortgage given by John Smith to Richard 

Black, DATED the second day of January, A.D. 1912, Recorded at 

Philadelphia in mortgage book F.G. No. 129, page 249, and etc., of

Thirty-five hundred ($3500.00) Dollars, AND that no part of said mortgage debt has been paid off, and that I have no charge, claim, demand, plea or set-off upon, for or against the same in any way or manner whatever.

It is to be noted that this certificate or declaration of no set-off, accomplishes two objects; it is an acknowledgment by the mortgagor, or the owner of the property, that he has received notice of the assignment which we found it incumbent upon the assignee to give. (See $102); and second, it is an admission of the debt and that no defense exists thereto. If there be more than one mortgagor, or owner of the property, the certificate of no set-off should be executed by all. The assignee of a bond accompanying a mortgage who fails to make inquiry of the obligor, takes it subject to any defense to which it is subject in the hands of the assignor (Federal 

Reserve Bank etc. v. Gearon, 331 Pa. 65-1938). 

103-A. Suggestions to Assignee as to What Must Be Done to Make Assignment of Mortgage Effective. 

In order therefore, for an assignee of a bond and mortgage to be protected against the world, he should, (a) demand production and delivery to him of the mortgage papers, (Brumbach v. McLean, Supra., $101A). (b) Record the assignment (Landis v. Robacker, 313 Pa. 271-1933), (c) give actual notice to the owner of the mortgaged property, (§102, and cases there cited). (d) Insist on a declaration of no set-off by the mortgagor or property owner and from both if reliance is placed on the personal responsibility of the mortgagor. ($103 and cases there cited).

The mortgagor or owner cannot be compelled to execute this certificate although few would be so ungracious as to refuse. But should the refusal be persisted in, it of course, puts the proposed assignee on his guard and he is bound then to make diligent inquiry before taking the assignment. 

It is to be noted that a subsequent assignee may avail him-

§103B  

self of a certificate of no set-off given to the first (Ashton's Appeal, 73 Pa. 153-1873). But the estoppel which is raised against the mortgagor, or owner, by reason of his execution of a certificate of no set-off, is available only to an assignee who is a purchaser for value without notice (Ashton's Appeal supra).

After notice of an assignment of a mortgage, the party liable cannot set off claims subsequently occurring against the assignor, so even in the absence of a declaration of no set-off, no claim arising in favor of the obligor against the assignor subsequent to the assignment, is available as a set-off or counterclaim (Much v. Gorsuch, 307 Pa. 56—1932). 

103-B. Right to Compel Assignment of Bond and Mortgage. 

Generally speaking, a mortgagee is not required on receipt of the indebtedness, to assign or transfer the mortgage. He can only be required to satisfy it. (Hopkins Mfg. Co. v. 

Ketterer, 237 Pa. 285-1912, and see §97(a) Supra.), unless the circumstances are such that an assignment is required for the protection of the party making the payment as in the case of a junior mortgagee or lien holder (id.), or where the mortgagor has parted with title to the property and is compelled to pay the mortgage to protect his bond as e.g. proceedings under Act of 1903 (21 P.S. 735). See §81B (b) this book

Supra. 

Attempts by property owners to "freeze" out junior encumbrances by buying the first lien and taking an assignment thereof to an agent or nominee instead of satisfaction, is a familiar device that has come all too frequently before our courts. In such cases the courts have not hesitated to grant full relief when the real purpose of the assignment was shown (Kiedaisch v. Elkins Bank, 325 Pa. 241-1937).

Frequently mortgagees themselves, when they sense such a trick, refuse to be a party to the fraud and decline to assign the mortgage and so arises the question to what extent and to whom a mortgage holder can be compelled to assign the mortgage and bond, upon tender of payment thereof. Upon this

§103B 

MORTGAGES. 

subject the following acts appear on the Statute Books. The 

Act of June 24, 1885, P.L. 157 (21 P.S. 731) gives to owner of land encumbered by a previous owner, the right to tender to the encumbrance holder (when due) the amount owing, together with interest and costs and require assignment of the encumbrance to the land owners nominee, but only in the following case, (1) where minors are involved and the court finds it to the interest of the minors that the encumbrance shown be assigned to the appointee of the guardian. (2) Where the land is held for life with remainder over. (3) Where lands are held in trust, (4) or where they have descended under the intestate laws. The Court is authorized to compel assignment upon failure of the holder of the mortgage or encumbrance to assign after proper tender and interest shall cease from the date of tender until the assignment is executed. The act also contains a proviso that it must first appear to the Court that "all parties in interest in the lands so encumbered, have joined in the application for assignment of such mortgage, judgment, recognizance or other security" (See Weimer v. 

Karch, 5 Pa. C.C. 203—1888; Wymbs v. Reilly, 7 Lack, L.N. 

98-1900 construing this act).

It is obvious the right to compel an assignment of a mortgage was by this act denied to the mortgagor and restricted to the subsequent land owner, is a distinctly limited one, and appears to have been infrequently invoked. 

The Act of May 4, 1927, P.L. 710 (21 P.S. 733-4) is much broader in scope and provides in substance the owner of lands encumbered by mortgage, judgment, recognizance or other security, after the same is due, shall have the right to tender to the owner of the encumbrance, the amount owing with interest and costs and to require him to assign the same to property owners nominee without recourse or liability on part of the assignor. Then follows a provision similar to that of the Act of 1885 just considered, authorizing the Court to enforce the assignment and with the same penalty of loss of interest from the date of the tender to the date of assignment. The Court is empowered to make such a decree as justice may require

§103B  

and forbids a decree unless it appears that all parties in interest have joined in the application for the assignment. The 

Supreme Court has very properly construed this proviso to mean that the owner of the encumbered property may not compel an assignment unless the subsequent lien owners assent, since they are parties in interest (Kiedaisch v. Elkins 

Bank, 325 Pa. 251-1937; Green v. Second Allegheny Building Assn., 311 Pa. 305-310-1933). It is obvious from these decisions that the act may not be used by an owner to compel an assignment to the injury or damage of any party in interest, including junior encumbrancers and lien holders, without their consent. So also a co-owner of the land must consent (Weimer v. Karch 5 Co. Ct. 203-1888). Though where the co-owner was the party primarily liable by reason of the fact that the mortgage was made for his accommodation, his assent was held to be unnecessary (Cecotti v. First Nat. Bank of 

Jessup, 37 D. & C. 539-1940). The provision requiring assent does not mean that all in interest must become parties to the litigation if their assent is otherwise sufficiently expressed. 

(Fitzpatrick v. Influential B. & L. 36 D. & C. 206-1939). 

Where mortgage foreclosure has been commenced before tender, a reasonable attorney's fee for counsel of the mortgage holder, must be paid by the person requesting the assignment (Fitzpatrick v. Influential B. & L. Assn. Supra.). 

There remains but to be said, that there is also the Act of 

1903, (Apr. 28, P.L. 327; 21 P.S. 735), which enables the mortgagor who has parted with title to the mortgaged land, to demand after maturity, that the mortgage and bond be assigned to him upon payment of the mortgage debt with interest and costs. Refusal to assign, upon tender, results in the mortgagor being relieved of all personal liability. This remedy, under this act, was held not to be so exclusive so as to oust the jurisdiction of the Equity Court, if other and further relief was necessary (Kiedasch v. Elkins Bank, 325 Pa. 241-1937). 

See also §81-B (b) Supra., where the Act of 1903 and decisions thereunder, is more fully discussed.

103-C. Extension of Mortgage Agreements. 

When the maturity date of a mortgage arrives, the mortgagee has the option of demanding its payment in whole or part. Or he may permit it to remain as is, in which case, as we have seen (§97 (a) ), it remains a lien until paid notwithstanding the maturity date has passed. Or he may, as is customarily the case, agree with the property owner for a definite period of extension. The agreement to extend a mortgage need not be in writing to be valid (Hoffman v. Lee, 3 W. 352-1834; 

Girard Trust Co. v. Cresson Co. Leg. Int. Aug. 26, 1940 (CIII 

L.I. 327), but the advantage of a written agreement of extension of mortgage is too obvious for comment. 

The extension of a mortgage does not impair either its priority or its lien (Beckman v. Altoona Trust Co. 332 Pa. 

545-546—1938), and a reduction of interest rate therein is binding since mutuality of the extension is itself sufficient consideration (Shoemaker v. Farrell, 64 Pa. Super. Ct. 341916).¹
