I. 

104. Definition and History of Ground Rents. 

The meaning of ground rent is generally more misunderstood than any other term in the science of conveyancing. 

This is in a great measure due to its inappropriate name, which leads most people to believe it to mean rented ground. 

The idea that a man who pays ground rent does not own the ground in fee is as unfortunate as it is erroneous. The real meaning of the term ground rent is best explained by briefly developing its history. 

In early English History there existed an estate in land called a Rent Service, which was created by a Lord conveying land to one of his vassals in fee, reserving to himself, however, the right to call upon his vassal's service so long as the vassal remained the owner of the land. Later, instead of reserving the right of demanding the actual service of the vassals, the Lords granting the land began to reserve to themselves the right to receive annually a certain sum of money instead. At common law, therefore, a rent service became an estate in land reserved by the grantor to himself out of the granted estate. This reserved part usually consisted of a right to services or right to receive a certain sum of money paid at fixed intervals according to the terms of the grant. The socalled ground rent is a lineal descendant of the old rent service. 

It possesses all its attributes (Ingersoll v. Sergeant, 1 Whart. 

336-337-1836) and is created in the same way. 

The method of creating a ground rent is as follows: The owner of the land conveys to a grantee his whole estate, reserving, however, for himself the ground rent out of it. The former owner or grantor then has the ground rent estate and the grantee owns the land subject to the payment of this rent. 

The owner of the ground rent is sometimes called the

§104 

99 "grantor," sometimes the "ground rent landlord" or the "covenantee." The owner of the land subject to the payment of the ground rent is sometimes called the "grantee, sometimes the "terre-tenant," and sometimes the "covenantor."

A ground rent can only be created by the person having a fee simple estate reserving it out of a conveyance to someone else. Therefore, if A desires to give B a ground rent in a certain piece of land, he must first convey unto B his whole estate, which makes B the owner in fee. B must now re-convey the land to A, reserving unto himself a sum of money or rental to be paid yearly. A is once again the owner in fee of the land, but he must now pay to B a certain tribute every year. Thus it will be seen that a ground rent is nothing more or less than "a rent (usually a sum of money payable at stated intervals) reserved by a grantor, to himself, his heirs and assigns in conveying land in fee." (Ingersoll v. Sergeant, 1 Whart. 336–337—1836). This rent, while usually a sum of money payable at stated intervals may, like the common law rent service, be either in kind, services or chattels and sometimes has been made merely nominal. Thus e.g. Charles II granted the province of Pennsylvania to William Penn upon ground rent which according to the Charter was stipulated to be "two Beaver Skins to Bee delivered att our Castle of Windsor on the first day of January in every year; and also the fifth part of all gold and silver oare which shall from time to time be found within the Limitts aforesaid."'1

The ground rent is generally unknown throughout the rest of this country. It is in use in some few of the states, perhaps in parts of New York or New Jersey. With these exceptions it is peculiar to Pennsylvania, and even in Pennsylvania, outside of the City of Philadelphia it is a rarity. In 

1 In Manheim, Lancaster County, Pa., the Zion Evangelical Church is erected on a plot of ground conveyed in 1772 by Baron von Stiegel by deed which reserved a ground rent of "one red rose annually in the month of June forever." The terms were carried out during the Baron's lifetime then forgotten till 1901, when the payments were resumed with payment of 156 roses as back rent. Since then the delivery of this ground rent to the descendants of von Stiegel is an annual ceremony.

§293 

GROUND RENTS. 

The 

Philadelphia, however, ground rents are very common. creation of ground rents was used for the building up of the City of Philadelphia, and was of inestimable value in doing it. 

The method was that the owner of a tract of land would convey it to B, reserving a perpetual rent generally with a condition that the rent might be paid off within a certain time upon the payment of an amount equal to the rent capitalized at 6%. Of course, the advantage of the ground rent was that the purchaser or grantee did not need to pay any ready money to complete his purchase, but simply had to go upon the land, improve it and so earn the purchase money. Again, the ground rent was used and to this day is still used as an encumbrance for the loaning of money, as in the case of a mortgage. In such case, as explained before, A being the owner of the land and desiring to borrow money on it, would convey it to B for a nominal consideration and B would immediately reconvey it to A, reserving the rent; in this way the ground rent estate would become a security for the money loaned.

The instrument by which a ground rent is created is called a ground rent deed. This deed contains covenants on the part of the grantor and grantee and is executed in duplicate as all indentures once were. (See $52). One copy is recorded and the other marked counterpart and they are retained by the owner of the land and of the ground rent, respectively. By examining the form set forth on page 293 it will be seen that a ground rent deed reads the same as an ordinary deed of conveyance until you reach the habendum (to have and to hold clause), where, after the word 'forever', is added what is termed the "Reservation" (See form, page 294), which begins with the words "yielding and paying" and ends with the word "procurement near" the very end of the deed.

Analyzing the reservation it will be seen that it provides, first, for the amount of rent reserved, in what, and how it shall be paid. Modern ground rent deeds set forth merely lawful money of the United States, the older ones usually stipulated the metal coin such as gold or silver of a specified weight and fineness. Then follows an agreement permitting the grantor or owner of ground rent, his heirs or assigns to enter to make distress if the rent is unpaid and following it a provision that if sufficient distress be not found the grantor, his heirs or assigns may re-enter and take possession. Modern ground rent deeds also have the next clause inserted providing for an attorney's fee in whatever amount agreed to, to be added to the arrearages of the ground rent, should it be necessary to commence suit thereon. This provision for attorney's fee relieves the grantor from this burden, which he bore under the older deeds, and saddles it on the grantee. 

Next a covenant on the part of the grantee to pay all the taxes

$106

assessed against the property which is important in that it relieves the grantor from paying any taxes on his ground rent. 

This provision is valid and enforcible (Van Beil v. Brogan, 65 

Pa. Super. Ct. 384-1917, Aff. 262 Pa. 362-1918 and see 

§120,-5 infra.). 

The clause in parentheses may be termed the "covenant to build." As here set forth, it requires the grantee to build a stable. If improvements are already erected on the lot and no additional ones contemplated, this clause should be omitted. 

The next clause is that waiving the Exemption Act. The remedy of distress is of little value unless the exemption Act is waived, so care should be taken to always insert it. Equally important is the waiver of exemption in case of a sale of the property subject to the ground rent. 

Then follows the agree ment that if at any time after the expiration of ten years, the owner of the ground rent is paid $1,000.00 (which is the capitalized principal of $60.00 per year at 6%) he will execute the necessary instruments to extinguish it. The rest is the usual covenant of quiet enjoyment and is self-explanatory. 

II. 

NATURE AND KINDS OF GROUND RENTS. 

106. A Ground Rent Is Real Estate. 

From the foregoing section it is readily seen that a ground rent is essentially different from a mortgage both in creation and effect. A ground rent is an estate in the land and is, therefore, real estate (Cobb v. Biddle, 14 Pa. 444-1850) whereas a mortgage is but a pledge of the land to repay a debt and is personal property. So also a leasehold for a term of 999 years, yielding an annual rent, with covenants for perpetual renewal, is but personal property and not the legal equivalent of an estate in fee simple reserving a ground rent (Sachse Estate 26 D.R., 709-1917, see also §4(a) of this book). 

A ground rent is an estate in fee, although separate and distinct from the fee estate of the land itself, out of which it issues. The ground rent being an incorporeal estate and the latter a corporeal estate. A ground rent being real estate

§

299 

GROUND RENTS. 

may itself be mortgaged (Weidner v. Foster, 2 P. & W. 231830; Bank of Commerce v. Peace, 27 Pa. Super. Ct. 644 

1905), and may be bound by a lien of a judgment (Huehner v. Fisher, 61 Pa. Super. Ct. 533, 535—1915). It is just like other real property, subject to the assessment and payment of real estate taxes and upon death of the owner it passes to the devisee or heir and not to the executor or administrators, and the doctrine of implied grant is applicable thereto (Huehner v. Fisher, supra.). The fact that a ground rent is real estate, is likewise reflected in the instrument creating it and in a way it is extinguished. 

107. Irredeemable Ground Rents. 

Ground rents in Pennsylvania are of two kinds, Redeemable and Irredeemable. Irredeemable ground rents, as the name implies, are such as can never be redeemed, that is, never paid off. These irredeemable ground rents were the older form, for originally ground rents were perpetual when the deeds reserving them used the words "In every year hereafter forever." Later it became customary to place in the deed reserving the ground rent a provision that if said ground rent should not be extinguished (i.e., paid off) within a specified period it should become irredeemable. Although at the present time there are few ground rents existing in Pennsylvania which were originally irredeemable, there are many still existing which have become irredeemable by operation of the clause such as above stated. Since the Act of June 24, 1885, P.L. 161—68 P.S. 161, 162), no new irredeemable ground rents can be created, for that act in positive terms forbids their creation and provides that notwithstanding any irredeemable clause in a ground rent created after the act, it shall nevertheless be redeemable. (Crean's Estate, 321 Pa. 216-1936). 

108. Redeemable Ground Rents. 

Redeemable ground rents are such as can be redeemed or extinguished at any time after their creation at the pleasure

§109  

of the owner of the land, that is, the grantee who must pay the ground rent. The ground rent owner or ground rent landlord can never demand the payment of the principal (Crean's Estate, 321 Pa. 216-1936) unless a clause giving him such a right is inserted, in which case he may demand the payment of the principal only at the expiration of the term fixed, notwithstanding any default. Some of the more recent ground rent deeds contain such a provision as well as a provision enabling the principal to be called in the event of a default. 

The remedy of the Ground Rent Landlord to enforce such right is by action of assumpsit and sale of the real estate under judgment so obtained. 

109. Apportionment of Ground Rents.

A peculiar attribute of a ground rent is that a ground rent becomes apportioned as the land out of which it issues is divided. 

That is, suppose a tract of land out of which a ground rent issues, is divided into three parts, out of each part of the original tract must be paid its proportionate part of the whole rent, in this case one-third. But the ground rent landlord is not, without his express consent, bound by the apportionment and may collect the whole rent from any part: (Ministers 

Trustees, etc. v. Limehouse, 19 D.R. 199—1910). If the holder of any part pays the whole rent he may maintain an action against the owners of the other parts for their proportionate contribution. The release of the ground rent as to any part of the divided tract has no effect on the remainder for that remainder's share of the ground rent, which still exists in full force until released or extinguished (Ingersoll v. Sergeant, 1 Whart. 336-337-1836). 

Not only may the land out of which the rent issues be apportioned but the ownership of the rent may also be divided among any number of persons, and the owner of any portion may maintain a separate action for his portion of the rent and the terre tenant is bound to pay each his due portion (Reed v. 

Ward, 22 Pa. 144-1853).

§

301 

GROUND RENTS. 

III. 

REMEDIES FOR COLLECTION OF GROUND RENT AND PRINCIPAL. 

110. When and How Rent Must Be Paid. 

The rent must be paid according to the terms of the deed. 

If it provides that rent is to be paid in lawful money of the United States, it may be paid in any legal tender. If it provides "payable in coin of a specified weight and fineness" it must be paid in coin of that weight and fineness, unless such coin is no longer legal tender, in which case it may be paid in legal tender (Cook v. Lovett, 17 D.R. 347—1908). It must be paid when due or the ground rent landlord may proceed to collect the rent by any remedies hereinafter set forth; which remedies are cumulative; i.e., the party entitled to the ground rent may invoke any or all until he is satisfied (Hiester v. 

Schaefer, 45 Pa. 537—1863). 

111. Remedy by Distress. 

The owner of the ground rent may distrain like the lessor of a term of years. This right is an incident of a ground rent at common law and existed without special provision in the deed. But in Pennsylvania is was held (Wallace v. Harmstead, 44 Pa. 492-1863), that an express reservation of the right to distrain must appear in the deed, hence the ground rent deeds usually have inserted a distress clause in which includes a waiver of exemption in order to make this remedy more complete. In distress for ground rent the procedure is the same as any other distress for house rent, and if the ground rent deed contains a waiver of the exemption law it is usually effective. Tenant's goods as well as those of the owner are liable for distress. 

112. Remedy by Re-Entry. 

This remedy is practically obsolete, although it may still be enforced. It is, however, a troublesome procedure and rarely

§113  

used because the following steps must be carefully taken:

Distress must first be made and if sufficient property be not found to pay the rent due, an actual demand must be made before sundown on the precise day when due for the exact amount (McCormick v. Connell, 6 S. & R. 151-1820). This demand must be made even though the land is unoccupied 

(Homet v. Singer, 35 Super. Ct. 491-1908). If possession of the land be refused, ejectment proceedings must be commenced to oust the tenant in possession. If there is no one in possession, then the ground rent landlord may enter without difficulty, but as there is nothing on record, equity proceedings should be commenced to perpetuate testimony (Cadwallader v. App. 81 Pa. 194-1876). 

113. Remedy by Action of Ejectment. 

Wherever the ground rent deed provides for a right to reenter upon the breach of covenants, then the ground rent landlord may begin an action of ejectment upon such breach. 

This is the more common method of proceeding where the right to re-enter is desired to be enforced, having the advantage of avoiding a personal conflict and being a matter of record. 

114. Remedy by Suit or Action of Assumpsit. 

The most common remedy to recover ground rent is to sue the grantee or the terre-tenant, the person liable to pay the ground rent in an action of contract. The ground rent deed is a contract or covenant to pay the rent, hence an action of contract lies. If the original grantee of the land out of which the rent issues, transfers the land, the assignee becomes liable to pay the rent and a personal action may be commenced against him (Act of April 25, 1850, P.L. 569, §8, 68 P.S. 211) and also independent of statute, see (Sachse v. Meyers, 15 Pa. 

Super. Ct. 425, 434-1900). But as to ground rents reserved since the Act of June 12, 1878, P.L. 205, (21 P.S. 655), the personal liability for ground rent remains only so long as such

§303 

GROUND RENTS. 

grantee owns the land (Sachse v. Meyers, 15 Pa. Super. Ct. 

425-1900). He is relieved of such personal liability on bona fide conveying the land to a purchaser, unless he has by express language in the deed assumed such liability: Act of 

1878, supra., §2 (21 P.S. 656). Of course, a grantee's liability to indemnify the original convenantor for rent actually paid after conveyance of title, remains: (May's Est. 218 Pa. 64.).

IV. 

LIEN AND DISCHARGE OF GROUND RENTS. 

115. Lien of Ground Rents and Arrearages of Rent. 

Strictly speaking a ground rent is not a lien, though its practical effect on the title is that of any other encumbrance. 

Therefore, a property subject to a ground rent would not satisfy the terms of an agreement of sale calling for a marketable title clear of all encumbrance. Not only is the ground rent in the nature of a lien on property but all the arrears of the ground rent, rent or interest unpaid, remain a lien against the property as of the date of the ground rent deed. This means that a mortgage on a property subject to a ground rent comes after ground rent arrearages that may have accrued after the mortgage because all of these arrearages become liens as of the date of the ground rent deed. Said the Supreme 

Court of Pennsylvania (Devine's App., 30 Pa. 348-351- 

1858): "The priority of the lien for arreas is determinable by the date of the ground rent deed without regard to the time when they accrued. It is to the deed alone that the subsequent encumbrancer or purchaser can look." 

116. Discharge of Ground Rents by Extinguishment. Form. 

A ground rent cannot be discharged on payment of principal sum, by merely satisfying the record, as in the case of a mortgage. It must be done by a formal instrument called a deed of extinguishment. As it is really a conveyance of real estate, all formalities incident to ordinary deeds must be observed. Thus, if the owner of the ground rent is married,

§116  

his wife must join in the deed of extinguishment to release her dower. A form of a Deed of Extinguishment is here given. 

It is really an assignment of the rent to the owner of the land and operates to extinguish the ground rent as explained in the next $(117). The same form can be used for assignments of ground rents to third parties.

117. Discharge by Merger. 

Richard Roe,

Notary Public. 

If the owner of the ground rent subsequently acquires title to the land out of which the rent issues, the ground rent is said to be merged and is extinguished. By operation of law, when the right to the land and the right to the rent are united in the same person, the rent becomes extinct (Charnley v. 

Hansbury, 13 Pa. 16-1850; Frank v. Guarantee Trust Co. 

216 Pa. 40-1906). But this does not happen where a mortgage intervenes which was given by a prior owner of the land (Cook v. Brightly, 46 Pa. 439). And it must, also, be the same person who holds the fee, so where a ground rent of a wife's real estate was acquired by the husband, it was held not to have merged even after the wife died and the husband became possessed of her real estate by curtesy (Penna. 

Co. v. Singheiser, 235 Pa. 241). 

118. Discharge or Extinguishment by Order of Court. 

(a) After Lapse of Twenty-one Years. 

The Act of April 27, 1855, P.L. 368, §7 (12 P.S. $80), provides, "Where no payment, claim or demand shall have been made on account, of or for any ground rent, annuity or other charge upon real estate, for twenty-one years, or no declaration or acknowledgment of the existence thereof, shall have been made within that period by the owner of the premises, subject to such ground rent, annuity or charge, a release or extinguishment thereof shall be presumed, and such ground rent, etc., shall thereafter be irrecoverable." This

§

307 

GROUND RENTS. 

presumption, by the very terms of the Act, is conclusive. It does not merely shift the burden of proof as in the case of a mortgage or bond unpaid for 20 years (see $98, supra.) but absolutely extinguishes the ground rent (Cadwalader v. 

Springsteen, 36 Pa. Super. Ct. 134–135–1908). In the case of Munce v. Eckard, (87 Pa. Super. Ct. 383–1926), it was held, the owner of the real estate subject to the ground rent is not bound to inform the owner of the ground rent of the existence of the ground rent, and his mere silence in this regard does not arrest the running of the twenty-one years, or estop him from claiming non-payment for that period of time. 

This act further provides that evidence of such payments may be recorded in the Recorder of Deeds Office by recording the duplicate of any receipt therefor, proved by the oath or affirmation to be a true copy of that signed and delivered in the presence of the payor, and witnessed at the time by the deponent. Such recorded duplicate, or exemplification of the record thereof, shall be evidence until disproved. Also, by this act it is provided that evidence of any such demand, claim or payment may be perpetuated by the record of any judgment recovered for such rent, annuity or charge in any court of record or the transcript of any recovery of judgment therefor before an alderman or justice of the peace. 

Appropriate proceedings exist whereby the court will order an extinguishment of record of a ground rent barred by this act (Acts of July 19, 1917, P.L. 1112, and June 14, P.L. 1897, 

149, 68 P.S. §184 to 190 and note; Brook v. Bromley, 28 D.R. 291-1919). 

(b) By Payment into Court in Philadelphia County. 

A local act applying only to Philadelphia (Act of Sept. 6, P.L. (1861), 804; 68 P.S. §182), provides a procedure whereby the owner of the land subject to a ground rent, desiring to pay it off, and finding it encumbered by liens or judgments against the ground rent owner, may, by petition, pay the money into court and obtain an order requiring the ground rent extinguishment. The court will then distribute the money to those entitled (See Ritter v. Leach, 97 Pa. Super. Ct. 386-1929).

§119 

 119. Discharge of Ground Rent by Judicial Sale. 

As in the case of a mortgage, if there is no lien prior to the ground rent, a sale on any subsequent lien will not discharge the ground rent. But a sheriff's sale will discharge a ground rent if there should be a judgment lien against premises prior to the ground rent. The rules laid down in $100, as to discharge of mortgages, applies equally to ground rents. 

V. 

120. Mortgages and Ground Rents Compared. 

Mr. Fallon (Pa. Law of Conveyancing on page 459), from the viewpoint of an investor, has compared the respective advantages of a ground rent and mortgage and a review of his comparison may be of some benefit.

First: A ground rent is real estate and is descendible to the heir, subject to curtesy and dower right to the real estate. On the other hand, a mortgage is personal property and goes to the administrator. A ground rent being real estate is, of course, subject to the lien of judgment, may even be mortgaged but a mortgage is not so subject to lien of judgment, but may only be attached on an attachment execution issued for that purpose.

Second: The holder of a ground rent can never demand the payment of the principal (unless specified to the contrary ¹) so that if the property should depreciate in value, he cannot protect his capital by withdrawing it; mortgages, on the other hand, are made for a fixed period, usually three to five years, and if the holder, at the end of that time, is not satisfied with his investment, he can call in the principal.

Third: Should it become necessary to sell the property for the non-payment of rent, the holder thereof is at the expense of the sale, although in recent years many deeds contain a provision for an attorney's fee (See Form, page 295). The recovery of the costs upon the ground rents not exceeding 

1 Added by the author.

§

309 

GROUND RENTS. 

$100.00, is however, secured by the Act of April 8, 1857, P.L. 

175 (68 P.S. 214). Mortgages, on the other hand, invariably provide for an attorney's fee, in case foreclosure is necessary and should the property not realize sufficient to pay off the debt, interest and costs, the holder can resort to the bond accompanying the mortgage for the balance due. 

Fourth: The cost of satisfying a mortgage is small compared to the extinguishment of a ground rent, which, it will be remembered, must be done by a deed, carefully drawn, executed and recorded.

Fifth: Ground rents, however, are usually not taxable, unless the deeds creating them do not contain the usual clause of covenant to pay all taxes on the rent and on the land. 

Where such clause reads that the covenantor shall pay without defalcation or abatement for "any taxes, charges or assessments" and that "he shall pay all taxes whatsoever that shall hereafter be levied or assessed by virtue of any law whatever" on the "granted lot and buildings thereon erected or to be erected as well as on the yearly rent now charged thereon" this imposed on the covenantor and his successors in title, the obligation to pay out of his own pocket, the ground rent landlord's income tax imposed thereon (Van Beil v. Brogan, 65 Pa. Super. Ct. 384—1917, Aff. 262 Pa. 362-1918). Mortgages, however, are subject to a state and county tax which is presently eight mills, but these eight mills are sometimes added in the mortgage to the rate of interest, hence for a five per cent mortgage, the rate is fixed at 5, 8-10 per cent.

Method of Recording 121. Recording of Deeds. Definition. Origin. 

By recording of deeds we mean the copying of the deeds by an official duly designated by the state, into a book which is preserved as a public record. In some states this is called "registering of deeds" and the official who copies the deed is called the "register of deeds." In Pennsylvania, this act is called recording of deeds, and the official is known as the recorder of deeds.

In early English history not all kinds of deeds were required to be recorded, with the result that the recording was haphazard and of little use in protecting innocent purchasers. 

William Penn, with the object lesson of the inefficient recording system of England before him, determined when he em- 310

§311 

barked for his domain, Pennsylvania, to establish among the first things, an efficient recording system so as to place Pennsylvania titles on a solid foundation. Accordingly, he caused to be passed various recording acts which were later revised and consolidated by the Act of May 28, 1715 1 Sm. L. 94, (21 

P.S. 41 et. seq., 16 P.S. 3241). This act provided a system of recording which has persisted in Pennsylvania with but few changes, to the present time. Later by the Act of March 18, 1775, 1 Sm. L. 422, (21 P.S. 444 et. seq.) the recording of all deeds was made obligatory. 

122. Object and Purposes of Recording. 

At common law a deed executed and delivered took precedence over subsequent deeds and mortgages. Hence a grantee's or mortgagee's only protection against the existence of a prior conveyance was the honesty of the grantor backed by his covenant of warranty which unfortunately in many cases proved to be no protection at all. It became manifest that further protection for purchasers and mortgagees was necessary, and out of this need developed the recording acts. The protection afforded by these acts was at first limited to purchasers and mortgagees, but as we shall see, was later extended to creditors. 

The object of recording deeds as stated by the Supreme 

Court of Pennsylvania (Salter v. Reed, 15 Pa. 260-1850), is "to protect purchasers against fraud and possible loss of evidence of title by providing books wherein their deeds might be recorded and to which interested parties might have access and be enabled to ascertain the condition of the title before lending money on it." In order to fully accomplish this purpose, the law also provides that exemplified copies from the record, i.e., copies made and certified by the recorder of deeds, of all instruments authorized by law to be recorded, may be evidence in court without formally proving execution. (Act of May 28, 1715, 1 Sm. L. 94 §5; 21 P.S. 471). So, if the original deed is lost, an exemplified copy of the record can be received as evidence of the contents of said deed, and this

§123 

even without proving its loss (Curry v. Raymond, 28 Pa. 144 -1857). The execution and recording of a deed raises a presumption in favor of its validity and one who asserts the contrary has the burden of proving it (Walkinshaw Est. 275 Pa. 121-1922). 

123. Notice. Recording Is Notice to the World. 

The failure to record a deed does not render it void under all circumstances, or as to all persons. Thus an unrecorded deed is valid as against the grantor himself or his heirs and devisees, or as against a subsequent grantee to whom the property was conveyed without consideration. Such an unrecorded deed is also valid and retains its priority against subsequent grantees or mortgagees, even though they may have paid a valuable consideration if they had notice of the existence of the prior conveyance (Jennings v. Bloomfield, 199 Pa. 638-1901).

Notice is of two kinds: actual notice, which means express or direct notice, and constructive notice, which means such notice as is assumed or implied. Actual Notice in order to be effective must have been received by a party to the title, otherwise it is considered as mere vague rumor and not sufficient to put a person on notice (Yaukey v. Forney, 231 Pa. 371, 3741911; Churcher v. Guernsey, 39 Pa. 84, 85-1861). On the other hand, the mention of a prior unrecorded deed in describing boundaries in a later deed, was held to be sufficient notice to put the later grantee on inquiry so that the unrecorded deed was not void as to him. (Detwiler v. Coldren, 101 Pa. Super. 

Ct. 189-1931).

As to constructive notice, “it is difficult to define with precision the rules which regulate implied or constructive notice, for it depends upon infinitely varied circumstances in the case" (Jaques v. Weeks, 7 Watts 261-1838, citing 4 Kent's 

Com. 179). The most familiar example of constructive notice is that which arises from the possession of the land about to be conveyed. Actual possession by a prior purchaser at the

§

313 

time the second acquired title from the owner of record, if open, notorious, distinct and unequivocal, is ordinarily sufficient notice, to the latter of the former title. (Smith v. Miller, 296 Pa. 340-1929). It is the duty of purchasers to make inquiry of the party in possession, and failing to do so, they are affected with constructive notice of such facts as would have come to their knowledge in the proper discharge of this duty (Lazarus v. Lehigh, etc. Coal Co., 246 Pa. 178—1914, and see generally, $188 infra.)

The recording of a deed gives notice of its existence to the world. Recording is made constructive notice by statute. 

When recording acts say that an instrument recorded, according to the terms of the act, shall be constructive notice, it means that from the mere recording every one is assumed to have notice of its existence although in point of fact, no one would know of its existence unless present at its execution or had examined the record. 

124. Effect of Not Recording Instruments. 

In order to make recording effective for the protection of people against frauds, the law must visit some disadvantage in the nature of a penalty on such who do not record their deeds and mortgages. This was done by the Recording Act of March 18, 1775, 1 Sm. L. 422; (21 P.S. 444); and the Act of May 25, 1878, P.L. 151, (applies to the City of Philadelphia only) and now by the Act of May 12, 1925, P.L. 613, §1, (21 

P.S. 351), as amended by the Act of June 12, 1931, P.L. 558

Act 191, which provided that if a deed is not recorded it shall be void as against any "subsequent bona fide purchaser or mortgagee without actual or constructive notice." 

By the 

Act of June 12, 1931, P.L. 558, (21 P.S. Anno. 351), there was added to the persons against whom such unrecorded deed is void, a "holder of any judgment duly entered in the Prothonotary's office in the County in which the lands are situate.” 

Observe, the unrecording of a deed does not make it totally void in Pennsylvania, but void only as to the parties mentioned in the recording acts. Thus, suppose "A" executes and

§124A  

delivers a deed to B, who fails to record his deed; A now afterwards makes another deed for the same land to C, who pays value for it; as against A, B's deed is still good, but as against C, B's deed is void unless he can prove that C gave no value for it or actually knew, or should have known of the prior transaction. In this way the law protects the innocent purchaser without enabling the grantor to derive any benefit from the non-recording of the deed. The law desires not so much to punish B as to protect C.

Prior to the Act of 1931, a judgment creditor was not protected against an unrecorded deed. (Cover v. Black, 1 Pa. 

493-1845; Reed's Appeal, 13 Pa. 475-1850; Rosa v. 

Hummel, 252 Pa. 578-1916). Though if he became a purchaser at a sheriff's sale under his judgment he was (Hultz v. Ackley, 63 Pa. 142-1869; and see Reisinger v. Garrett, 262

Pa. 530-1919). It should be noted that the Act of 1931, protecting holders of judgments entered in the Prothonotary's office, was held to have no retroactive effect and did not apply to an unrecorded deed executed before its passage. (Farmers 

National Bank, etc., to the use, etc. v. Berks County Real Estate Company, 333 Pa. 390-1939).

The Act of April 1, 1863 P.L. 188, §1, (21 P.S. 352), pro vides a procedure by which a former owner can be compelled by the present owner of real estate to record deeds or other instruments in writing concerning the same.

The recording acts are also made to apply to contracts of sale of timber by the Act of May 22, 1895, P.L. 113 (21 P.S. 

521-522), and by the Act of Apr. 24, 1931, P.L. 48 (21 P.S. 

356 Anno.) to any agreements relating to permanent privileges or easements in land. 

124-A. Extent of Notice Imposed by Recording. 

The record of a deed is notice of its contents to those who are bound to search for it, and therefore, where an owner of lots conveys several of them by a deed containing building restrictions with a covenant that he will impose similar restrictions in deeds for remaining lots owned by him, and the

§315 

deed is recorded and subsequently conveys the remaining lots without such building restrictions, his later grantee is bound by the terms of the deeds of the former grantee though he had no actual notice of such terms. In examining the record he is bound to read the whole of the former deed and if he fails to do so, he is affected by notice of all that it contains (Finley v. Glenn, 303 Pa. 131-1931, but see Ladner v. Siegel, 294 Pa. 360-1928). 

125. Time Within Which Deeds Must Be Recorded. 

Before 1925, deeds were accorded priority according to the date of their execution provided they were recorded within the period fixed by law. Under the Act of March 18, 1775, 1 Sm. L. 422, (21 P.S. 444) deeds executed within the commonwealth were allowed six months within which to be recorded, and those executed outside of the commonwealth, twelve months. By the Act of May 19, 1893, P.L. 108 (21 P.S. 444), these periods were reduced to ninety days and six months respectively. The Act of 1775 was interpreted in the case of 

Fries v. Null, (154 Pa. 573-1893), as protecting a deed recorded within the allotted time against deeds executed subsequently but not as against prior unrecorded deeds which were actually recorded before the later deed. This was also stated in Davey v. Ruffell, 162 Pa. 443-1894, to be the rule under the Act of 1893.¹ That statement, however, was disproved in the case of Smith v. Young, (259 Pa. 367—1918), where it was held that the Act of 1893 carefully and deliberately changes the law relating to recording of deeds and conveyances and that thereafter, all deeds and conveyances were required to be recorded within the stipulated period, so that a prior deed not recorded within the period, was void as to a subsequent deed recorded within the period even though the prior deed was first recorded. "It is only when both deeds are outside of the ninety day period that it becomes a race between which shall get on the record first.' 99 1 See discussion of the matter in the first edition of this book, $125, page 160.

§126 

The period allotted to record, had its origin in the days when travel to county seats was difficult and uncertain, but it has no real justification in the days of motor vehicles and roads open at all seasons, so the Legislature of 1925, pursuant to a broad hint contained in the opinion of Smith v. Young (supra.) abolished it altogether by the Act of May 12, 1925, P.L. 613 (21 P.S. 351). This Act provides, in effect, that all deeds, contracts and other instruments in writing by which it is intended to grant and convey land shall be adjudged fraudulent and void as to any bona fide purchaser or mortgagee without actual or constructive notice, unless such deed, contract, or instrument shall be recorded before the deed or conveyance under which such subsequent purchaser or mortgagee claims. Thus, as the law now stands, the instrument first of record, in absence of notice, is first in priority. There is but one exception, and that is in the case of purchase money mortgages executed to the seller, which will be discussed in the next $126.

As noted in $124, by the amending Act of June 12, 1931, P.L. 

558, Act 191 (21 P.S. 351 Anno.) the "bona fide * * * holder of any judgment duly entered in the Prothonotary's office of the county in which the lands, tenements or hereditaments are situate," is included among those protected against an unrecorded deed. A bona fide Judgment creditor has been defined to be one who in good faith without fraud or collusion, recovers a judgment for money honestly due him (Rochester Trust Co. v. White 243 Pa. 469-1914). 

126. Time Within Which Mortgages Must Be Recorded. 

All mortgages except purchase money mortgages should be recorded immediately after execution, if they are to be a lien from that time. The Act of April 27, 1927, P.L. 440 (21 P.S. 

622) sets forth in effect that all mortgages and defeasible deeds in the nature of mortgages, should have priority according to the date of recording the same, without regard to the time of execution. And the recorder is required to indorse

§317 

the time upon the mortgages or defeasible deeds when left for record, and if two or more are left on the same day they shall have priority, according to the time they are left for record, and no mortgages or defeasible deeds shall be a lien until left for record. A mortgage properly executed and acknowledged for recording is recorded the moment it is left with the recorder of deeds and so continues for all time (Brubaker's Est. 

7 D. & C. 19—1925; Musser v. Hyde, 2 W. & S. 314—1841).

The meaning of the Act of 1927 requires but little explanation, and by it mortgages, except purchase money mortgages, given by the purchaser to the seller, become a lien only from the time of recording. Title Insurance Companies have adopted a method of requiring the mortgages they are asked to insure, to be recorded for two days prior to settlement. 

The searches are then brought down to cover these two days so as to disclose the fact if any other mortgage or lien has crept in ahead of the one they insure. While under this Act of 1927, an unrecorded mortgage is not a lien as to creditors or subsequent mortgagees or purchasers, it is nevertheless a good lien as against the mortgagor. 

An exception is made as to purchase money mortgages given by the purchaser to the seller (Martin's Est. 135 Pa. Super.

Ct. 136-1939) which are a lien from time of delivery, if recorded within 30 days from the date. (See supra. purchase money mortgages $88.) This exception is confirmed by the 

Act of June 12, 1931, P.L. 558, Act 191 (21 P.S. 351 Anno.) 

The Act of 1927 repealed and supplied the prior Acts of March 

28, 1820, 7 Sm. L. 303, and May 28, 1915, P.L. 631 couched in the same language except that the Act of 1820 allowed purchase money mortgages 60 days without restricting exception to purchase money mortgages given by the purchaser to the seller.

As set forth in §88, if two purchase money mortgages, executed on the same day, are recorded within the thirty days, both are equal in lien unless one be made expressly subject to the other (See §92).

§127  127. Defective Recording and Indexing. Result Thereof. 

For recording to be effective it must be properly done. The instrument must not only be correctly transcribed in the proper book, but must be correctly indexed as well. The rule of law governing the question as to what book an instrument should be recorded in has been stated as follows: "Where certain instruments of writing are not required by law to be recorded in a particular book, they may be recorded in any book kept by the recorder" (Glading v. Frick, 88 Pa. 4601879). Deeds and mortgages are required to be indexed in the deed book and mortgage book indexes respectively. A list of all instruments which may be recorded and the acts of assembly relating thereto, will be found in $130 (infra.). 

(a) Defective Indexing. 

Before the Act of March 18, 1875, P.L. 32, (16 P.S. 3391) a general index was not required by law and it was then held that "where an instrument was properly recorded but not indexed in a general index it was nevertheless effective, since the only index then required by law to be kept was index for each book" (Schell v. Stein, 76 Pa. 398-1874). The Act of 

March 18, 1875, P.L. 32, (16 P.S. 3391-2-3), requires the recorder to keep two general indexes, one for deeds and one for mortgages, and makes it his duty to index in the proper index every deed and mortgage left at his office for record. "Since this Act, therefore, deeds and mortgages must be both indexed and transcribed properly, and failure to do either is such defective recording as to make it a nullity as to subsequent purchasers or mortgagees". (Pyles v. Brown, 189 Pa. 164 -1899). 

One searching an index is only entitled to rely upon such information as the Act of Assembly requires to be contained therein, so where in re-writing the indexes, the recorder used index books which, in addition to the names of the mortgagor and mortgagee and place of record, as required by law, also had a space in which was written the location of the property

§

319 

mortgaged, and in that space, noted the location of only one of two properties covered by the same mortgage, it was held, the title searcher could not rely on such information which the Act of March 18, 1875, P.L. 32, did not require to be included in the index, but was in duty bound to examine the mortgage record to determine the coverage of the lien (Gulf 

Refining Co. v. Camp Curtin Trust Co., 323 Pa. 465-1936). 

(b) Defective Transcription. Wrong Book. 

Not only does omission to record and index constitute a defective record, but failure to index and transcribe correctly is equally defective. Thus where a mortgage was indexed and recorded under the name S. J. Marshall instead of L. J. 

Marshall, the Supreme Court said (Prouty v. Marshall, 225 

Pa. 570, 574—1909): "In this case the mortgage was neither recorded properly nor indexed properly; both recording and indexing were alike defective and each of the defects was fatal to the claim of the mortgagee". As a result of this development of the law a mortgagee or grantee ought to do more than merely leave the instrument for record, he ought to examine the record and see that no mistake has been made by the recorder, either in indexing or transcribing. Says the Supreme Court in the same case of Prouty v. Marshall, 225 Pa. 

570-574: "The chief object to be obtained, by recording and indexing an instrument, affecting real estate, is to give notice of the incumbrance. It is therefore the duty of a person offering an instrument for record to see that it is properly recorded and properly indexed. If he fails to do so, he cannot shift the consequence upon an innocent purchaser. But where a deed was executed "Herman Bergold” it was held the grantee was bound to take notice of a prior recorded and indexed mortgage executed by the signature "Herman A. Bergold" 

(Crippen v. Bergold, 258 Pa. 469-1917). For further dis cussion of this subject see "Searches" §172 of this book. 

Wrong Book. Where an instrument is recorded in the wrong book or place, it is no notice to those entitled to notice. 

Thus where an agreement limiting the scope or lien of a

§127  

mortgage was recorded in the deed book instead of the mortgage book, it was held to be void as against a purchaser at sheriff's sale of the mortgaged land. (Reisinger v. Garrett, etc. Co., 262 Pa. 530-1919.) (c) Recorder of Deed's Liability for Defective Indexing and Recording.

The Recorder who makes a mistake in indexing or recording an instrument is liable for damages resulting therefrom and suit may be brought on his official bond (Act of March 18, 1875, P.L. 32, §2–16 P.S. 3392).

To a certain extent this affords protection to a grantee or mortgagee whose instrument was improperly indexed or recorded, but since action must be commenced within seven years from the time the mistake was made (Commonwealth v. 

Donnelly's Estate, 33 Pa. C.C. 601-1907), the only complete protection is to follow the advice of the Supreme Court and personally examine both index and record to see that no mistake is made. In Hutchinson's Appeal, (92 Pa. 186, 187 -1879), it was said, "It is always the duty of a plaintiff to see that his judgment is correctly entered in the index." (d) Defective Recording Due to Defective Acknowledgment. 

Defective recording may also arise from the lack or improper execution of the instrument or its acknowledgment. 

It makes no difference whether the deed or the instrument actually appears on the record for the question is, should it have been recorded? If owing to such defects, the Recorder of Deeds should not have accepted the instrument for record, it is as though it was never recorded and therefore not entitled to the protection of the recording act. A recorded paper, not acknowledged or defectively proved or acknowledged, is constructive notice to no one (Lancaster v. Flowers, 198 Pa. 614 –1901; Powell's Appeal, 98 Pa. 403-1881). The necessary ingredients of a valid acknowledgment are set forth in $69 and see also Myers v. Boyd, (96 Pa. 427—1880). In order to overcome this hardship, the Legislature, from time to time,

§321 

passes acts of assembly validating the recording of defectively proven or acknowledged instruments. (See $69.) An example of such validating act is the Act of Apr. 11, 1931, P.L. 28 

(21 P.S. 281 Anno.). 

128. Recording of Forged Instruments.

The recording of an instrument gives it no greater validity, as far as execution is concerned, than it had before. Thus where a forged deed was recorded, one who buys relying on the record, takes no title. As said by our Supreme Court 

(Reck v. Clapp, 1 Pennypacker 339-1881): "Of course a purchaser who examines the records is protected by them as far as they can protect him, but he necessarily takes the risk of having the actual state of title correspond to that which appears of record." 

Reliance on a forged deed, recorded on an absolutely false certificate of acknowledgment may bring loss on him who so relied, but neither such deed nor such certificate appended to it can ever affect the owner of the property. (Smith v. Markland, 223 Pa. 605-1909). 

129. Method of Recording. 

The method of recording a deed or other instrument is to take or send the instrument to the recorder of deeds office. 

The recording fee is then paid, and receipt for the instrument is issued by the recorder or his clerk. The instrument is left there and when copied into the book and properly indexed is returned to the owner upon surrender of the receipt. The instrument is stamped "recorded," the moment it is received by the recorder. Its recording dates from the time it is left with the recorder and not from the time it is copied into the book (Brubaker's Est., 7 D. & C. 19-1925).

131. Descent.

MODERN LAWS OF DESCENT. 

Definition.

Descent or hereditary succession says Mitchell (Real Estate and Conveyancing in Pennsylvania), is the title whereby a man on the death of another acquires his estate by right of representation as his heir. Blackstone (2 Blacks. 11), states that the right of an heir to inherit was not a natural right, but a civil one established by long custom.' But whether the right is natural or has arisen from the long acquiescence in a proper custom, the right of a decedent's family to inherit is now established by law.

At common law real estate descended to heir according to certain rules known as canons of descent. They are set forth in detail and fully explained by Blackstone in his commentaries (2 Blacks. 220). They have been so altered by statute that it would only be confusing to set them forth here. 

At the present time they are chiefly useful for the courts to refer to in construing the modern laws of descent of which they are the foundation. The modern rules of descent are provided in different jurisdictions, by the leglislature of the respective states and differ more or less in each jurisdiction. 

These modern rules of descent are usually termed the intestate laws. 

132. Who May Inherit by Descent Under Intestate Laws. 

In general the intestate laws provide that only some one related to the decedent by consanguinity, that is, blood ties, 1 See interesting discussion of the origin of intestate laws in England and 

Pennsylvania in Horner et al v. Hasbrouck, (41 Pa. 169-1861).

§132  

shall inherit by descent, in other words, what is commonly called the "family" of the decedent. This means of course any one who is related by blood to the decedent whatever the degree. The widow although not related to the decedent by blood is under the intestate laws of practically every jurisdiction also allowed to inherit to some extent. The relationship between husband and wife is termed "affinity" as distinguished from "consanguinity" which means relationship by blood, but by statute, adopted children gain the rights of natural heirs (see infra. "e" this sec.). A man's blood relations are called his kin or kindred while his relationship by marriage should be properly termed his connections 

(Mitchell 285 Note). 

(a) Natural Heirs. By natural heirs we mean of course, all blood relatives such as children, nephews, nieces, uncles, aunts, cousins, etc. They may all inherit under the intestate laws in the order therein set forth (See $134, infra.). (b) Illegitimates. At common law an illegitimate child or a bastard child was one born out of wedlock and could not inherit even from his mother, unless he was made legitimate by Act of Parliament. In no other way could he be made legitimate, not even by marriage of the mother and father after his birth. In Pennsylvania as in every other jurisdiction the harshness of this common law rule has been relaxed and today the marriage and cohabitation of the father and mother at any time after the birth, legitimates their child Act of May 14, 1857, P.L. 507 (48 P.S. 167). But the Act of June 7, 1917, 

P.L. 429, §15-D (20 P.S. 95), which now supplies the Act of 

1857, omits the requirement of cohabitation. (Buchar's 

Estate, 44 York, 173—1930).

If the illegitimate child has not been legitimated by the marriage of the parents, such child is nevertheless permitted to inherit from the mother and her family. This right was originally given by the Act of April 27, 1855, P.L. 368, and enlarged by subsequent legislation. Since title of real estate under the intestate laws, depends upon the law in force at the

§331 

time of the death, it would seem advisable to trace the expansion of an illegitimate's right to inherit through the various acts (See Goughnour v. Zimmerman, 237 Pa. 599—1912). 

The Act of Apr. 27, 1855, P.L. 368 §3, gave an illegitimate child and its mother the right to inherit real and personal estate from each other. The Act of June 5, 1885, P.L. 88, §1, gave illegitimate children of the same mother, capacity to inherit personal property from one another. The Act of June 

14, 1897, P.L. 142, §1, amended §3 of the Act of 1855 (supra.) so as to enable illegitimate children and their issue and their mother and grandmother (presumably maternal) to take or inherit from each other, real and personal estate, and to transmit the same according to the intestate laws of the state. 

Next, the Act of June 10, 1901, P.L. 551, §1, provided, that all children of the same mother, whether legitimate or illegitimate, dying without leaving children or others entitled to inherit under existing laws, shall have the capacity to inherit from each other to the exclusion of the grandmother of said illegitimate child or children. This right as to real estate was, however, limited to the extent which any legitimate child of the half blood might inherit. 

Finally, the intestate Act of June 7, 1917, P.L. 429, §15(a) and (b), (20 P.S. 92-93) supplied the Act of 1901, and since that act the law now reads (a) "The mother of an illegitimate child, her heirs and next of kin, the maternal grandfather and grandmother of said illegitimate child, and the said illegitimate child, its heirs and next of kin, shall have the capacity to take and inherit from each other personal estate as next of kin, and real estate as heirs under the foregoing provisions of this act in the same manner and to the same extent as if said child or children had been born in lawful wedlock." (b) "Every legitimate child shall be considered as a brother or sister of every other child of its mother, legitimate or illegitimate." 

In considering the rights of illegitimates to inherit it must 1 The Intestate Act of 1917 as we shall see hereafter, ($134) has abolished the distinction between the children of the half and of the full blood which formerly existed as to real estate.

§132  

be remembered that the laws of a state have no extra-territorial effect and that the law of that state governs wherein the land lies. So a non-resident illegitimate may inherit land in Pennsylvania from its mother. (Waesch's Est. 166 Pa. 204-1895.) (c) Adopted Children. Adoption has been defined as "the taking of the child of another in the manner provided by and with the consequences specified in the statute." (Fischer v. 

Robison, 329 Pa. 305-1938). Adoption is purely statutory. (Thompson's Adoption, 290 Pa. 586-1927). There was no adoption at common law (Ballard v. Ward, 89 Pa. 358-1879).

In Pennsylvania, adoption is now regulated by the General Adoption Act of April 4, 1925, P.L. 127, as amended by the 

Act of April 26, 1929 P.L. 822 (1 P.S. 1 et. seq.). This act authorizes adoptions of adults as well as minors, provides the procedure and confers jurisdiction on the Orphans' Court which jurisdiction, by virtue of the repeal of earlier statutes, is now exclusive except in Philadelphia County where the Municipal Court has concurrent jurisdiction because the Act of May 11, 1923, P.L. 201, (17 P.S. 693), conferring jurisdiction on that court, was not repealed. (McCann's Adoption, 104 Pa. Super. Ct. 196, 1931).

Before the Act of 1925, there were two methods of adoption in Pennsylvania, (a) by decree of court, (b) by deed duly recorded. The former method was authorized by various acts beginning with that of May 4, 1855, P.L. 430, (the Act of June 

11, 1879, P.L. 142 expressly vesting jurisdiction in the Common Pleas Courts), all of which acts are carefully reviewed and their effect commented upon by the Superior Court in 

McCann's adoption (supra.). To this case reference can be had if the status of the adoption prior to 1925 is called into question. Adoption by deed, was authorized by the Act of 

April 2, 1872, P.L. 31, and was equally effective as by decree of court provided the deed of adoption was recorded (Evans's 

Estate, 47 Pa. Super. Ct. 196-1911). Since the Act of 1872, authorizing adoption by deed was expressly repealed along with the other acts authorizing adoption by decree of the

§333 

Court of Common Pleas, the only method of adoption at present available is by petition to the Orphans' Court (and in Philadelphia County, to the Municipal Court also), under the 

Act of 1925 (supra.).

When a person has been legally adopted, he is in effect translated into a natural born child so far as the intestate laws are concerned. This because $16 of the Intestate Act of 1917 (June 7, P.L. 429, 20 P.S. 101-102), gives to such adopted child the same rights of inheritance as a natural child (Cave's Est. 326 Pa. 358-1937; Reamer's Est. 331 Pa. 

117-1938). Conversely, the act in express language ends the right of the "adoptee" and his or her natural parents thereafter to inherit from each other. So, in Fischer v. 

Robison, (329 Pa. 305-1938), it was held that when a person is adopted according to law, the adoptive relatives of the adoptee are entitled to inherit to the exclusion of his or her natural parents. In that case the court ruled that even the natural mother, whose second husband had adopted her child by proceedings in which she did not join, was precluded by the intestate law from inheriting from her child. Care must therefore be taken in adoption proceedings under such circumstances to have the natural parent join as co-petitioner with the adopting spouse.

Finally, it should be observed that while the validity of an adoption is governed by the laws of the state which created the adoption because entitled to full faith and credit under the Constitution, the right to inherit pursuant to the adoption depends on the laws of the state governing the descent of property (Crossley's Est. 135 Pa. Super. Ct. 524-1939). 

That case holds also that the intent of §16(b) Interstate Act of 1917 (supra.) excluding the natural kin of an adoptee, applies to adoption generally whether the persons were adopted under the laws of Pennsylvania or elsewhere. 

133. Lineal Heirs and Collateral Heirs.

Heirs inherit in the order and as the law provides. Heirs are divided into two lines or classes. "Lineals" and "col-

§134  

laterals." Lineal heirs are such as are descended one from the other in a direct line, as between a man and his son, his grandson, etc. In ascertaining the nearness of relationship or consanguinity each generation counts one degree. Thus the son is removed one degree from his father and two from his grandfather.

Collaterals are such who descended from the same stock or common ancestor, but do not descend one from the other. 

Thus brothers are collaterals because they are not descended one from the other, but are descended from the same common ancestor, their father. So also cousins are collaterals. In computing the nearness of relationship or consanguinity the method now adopted by law is to count from one collateral up to the common ancestor and then down to the other. This is known as the civil law method. If the reader desires to have a fuller exposition of the method of computing consanguinity he is referred to the 2nd book of Blackstone's Commentaries, Ch. XIV, p. 199, where a most interesting, full and plain explanation replete with illustrations is made by the learned author. But observe that the common law method of computing the degree of collaterals is no longer used. 

134. Intestate Laws of Pennsylvania. Order of Inheritance. 

The order in which heirs shall inherit in Pennsylvania is now regulated by the Act of June 7, 1917, P.L. 429 (20 P.S. §1 et seq.) and its amendments, commonly called the Intestate 

Laws.¹ These acts are here set forth in full and then a synopsis of them added so that they may be more clearly understood.2 

$1. Surviving Spouse and Issue. 

The real and personal estate of a decedent, whether male or female, remaining after payment of all just debts and legal 1 The Intestate Act of 1917 was a codification and revision of the earlier Act of April 8, 1833, P.L. 315 and its supplements. Those interested in the law as it stood before 1917 are referred to the 1st edition of this book where it is set forth extenso in $134. 

2 Students will find it helpful to a better understanding of the Intestate Laws if they will first study the general rules set forth in the next section (§135).

charges, which shall not have been sold, or disposed of by will, or otherwise limited by marriage settlement, shall be divided and enjoyed as follows: namely— 

(a) Surviving Spouse, One Child or Issue of One Child. 

Where such intestate shall leave a spouse surviving, and one child only, or shall leave a spouse surviving and no children, but shall leave descendants of one deceased child, the spouse shall be entitled to one-half part of the real and personal estate. 

(b) Surviving Spouse and More Than One Child or Issue. 

Where such intestate shall leave a spouse surviving and more than one child, or one child and the descendants of a deceased child or children, or the descendants of more than one deceased child, the surviving spouse shall be entitled to one-third part of the real and personal estate. 

$2. Surviving Spouse and No Issue. 

(a) Allowance of $5,000. and Half of Remaining Estate.

Where such intestate shall leave a spouse surviving and other kindred, but no issue, the surviving spouse shall be entitled to the real or personal estate, or both, to the aggregate value of Five Thousand ($5,000.00) Dollars in addition, in the case of a widow, to the widow's exemption as allowed by law; and, if such estate shall exceed in value the sum of 

Five Thousand Dollars, the surviving spouse shall be entitled to the sum of Five Thousand $5,000.00 Dollars absolutely, to be chosen by him or her from the real or personal estate, or both, and in addition thereto, shall be entitled to one-half part of the remaining real and personal estate; provided, that the provisions of this clause as to the said Five 

Thousand ($5,000.00) Dollars in value shall apply only to cases of actual intestacy of the husband or wife, entire or partial, and not to cases where the surviving spouse shall elect to take against the will of the decedent spouse.

Procedure in Setting Aside $5000. Allowance for Spouse.

The rest of $2, being sub-divisions (b) (c) (d) (e) (f) (g) and (h) are not here set forth in extenso. Sub-divisions (b) and (c), provided the procedure in the Orphans' Court by which the property, real or personal or both, chosen by the surviving spouse is appraised. Sub-divisions (d) and (e) provide the procedure where real estate is claimed which is appraised at more than Five Thousand ($5,000.00) Dollars.

Where it cannot be divided, the court may award it to the spouse conditioned on the spouse's paying the excess value within one year.

Where the spouse refuses to take the real estate at the appraisement, or fails to make the payment, the court, on application of any party in interest, will direct the administrator to sell the same, and to pay the Five Thousand Dollars allowance out of the proceeds. Sub-division (f) provides that where the title to real estate chosen by the spouse is confirmed, the spouse is entitled to the rents, issues and profits from the date of the intestate's death; and where the real estate is sold, and adjustment is provided for, based on the proportionate part of such rent to which the spouse is entitled. Sub-division (g) regulates the procedure where the real estate chosen is situate in a county other than that in which the intestate was domiciled. In such cases orders of sale are under the direction of the Orphans' Court of the county in which the real estate is situated, while matters of distribution remain in the exclusive jurisdiction of the Orphans' Court of the intestate's domicile. Provision is made for a record of the proceedings in the courts of both counties. 

Sub-division (h) provides for the recording, in the office for recording of deeds of the county in which the real estate lies, of a certified copy of the decree setting the same apart for the spouse and for its indexing in the grantor's index in the name of the decedent, and in the grantee's index in the name of the surviving spouse. Provision is also made for registering the title in the survey bureaus, or with the proper authorities of the same county.

$3. Widows Share in Lieu of Dower.

The shares of the estate directed by this act to be allotted to the widow shall be in lieu and full satisfaction of her dower at common law, so far as relates to the lands of which the husband died seised; and her share of lands aliened by the husband in his life time, without her joining in the conveyance, shall be the same as her share in the lands of which the husband died seised. The widow shall be entitled to the same share in an estate in remainder vested in interest in the husband during his life time, although the particular estate shall not terminate before the death of the husband.

No husband who shall have, for one year or upwards, previous to the death of his wife, wilfully neglected or refused to provide for his wife, or shall have for that period or upwards wilfully and maliciously deserted her, shall have the right to claim any title in her real or personal estate after her decease, under the provisions of this act. §134  $6. Wife's Right Barred by Desertion. 

No wife who shall have, for one year or upwards, previous to the death of her husband, wilfully and maliciously deserted her husband, shall have the right to claim any title or interest in his real or personal estate after his decease under the provisions of this act. (See $145 (c) for discussion and cases construing this section of the Act). 

$7. Issue. 

The real and personal estate of such intestate, not heretofore given to the surviving spouse, if any there be, shall descend to and be distributed among his or her issue, according to the following rules and order of succession: namely,— (a) Children. If such intestate shall leave children, but no other descendants, being the issue of a deceased child, the estate shall descend to and be distributed among such children. (b) Grandchildren. If such intestate shall leave grandchildren, but no child or other descendant, being issue of a deceased grandchild, the estate shall descend to and be distributed among such grandchildren. 

(c) Descendants in the Same Degree of Consanguinity. 

Descendants in the same degree of consanguinity to the intestate, share equally. 

(d) Descendants in Different Degrees of Consanguinity. 

If such intestate shall leave descendants in different degrees of consanguinity to him, the more remote of them being the issue of a desceased child, grandchild, or other descendants, the estate shall descend to and be distributed among them as follows: namely,- 

(1) Shares of Children. Each of the children of such intestate shall receive such share as such child would have received if all of the children of the intestate, who shall then be dead, leaving issue, had been living at the death of such intestate. (2) Shares of grandchildren. Each of the grandchildren, if there shall be no children, in like manner, shall receive such share as he or she would have received if all the other grand-

children, who shall then be dead, leaving issue, had been living at the death of the intestate, and so in like manner to the remotest degree. (3) Issue Taking by Representation. In every such case, the issue of such deceased child, grandchild, or other descendants, shall take by representation of their parents, respectively, such shares only as would have descended to such parents if they had been living at the death of the intestate. $8. Parents.

In default of issue, as aforesaid, the real and personal estate of such intestate, not herein before given to the surviving spouse, if any there be shall go to and be vested in the father and mother of such intestate; or, if either the father or mother be dead at the time of the death of the intestate, the parent surviving shall take such real and personal estate.¹ $9. Collateral Heirs.

In default of issue, father and mother, the real and personal estate of such intestate, not hereinbefore given to the surviving spouse, if any there be, shall descend to and be distributed among the collateral heirs, and the kindred of such intestate without distinction between those of the whole and those of the half blood, according to the following rules and order of succession: namely,- (a) Brothers and Sisters. If such intestate shall leave brothers and sisters or either, and no nephew or child or children of a deceased nephew or niece, being the issue of a deceased brother or sister, the real and personal interest shall descend to and be distributed among such brothers and sisters. (b) Nephews and Nieces. If such intestate shall leave neither brother nor sister, and no child of any deceased nephew or niece, being the issue of a deceased brother or sister, but nephews or nieces, being children of such deceased brother or 1 Parents take this estate by entireties under the intestate act of 1917 as they did under the prior intestate laws (Walls Estate 72 Pitts. (d) Descendants of Brothers or Sisters. If such intestate shall leave brothers or sisters, and nephews or nieces, being children of a deceased brother or sister, and children of deceased nephews or nieces, being the children of deceased brothers and sisters, or shall leave members of any two of these three classes, the real and personal estate shall descend to and be distributed among such brothers and sisters, nephews and nieces, and children of deceased nephews and nieces, as follows: namely,—

Each brother and sister shall receive such share as he or she would have received if all brothers and sisters who died before the intestate, leaving children, or children of deceased children surviving intestate, had been living at the death of the intestate.

Each nephew and niece, if the intestate shall leave any brother or sister, shall receive an equal portion of the share which his or her parents would have taken if then living, which portion will be what he or she would have taken if all the children of his or her parent who died before the intestate, leaving children surviving the intestate, had been living at the death of the intestate; but if such intestate shall leave neither brother nor sister, the nephews and nieces shall take per capita.

Each child of a deceased nephew or niece, whether the intestate shall leave members of one or both of the other classes, shall receive an equal portion of the share which his or her parents would have received if living at the death of the intestate.

§11. Limits of Representation. 

The grandchildren of brothers and sisters, and children of uncles and aunts, shall be entitled to take, by representation the shares of real and personal estate which their parents would have taken if living; but, except as hereinafter provided, there shall be no representation admitted among collaterals after grandchildren of brothers and sisters and children of uncles and aunts. $12. Grandparents and Issue of Deceased Grandparents.
