The effect of this section, and the section which follows it, namely, §15, relating to the inheritance of and from illegitimates, has been heretofore discussed in §132(b), (supra.) to which reference is made. $16, which relates to inheritance of and from adopted children has likewise been covered in §132(c), (supra.) to which the reader is referred. $17. Surviving Spouse and No Known Heirs or Kindred. (a) Rights of Surviving Spouse. In default of known heirs or kindred, competent as aforesaid, the real estate of such intestate shall be vested in the surviving spouse of such intestate, if any, and the surviving spouse shall be entitled to the whole of the personal estate. (b) This provides the procedure to be followed where a surviving spouse claims there are no next of kin. The decree of the Orphans' Court, obtained pursuant to this procedure when recorded, becomes indefeasible six months after the decree has become final. $18. Character of Estate Passing to Persons Entitled Under this Act.

The real estate of such intestate shall be vested in the person or persons entitled thereto, under the provisions of this act, for such estate as the intestate had therein, and such person or persons shall be entitled to the personal estate absolutely. $19. Persons in the Same Degree of Consanguinity Take Equally.

Wherever real or personal estate shall descend to or be distributed among several persons, whether lineal or collateral heir or kindred, standing in the same degree of consanguinity to the intestate, if there shall be only one of such degree, he shall take the whole of such estate; and if there shall be more

§134 

than one, they shall take in equal shares, and if real estate, shall hold the same as tenants in common. $20. Posthumous Children.

Descendants and relatives of an intestate begotten before the death of the intestate, and born thereafter, shall in all cases inherit and take in like manner as if they had been born in the life time of the intestate. §21 provides a limitation of seven years for the protection of administrators who have made a bona fide distribution. It does not apply to real estate, hence need not be considered in this work. (See Vogest's Estate, 31 D. & C. 169-1937). $22. Advancements.

As this subject will be hereinafter considered in $137 of this book, the reader is referred to that section. $23. Persons adjudged guilty of murder not to inherit from the murdered person.

No person who shall finally be adjudged guilty either as principal or accessory of murder of the first or second degree shall be entitled to inherit or take any part of the real or personal estate of the person killed, as surviving spouse, heir or next of kin of such person under the provisions of this act. $24. Escheat.

In default of all such known heirs or kindred or surviving spouse, competent to take as aforesaid, the real and personal estate of such intestate remaining after the payment of all just debts and legal charges shall be sold by the executor of the will or the administrator of the estate, and the net proceeds of such sale shall be, by him paid into the State Treasury for the use of the Commonwealth. Such sale shall be made only under the supervision of the court having jurisdiction of the estate, and in accordance with the laws of the Common-

§345 

wealth providing for the payment into the State Treasury of unclaimed funds in the hands of fiduciaries. For procedure governing the sale of real estate escheated under this section, see Rooney's Est. 38 D. & C. 524-1940. 

$25 provides that the Act does not apply to personal estate of an estate dying domiciled outside of the Commonwealth. $27. When the Act shall go into effect. 

This act shall take effect on the 31st day of December, 1917, and shall apply to estates, real and personal, of all persons dying intestate on or after said act. As to estates, real and personal of all persons dying before that day, the existing laws shall remain in full force and effect. 

135. General Rules Helpful to Understanding the Intestate Laws of 1917. 

The following general rules will be helpful in an accurate understanding of the Pennsylvania Intestate Laws. (1) Lineals. (a) Lineals (see §133), in the ascending series inherit equally. No distinction is made between males and females, nor is any now made between those of the full blood and half blood (See $136). Thus the property of the father is inherited by his lineal descendants, say, his children, equally. (b) Lineals in the ascending series will take in preference to the collateral kindred. If the decedent dies without issue, his parents get the estate in preference to his uncle or cousins. 

(2) Per Capita and Per Stirpes. (a) Per Capita means taking "by heads", i.e., one equal share to each person entitled. 

It is the opposite of taking "per stirpes." (b) Per Stirpes sometimes called "taking by representation", means the person who takes, represents the parent in taking, and if he has one or more brothers, he divides his parent's share equally with them.

These terms can be better understood by illustration than by definition. Suppose a man dies intestate who had originally two children, one of which predeceased him so that at

§135 

his death there survived him, one child and two grand-children of i.e. children of his deceased child. The son takes onehalf of the estate i.e., he takes per capita; the grandchildren take each half of what their parent would have received; that is one-fourth of the whole; they take per stirpes; i.e., they represent their father and divide what he would have gotten. 

(3) Whole Blood, Half Blood and Blood of First Pur chaser.

There is now no distinction between the descent of real estate and the distribution of personality so that consequently there is no longer any distinction between heirs of the full blood and of the half blood, or blood of the first purchaser in inheriting real estate (See §136 infra.). 

(4) Computing Degree of Relationship. Relationship is computed by counting from the decedent back to the common ancestor and then down to the heir. Each step is counted one degree. 

(5) What Property is Governed by the Pennsylvania Intes tate Law. Remember our intestate laws are effective to pass title only to such real estate as is situate within this state. 

Real estate outside of this commonwealth, which belongs to an intestate, though domiciled here, passes under the law of the state wherein it lies. (Wolfe v. Lewisburg, T. & S. D. Co., 305 

Pa. 583, 589-1932). On the other hand, personal property passes according to the law of the state in which the intestate is domiciled. Our intestate laws therefore govern the succession of personal property whether it happens to be in or out of this commonwealth if its owner was domiciled here at the time of his death. (Mallory's Est. 300 Pa. 217-1930; Dent's 

Estate, 22 Pa. 514–1854).

§135A 

347 

135-A. Synopsis of Intestate Act of 1917. 

I.

WHERE A PERSON DIES UNMARRIED OR A WIDOW OR WIDOWER WITHOUT CHILDREN. 

The estate, real and personal, descends: (a) To the father and mother and survivor of them absolutely, i.e., by entirety (See §5 (d) p. 9. Entireties Supra.). 

If neither survive 66 (b) To brothers and sisters, and to their children, and grandchildren, the parent being deceased; in equal shares 'per capita", if all such collaterals are in the same class or degree of relationship. If not, then "per stirpes', the children or grandchildren taking among them the deceased parent's share. (c) In default of persons named in (a) and (b), to grandparents or descendants of deceased grandparents.' (d) In default of parties named in (a) (b) and (c) then to the intestate's next of kin. (e) In default of any know heirs, the estate escheats to the 

Commonwealth. (See $147 infra.).

II. 

WHERE DECEDENT IS A WIDOW OR WIDOWER LEAVING CHILDREN OR LINEAL DESCENDANTS. 

The Real Estate and Personal Property descends: 

(a) To the lineal descendants who, if they stand in the same degree, take equally per capita, e.g., as if all be children or all be grandchildren. 

1 If those entitled to take include one or more grandparents, and there shall be living at the decedent's death, children or other descendants of any deceased grandparent, then the children or the other descendants of any such deceased grandparent shall take per stirpes that deceased grandparent's share. With the exception of that case, there is no representation admitted among collaterals after grandchildren of brothers and sisters and children of uncles and nieces.

§135A  

(b) But if lineals be of different degrees, they take by representation (per stirpes), e.g., if some be children and others be grandchildren, the grandchildren do not take equally with the children, but divide their parents' share. 

III. 

MARRIED PERSON LEAVING SPOUSE SURVIVING 

The Real estate and personal property descends: 

1. If no issue (i.e. lineal descendants), 1 (a) Five Thousand ($5,000.00) Dollars worth thereof out of either real or personal property or both to the spouse ¹ absolutely. And one-half of the estate remaining, if any, absolutely. 

2. If issue survive, (a) If there be one child only or descendants of one child, one-half of the estate goes to the surviving spouse absolutely, and the other half to the child or descendants of the child. (b) If there be more than one child, and one child and descendants of a deceased child, or children, or no child but the descendants of more than one deceased child, then one-third of the estate goes to the surviving spouse absolutely, and the balance to the children or descendants of deceased children, as in Part II. 

3. In default of all known heirs or kindred, the whole estate goes to the surviving spouse absolutely. 

IV. 

FORFEITURE OF THE RIGHTS TO INHERIT. 

1. Husband forfeits his right by wilful and malicious desertion, or wilful neglect to provide for his wife for one year or more preceding the death of the intestate. (See §141 infra.). 

2. Wife forfeits her right by a wilful and malicious desertion of her husband for a year or more preceding the death of the intestate husband. (See $145 infra.). 

1 If the surviving spouse be a widow this allowance is in addition to the widow's exemption of $500.

136. Whole Blood and Half Blood. 

Blood of First Purchaser. 

Prior to the present intestate laws of 1917 there was a distinction made in the right to inherit real estate between persons of the whole blood and half blood, and between persons not of the blood of the first purchaser. Though these distinctions no longer prevail, those examining titles that descended before that time must bear the distinction in mind. Hence a few words of explanation. 

(a) Whole Blood and Half Blood. 

Relationship by the whole blood is where two persons are descended from the same pair of ancestors as where two persons have the same grandfather and same grandmother. Relationship by the half blood is where two or more persons have

§351 

only one common ancestor; as where they are descended from the same grandfather, but from different grandmothers.

Under the Intestate Laws in force prior to 1917,¹ collateral heirs who were of the half blood were postponed in their right to inherit real estate until all heirs of the whole blood were extinguished. 

(b) Blood of First Purchaser. 

By this phrase was meant one of the blood of the person who first acquired the real estate in question by purchase. "A first purchaser" is the person "first" reached, counting back who acquired the real estate in any manner except by descent under the intestate laws. Under the former intestate laws, so far as real estate was concerned, the next of kin of the blood of the first purchaser was preferred to the exclusion of those who were not. The latter could take only in default of heirs of the blood of the first purchaser. In fact, just before the real estate would escheat. This rule is now wholly abolished. 

137. Advancements.

An advancement is an irrevocable gift by an intestate to an heir of the whole or part of what it is supposed the heir would be entitled to at the death of the intestate. (Eshleman's Ap peal, 74 Pa. 42-1873). The Intestate Laws of 1917, §22 (20 

P.S. 135) provides: "If any person other than surviving spouse *** shall have any estate by settlement of such intestate, or shall have been advanced by him in his life time, either in real or personal estate, the amount of such settlement or advancement shall be charged against the share of the person who shall have received it, so that the total received by him, including the amount of settlement or advancement shall not exceed the amount received by each of the other persons who are equally entitled" to inherit. 

Advancements under the former intestate law were re- 

1 See $5 p. 174 of the 1st ed. of this work.

$138 

stricted to children. The purpose of this provision is that all heirs under the intestate laws should be equalized. Thus an advancement bars the recipient from participating in the decedent's estate to the amount of the advancement received. 

To make a gift an advancement it must have been intended as such when made. (Dare's Est. 9 D.R. 431, 1900; Brahm's 

Est. 269 Pa. 82-1920). Where real estate is conveyed or purchase money paid, the legal presumption is that it is intended as an advancement which is greatly strengthened when the value bears any considerable proportion to the donor's estate. (Cooper v. Duval, 10 D.R. 475—1901; Kern v. Howell, 180 Pa. 315-1897). As between a loan, gift and an advancement, the presumption is in favor of an advancement because of its tendency to equality. (Knoppel's Est. 1 D. & C. 2621922). 

138. Form of a Recital in a Deed of One Who Has Inherited His Title by Descent. 

When the owner of real estate dies, the record at the recorder of deeds office still shows title in the decedent's name because the heir gains title not by virtue of deed, but by mere operation of law. When therefore the heir conveys the land he should show by deed how he gained title in order to fill up the gap existing on the record between his grantee and his ancestor. This is done by the recital. The following is a form of recital to be inserted in a deed drawn for a conveyance from a grantor who has derived his title by operation of the intestate laws:

BEING the same premises which Adam Smith by Indenture bearing date the 23rd day of February, 1896 and recorded in the Office for the Recording of Deeds in and for the City and County of Philadelphia in Deed Book J.V. No. 23, Page 322, &c., granted and conveyed to Samuel Moore in fee.

And the said Samuel Moore being seised of said premises departed this life intestate on the Fifteenth day of September, A.D. 1912, leaving surviving him as sole heir, Robert Moore to whom said premises descended in fee.

$353 

II. 

ESTATE BY CURTESY. 

139. Estate by Curtesy. 

(a) Prior to 1917. 

This estate has already been defined (See §3). At common law it was the right of the husband to enjoy a life estate in all his wife's real estate at her death. Then, the husband was not entitled to his curtesy unless there was a child born of the marriage, but this condition as well as others stipulated by the common law long ceased to be in force in Pennsylvania. 

By marriage alone, whether a child be born thereof or not, the husband became vested in his estate by curtesy, which became consummate upon his wife's death (Act of April 11, 1848, P.L. 536, §10; see also Act of May 4, 1855, P.L. 430). His estate was an absolute one and could only be divested once vested, by his own act. It subsisted and followed such land which his wife may have conveyed without his joining in the deed. While the estate vested the moment of marriage, the enjoyment thereof was postponed until the death of the wife. 

Nor since the Act of 1850 (Act of April 22, 1850, §20, P.L. 553) could the creditors of the husband levy upon and sell this interest during the lifetime of the wife. Nor was a judgment against the husband during the life of the wife a lien against his curtesy (Act of April 1, 1863, P.L. 212; 48 P.S. 66). (b) Since 1917.

Since 1917 (Intestate Act of 1917 P.L. 429 §4, 20 P.S. §32), the estate by curtesy as it existed in Pennsylvania prior thereto may now be regarded as abolished, for by that act it is expressly provided "The shares of the estate directed by this act to be allotted to the surviving husband, shall be in lieu and full satisfaction of his curtesy at common law. The surviving husband shall be entitled to the same share in an estate in remainder, vested in interest in the wife during her lifetime, as in property of which she dies seized, although the

$140 

particular estate shall not terminate before the death of the wife."

As we have seen (§§134, 135) each spouse's rights directed by that act to be allotted to the survivor is one half of the entire estate, real and personal, if there be one child, one third if there be more than one child, and if there be no children, $5,000.00 and one half of the remainder. 

Neither spouse as we shall see hereafter (§165) can be deprived by will of this right given in lieu of curtesy or dower except as to the $5,000.00 allotment, the right to claim which is restricted to actual cases of intestacy. 

Though the Act of 1917 has substituted a greatly enlarged share of the wife's estate in lieu of curtesy, so that it ought not, properly speaking, be any longer called by the old name curtesy, nevertheless in common parlance the name persists and its use is now generally regarded as referring to the Statutory rights given the spouse under the Intestate Law of 

1917. So in Paczosa's Estate (9 D. & D. 706—1927), where a decedent dying in 1925 by her will referred to her husband's share as "tenant by the curtesy", it was held that while tenancy by curtesy was abolished by the Intestate Act of 1917, the language used would be construed as referring to his statutory share under the Intestate Law. We will therefore, in this section, continue to use the old name to designate the new right given in substitution thereof. 

140. Against What Land Curtesy Attaches. 

In general it may be stated that a husband's right of curtesy attaches to all land to which his wife has title at time of marriage or to which she acquires title thereafter, whether by deed, descent, will or otherwise, including a vested estate in remainder. Prior to the Intestate Act of 1917 the husband's curtesy attached to his wife's estate in remainder only if the particular estate terminated before the death of the wife, (Hitner v. Ege 23 Pa. 305-1854), this was expressly changed by the Act of 1917 (see Commissioners' note $4). There is, however, this exception viz., such land as may be expressly

§355 

devised to her by will or conveyed by deed of trust wherein the instrument stipulates that the land is to be for her sole and separate use, free from control of her husband and specifically shows the intent of the testator or grantor, that the husband's right of curtesy should be barred. 

141. How Curtesy May Be Barred.

The husband's estate of curtesy is absolute and exists unless barred by the husband's own acts in any of the following methods. 

(a) By Voluntary Joinder in a Deed of Conveyance. 

Should the husband join in his wife's deed conveying away her land, his curtesy is barred. (Commissioners of Rouse 

Est. v. Poor Directors, McKean County, 169 Pa. 116-1895).

Mere consent given by husband to his wife to sell does not bar him; he must join in the deed. If he, however, signs the agreement of sale with his wife he can be compelled to sign the deed. 

(b) By Divorce A. V. M. Divorces are of two kinds: a vinculo matrimoni, usually abbreviated A.V.M., which means literally from the bonds of matrimony, and is the so-called absolute divorce entitling both parties to re-marry. The other is "a mensa et thoro", meaning literally from bed and board, which in effect is really a legal separation and does not entitle either party to re-marry. The former, viz.: the absolute divorce, bars the husband's curtesy (Schock's Appeal, 33 Pa. 351-1859), the latter does not (Rudolph's Estate, 128 

Pa. Super. Ct., 459—1937). (c) Non-support or Desertion by Husband. Under the Act of May 4, 1855 (P.L. 430-48 P.S. 42), as well as by §5 of the 

Intestate Act of 1917 (20 P.S. 41), a husband who has for the period of one year or upwards before his wife's death, wilfully neglected or refused to support her, or for that period or upward, wilfully and maliciously deserted her, shall have no claim to her real or personal estate after her decease, whether

§141  

by the curtesy or under the Intestate Laws of Pennsylvania. 

It is to be noted that under these Acts the husband loses his curtesy either by neglect or refusal to support his wife, or by wilful and malicious desertion (Kvist's Estate 256 Pa. 301917; Nixons' Estate 104 Pa. Super. Ct. 506-1931). 

1. Non-support. The refusal or neglect to support must be wilful, i.e. voluntary, if involuntary as e.g. where due to physical incapacity, the curtesy rights will not be barred 

(Roop's Estate 15 D. & C. 752-1931). The burden of proof that the surviving husband wilfully neglected or refused to support the wife during the last year of her life, is upon those who assert the husband forfeited his right. (Rudolph's 

Est. 128 Pa. Super. Ct. 459-1937).

Where husband and wife lived separately as domestics, the mere fact that the deceased wife did not demand support did not excuse the husband from performance of his duty to her and his failure to support her barred his rights (Kvist's Est. 

256 Pa. 30-1917). 

2. Desertion. Separation by mutual consent is not wilful and malicious desertion (Maurer's Est. 17 Berks Co. 2041925; O'Connor's Est., 2 D. & C. 229—1922).

Where a husband has been expelled from the home of the decedent there is no wilful desertion (Kaznowski's Est. 4 

Erie 132-1922).

But the burden is on the husband who has left his wife to justify his desertion and to do so he must show such cause as would have entitled him to a decree of divorce A. V. M. against her (Hahn v. Bealor, 132 Pa. 242-1890; Weller v. 

Weller, 213 Pa. 265-1906). Where a wife left her husband and the reason does not appear, the husband's rights are not barred (Powell's Est., 26 D. & C., 369—1936).

A separation of husband and wife, consensual in its origin becomes wilful and malicious desertion on part of the husband barring his rights, upon commission of adultery by him (Bowman's Est. 301 Pa. 337-1930; McMullin's Est., 18 D. & C., 397-1933).

§357 

3. Evidence. By the Act of April 24th, 1931 P.L. 46 a surviving spouse is made competent to testify in any proceeding where the matter in issue is the right of the surviving spouse to share in a deceased spouse's estate, and is disputed by reason of desertion or non-support. Formerly such a spouse was incompetent if he sought to claim against the will (Bowman's Est. 301 Pa. 337-1930; Schreckengost's Est., 77 

Pa. Super. Ct., 235—1921), though competent where the deceased spouse died intestate (Kvist's Est. 256 Pa. 30-1917).

The declarations of a decedent that her husband had deserted her are inadmissible to prove to the fact at the audit of her estate (Schultz's Est., 24 Pa. D. & C. 546—1935). 

(d) By Feme Sole Trader Decree. A Feme Sole Trader 

Certificate issued by a court of competent jurisdiction, will bar her husband from any right of curtesy in the wife's estate, although family relations have been maintained, where the court's decree was based on the ground of drunkenness and failure to support. This because the Second Section of the 

Act of May 4, 1855, P.L. 430; 48 P.S. 42 confers on the wife the right of free and absolute disposal of her property during her life or by will without interference of the husband 

(Browarsky's Estate, 252 Pa. 35—1916). 

(e) By Voluntary Agreement or Release. A husband may agree in writing either before marriage (McCready's Est. 

316 Pa. 246-1934), or thereafter to forego all claims of curtesy against his wife's estate. Such agreement when properly executed is valid and bars his curtesy (McBride's 

Est., 81 Pa. 303-1876; Singer's Est., 233 Pa. 55—1911). (f) By Sheriff's Sale. A sheriff's sale of the wife's real estate on a judgment confessed by or obtained against her bars the husband's curtesy (Wells v. Bunnell, 160 Pa. 4601894). But if the judgment is collusive or a mere fraudulent scheme to deprive either husband or wife of their interests it will be set aside (Waterhouse v. Waterhouse, 206 Pa. 4331903).

§141  

(g) Devise in Lieu of Curtesy. Where a wife devises a portion of her property by will to her husband and he accepts said provision of the will, it is presumed to be in lieu of dower. He may, however, refuse the provision made in the will and elect to take under the intestate laws instead (See right to take against will, §165 infra.). 

(h) Sale by Orphans' Court for Payment of Debts. Since the Intestate Act of 1917, §1, expressly says "the real and personal estate of a decedent whether male or female, remaining after payment of all just debts and legal charges shall descend" etc., it necessarily follows that a husband's curtesy is discharged upon a sale of his deceased wife's real estate by order of the Orphans' Court or under a testamentary power of sale by an executor (Miller v. Sheaffer, 75 Pa. Super. Ct., 584 -1921). See also the cases cited in §145 (h) (infra.) as to dower, which cases, since the curtesy and dower rights of husband and wife are now the same, are equal authority for the proposition stated. (i) Sale in Partition Proceedings. A sale in partition proceedings of the wife's real estate, bars curtesy of the husband (Wilson v. Sailer 18 D.R. 435-1909 approved in 

Briegel v. Briegel, 307 Pa. 93, 99-1931). See also §145 (c) infra. (j) Eminent Domain. Condemnation of the wife's land by eminent domain proceedings would seem to bar the husband's curtesy for it was so held as to wife's dower (See $145 (j) and Briegel v. Briegel, 307 Pa. 93-1931). (k) Pre-Nuptial Conveyances. Either spouse may challenge as fraudulent, a conveyance of real estate or gift of personal property made during a treaty of marriage (as, e.g., a conveyance of real estate made after the parties became "engaged" but before marriage), but the mere proof of a voluntary conveyance or gift, without knowledge of the other party does not of itself prove fraud. (Kirk v. Kirk, 340 Pa. 203-1940).

§

359 

III. 

DOWER. 

142. Dower. (a) Prior to 1917. At common law, dower meant a life estate which the law gave to a widow in one-third of the land and tenements of her husband of which he was seised at any time during the marriage.

Common law dower was taken away in all cases where a husband dies intestate, seised of lands and in its place a statutory provision consisting partly of real and partly of personal estate was given to the widow by the intestate laws 

(Act of April 8, 1833, P.L. 249, §11, and amendments thereto as further amended by Act of April 1, 1909, P.L. 87). By this provision of the former law, the widow, if there were children, was given one-third of the personal property absolutely and one-third of the real estate for life. If no children,' the widow was given $5,000.00 absolutely out of real or personal property or out of both together, with one-half of the remaining personal property absolutely and one-half of the remaining real estate for life. This provision being given in lieu of dower. (b) Dower since 1917. Just as in the case of curtesy, the

Act of June 7, 1917 P.L. 429 substitutes in lieu of dower (see $3 of that Act 20 P.S. 31) a greatly enlarged share of the husband's estate which is exactly the same as that given by the Intestate Act of 1917 to the husband out of his wife's estate (see $139 (b) Supra.). That is to say, each spouse's rights directed by that Act to be allotted to the survivor, is one half of the entire estate real and personal absolutely, if there be one child; one third absolutely if there be more than one child and if there be no children, $5,000. and one half of the estate that remains absolutely (see $$134, 135 Supra.). 

Neither spouse (see $165 infra.) can be deprived of these 

1 An adopted child was held to be a child within the meaning of this Act, McQuiston's Est. 238 Pa. 313-1913.

§143  

rights by will except as to the $5,000. allotment, the right to claim which is restricted to actual cases of intestacy. Though strictly speaking dower no longer exist in Pennsylvania the name, just as in the case of Curtesy, continues to be used to designate the share of the estate which a widow now receives in lieu thereof. 

143. Common Law Dower in Lands Aliened During Husband's Life, Prior to 1917. 

The provision of the laws giving the rights to the widow mentioned in §142(a) in lieu of dower, did not contain the clause of §3 of the Act of 1917 which expressly includes lands aliened by the husband in his life time without her joinder. 

So that it followed that prior to the Intestate Act of 1917, a widow still had a common law dower interest in land aliened by her husband in his life time without her joinder in the conveyance. $3 of the Intestate Act of 1917 for the first time gave to a widow the same share in lands conveyed by her husband in his life time without her joinder, as in those of which he died seised. In Merrick v. DuPont, (285 Pa. 3681926), it was held that §3 of the Intestate Act of 1917, applies only to land so conveyed after its enactment and Bridgeford v. Groh, (305 Pa. 554-1932), holds this section of the Act of 

1917 to be constitutional. Common law dower may therefore be said to still exist where a husband has aliened land in his lifetime without joinder of his wife by a conveyance made before the Intestate Act of 1917.

Where a widow claims dower rights against real estate conveyed in her husband's life time, by a deed of general warranty in which she did not join, the grantee has a claim of damages against the husband's estate measured by the value of widow's interest (Inblum's Estate, 26 D.R. 8521917; Terry v. Drabenstadt, 68 Pa. 400-1871). 

144. When the Dower Right of the Wife Vests. 

Just as in the case of tenant by curtesy the dower right of a wife vests from the instant of marriage. From that time

$361 

on she has her interest in the husband's land or such as he may acquire thereafter, but her right is inchoate and she cannot enforce the same until her husband's death, though it is an encumbrance on the title conveyed without her joinder (Muirhead v. Clabby, 7 Phila. 345, 347-1870). The interest which she acquires by marriage however can only be barred by one of the methods set out in the next section (145). The nature and effect of modern dower rights has been explained in the case of Briegel v. Briegel (307 Pa. 93-99-1931) as follows: "Before dower exists three things must occur, marriage, feasance of the husband and his death before the death of his wife. Prior to his death dower is a mere intangible, inchoate, contingent expectancy; it is not an interest in land and cannot rise to the dignity of a vested right; it vests only at the death of the husband. Such a contingent expectancy is not the subject of a gift, sale, attachment or devise." Neither can a wife claim dower rights in real estate conveyed away by her husband before marriage without her knowledge unless she can prove actual fraud (Kirk v. Kirk 340 Pa. 203-1940). 

145. How Dower May Be Barred.

Dower may be barred or forfeited by various acts of a wife just as we have seen a husband's curtesy may be barred. 

These methods are:- (a) By Voluntary Joinder in a Deed of Husband. If the wife joins in a husband's deed of conveyance she thereby is held to have signed away or relinquished her dower rights. 

Mere consent to the transaction does not bar her rights unless she actually signs the deed or agrees to do so by signing the agreement of sale. 

(b) Divorce A. V. M. A divorce A. V. M. (See §141 (b), i.e., an absolute divorce, also bars her right (Richardson's 

Estate, 132 Pa. 292-1890; Miltimore v. Miltimore, 40 Pa. 

151-1861). But not a mere separation (Arnout's Est. 283 

Pa. 49-1925) or even desertion unless it be for one year or upwards previous to husband's death (see (c) infra.).

§145 

 (c) Desertion or Elopement and Adultery of the Wife. §6 

of the Intestate Act of 1917 provides "that no wife who shall have for one year or upwards, previous to the death of her husband, wilfully and maliciously deserted her husband, shall have the right to claim any title or interest in his real or personal estate after his decease under the provisions of this act." But an agreement between husband and wife to live separate and apart is not desertion and does not bar dower 

(Lawton's Est. 266 Pa. 558–1920). 

It is to be noted that the same rules of evidence apply here as in the case where it is sought to bar a husband's right of curtesy by his desertion or non-support (See §141 (c)). 

Should the wife elope from the husband and commit adultery her dower rights are barred (Lewis v. Parrott, 37 

W. N.C. 330-1895). Though if the husband deserts her first, her subsequent adultery will not bar her dower (Reel v. Elder, 62 Pa. 308-1869). At common law, mere desertion by the wife, did not bar her dower, nor did mere adultery, both had to combine (Heslop v. Heslop, 82 Pa. 537-1876). (d) Devise in Lieu of Dower. Where a husband devises a portion of his property by will to his widow and she accepts said provision of the will, it is presumed to be in lieu of dower. 

She may, however, refuse the provision made in the will and elect to take under the intestate laws instead (See Right to 

Take against Will, §165, infra.). 

(e) Ante Nuptial or Post Nuptial Agreement. An ante nuptial agreement is one made by the parties about to marry in which one or the other releases his or her interest in the other's estate. When such an agreement releases dower it is barred. A post nuptial agreement is one entered in after marriage (See (ƒ) infra.). (f) Release and Agreements. The wife may by writing or agreement release her dower interest (Singer's Estate, 233 

Pa. 55-1911; Ray's Est. 304 Pa. 421-1931). So, too, agreement or deed of separation may contain release of dower and operate to bar it (Fennell's Estate, 207 Pa. 309—1904).

§363 

Such deeds of separation releasing dower may be and should be recorded, though they have been held valid even when not acknowledged (Kaisers Est. 199 Pa. 269-1901). Merely living separate and apart does not operate to abrogate dower, its release must be specifically agreed to in writing (Walsh v. 

Kelly, 34 Pa. 84-1859), and there must be no fraud and proper consideration (Inskipt's Est. 324 Pa. 406—1936). (g) Sheriff's Sale. Where land is sold out under foreclosure of mortgage or under the judgment obtained by a creditor against the husband, the dower is barred (Scott v. 

Crosdale, 2 Dallas 127-1791; Directors of Poor v. Royer, 43

Pa. 146-1862). But where the mortgage is made or judgment permitted to be obtained by connivance of husband with intent to bar dower, the court will declare it to be a fraud and preserve the wife's rights (Killinger v. Reidenhauer, 6 S. & R. 

531; Waterhouse v. Waterhouse, 206 Pa. 433-1903 but see 

Beirne v. Continental Equitable T. Co. 307 Pa. 570-1932). 

(h) Sale by Orphans' Court for Payment of Debts. Where land of decedent is sold by Orphans' Court for payment of decedent's debts, dower is also barred (Hay v. Meyers 114 

Pa. Super. Ct. 269-1934) unless the order of the Orphans'

Court expressly preserves it (Ohio-Pennsylvania etc. Bank v. Blough, 119 Pa. Super. Ct. 34-1935). So also a sale under a testamentary power for payment of debts discharges the land from the dower of the testator's widow, (Mitchell v. 

Mitchell, 8 Pa. 126-1848; Directors Etc. v. Royer, 43 Pa. 

146-1862). So also a sale by an executor under authority given by will and without order of Court (Miller v. Sheaffer, 75 Pa. Super. Ct. 584–1921). (i) Sale in Partition Proceedings. A sale in partition divests inchoate dower rights of the wives of co-tenants even though not made parties to the proceeding. (Carl v. Jauss, 22 D.R. 407-1913). In fact they are not considered necessary parties to a partition proceeding (Powell's Est. 3 D.R. 

508-1894). Even though they may be joined as proper parties (McCoy's Est. 1 D.R. 60-1892). The Act of April

§146 

24, 1929-646 (20 P.S. 1202, 1321) amending the Orphans'

Court Partition Act, now expressly provides that the spouses need not be made a party to the proceedings. Where a spouse however obtains a vested interest in a remainder by death of the spouse during the pendency of the particular estate (see §§3 and 4, Intestate Act of 1917), then the spouse is a necessary party to the partition proceedings in the Orphans' Court, (Hughes Est. 29 D. & C. 110—1937). (j) Eminent Domain. Condemnation of the husband's land by eminent domain proceedings bars the wife's dower and the fund raised thereby is not subject to a claim by the wife by virtue of her contingent dower interest in the land 

(Briegel v. Briegel 307 Pa. 93—1932). 

(k) Pre-Nuptial Conveyances. Either spouse may challenge as fraudulent a conveyance of real estate or gift of personal property, made during a treaty of marriage (as, e.g., a conveyance of real estate made after the parties became "engaged" but before marriage), but the mere proof of a voluntary conveyance made three days before marriage, without knowledge of the intended wife, was held not to be sufficient, of itself, to establish the fraud necessary to set aside such conveyance (Kirk v. Kirk, 240 Pa. 203—1940). 

146. Bankruptcy Now Bars Dower and Curtesy. 

Prior to the Act of June 2, 1919, (P.L. 363 68 P.S. 141), sale of a bankrupt's real estate by his receiver or trustee or assignee for creditors, did not bar dower (Porter v. Lazear, 109 U.S. 84-1883; Mills v. Ritter, 197 Pa. 353, McFadden v. 

McFadden, 32 Pa. Super. Ct. 534-1907), but now by that

Act such a sale confirmed by the Court, bars dower. 

By amendment of April 27th, 1927 P.L. 441 (68 P.S. 141) 

the same is true of curtesy, which is also barred by the bankruptcy of the wife.

147. Escheat. 

Definition. 

Escheat at common law was the term used to signify the reverter of lands held in fee to the over-lord by reason of failure of heirs to inherit. More modernly, escheat means the reverter of property to the commonwealth or sovereign state because of absence of kin or kindred. It is, therefore, a method by which the commonwealth acquires title. The Pennsylvania Intestate Laws (See 24, of §134, this book) provide that in default of "all such known heirs or kindred, widow or surviving husband as aforesaid, the real and personal estate shall go to and be vested in the commonwealth by escheat." 

For the procedure of sale of real estate of a decedent passing by escheat to the commonwealth see (Rooney's Est. 38 

D. & C. 524-1940, and Lutton v. Powell 7 D. & C. 245—1925). 

Escheat is not limited to the single instance of an intestate dying without kin, but exists also in cases where a person or corporation, forbidden to do so, attempts to hold land. And in general it may be said a State has the power to take by escheat all unclaimed property within its borders (Re Escheat 365

§148 

of Money in U.S. Treasury, 322 Pa. 481-1936, 326 Pa. 2601937 Aff. 303 U.S. 276). 

148. Escheat of Lands Held by Aliens. 

In considering the capacity of persons to take, hold and convey title to land we found that the capacity of aliens was limited to 5,000 acres in quantity and $20,000 in net annual value (See $28 of this book). Should he acquire more, the excess escheats to the State. Where an alien sells such land before escheat proceedings are commenced a good indefeasible title vests in the purchaser (Act of April 6, 1859, P.L. 383, §1 

68 P.S. 54). But an alien is allowed to take and acquire by descent or devise "real property in the Commonwealth and to hold and dispose of the same in as full an ample manner as citizens of this State may or can do" Act of Feb. 23, 1791, 3 Sm. L. 4 §1 (68 P.S. 22) though not, it seems, from an alien ancestor (Rubeck v. Gardner 7 W. 455-1838). 

149. Escheat of Land Held by Charities. 

So also religious and charitable societies, churches or institutions whether incorporated or unincorporated were limited in the amount of land and the purposes for which they might hold. At first they were limited in their capacity to real estate to a greater amount than a yearly value of $30,000.00 without express legislative sanction (Act of April 26, 1855, P.L. 328, amended by Acts of April 22, 1889, P.L. 42, 10 P.S. 

31, 33). By the Act of May 15, 1913 P.L. 214 as amended by

June 1, 1915 P.L. 701, this limit was increased to $50,000 and by the Act of March 13, 1929 P.L. 21 (10 P.S. 33) to $350,000.

These acts were repealed so far as relates to corporations by the Non Profit Corporation Act of 1933 Article XI §1102, P.L. 

289 (15 P.S. 2851-1102) and such corporations, now by $306, may now take and hold for the purposes set forth in its articles, real and personal property without limitations as to value. (See $38(b) of this book). Here, again, any land held in violation of the restriction as to purpose, escheats to the State.

$367 ESCHEAT. 

150. Escheat of Land Held by Trustees. 

Where the cestui que trust has been unknown and absent for seven years and still remains unknown, all property in the custody of the trustee may be escheated to the Commonwealth as in other cases (Act of May 11, 1911, §1, P.L. 281, 27 P.S. 333). 

151. Escheat of Land Held by Corporations. 

We have seen (§§38-39 of this book) that prior to the 

Business and Non Profit Corporation Acts of 1933 (15 P.S. 

2851, 2852), foreign corporations and to a lesser extent domestic corporations, were limited in their right to hold real estate. By these Acts the foreign corporations as regards the right to hold real estate, are now on a parity with domestic corporations, and both may now take and hold real estate regardless of value, "appropriate to enable them to accomplish fully and properly their corporate purposes. See §§38, 39 of this book where the matter is more fully discussed. 

Real property taken or held beyond the corporate needs remains however still escheatable. 

152. Escheat Not Complete Until Commonwealth Begins Proceedings. 

At common law when property escheated title vested in the overlord without more. True it is that he had often to commence proceedings to eject the occupiers or to gain possession, but title vested in him absolutely upon the mere happening of the event. But this is not true under the escheat law in 

Pennsylvania. Title of the Commonwealth to escheated property is not perfect until it is determined by inquest that there are no heirs or known kindred of the intestate (Crawford v. 

Com., 1 Watts 480, 485-1833; Mitchell on Real Estate etc. 

316). But the rights of the Commonwealth to property after escheat is decreed, dates from the death of the decedent and

§153  

it is entitled to rents from that time (Kephart v. Straub et al., 21 D.R. 477-1911).

So, also, until the Commonwealth commences proceedings to escheat the title to escheatable land held by aliens, religious societies or corporations, its title does not become perfect. Delay on the part of the Commonwealth to assert its title can not inure to the benefit of the alien, religious society or corporation that holds the property in violation of its limitation, but while the Statute of Limitations does not run against the Commonwealth laches may be imputed to her as well as to an individual, (Bailey's Est. 241 Pa. 2301913; Comm. v. Turnpike Co., 153 Pa. 47-1893). However, in the case of escheat for failure of heirs there is a limitation imposed on the Commonwealth by the Act of May 2, 1889, P.L. 66, §26 (27 P.S. 101), which provides that the Commonwealth must commence escheat proceedings within twenty-one years after the decease of intestate dying without heirs, or be forever barred. This limitation applies only to estates in possession. It begins to run as to remainders only when the life estate falls in. (Comm. v. Naile, 88 Pa. 429-1879). 

153. Bona Fide Purchasers Before Escheat Gain Good Title. 

The effect of this development of the escheat doctrine in Pennsylvania was that if in order to perfect its title it was necessary for the Commonwealth to begin proceedings and if before such proceedings were commenced, the land in question was conveyed to a bona fide purchaser for value without notice, such purchaser ought to have a good title as against the Commonwealth. This was the position eventually taken by the legislature of Pennsylvania, which, after passing laws from time to time confirming title of innocent purchasers gained before escheat was commenced, passed the very broad 

Act of June 24, 1895 (P.L. 264, §1 68 P.S. 56), which provided, that "Where any conveyances of real estate in this Commonwealth have been or shall be made by an alien or any foreign corporation or corporations of another or of this State to any citizen of the United States or to any corporation char-

$369 

ESCHEAT. 

tered under the law of this Commonwealth, and authorized to hold real estate, before any inquisition shall have been taken against the real estate so held to escheat the same, such citizens or corporation, grantee as aforesaid, shall hold and may convey such title and estate indefeasible as to any right of escheat in this Commonwealth by reason of such estate having been held by an alien or corporation not authorized to hold the same by the laws of this Commonwealth." (See also Acts of June 15, 1897, P.L. 164, March 26, 1903, P.L. 67, (68, P.S. 

57) and also Act of May 25, 1939, P.L. 202 (68 P.S. 61 Anno.) 

154. Proceedings to Escheat. 

Escheat proceedings may be begun by anyone who knows of escheatable property, informing the Commonwealth. This is done by notifying the Secretary of Revenue (prior to the 

Administrative Code 1929; (Act of Apr. 9, 1929, P.L. 177; 

71 P.S. 51); the Auditor General), in writing, signed and witnessed by two subscribing witnesses. The informer, as he is known, receives one-fourth of the proceeds of the real or personal property escheated, less costs and expenses. He must, however, file a bond to refund said one-fourth share if a claimant subsequently appears and establishes his claim within the time limited (Act of May 11, A.D. 1911, §4, P.L. 

281, re-enacted by Act of April 9, 1929 P.L. 343 Article XIII 

$1304; 72 P.S. 1304). Upon the receipt of the communication, the Secretary of Revenue appoints some suitable person of the proper county as escheator. But the Secretary of

Revenue is not required to appoint an escheator; he may in his discretion adopt the alternative procedure available under the 

Act of June 25, 1937, P.L. 2063 (27 P.S. 434), and demand that the escheatable property to be delivered without escheat. He cannot be compelled to accept the information and appoint an escheator (Edelman v. Boardman Sec. etc., 332 Pa. 85-1938). 

The escheator, if appointed, conducts the proceedings as laid down by the Act of May 2, 1889, P.L. 66 as amended by 

Act of May 11, A.D. 1911, (27 P.S. 41) and Chapter XIII of Fiscal Code, Act of April 9, 1929, P.L. 343 (72 P.S. 1301).

§154  

After decree of escheat has been obtained, the escheator applies to the Court having jurisdiction of the escheat proceedings, for an order directing sale of the escheated real estate and after it has been sold the proceeds are paid into the State Treasury. The Court may direct a private sale. 

See Rooney's Est. (38 D. & C. 524-1940), where the applicable statutes are reviewed and the proper procedure outlined.

155. Definition of Wills and Terms Thereof. 

417 "A will", says Chancellor Kent (4 Kent Com. 50), “is a disposition of real and personal property to take effect after the death of the testator." Lewis' Est. 139 Pa. Super. Ct. 

83-1940 cites Blackstone's definition viz. A will is a legal declaration of a man's intentions which he wills to be per-

$373 

WILLS. 

formed after his death (2 Blacks. 499). Correctly speaking, a will of personal property is called a testament. A will of real estate is called a devise (Mitchell on Real Estate and 

Convey. 513).

The person who makes a will is called the testator, if female, testatrix. The person to whom the will gives real estate is called the devisee; and what he receives, a devise. One who receives personal property is called legatee, and what he receives, legacy. The apt words to be used in willing real estate are devise and for personal property bequeath. (Fleck v. Harmstead et al. 304 Pa. 302-1931). Latterly, however, this distinction has not been maintained and it has become customary to use the form, "I give, devise and bequeath", indiscriminately. When a will is written wholly by the testator, it is called a holographic will. A codicil is a supplement to a will altering or changing some part or parts of it. 

156. Origin of Wills. 

During the early history of mankind the only right, man had to acquire and possess property was the right of might. 

Upon his death, whatever he possessed or occupied was by law of nature open to any who chose to take it, and so the next occupant acquired title. Usually the next occupant was a member of the decedent's family for the obvious reason that a member of the family was usually nearest to the property when the death occurred. With the dawn of civilization and as society organized, to prevent this unseemly scramble and its attendant disturbance, the law declared who should be entitled to the decedent's possessions. Later, the dying person was given the right to dispose of his possessions by will. 

The right, therefore, to make a will, just as is the right to inherit under the intestate laws, is purely a matter of grace on the part of the organized society which we call the state. (Links Est. No. 1, 319 Pa. 513, 516-1935). During the early days of the common law only personal property could be willed. Land descended by the inexorable laws of Descent. 

It was not until the 16th century, after the advantage of will-

§157 

ing estates in land became manifest, from the practice of devising equitable estates or uses that the parliament of 

England passed an act (Stat. 32, Hen. VIII, C.1) enabling land to be devised by will.

157. Modern Requirements of Wills. What Law Governs. 

Since the right to make a will is derived from the permission given by the state, it follows that each state may prescribe the manner and form in which the will shall be made. This has been done by the states enacting various statutes, usually termed statutes of wills. Sometimes the question arises whether the will must conform to the law of the state in which the testator is domiciled, or to that of the state where the land lies. The rule is settled that in construing devises of real estate, the law of the state in which the land lies, governs all questions concerning the form and validity of the will. (Pepper's Est. 148 Pa. 5-1892). But with personal property it is otherwise. The law of the state in which the testator lives, governs the disposition of his personal property, no matter where located. (Beaumont's Est. 216 Pa. 350-1907). 

In drawing a will containing a devise of real estate care should be taken to conform to the requirements prescribed by the state in which the real estate is situated. Happily, the requirements of the various states do not differ greatly. Still differences exist, e. g., in Pennsylvania, a will ordinarily does not require subscribing witness. In New Jersey a will would not pass title to real estate unless witnessed by two subscribing witnesses, some states require three. Generally speaking, however, it will be found that a will, in writing, made by an adult of sound mind, and signed by him in the presence of three subscribing witnesses, will be effectual to pass title in most any jurisdiction. 

158. Statute of Wills in Pennsylvania. 

The earliest statute of wills in Pennsylvania was the act of 1705 ( 1 Sm. L. 33), which was afterwards replaced by the 

Act of April 8, 1833 (P.L. 249), which provided in effect that

$375 WILLS. every person of sound mind might by will dispose of his or her real estate, whether held in fee or for life, and whether by severalty, joint tenancy or common, and also his or her personal estate. Married women were excepted by this act, but later were given equal right to will (Acts of April 11, 1848, 

§7, P.L. 536, and June 8, 1893, (Act No. 284) §5, P.L. 344.) 

The present governing Statute in Pennsylvania is the Wills 

Act of 1917, (Act of June 7, 1917, P.L. 403, 20 P.S. 181 et. seq.) which largely re-enacts the previous Wills Act of 1833 and its supplements. This Act like its predecessor of 1833, requires that a will must be in writing and signed at the end thereof. 

Provision is also made by the same statute for the making of a nuncupative will, i.e., an oral will. As personal property only can be bequeathed by a nuncupative will, we will limit ourselves strictly to the consideration of the wills by which title to real property may be passed. Let us, therefore, consider the essential requirements of a valid will under the 

Pennsylvania Laws. 

159. Who May Make a Will. Capacity. 

Any person, whether male or female, married or single, at least twenty-one years of age who is of sound mind may make a will.

What constitutes soundness of mind is difficult to define by general rule, nor can we do more in this book than to indicate generally what the law means. Probably the best known rule is that laid down by Judge King, in the case of Leech v. Leech, 1 Phila. 244-1851, which, reduced to simple verbiage, is: 

If a testator at the time of making the will knows what he is doing, knows what he is giving and knows to whom he is giving, he possesses sufficient capacity to make a will (See 

Lindsay's Est. 240 Pa. 19—1913). As indicated by this rule, something more than mere weakness of mind must exist before the will can be set aside on the ground of want of capacity (See also McNitt's Estate, 229 P. 71-1910).

Where a person is of weak mind, especially when the weakness results from a great age, the usual allegation of those who

§160 

seek to set the will aside is that it was made under undue influence. Undue influence is not to be confounded with want of capacity. The latter means the testator never had the requisite qualifications to make a will; in other words, was of unsound mind. But even if the testator had the requisite capacity a will may be set aside if made under undue influence, for then it is not really the testator's will, but the will of the person who dictated it. By undue influence is meant not mere solicitation or coaxing but such influence or constraint brought to bear upon the mind of the testator that at the time of the making of his will he was not a free agent (McMahon v. 

Ryan, 20 Pa. 329-1853; Englert v. Englert, 198 Pa. 3261901). 

160. Will Must be in Writing.

The statute requires that the will must be in writing (§2 

Wills Act 1917, 20 P.S. 191). Title to real estate cannot be passed by nuncupative will (Weisner's Est. 17 Berks 2821925). A will whether in typewriting, in lead pencil (Smith v. Beales, 33 Pa. Super. Ct., 570-1907) or in ink is considered to be in writing within the meaning of the statute. It may be written on parchment or paper or any substance which will preserve writing permanently. Thus a letter (Scotts Est. 

147 Pa. 89-1892), a contract (O'Connor's Est. 273 Pa. 3911922), an assignment (Coulter v. Shelmadine, 204 Pa. 1201902), a deed (Turner v. Scott 51 Pa. 126-1866), a power of attorney (Rose v. Quick 30 Pa. 225-1858), and even a signed endorsement on an envelope (Glass' Est. 331 Pa. 561-1938), have been held to be wills if so intended and testamentary in character. 

161. Will Must be Signed at the End. Execution. 

The will must be executed by the testator signing at the end thereof or by some person in his presence and by his express direction; unless he shall be prevented by the extremity of his last illness; Wills Act, 1917 §2 (Act of June 7, 1917 P.L. 

403; 20 P.S. 191, Hunter's Est. 328 Pa. 484-1938).

§377 

WILLS. 

(a) Signing by Mark. If a testator is unable to sign for any reason other than the extremity of his last illness, he may sign by mark; Wills Act 1917 §3 (20 P.S. 192). The proper method of signing by mark has been indicated in Kelly's Est. 

306 Pa. 551-1932 by Mr. Justice Maxey, to be "First, his or her name must be subscribed to the will in his or her presence and by his or her direction and authority. Second, after this is done, he or she must make his or her mark or cross at the appropriate place in the signature. A mark for a name or signature is the sign of a cross made in a little space left between the Christian name and the surname, and the word 'his' is usually written above the mark and the word 'mark' below it, 2 Blackstone Com. 305". If this method be faithfully observed the requirements of §3 of the Wills Act (20 P.S. 

192) will be complied with and the execution good. Though it is not the only way which it can be done, (Cassell's Est. 

334 Pa. 381-1939), deviation therefrom is perilous (James'

Est. 329 Pa. 273–1938, Hughes's Est. 286 Pa. 466—1926, Drews' Est. 32 D & C 297-1938). 

(b) What Is a Signature. Signing in the usual acceptation of the word and in the sense which presumably, it is used in the Act, is the writing of a name or affixing what is meant as a signature, thus a paper signed, "your misserable father", was held in Brennan's Est. 244 Pa. 574–1914, not to be a sufficient execution, but in Kimmel's Est. 278 Pa. 435–1924 a letter testamentary in character, signed "Father" was held to be sufficiently executed under the Act because it was intended as a full and complete signature. So also, in Knox's 

Estate 131 Pa. 220—1890 a testamentary paper signed “Harriet" was held sufficiently executed it being said "The form which a man customarily uses to identify and bind himself in writing is his signature whatever shape he may choose to give it, and under the Statute of Wills as under the Statute of Frauds, what is a sufficient signature depends largely upon the custom of the time and place, the habits of the individual and the circumstances of the particular case.

§161 

(c) What is Meant by End of Will. The question has often arisen, what is the end of the will? It arose in a case (Baker's 

Appeal, 107 Pa. 381-1884) where a will was written on the first and third pages of a sheet of foolscap paper, and was signed and sealed by the testator at the foot of the third page and there attested by subscribing witnesses. On the fourth page was an unsigned and unattested clause which read as if it was meant to form part of the body of the will. The court held that although the instrument was not signed at the end thereof in point of space, it was signed at the end of the will in point of fact, and that it was, therefore, a valid will under the statute. "The end of a will is the logical end of the testator's disposition of his property wherever it manifestly appears on the paper, and the position of the signature with regard to the bottom or end of the page is only evidence as to whether the testator has completed the expression of his intention; prima facie the bottom or end of the will is the natural place for the signature to show the full expression of the testator's wishes, and is, therefore, presumptively the right place for it; but it is only evidence and must give way to evidence of a different intent" (Stinson's 

Estate, 228 Pa. 475, 480-1910. See also Churchill's Est. 260 

Pa. 94-1918). 

§2 of the Wills Act of 1917 (20 P.S. 191) now provides that the presence of dispositive or testamentary words or directions, after the signature whether written before or after the execution shall not invalidate that which precedes the signature. Before this Act, the law was, a clause written after the signature, if it had no bearing on the contents of the rest of the will or its interpretation, was ignored (Wikoff's Appeal 15 Pa. 281-1850). But if it bore upon the will or was essential to its interpretation the whole will was considered invalid (Wineland's Appeal, 118 Pa. 37-1888; Taylor's Est. 

230 Pa. 346-1911). The law now is, however, that only what is written after the signature becomes invalid and is to be disregarded, but does not operate to invalidate what is written above the signature. But this section does not obviate the

§379 

WILLS. 

necessity of signing a will at the end thereof, (Bridge's Est., 139 Pa. Super. Ct. 606-1940). 

162. Subscribing Witnesses. Gifts to Charities. 

A will whether devising real estate or bequeathing personalty does not require subscribing witnesses in Pennsyl vania. Prior to 1935 (see Act of July 2, 1935 P.L. 573, 20 

P.S. 195 Ann.), there was an exception to this general rule in the case of devises or bequests to a Church or other religious or charitable use, this because of the Act of April 26, 1855 P.L. 

328 §11 as amended by the Act of June 7, 1911 P.L. 702 (10 

P.S. 12), re-enacted so far as wills are concerned by §6 of the 

Wills Act of 1917 P.L. 403 (20 P.S. 195), which required such a will to have "two disinterested, credible, subscribing witnesses", and to be executed at least one calendar month before the decease of the testator. The latter requirement being changed to 30 days by the Wills Act of 1917 §6 (20 P.S. 195). 

(a) Gifts to Charities to Take Effect After Death. Though the Act of 1935, (20 P.S. 195 Ann.), effective July 2, 1935, has removed the requirement as to subscribing witnesses, it still provides "no estate real or personal, shall be bequeathed or devised to any body politic, or to any person in trust for religious or charitable uses, except the same be done by will at least 30 days before the decease of the testator; and all disposition of property contrary hereto shall be void and go to the residuary legatee or devisee, heirs or next of kin according to law. This dispensation of the need of subscribing witnesses by the Act of 1935 was held to operate to validate a charitable bequest of a will executed without subscribing witnesses before its enactment where the testator died after its enactment (Spain's Est. 327 Pa. 226—1937). 

By the recent Act of May 16, 1939, P.L. 141, Act No. 70, (10 P.S. 17), it is provided that "any gift for religious or charitable uses hereafter made, to take effect in possession or enjoyment at or after death of the donor shall be void unless made at least 30 days before such death, and any promise

§163 

hereafter made to give real or personal property for religious or charitable uses, shall be unenforceable unless made at least 

30 days before the death of the promisor. The thirty days period provided for in this Act shall be computed as to exclude the first and include the last day thereof". Thus whether by will or by other instrument, a gift to charity to take effect at or after death, is void unless executed 30 days or more before the death. This Act of 1939 has repealed absolutely the Act of 1855 as amended by the Act of 1911 P.L. 

702 (10 P.S. 12) which required subscribing witnesses to deeds of conveyance where the gift was made inter vivos, and the thirty day restriction is now limited to bequests or gifts designed to take effect at or after death. (b) What is a Charity. As to what the law deems to be a charity within the restrictions of these acts see Archambault's 

Estate, (308 Pa. 549, 555-1932), where the Court cited with approval the definition from Fire Ins. Patrol v. Boyd, (120 

Pa. 624-1888, where it was said "a charity in a legal sense may be defined as a gift to be applied consistently with existing laws for the benefit of an indefinite number of persons, either by bringing their minds or hearts under the influence of education or religion, by relieving their bodies from disease, suffering or constraint, by assisting them to establish themselves in life or by erecting or maintaining public buildings or works or otherwise lessening the burdens of government". 

See also Lowes Est. (326 Pa. 375-1937), and Jordan's Est. (329 Pa. 427-1938). If title search requires the consideration of the question; who was deemed a "disinterested" witness under the prior law? the reader is referred to $162 of the first edition of this book where the subject is adequately discussed and see also Archambault's Est. (15 D. & C. 785, 308 Pa. 549-1932) and Aiken's Est. (103 Pa. Super. Ct. 279 -1931). 

163. Form of Will. 

No set form of words is essential to the validity of a will. 

No particular words are necessary. All that is required is

§381 

WILLS. 

that the intention of the testator be made clear. (Hengen's 

Estate, 337 Pa. 547-1940). Yet, nevertheless, the preparation and execution of a will is so serious a responsibility as not to be attempted by any one not learned in the law (Drew's 

Est. 32 D. & C. 297-1938). Drawing of wills by laymen has been declared to be unauthorized practice of law by the Supreme Court in Childs et al. v. Smelzer, 315 Pa. 9—1934), and the unauthorized practice of law is made a misdemeanor by the 

Act of July 12, 1935 P.L. 708, Act No. 271, (17 P.S. 1610). 

After all, it is not the province of a modern conveyancer, who is not a lawyer, to draw wills and untold litigation may be avoided by his refusal to do so. A person has the right however to draw his own will. Such a will is termed a holographic will but while the right exists the books are full of cases showing the litigation which inevitably follows the obscure and inaccurate phraseology in such wills usually employed. The following is a simple form of will:

LAST WILL AND TESTAMENT. 

I, Abram Jones, residing at 1342 Blank Street, Philadelphia, Pa., being of sound and disposing mind, memory and understanding, do make, publish and declare the following as and for my last will and testament, hereby revoking any and all wills by me at any time heretofore made.

First: I direct that all my just debts and funeral expenses be paid as soon as conveniently can be after my decease. 

Second: I give, and bequeath to my son John my gold watch and chain.

Third: All of the rest, residue and remainder of my estate, whether real, personal or mixed, and wheresoever situate, I give, devise and bequeath unto my beloved wife, Rebecca Jones, absolutely and forever.

Lastly: ¹ I hereby designate, constitute and appoint my said wife, Rebecca Jones, to be the executrix of this my last will and testament. 

In witness whereof I have hereunto set my hand and seal this 2nd day of September, A.D. 1940.

Abram Jones. (Seal).

Signed, sealed, published and declared by the testator as and for his last will and testament in our presence, who, in his presence and in the presence of each other and at his request have hereunto subscribed our names as witnesses.
