163-A. Construction of Devises of Real Estate. 

In devising real estate, words of inheritance (i. e., heirs) need not be added to the name of the devisee, as in the case of a deed (§54d of this book). The words, "give, devise, and bequeath to John Smith absolutely and forever" will convey a fee for by §12 of the Wills Act 1917 (20 P.S. 224) which reenacts §9 of the earlier Act of 1833, such a devise operates to pass the testator's whole estate in the premises devised, without words of inheritance (Gohn's Est. 324 Pa. 177-1936, Rengier v. Kunzler 246 Pa. 445-1914). Also a general devise of real estate will pass real estate over which the testator has a general power of appointment, §11 Wills Act 1917 (20 P.S. 223). Real estate devised need not be described by metes and bounds. The street number in a city for example is sufficient. Any description which will identify the land intended to be given is enough. The residuary clause, which is that clause beginning with the words, "All the rest, residue and remainder of my estate", etc., when drawn broadly as set forth in the foregoing form, will operate to pass a fee to any real estate and all personal property not specifically devised or bequeathed before.

A will (unless a contrary intention is manifest on the face of the will) speaks not from the time of its date but from the time of the testator's death; §9 of Wills Act of 1917 (20 P.S. 

221). Thus, if the testator acquired real estate after the date of the will it would nevertheless pass to the devisees in accordance with the terms of said will; §10 Wills Act of 1917 (20 

P.S. 222). Unless a testator directs otherwise the devisee of real estate subject to a mortgage, takes the real estate subject thereto; §18 Wills Act of 1917 (20 P.S. 242). Prior to

§383 

WILLS. 

1917 a devisee of real estate subject to a mortgage executed by the testator was entitled to have the mortgage paid off out of the personal estate of the testator (Stuard's Est. 17 Phila. 

498-1885), but not where the mortgage was created by previous owners (Hirst's Appeal 92 Pa. 491-1880). 

Since the Wills Act of 1917, §16a (20 P.S. 227) a devise to a child or children of the testator without naming such child or children (unless a contrary intention shall appear by the will), includes testator's adopted children. But such a devise or bequest made to the child or children of a person other than the testator includes only adopted children who were adopted before the date of the will (unless a contrary intention shall appear by the will), §16b Wills Act 1917 (20 P.S. 228); Ashhurst's Est. (32 D. & C. 547 aff. 133 Pa. Super. Ct. 526-1938). 

164. Codicil, Form of. Effect of. 

Sometimes it happens that a testator desires to change a single clause or bequest in his will without changing the rest of it. This is done by a writing executed similar to the will, which recites its purpose and then makes the change. The codicil need not be in any particular set form of words. A 

convenient form is as follows: 

CODICIL. 

I, ABRAM JONES, of Philadelphia, Pa., having made my last will and testament dated the second day of September, A.D. 1940, whereby 

I bequeath to my son John Jones my gold watch and chain. Now, therefore, I do hereby revoke the said legacy as given by my said will and hereby give said gold watch and chain to my son Philip Jones. In all other respects I do hereby ratify and confirm my said will.

In witness whereof I have hereunto set my hand and seal this 30th day of September, A.D. 1940.

Abram Jones. (Seal.) 

Signed, sealed, published and declared by the said Abram Jones, as and for a codicil to his last will and testament in the presence of us, who, in his presence and in the presence of each other, have, at his request, subscribed our names as witnesses thereto. 

John Doe. 

Richard Doe.

§165 

The effect of a codicil is to confirm and republish the will as of the date of the codicil in all respects except as altered by the codicil (Gilmor's Estate, 154 Pa. 523-1893; Davis' 

Estate, 27 Montg. (Pa.) 30-1911); and a defectively executed will is cured by its republication through a properly executed codicil (Kelly's Estate 236 Pa. 54-1912).

A codicil is to be distinguished from a later will for the latter works essentially a revocation, while a codicil is a confirmation of the will, except as to the express alterations which it may contain. Notwithstanding a codicil, the provisions of the will are to stand unless in order to effect the purpose of the codicil it is absolutely necessary that the provisions of the will shall give way (Wright's Estate 68 Pa. Super. Ct. 

177-1917). A codicil being essentially a supplement to a will, both must be considered together as constituting a single instrument (Ketcham's Estate, 22 D.R. 966-1913). The codicil changes the will only so far as the changes are directed or necessarily implied. In all other respects, a codicil confirms and re-publishes it (Sigel's Estate No. 1, 213 Pa. 141905).

A second codicil may be added after the first, and so on. 

A confirmation of a will by a second codicil confirms it as modified by the first codicil (Lees Est. 16 Pa. Super. Ct. 6271901). The codicils should be kept with the will and are probated with it. 

165. Election or Right to Take Against the Will. Of De ceased Spouse.

A parent may disinherit children by a will which fails to make any provision for them whatsoever, and give the entire estate to strangers. But one spouse cannot by will deprive the other of the provision given by law in lieu of curtesy or dower. By §23(a) of the Wills Act of June 7, 1917 

P.L. 403 (20 P.S. 261) it is provided that if a surviving spouse shall elect to take against the will, such surviving spouse shall be entitled to such interest in real and personal estate of the

$385 

WILLS. 

deceased spouse as he or she would have been entitled to had the testator died intestate.

We have seen that under the intestate laws Sections one and two (See also $134, of this book 1 & 2), a surviving spouse is entitled to one half of the entire estate, real and personal if there be one child or none, and one-third if there be more than one child. The preferential allowance of five thousand ($5,000.) dollars is restricted to actual cases of intestacy and cannot be claimed where the spouse elects to take against the will of the deceased spouse; §2(a) Intestate Act of 1917 P.L. 

429 as amended by Act of July 11, 1917 P.L. 755 (20 P.S. 11).

This restriction has been held constitutional, (Langerwisch's 

Est. 267 Pa. 319-1920). 

The right of both husband and wife to take against each other's will, was quite different before the Wills Act of 1917, for then if a husband died without children, the wife could claim against his will $5,000.00 and in addition one half of the remaining personal property absolutely and half of the real estate for life; and if children, the wife took only one-third of the personal property absolutely and one-third of the real estate for life. A surviving husband, before 1917, had two choices, (a) he could take against his wife's will, his curtesy, which then was all of the real estate for life, or (b) he could take against her will the same share out of real and personal estate which the law gave her in his estate (Moores Est. 50 

Pa. Super. Ct. 76-1912). Now, under the Act of 1917, the rights of the husband and wife are not only greatly enlarged, but are precisely the same. 

166. Proceedings Necessary to Take Against the Will. 

The right to take against a will is an optional right and is technically called an election. The Wills Act of 1917 P.L. 403, 

§23(b) as amended by the Act of July 8, 1935, P.L. 611 (20 

P.S. 262), makes it the duty of a surviving spouse (unless the sole beneficiary), to indicate whether he or she is satisfied to take under the will or is dissatisfied, and desires to take against the will. This must be done by executing and acknowledging

$166

a writing to that effect, within one year of the issuance of letters testamentary. Neglect, refusal or failure to deliver such writing to the executor or administrator within said period is deemed an election to take under the will. The time of making and delivering an election may be extended by the court if application is made within seven months from the death of the testator, (Act of June 24, 1939, P.L. 705 20 P.S. 266). $23(c) of the Wills Act, (20 P.S. 263,) forbids any payment from the estate of the decedent, (except the widow's exemption), to any surviving spouse, unless his or her election shall have been first executed, acknowledged and delivered, and $23(d) (20 P.S. 264) provides a procedure whereby the 

Orphans' Court, on application of any person interested, may have the surviving spouse cited at any time after six months from the death of the testator, to appear and make his or her election to take under or against the will. Failure to appear is deemed an election to take under the will and decree of court will be made accordingly. $23(e) of the Wills Act of 1917, (20 P.S. 265), provides that the surviving spouse's election or decree of the court, except when the decedent died seised and possessed of personal property only, shall be recorded in the Deed Book, at the cost of the estate, by the personal representative of the decedent, in the office for recording of deeds of the County where the decedent's will is probated, and shall also be indexed by the recorder in the grantor's index under the name of the decedent and in the grantee's index under the name of the surviving spouse. Where the decedent's estate, however, consists only of personal property, the election or the decree need only by filed with the Clerk of the Orphans' Court. No time limit seems to have been set for the recording and filing, by the executor or administrator, of the election (Cramm's 

Est. 127 Pa. Super. Ct. 446-1937 aff. 329 Pa. 528-1938), but the requirement, that notice of an election to take against the will be filed with the executor or administrator within one year after issuance of letters testamentary or of administra-

§166A 

387 

WILLS. 

tion, must be complied with if such election is to be effective. (Broad's Est. 325 Pa. 541-1937). Since the duty of recording the election is placed upon the personal representative, it was held that an executrix's failure to record and file a widow's written election to take against the will, delivered to the executrix within a year after issuance of letters testamentary, cannot deprive the widow of her legal rights thereunder. 

(Cramm's Estate 127 Pa. Super. Ct. 446-1937 aff. 329 Pa. 

528-1938). Neither will a recorder's error in indexing, invalidate an election, (Dalsen's Estate 310 Pa. 190-1933).

An election to take against a husband's will may be signed by the widow's attorney in fact, (Celenza's Estate 308 Pa. 186-1932).

Where the surviving spouse is mentally incompetent, her guardian or her committee in lunacy, may elect for her and the court which appointed the guardian or committee, may instruct the guardian whether to elect to take under or against the will of the imcompetent's deceased spouse. The authorization to elect should be determined by the Court with view primarily to the best interests and welfare of the incom petent. (German's Case 318 Pa. 200-1935). 

166-A. Effect of Election to Take Against a Will on Other Provisions Thereof. 

The rights of devisees and legatees under a will are subject to the rights of decedent's surviving spouse's election to take against the will, (Cramm's Estate, 127 Pa. Super. Ct. 446-452 -1937 Aff. 329 Pa. 528-1938). When a spouse elects to take against a will the election relates back to the date of the testators' death (Fitzgibbon's Est., 276 Pa. 105-1923) and speaks as of that time (Ward's Est. 25 D. & C. 674-1936). 

When the will taken against, provides a life estate for the spouse with remainders over, the election frequently gives rise to troublesome questions concerning the effect on the remainders. The general rule is that a spouse's election is to be considered as equivalent to the death of the spouse and therefore accelerates the vesting of the remainders (Coover's

§166A  

Appeal, 74 Pa. 143-1873; Ferguson's Estate 138 Pa. 2081890). That is to say, the rule is that as to provisions in a will for legacies subordinate to a life interest in the widow and contingent upon her death or payment of which is postponed until then, her election to take against the will is equivalent to her death. By such election, the widow takes her share as if the husband had died intestate and the will then operates on the rest of the estate precisely as if the widow were dead. (Vance's Est. 141 Pa. 201-1891; Woodburn's Est. 151 Pa. 586-1892).

In later cases the generality of the rule quoted has been restricted and held not applicable when the will shows a plain purpose that those who are to take the principal shall be ascertained at the actual death of the spouse (Reighard's Est. 253 

Pa. 43-1916); "Or where the will fixes a definite time for distribution independently of the widow's death or expressly provides as to the effect of her refusal to take under the will; or where a trust is created not simply to guard the widow's life interest but also for the benefit of a third party other than the widow or remaindermen; or again where during the life of a widow, the whole income is given to her and another, the latter of whom, for apparent reasons the testator, would specially desire to enjoy his bounty to the full extent indicated. (Disston's Est. 257 Pa. 537, 543-1917. See also Ammon's 

Est. 269 Pa. 159–1920, and Feeney's Est. 293 Pa. 273–1928).

But the general rule has been held to apply where remainders are not vested, but contingent upon the remaindermen surviving the widow, even though substitutionary gifts are made if they do not; it being considered that the principal intent of a testator is in favor of the first takers and the acceleration takes place (Lynn's Est. 23 D. & C. 139; 1935 Ward's 

Est. 25 D. & C. 674-1936; Wyllner's Est. 65 Pa. Super. Ct. 

396-1917). There is another qualification of the general rule that should be mentioned and that is where the election of the spouse results in a depletion of the estate so that other gifts made cannot be paid in whole or part. In such cases it was held in Lonergan's Est. 303 Pa. 142–1931, that where a 1-

§166B 

389 

WILLS. 

widow elects to take against the will, bequests and devises to her must ordinarily be sequestered to make good as far as possible, the losses thereby caused to the distributees and this principle applies in favor of the remaindermen as well as specific legatees and devisees. If both specific and residuary legatees or devisees suffer by reason of such election, the former must be made whole before the latter receive anything; but if only the latter suffer, the gifts to the widow will be sequestered for their benefit. See also Edelman's Est. 336

Pa, 4-1939. 

166-B. How Right of Election May be Barred. 

Since the surviving spouse's rights to take against the will is predicated upon the Intestate Laws, whatever would serve to bar the interests there given in lieu of dower or curtesy, would also serve to bar the right of election. The reader is therefore referred to §§141 and 145 of this book, setting forth when curtesy and dower is barred. 

Death of the spouse before electing also bars, for the right of election is a personal privilege which perishes with the surviving spouse and cannot be exercised by the deceased surviving spouse's personal representative. (McClintock's Estate, 240 Pa. 543-1913). 

167. Revocation of Wills. Express Revocation. 

Since a will does not take effect until the death of testator it follows that it may be revoked at any time prior to testator's death. A will may be revoked either by express act of the testator, which is called an express revocation, or by operation of law, which is termed an implied revocation. In Penn sylvania the Act of June 7, 1917, P.L. 403, §20(a), (20 P.S. 

271), provides that wills devising real estate shall not be revoked except by "some other will or codicil in writing or other writing declaring the same, executed and proved" like a will, or "by burning, cancelling or obliterating or destroying the same by the testator himself or by some one in his presence

§168  

and by his express direction." A will bequeathing personal property only, must be revoked in the same way, unless a later nuncupative will be made. $20 (b) of Wills Act of 1917 (20 

P.S. 272).

It is a good practice in drawing a will to put in a clause revoking all prior wills (See Form, §163), although not strictly necessary since if the later will is totally inconsistent with the prior will it prevails and the prior will is revoked. (McClures 

Est. etc. No. 2, 309 Pa. 370-1933; Hartman's Estate 320 Pa. 

321, 326—1936). If, however, not totally inconsistent, the prior will is only revoked pro tanto, that is, only in such parts as are inconsistent with the last will. (Fox's Estate 55 Montg. 

110-1939). The writing revoking a will need not necessarily be a will, it can be any writing provided it is executed and proved like a will. (Harrison's Est. 316 Pa. 15—1934).

Revoking a will by cancellation or obliteration means cancelling in the popular sense. Thus scratching out or drawing a line through the signature (Evans' Appeal, 58 Pa. 2381868), writing the word cancelled or annulled across its face, or tearing it up, are all acts of revocation (Evans' Appeal, 58 Pa. 238-1868). A bequest was held cancelled by the testator drawing lines through the paragraph whereby the bequest was made (Wood's Est. 247 Pa. 377-1915 Lindemans Est. 

141 Pa. Super. Ct. 225-1940). Destruction means tearing it up or directing some one to do so in testator's presence with the intent that it be revoked (Ford's Est. 301 Pa. 183-1930). 

168. Implied Revocation. 

(a) By Subsequent Marriage, Birth or Adoption of Child. 

Marriage or subsequent birth of child not provided for in the will, operates as revocation of the will so far as the surviving spouse or subsequently born child or children is con cerned (§21 of Act of June 7, 1917, P.L. 403, 20 P.S. 273). 

This is termed an implied revocation. By the terms of the act such revocation is not, however, total, but partial i. e. only so far as the spouse or after-born child is concerned. The

$391 WILLS. testator is only considered to have died intestate as to a spouse he or she married, or the child that was born, after the making of the will; the rest of the will is good. A single person should therefore immediately after marriage, execute a codicil confirming his or her will and should execute such a codicil after the birth of each child. But this is only necessary if the will contains no provision for after-born children. If it does there is no pro tanto revocation (Newlin's Est. 209 Pa. 456–1904).

Nor is the extent of the provision important. (For Form, see $316. "All that is required relative to the provision for an unborn child is that the testator shall have the child in mind and shall make clear his intention that the will shall apply to it. Any provision that does this is sufficient and the inquiry whether large or small, equal or unequal, vested or contingent, present or future, is irrelevant and outside the jurisdiction of the court except so far as it tends to throw light on the question of intention." (Randall v. Dunlap, 218 

Pa. 210—1907). There a provision as follows: "I declare this to be and contain my last will and testament and that after-born children are herein provided for" was held sufficient.

By the Act of May 20, 1921 P.L. 937, (20 P.S. 273) §21 of the Wills Act was amended so as to extend its provisions to adopted children. Prior to that Act, a child adopted after the adopting parent made a will was not entitled to any rights against it as in the case of natural born children (Goldstein v. Hammell 49 Pa. Super. Ct. 39–1912, aff. 236 Pa. 3051912).

So far as the spouse who married a testator after the execution of the will is concerned, apart from this section of the Wills Act, he or she has in all cases the election to take against the spouse's will (under section 23) no matter when made or what may be the provisions thereof unless by valid agreement, antenuptial or otherwise, the right to do so was waived. (McGarry's Est. 9 D.R. 172-1900). Where a spouse claims under $21 (20 P.S. 273) however, actual intestacy is created as to the surviving spouse and where there are no

§169 

children, can claim $5,000 and in addition thereto one half of what remains of the deceased's estate. (Shestack's Est. 267 

Pa. 115-1920). The right of the surviving spouse to have an intestacy declared as to him or her is personal, and is really to be regarded as an additional right of election. So where a spouse was satisfied to take under a will executed before the marriage because the entire estate had been bequeathed to him and there were no children, it was held the next of kin could not compel the application of §21 of the Wills 

Act (Lintner's Est. 297 Pa. 428—1929). (b) By Ademption. A will may also be impliedly revoked either in whole or in part by the testator conveying away in his lifetime the property devised. Thus A, by his will, devised a house to B; later he sells the house; the devise to B is thereby impliedly revoked. If the testator has conveyed away so much of his real estate during his lifetime so that it is impossible to distribute the balance in accordance with his will, i. e., if his whole testamentary scheme is destroyed the whole will is revoked except possibly as to the appointment of an executor, if there is any need of one (Cooper's Estate, 4 Pa. 88-1846; Horton's Est. 304 Pa. 112—1931).

Ademption involves action upon the part of testator; the doing of some act with regard to the subject matter which interferes with the operation of the words of the will, and by which he anticipates the gift there made by bestowing it during his lifetime upon the legatee or devisee, or disposes of the subject matter in some way which puts it out of question to follow his directions as set forth in the will. Therefore an absolute divorce was held not to operate to revoke a bequest to the divorced wife who was described therein as "my wife Mary Brown Jones" (Jones's Estate 211 Pa. 3641905). 

169. Probate of Wills. 

Limitations.

By probate of wills is meant the proving of the will to be the last will and testament of the decedent before the proper

$393 WILLS. officer. The officer before whom the will is proved is called the surrogate in some states. In Pennsylvania he is called the Register of Wills. The will is "probated" by taking it to the Register's office, where affidavits are taken from the subscribing witnesses that they were "present and did see the testator execute the will." If there are no subscribing witnesses any two persons who are familiar with the decedent's signature can be called to swear to its authenticity. If there are subscribing witnesses who are dead or permanently beyond the jurisdiction, two witnesses must be produced who can identify the signature of the subscribing witnesses. The register then issues "letters testamentary", which constitutes the executor's authority to act as such. 

A will may be offered for probate at any time¹ but unless it is offered for probate within three years from the date of the death of the testator it will be void and of no effect against a bona fide conveyance or mortgage of the real estate of the decedent "duly recorded before the date of the offering of said will for probate (Act of June 7, 1917, P.L. 415 §16(b), (20 P.S. 1887). But will be good against a devisee (Kellner v. Stahl, 3 D & C 389-1923). 

The three year limitation by its express language, only protects a bona fide grantee or mortgagee who takes title after three years. Thus a title acquired from or mortgage given by an apparent heir under the intestate laws within three years of decedent's death, would be voided, if a will is discovered and probated thereafter and before the expiration of the three years.

The Register of Wills decree of probating or refusing to probate a will becomes conclusive 2 years after made unless within that time an appeal is taken to the Orphans' Court (Act of June 7, 1917 P.L. 415 §16(a) 20 P.S. 1886). Such will so probated then becomes conclusive as to transfers of real and personal property (Young v. Fager 200 Pa. 329-1901; Hick- 

1 While a will may be accepted for probate at any time, the Register may not grant letters testamentary thereon after 21 years from decedent's death, except on order of the Orphans' Court on due cause shown $2(b) Fiduciaries Act of 1917, P.L. 447 (20 P.S. 342). See Comm. et rel v. Fisher, 2 D & C 300—1922.

§170 

 man's Estate 308 Pa. 230-1932). In Culbertson's Est. 301 

Pa. 438-1930, however, the decree probating a forged will was set aside twelve years after probate but it was expressly held the rights of grantees and mortgagees accruing after probate, were not affected. The true meaning of these two sections was clearly explained by Judge Trimble in an excellent opinion in Hetzel's Estate (37 D & C 440—1939), in the following language. "The purpose of these two sections 

(16(a) and 16(b) of the Register of Wills Act of 1917 P.L. 

415) is to make marketable the property of decedent passing under his will, or by conveyance from his heirs, or by transfers by his administrators. The result is when the bar becomes effective, titles of bona fide purchasers for value are free from direct or collateral attack after the expiration of 2 years in $16(a) and 3 years in §16(b). It is not the purpose of the Act of Assembly to prohibit the probate of a last will and testament offered after the expiration of the time limit. This would be in contradiction to the direct declaration of $16(b) which says the last will and testament may be probated at any time". Consequently that case held that where no transfer of property was involved, no administration conducted or account filed and only the rights of legatees involved, a probate could be opened and a later will offered for probate after the expiration of the 2 year period. 

The will should be probated in the county where the decedent resided, or if he had no particular residence, then in the county where the principal part of his estate is located.

II. 

LIENS OF DEBTS AND LEGACIES ON DECEDENT'S REAL ESTATE AND SALE THEREOF. 

It is of course, not the province of a book on conveyancing to delve deeply into the law of decedents' estates or of that governing the construction of wills, but an understanding of certain fundamental principles is essential to enable a conveyancer searching titles, to be competent to pass on such as are derived from or through decedents. These principles will be briefly, though it is hoped, adequately, set forth in the following sections of this chapter. 

170-A. Lien of Decedent's Debts. 

(a) Origin of the Lien of Decedent's Debts. 

Lands at common law in England were not assets for payment of decedent's debts (Horner et al. v. Hasbrouck 41 Pa. 

169, 177-1861). In Pennsylvania however, the original charter to William Penn made land assets for payment of decedent's debts first to the extent of one third, if decedent left issue, then by Act of Dec. 7, 1682 to the extent of one half and finally by the Act of May 31, 1693 (votes and Proceedings of House of Rep. of Province of Pennsylvania, Vol. 1, p. 75), all lands were made liable for payment of debts without limitation in favor of heirs. (Kirk v. Van Horn 265 Pa. 549,

§170A (b)1  

553-1920). Under these acts and the Acts of 1700 and 1705 (1 Sm. L. 7 and 57) which followed, the lien of a decedent's debts on his lands were of indefinite duration (Graff v. Smith's 

Administrators 1 Dallas 481-1789; Konigmaker v. Brown 14

Pa. 269-1850). As we shall hereafter see, the liens of debts not of record were step by step reduced in duration until they remain liens only one year from the date of decedent's death unless continued in the manner provided by law. 

Decedent's debts fall naturally in two classes (1) those which are simple debts, neither recorded nor reduced to judgments. They are usually termed "debts not of record." (2) Debts of record which comprise judgments, mortgages, etc. 

(b) Lien of Debts Not of Record. 

(1) What Are Debts Not of Record. In a general way it may be said, a debt not of record is any enforcible claim against the decedent which has not been reduced to a judgment in his lifetime. It includes debts due the Commonwealth (Koering's Est. 34 Pa. Super. Ct. 425-1907); or to a County for maintenance and support (Wurster's Est. 22 D. & C. 278 

-1934); a claim under an agreement to pay claimant certain moneys out of the proceeds of sale of real estate (Green v. 

Green 255 Pa. 224-1916). A right to an accounting from a deceased partner (Hook v. McCune 184 Pa. 292-1898). A claim on an antenuptial agreement was held also to be a debt in (Goeckel's Est. 131 Pa. Super. Ct. 36-1938). Costs of administration and funeral expenses are by the specific words of $15 (a) of Fiduciaries Act 1917, P.L. 447 (20 P.S. 521) included in the same category as debts. This has been held to mean that the lien of both administration costs and funeral expenses will be lost if an action is not commenced thereon and indexed as required in cases of other debts not of record. 

(Laziansky Est. 29 Schul. L.R. 181–1931). 

(2) Duration of Lien of Debts Not of Record. Since the passage of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917 (Act of June 7, 1917, 

P.L. 447 §15; 20 P.S. 521), debts not of record remain a lien

§170A (b)2 

397 

WILLS. 

1 against the deceased debtor's land not longer than one year after decease of the debtor unless continued by an action brought within the year against his executor or administrator and indexed, in the judgment index in the County where decedent's land lies. If such action is so brought then the lien continues for five years more. To continue the lien thereafter, it must have been duly prosecuted to a judgment and be revived by writ of Scire Facias, directed against the heirs, executors and administrators, devisee, alienee or owner of the land in question (§15 (a) Fiduciaries Act of 1917 Supra. 

20 P.S. 521).

If the decedent's land lies in a County other than that in which the executor or administrator resides, suit brought in the latter County to be availing, must be indexed in the County where the land lies. This is done by the Prothonotary of the 

Court in which the suit is brought certifying a copy of the praecipe to index, which may then be filed with the Prothonotary of the County where the land lies, who is required to index the same in the Judgment Index of that County, (§15 (d) id., 20 P.S. 524).

In order to preserve the liens of debts not of record, suit must not only be commenced within a year from the time of death but the action must be indexed (Negley v. Reiser, 324 

Pa. 190-1936; McDermotts Estate 19 D.R. 385-1910).

Neglect of the Prothonotary to index will not restore the lien against an innocent grantee. The party injured by the 

Prothonotary's neglect is referred to his action of damages against that official (Germantown Trust Company v. Buckley, 21 D.C. 397-1934). An action in equity for an accounting against a deceased partner's administrator was held to be a sufficient action. (Hook v. McCune 184 Pa. 293-1898).

Prior to that act the period was five years (Act of Feb. 2, 1834 (24). Prior to 1834 the period was seven years, (Act of April 4, 1797; 3 Sm.L. 296), and prior to 1797 the lien of such debts was of indefinite duration.

§170A (b)2 

Ch within a year from the debtor's death, its lien may be continued by the creditor filing within that year a "copy" of the instrument on which the debt is founded, or a "particular written statement of the debtor's demand", must be filed and indexed in the Prothonotary's Office of the County where the real estate, sought to be charged, lies. This will serve to continue the lien for a period of one year from the time the debt becomes due. To continue the lien thereafter, suit must be brought, and indexed within that year, otherwise the lien is lost. If the lien should not become due within 5 years from the date of debtor's death, the lien expires after 5 years unless a renewal of the entry is made on the judgment index upon order filed by the creditor or his attorney within the 5 years and every recurring period of 5 years (§15 (b); 20 P.S. 522).

If the lien of a decedent's debt is not continued by suit brought and indexed within a year after the decedent's death, it is wholly lost and the land is relieved from the payment of the debt in the hands of the heirs as well as in the hands of a bona fide purchaser for value without notice. (Tourison's 

Estate, 321 Pa. 299-302-1936; Brennan's Est. 277 Pa. 509 -1923).

Execution on judgments obtained against the personal representative of a decedent are by §15 (e) (20 P.S. 525), forbidden to issue unless the surviving spouse, heirs, devisee, alienee or owner of the land were either made parties to the action or are first warned by a sci. fa. issued on such judgment. In view of this provision, it is wise in commencing a suit to continue the lien of a debt not of record, to join in the suit the parties mentioned in this section, which may be done according to an express provision in §15 (a) (20 P.S. 521).¹

(c) Lien of Debts of Record. 

Debts of record naturally would include judgments, mortgages and the like. But a mechanic's lien was not so con sidered (Hershey v. Shenk, 58 Pa. 382-1868). 

As to Judgments, §15 (g) (20 P.S. 527) provides that judgments which at the death of the decedent shall be liens on real estate owned by said decedent at the time of his death, or on real estate which shall have been conveyed by deed not duly recorded during his lifetime, continue to remain liens for 5 years from his death, without necessity of revival and shall rank according to their priority at the time of his death. To continue the lien beyond the period of 5 years, revival proceedings must be pursued according to the law regulating revival of judgments.¹

This section preserves the lien only where it is a lien at the time of decedent's death. So where a judgment against a decedent in one county was transferred after his death to another County in which he owned real estate, it was held not to be within the provisions of this section, so that failure to proceed thereon and index the same within one year after death, terminated the lien as to the real estate in the County 

1 See for further discussion of this subject (177(b) of this book.

§170B  

to which the judgment was transferred. (Higgins's Est. 325 

Pa. 106-1937).

As to mortgages, §15 (h) (20 P.S. 528) provides that nothing in this section is intended to impair or affect the lien of any mortgage executed and recorded in decedent's lifetime, but the bond securing such mortgage except as to real estate on which the mortgage is a lien, is subject to the provisions of this section. In other words a mortgage duly recorded remains a lien against the mortgaged real estate of the decedent without any action thereon being necessary. But if the holder of the mortgage desires to make the bond a lien on other real estate of the decedent, he must proceed as in the case of an ordinary debt. 

170-B. Liens of Legacies. 

Prior to the Wills Act of 1917 (June 7, 1917, P.L. 403, §17; 

20 P.S. 241), pecuniary legacies were payable only out of the personal estate unless made a charge upon real estate either by express language or clear implication. $17 of the Wills 

Act (Supra.) changed the law in this regard and provides that: "All pecuniary legacies contained in any will, shall be charged upon and payable out of any real estate not specifically devised, where the personal estate is insufficient for their payment, or where the personal estate, although originally sufficient, has been wasted or mis-applied by the executor, unless a contrary intention shall appear by the will."

It is only real estate not specifically devised that is charged with pecuniary legacies. Even though the personal estate is insufficient to satisfy the legacies, specifically devised real estate cannot be resorted to (Strahley's Est. 314 Pa. 5151934).

Legacies charged on real estate remain liens until discharged by payment, release or decree of Court. There is perhaps no more troublesome¹ lien to the title searcher than

Feb. 18, 1939.

this lien when there is no clear evidence of record showing its payment. Of course, where an account of the estate is filed, confirmed and awards made, a satisfaction of award is customarily filed in the office of the Clerk of the Orphans' Court, which establishes of record, payment of the legacy. 

But sometimes satisfaction of awards are not filed, or in cases where accounts have not been filed and estates are settled informally, receipts are taken which after the passage of time are lost. Consequently the residuary devisee of the real estate subject to the charge of legacy, should see to it that a satisfaction of award is filed or in absence of an accounting, see that a formal receipt and release, witnessed by two witnesses and duly acknowledged, is obtained at the time of payment and recorded in the office for recording of deeds. 

Such releases are recordable, see $130 of this book, but not unless acknowledged (Powell's App. 98 Pa. 403-1881). If this is not done the devisee when he comes to sell his real estate, may, if the receipt be lost and the legatee dead, find great difficulty in making a clear title. 

When no proper acquittance or evidence of payment appears of record and sufficient proof of payment cannot be shown, the devisee of the land or his successor in title, will have to depend upon the presumption of payment which arises after 20 years (See §27 (b) 1 of the Fiduciaries Act, June 7, 1917 P.L. 447; 20 P.S. 693). Procedure under this statute however, will not necessarily bar the debt, for the presumption is a rebuttable one and the burden of proving demand and non-payment is merely shifted to the legatee (Yeates' Est. 22 

Dist. R. 445-1913). For this reason it is far better to wait

Davies' Estate, 60 Pa. Super. Ct. 360—1915); see also discussion of this Act in relation to extinguishment of ground rents 

§118 (a) of this book.

§170C (a)  

Where it is desired to relieve land charged with the payment of legacies from the lien thereof before the settlement of the estate, in order to sell the land charged, this can be effectually accomplished by having the legatees sign and acknowledge a release of legacy (see $281 this book for form of such release). If the legatees refuse to execute such release or the legatees cannot be found, or where no other means exist for relieving the land from the lien of legacies charged thereon, then §27 (a) 1, 2, (c) and (d) of the Fiduciaries Act (20 P.S. 691, 692, 697, 698), furnish a complete procedure by which an appropriate decree of court may be obtained to relieve the land charged, from such lien. These Sections also provide that a certified copy of the Court's decree may be recorded in the Recorder of Deeds Office of any other County where decedents' land may be situate. (See Remick's Pa.

Orphans' Court Practice Vol. 1, §§203 to 209 for further details and forms.) 

170-C. Lien of Inheritance Taxes. 

Inheritance Taxes, both State and Federal, are a lien on real estate of a decedent by Acts of Legislature and Congress respectively. 

(a) Lien of State Transfer or Inheritance Tax. 

By the Act of June 20th, 1919, P.L. 521, Art. IV, §39, as amended by the Act of May 16, 1929, P.L.

1795 $2, and the 

Act of July 14th, 1936, 1st Ex. Sess. P.L. 44, §3 (72 P.S. 2443), it is provided that the lien of the transfer inheritance tax "shall continue until the tax is settled and satisfied and shall be limited to the property chargeable therewith. All such taxes shall be sued within five years after they are due, otherwise they shall be presumed to have been paid and cease to be a lien against any purchasers of real estate.” But if the 

Department of Revenue within said five years, files in the Prothonotary's office of the County where the land is situate, a certificate certifying to the non-payment thereof, such taxes

§170C (b) 

403 

WILLS. 

become a lien against the decedent's real estate for a further period of five years from the date of filing. Such lien is required to be indexed in the Judgment Index in the name of the decedent as defendant. The Amendment of 1936 provides for a further extension or an additional five years by filing another certificate in the same manner, if the taxes are not by that time paid.

It has been held that failure of the Commonwealth to file within the 5 years, its certificate of non-payment does not preclude its right to file and collect the inheritance tax against the heirs or devisees, nor against the real estate of decedent still held by them; but the lien is discharged and cannot be collected from real estate conveyed bona fide to third persons. (Comm. v. Kirk's Estate, 39 D. & C. 276—1939). 

(b) Lien of Federal Estate Tax.¹ 

The Federal Law makes the amount of Federal Estate Tax due and payable, whether disclosed by the return or not, a lien for a period of ten years on all property constituting the gross estate of a decedent. This, whether it comes into the possession of the executor or administrator or not (Internal 

Revenue Code Feb. 10, 1939 Ch. 2; 53 Stat. 1, 26 U. S. C. A. 

827). This provision is derived from the Revenue Act of 

February 26th, 1926, C. 27 §315 (a) 44 Stat. 80 and its amendments. The lien is impressed on the decedent's estate as of the date of death (Rosenberg v. McLaughlin, 66 Fed. (2) 2711933 cert. den. 290 U.S. 696-1933; Page v. Skinner, 298 Fed. 

731-1924 cert. den. 266 U.S. 625-1924). The lien continues until the tax is paid or the period expires. (Neustadter v. 

U.S. 90 Fed. (2) 34—1937).

The Act of 1939 provides certain limitations governing the release, extent and removal of the lien. Thus (1) That part of the gross estate as is used for the payment of charges against the estate and expenses of its administration allowed 1 See for further discussion of this topic $176-A (a) of this book.

by the Court having jurisdiction thereof, is divested of the lien. (3) If the property is not sold bona fide for an adequate and full consideration by the decedent, but transferred in trust or otherwise in contemplation or intended to take effect at or after decedent's death, or transfer by trust or otherwise under which decedent retained a life estate or for any period not ascertainable without reference to his death or for any period which does not in fact end before his death (A) the possession or enjoyment of, or the right to income from, the property or (B) the right, either alone or in conjunction with any person, to designate the persons who shall possess or enjoy the property or income therefrom, then the transferee, trustee or beneficiary becomes personally liable for such tax, and such property to the extent of the decedent's interest therein at the time of the transfer, shall be subject to a like lien to the amount of such tax. III. 

POWER AND AUTHORITY OF ADMINISTRATORS AND EXECUTORS TO ADMINISTER OR SELL REAL ESTATE. 

170-D. Administrators Power Over Real Estate. 

(a) In General. Generally speaking, an administrator is appointed to administer only the personal property of a decedent, which he is authorized to take in possession, convert into cash, pay the cost of administration, the inheritance taxes, debts and account for and distribute the balance to the parties entitled under the Intestate Laws. While lands are assets for payment of debts, they are not assets in the hands of an administrator and without an order of the Orphans' Court, he has nothing to do with them. In case of intestacy they descend to the heirs, and if needed for payment of debts, they must be converted in the manner provided by the Statute (see $170-F of this book; Herron etc. v. Stevenson, et al., 259 Pa. 354—1918; Wolfe v. Lewisburg Trust etc. Company, 304 Pa. 583-1932). It naturally follows from this that an administrator ordinarily has no right to inter-meddle with nor collect the rents upon the decedent's death, without first obtaining authority of the Court. Should he assume to do so, he is regarded as acting merely as agent for the heirs, (Morrison's Estate, 196 Pa. 80-1900; Thord-Gray's Estate, 9 Erie 1-1926; Alexander's Estate No. 2, 34 D. & C. 1691938), but it has been held where the personal property is insufficient to pay the debts and the executor has collected the same with acquiescence of both creditors and heirs, the Orphans' Court may ratify and approve upon his accounting, what they might have previously authorized Downes' Est. 27 

Del. 319-1938; Joerger's Est., not reported (O.C. Phila. Co. 

No. 667 of 1932).

When the rents or the real estate itself are required for the satisfaction or the payment of the creditors, or the decedent has entered into a contract with reference to the real estate, then the administrator will be authorized by the Court, upon appropriate petition first made to it, to collect the rents

§170D  

and account for the same or sell the real estate and account for the same. Where an administrator presumed to sell decedent's real estate without order of the Court within the period during which decedent's debts were a lien, the lien was not discharged even though the proceeds of the sale were included in the administrator's account (Old Man's Home v. 

Fisher 252 Pa. 541-1916). 

(b) When and How Power to Collect Rents may be 

Obtained.

Rents accruing after death are made by $14 of the Fiduciaries Act, June 7, P.L. 447; (20 P.S. 503), assets for the payment of debts of the decedent whenever the personal property shall be insufficient therefor. This was a change in the law, as prior thereto, the rents belonged to the heir even where an estate was insolvent, until the land had been brought into the administration by a process of law. (Fross's Appeal, 105 Pa. 258-1884). §14 of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917 (20 

P.S. 503) now provides that whenever the personal estate of a decedent shall appear to be probably insufficient for the payment of debts, the Orphans' Court, having jurisdiction of the accounts of the executor or administrator, upon application of any creditor or of the executor or administrator, will authorize and direct the executor or administrator to collect such rents for such period as the Court shall fix. 

This power of the personal representative of the decedent to collect rents thus given, does not operate to prevent a mortgagee from entering into possession where the mortgage is in default (Merten's Est. 18 D. & C. 310—1932), or if the estate should prove insolvent, to prevent the subjection of the rents to the lien of the mortgage on the property out of which they issue (Bausman's Appeal 90 Pa. 178-1879; Wolf's 

Appeal, 106 Pa. 545-1884, Alexander's Est. No. 2, 34 D. & C. 

169, 178-1938).

The rents when collected are assets for the payment of unsecured creditors having no lien on the real estate, (Reel's 

Estate, 272 Pa. 139-1922) but subject to priority of creditors

§170D 

407 

WILLS. 

holding liens of record at the time of death if the estate prove insolvent and if application for authority is made within a year of decedent's death. If application is not made for authority to collect the same until a year after decedent's death, in granting authority, the Court will restrict the benefit of such rents to the creditors who have preserved their lien against decedent's real estate by appropriate proceedings within the year (See §170-A of this book). (c) Power over Real Estate which Decedent Contracted in his life time, to sell or buy.

We have seen that the legal effect of an agreement of sale is to vest in the vendee an equitable title to the land and in the vendor, an equitable title to the purchase money, which both may enforce by appropriate proceedings, (See §48 this book). When one of the parties to such a contract dies before settlement thereunder, the exclusive jurisdiction to enforce such contract, is, by the Fiduciaries Act of 1917 P.L. 447 §18 (b); (20 P.S. 612) in the Orphans' Court, (Manzer v.

Wycoff et al., 78 Pa. Super. Ct., 560-1922). The act applies to all cases, i.e., whether the vendor or the vendee dies. If the vendor is dead, enforcement of the contract, so far as his estate is concerned, can only mean payment to his personal representative, of the purchase money or any balance remaining due, and authorization, upon such payment to execute and deliver a deed for the land. By the agreement of sale as respects the vendor, the land is converted into personalty, and upon his death, before conveyance, the purchase money becomes assets in the hands of his personal representatives. (See $48 this book for cases in point.)

The administrator or the executor, as the case may be, is the proper person to carry out the terms of the decedent's contract under the Act, (Manzer v. Wycoff, also Bell v. Bell, 287 Pa. 269-1926). Either he or the other party to the contract, is empowered to petition the Court for a decree of specific performance. The procedure necessary to be followed is set forth in Vol. 1 of Remick's Orphans' Court

§170E  

Practice, $91. When a petition for specific performance is filed, it becomes the duty of the Clerk of the Orphans' Court to certify the same to the Prothonotary of the Common Pleas Court of the County in which the real estate lies, who is required to enter the same upon the judgment index under the name of the respondent in such petition and to certify the same as "lis pendens" in any certificate of search that he may be required to make by virtue of his office, §18 (c) of the 

Fiduciaries Act of 1917, (20 P.S. 613). The administrator then executes the deed, receives the purchase money and accounts for the same when he files his account. 1 

170-E. Power of Executors Over Real Estate. 

Executors, generally speaking, must be regarded as being subject to precisely the same limitations with regard to a decedent's real estate and rents as an administrator, unless the decedent in his will has granted to his executor further power to administer and sell real estate or has directed it to be sold and converted. 

(a) Powers by Will 

Testators usually grant to an executor power and authority to sell or administer real estate not specifically devised, but the nature and extent thereof, varies greatly in different wills. 

Sometimes the executor is merely authorized to sell the real estate. Sometimes he is expressly directed to do so. While the subject of powers under wills cannot be exhaustively considered, yet it is desirable that the following principles be understood because of their effect on titles of real estate. 

1 This must be taken generally to include administrators c.t.a. and adminis trators d.b.n.c.t.a., unless otherwise specified. 

2 In presenting this brief résumé on the question of powers, the author obtained much help from two excellent papers on the subject, one by Roland C. 

Heisler, Esq., read to the Pennsylvania Title Association in 1938 and reported in the proceedings of its 17th annual convention (1938), and the other by Pierce 

Mecutchen Esq., read to the Philadelphia Bar Association and printed in the

Legal Intelligencer of Feb. 18, 1939. Title under wills-with some practical suggestions. The reader is referred to these papers for a fuller discussion of the subject.

§170E (a)1 409 WILLS. 

The powers to sell real estate may be generally divided into two kinds, (1) the discretionary power of sale (2) a direction to sell, often termed a power working an "equitable conversion". Under the former power, real estate remains real estate until the power is exercised. In the latter, the direction to sell in the eyes of the law, is regarded as "converting" the real estate directed to be sold into personalty from the date of the decedent's death. These two powers and their incidents will be briefly considered, separately. 

(1) Discretionary Power of Sale. Where a testator gives his executor authority to sell but does not make it obligatory for him to do so and he may exercise or not exercise it as he chooses, the power so given is a discretionary power. The ordinary case of discretionary authority or power, is usually found expressed in the following language: "I hereby authorize and empower my executors to sell all or any part of my estate, real or personal, not herein specifically bequeathed and devised, either at public or private sale, and to execute and deliver good and sufficient deeds for all real estate sold, etc."

Under such a discretionary power the real estate of the decedent remains real estate until actual sale thereof. The death of a devisee before "exercise of the power", i.e. actual sale by the executor, transmits devisee's share to his devisee or heir as real estate and a subsequent sale does not divest his rights. (Reed's Estate 63 Pa. Super. Ct. 171-1916).

But a judgment debt against a devisee is divested when decedent's land is sold under a testamentary power (Kemerer v. Johnstone 318 Pa. 526-1935). It has been held that where there is no necessity to sell for payment of debts, the executor cannot sell the real estate without consent of a life tenant even though the will gives him a general (discretionary) 

power of sale (Werkheiser v. Friedman 29 D.R. 411—1920). 

(2) Power Working a Conversion. A power to sell given in such terms as to make a sale mandatory is said to work an "equitable conversion" of real estate into personalty. The theory behind the doctrine of equitable conversion, (fre-

§170E (a)2  

quently just called "conversion") was stated in Chew v. 

Nicklin 45 Pa. 84-1863 as being "nothing more than the application to deeds and wills, of the principle of equity which treats that as done which ought to be done. Where land is directed to be converted into money or money into land, it is to be treated as that species of property into which one or the other is directed to be converted." Conversion then is a question of intention which must clearly appear by express words or by necessary implication. "Whenever it appears from the will, that there is a (1) positive direction to sell or (2) an absolute necessity to sell in order to execute the will or (3) such a blending of real and personal estate by the testator in his will as to clearly show that he intended to create a fund out of both real and personal property and to bequeath said fund as money, the will is said to work a conversion (Hunt's & Lehman's Appeal 105 Pa. 128, 141-1884).

There is usually little difficulty in recognizing the first class, i.e., where there is a simple and express direction in the will to sell all or a specified part of decedent's real estate. (Sears v. Scranton Trust Co. 228 Pa. 126-1910 where the will provided "I do hereby order and direct that all of my real estate be sold by executor etc." See also Rieker v. Kaetz, 69 Pa.

Super. Ct. 182-1918). But if a will authorizes, directs and empowers an executor to sell "any or all" of the real estate, the words any or all implies a choice and the power to choose implies the power to keep, hence there is no positive direction to sell (See Conrad's Estate 32 D. & C. 677-1938).

Greater difficulty arises in recognizing the second and third classes. In order to arrive at a determination of whether a particular will works a conversion under these classes, the whole will must be carefully examined. In Fahnestock v. 

Fahnestock 152 Pa. 56-1892, the necessity was gleaned from the fact that a devise was made of the real and personal property, to the wife for life, and the rest to children and grandchildren and there was a direction that the same be invested in mortgages or other safe security. The positive direction to so invest could not be obeyed unless a sale was first made.

§170E (a)2 

411 

WILLS. 

Where it is impossible to carry out the testator's directions without a sale of the real estate, then the absolute necessity to sell, referred to as class 2, appears. (Suppes's Estate, 322 

Pa. 385-1936). But the necessity must have been contemplated by the testator himself and not arise from an unexpected shortage of his estate. (Hunt and Lehman's 

Appeal (supra.); Reel's Estate; Foreman's Appeal 272 Pa. 135-1921).

Illustrative of the third class is Battenfeld v. Kline 228 Pa. 

91-1910, where it was said "the requirement to sell, whether expressed or implied, must be unconditional, irrespective of contingencies, independent of discretion and imperative. (Cooper's Estate, 206 Pa. 628, 631-1903). But where it is clear that the provisions of the will cannot be carried out without a sale, it is not material that the language used in speaking of it is in form permissive and authoritative, rather than mandatory, nor that the time of the sale is postponed or left to the discretion of the executor (Severns's Estate 211 

Pa. 65, 67-1905). And so in the case of blending of realty with personalty (Tarrance v. Reuther 185 Pa. 279-1898).

The impossibility in such a case of making the division directed of the entire estate, without previous conversion of it into money, satisfies the needful, clear requirement of a sale of realty. (Laughlin's Estate 131 Pa. 333, 336-1889).' 99 When a conversion has been worked by directions in the will to sell, the legal effect thereof is to convert the real estate into personal property, at the testator's death. Various consequences flow from this result, thus on a legatee's subsequent death, it devolves as personal property to his legatees, spouse or next of kin. (Bergdoll's Estate, 258 Pa. 108-1917; 

Downer's Estate, 245 Pa. 580—1914).

So where there is a conversion, partition is barred (Severen's Est. No. 1, 211 Pa. 65-1905). A conversion frees the land from the lien of debts and as a consequence creditors may claim against the proceeds when the land is actually sold even though no suit was brought within a year of decedent's death, for in contemplation of the law, the real estate

§170E (a)2  

is regarded personalty as of date of decedent's death. (Mustin's Estate, 194 Pa. 437-1900).

From the viewpoint of enabling clear title of a decedent's real estate to be promptly conveyed with a minimum of litigation and court intervention, a power which works a conversion has many advantages which Mr. Mecutchen¹ in his paper sets forth as follows: (1) It obviates the necessity of all parties in interest agreeing upon any sale. Differences between them often involve an expensive partition proceeding to make title. (2) The spouses of all parties in interest need not execute deeds, which often causes complication. (3) Some of the parties may have judgments against them which cannot be disposed of without partition proceedings, see Battenfeld v. Kline, 228 Pa. 911910 holding that a judgment against a legatee obtained before actual sale, is not a lien where there is an equitable conversion. (4) The death of any of the parties may create any number of new complications, such as heirs that are minors, devisees, lien of debts, etc. (5) Where there is a conversion, legatees never acquire any lien on real estate nor are the debts of the decedent a lien thereon. All of these are manifest advantages from the standpoint of ease of making a good legal title. Mr. Mecutchen then makes the following suggestion for clear phraseology to enable a conversion to be accomplished. "I devise all my real estate unto my executor and his successors in office, in trust to sell and convey the same for such price or prices as to him or them may seem best, without liability on part of the purchaser to see to the application of the purchase money. I direct my said executor and trustees to complete the sale and conversion of said real estate within a period of years (not exceeding 21 

Years) following my death. The net proceeds of such sale or sales, after payment of any debts or legacies still remaining unpaid, shall be distributed as part of my residuary estate". (This might be followed with provisions for leasing, collection and distribution of rents and the like if desired, while the real estate remains unsold. Then add a residuary clause about as follows): "All the rest of my per- 

1 See footnote page 408.

413

sonal estate together with the proceeds of sale of my real estate, I give and bequeath as follows: (set forth the names and shares of the legatees) 

(b) Duration of Powers to Sell. 

Whether the power be discretionary or imperative, unless the period for its exercise be fixed definitely by a time limit or by statement of a specific purpose, much trouble may issue where it is not exercised until some years after decedent's death. Mr. Heisler in his paper suggests the following principles gleaned from the leading cases as a guide to the determination of the question. 1 1. A general power of sale given to executors, where by the will the property is vested absolutely in persons sui juris, will be presumed to be for administrative purposes and will ordinarily terminate when the lien of debts ceases. (Kolb v. 

O'Hay 28 D.R. 194-1918; Kreise v. Cartledge 262 Pa. 551918; Eberly v. Koller 209 Pa. 298-1904; Swift's Appeal 87 

Pa. 502-1878.) 

2. Where the real estate is left in trust, or life estates therein are given without the creation of trusts, the power of sale will continue during the period of trust. Wilkinson v. 

Buist 124 Pa. 253-1889; Fidler v. Lash 125 Pa. 87-1889; 

Carter's Est. 225 Pa. 355-1909; Cresson v. Ferree, 70 Pa. 

446-1872; Stiffler v. Penna. Coal & C. Co. 298 Pa. 152-1929. 

3. Where there is no trust, but a life estate given in the realty, the power of sale in the executor is continued for the benefit of the life estate (Rieder v. Miller 68 Pa. Super. Ct. 

529—1917, but see Schenck v. Clyde 53 Pa. Super. Ct. 652–— 1913). 

4. If it reasonably appears that the power was given for the purposes of ultimate distribution, or if an equitable conversion results from the will, so that a sale is essential, the power will continue for a reasonable time after the termination of the trust or the falling in of the life estate to enable 

1 See footnote page 408.

§170E (b)  

such purpose to be accomplished. In such event it seems that a sale must be made with reasonable promptness. (Battenfeld v. Kline 228 Pa. 91-1910; Tarrance v. Reuther 185 Pa. 

279-1898; Potts v. Breneman 182 Pa. 295-1897). 

5. A will sometimes directs a sale of real estate by the executors but mentions a specific time within which the power is to be exercised. In such case the rule is that the power does not cease because of a failure to exercise it within the time prescribed, but it may be exercised thereafter, in absence of a clear expression to the contrary. (Rieker v. Kaetz 69 

Pa. Super. Ct. 182-1918; Messmore's Est. 290 Pa. 107–1927). 

6. It would appear however that if a sale is not directed but is merely discretionary, and a specific time is limited for the exercise of the power *** the power would not be valid after the expiration of the time limited. (Herb v. Walther 

6 D.R. 687-1897). 

7. If a will provides the power is not to be exercised until the happening of a particular event e.g. death of life tenant, the power may nevertheless be exercised provided the life tenant joins in the deed. (Gast v. Porter 13 Pa. 533—1850;

Hupp v. Union Coal Co. 284 Pa. 529-1925; Hamlin v. Thomas 

126 Pa. 20-1889; Styer v. Freas. 15 Pa. 339-1850; Knapp v. 

Nissley 254 Pa. 379-1916). 

8. If a power is given for a specific purpose and that purpose fails, the power is ended. (Moore v. Gilbert 287 Pa. 102-1926). 

Mr. Mecutchen suggests the desirability of making plain the duration and extent of a power conferred in an executor to sell real estate in which the will has created a life estate but no trust, and a conversion is not desired, by using a provision such as the following. "At any time during the running of the life estate (or estates as the case may be) hereby created, and thereafter for the purpose of distribution, I hereby authorize and empower my executor and his successors in office to sell and convey etc."

§170F 

415 WILLS.

Where the estate is devised to a trustee, the power when a conversion is not desired, may be well given in the following form. "For the purpose of investment or any other purpose during the pendency of any of the foregoing trusts as to any share of the corpus thereof, and after termination of the trusts for the purpose of division and distribution, I hereby authorize and empower my said trustees, and the survivor and survivors of them and their successors in office, in their absolute discretion, to sell any of my residuary real estate or any other real estate which may, at any time, form any part of my trust estate, and to convey the same etc.’ 

9. Death of the original fiduciary does not terminate a power unless it appears by the clear language of the will that it is intended to be exercised only by the particular person named as executor or trustee. The general rule is that a power, unless so restricted, may be effectually exercised by the successor in office of the deceased fiduciary (Kemerer v. Johnson 318 Pa. 

526-1935; Battenfeld v. Kline 228 Pa. 91-1910 and see $170-I of this book for a fuller discussion.) 

170-F. Sales for Payment of Debts. 

A decedent's personal property is the primary fund out of which the debts and administration expenses must be paid. (Jones's Estate, 275 Pa. 143-1922). When the personal estate is not sufficient, it is the duty of the personal representative to proceed to sell real estate for the payment of debts. 

§16(a) of the Fudiciaries Act of June 7, 1917, P.L. 447, (20 

P.S. 551) provides, "whenever it shall satisfactorily appear to the executor or administrator, that the personal estate of the decedent, together with the rents of real estate, is insufficient to pay all just debts and expenses of administration, he shall proceed without delay, in the manner hereinafter provided, to sell or mortgage under direction of the Orphans' Court, having jurisdiction of his account, so much of the real estate as shall be necessary to supply the deficiency." The rest of the section sets forth the procedure, as to which see Remick's 

Orphans' Court Practice, $98.

§170G  

Of course this application must be made before the lien of debt against the real estate has expired,' (Emerick's Estate, 172 Pa. 191–1896; Golden's Estate, 56 Super. Ct. 300-1914); but this is so only where all liens have been lost for want of prosecution. If the lien of some of the debts have been preserved against the real estate, the Orphans' Court has jurisdiction to decree such a sale even though more than one year has elapsed since the decedent's death. (Leo's Estate, 9 Erie 

77-1926). The Orphans' Courts are empowered to direct a private sale, if in the opinion of the Court, under all circumstances, a better price can be obtained at private than at public sale. (See Fiduciaries Act of 1917, §16 (m) 1) (20 

P.S. 570). If an administrator refuses to apply for leave to sell for payment of debts, appropriate proceedings exist whereby he may be cited into court and compelled to (§16 (b) 

2, Fiduciaries Act 1917, 20 P.S. 553). (See also $15 (k) and (1) (20 P.S. 531-532).) 

170-G. Sales for Payment of Legacies. 

The Fiduciaries Act of 1917 P.L. 447, by §§24 to 26 (20 P.S. 

651 to 654 and 671 to 677) provides a procedure in the

Orphans' Court for collection of legacies by sale of decedent's real estate charged therewith as well as proceedings by which the residuary estate may be discharged from annuities and legacies payable in the future. This is done by petition of the legatee citing into court the fiduciary, the devisee or heir and the present owner of the real estate charged with the payment of the legacy. (Beyers Estate 20 D. & C. 128-1933.)

Whereupon the court is empowered to make a decree directing the devisee, heir or owner to pay the amount of such legacy and interest then due, within the time fixed. The decree made, will provide that in case such payment is not made within the time fixed, the fiduciary or a trustee appointed by the court will sell the real estate in question, at public sale after notice in the manner provided by the act, or so much thereof as may be necessary to pay the sum due. The proceeds of the sale are then distributed under direction of the 1 It should be noted that if the sale is made and confirmed within the year all creditors, whether they commenced suit or not within the year, are entitled to participate in the proceeds even though the account is not filed until after the year has expired (Weidner's Est. 40 D. & C. 407—1940).

Court as in the case of judicial sales, to the persons entitled thereto. The Act of April 14, 1931 P.L. 32 (20 P.S. 652), authorizes the court to direct a private sale, if in the opinion of the court, a better price could be so obtained than by public sale. See Remick's Orphans' Court Practice, §215 et sec. for procedure. 

170-H. Sales by Order of Court Where Power to Sell Omits to Specify the Person to Exercise It. 

Sometimes a will directs real estate to be sold but omits to specify the person by name or description authorized to exercise the power. In such case the power of sale is "deemed to have been given to the executors" (§28 (c) Fiduciaries Act of 1917; 20 P.S. 713), but, continues the Act, "such power, authority or direction shall be carried into effect by them only under control and direction of the Orphans' Court having jurisdiction of their accounts and after entry of security if the Court so directs". As to the nature, extent and character of the Orphans' Court control and supervision see Dundas's 

Appeal 64 Pa. 325-1870; Rose's Estate 20 D.R. 25-1910, 38 

Pa. C.C. 267-1910; Hancock Estate, 9 D.R. 231, 28 Pa. C.C. 

592-1900. This section applies where a testatrix in her will directed her real estate to be sold without specifying who should sell it (Beecher's Est. 31 Lanc. 26-1913). But where the real and personal estate was so blended by a testatrix as to work a conversion it was held no decree of the Orphans' Court was necessary to convey title (Himber v. Unks, 71 

Pitts. L.J. 632-1923). When an order of the Orphans' 

Court is made under this section it is to be regarded as a judicial sale and as such operates to divest the judgment on a municipal claim where the proceeds were sufficient to pay the judgment and costs (New Castle v. Whaley's Heirs 102 

Pa. Super. Ct. 492—1931). 

170-1. Fiduciary's Power and Authority Is Generally Exer cisable by the Successor.

Sometimes an executor designated by will, refuses to act and renounces his right to do so. Sometimes he dies before

$170-I 

the testator and the testator neglects to fill his place and sometimes indeed, a testator fails to name an executor. In all such cases the Register of Wills is authorized to appoint an administrator cum testamento annexo (i.e., administrator with the will annexed), usually abbreviated c.t.a., (§3 (a) 

Fiduciaries Act, June 7, 1917, P.L. 447; 20 P.S. 349). In cases where an executor dies after he has qualified and has only partly administered the estate or where assets not accounted for are afterwards discovered which require administration and the executor is dead, or has been discharged, an administrator de bonis non, cum testamento annexo, (usually abbreviated d.b.n.c.t.a.), may be appointed to complete the settlement of the affairs of the estate; (see §3 (b) Fiduciaries 

Act 1917 June 7 P.L. 447; 20 P.S. 350).

The question at once arises, whether these successors in office have the same power and authority to sell real estate as may have been conferred on the original executor. It is settled that they do. §3 (d) of the Fiduciaries Act 1917 (20 

P.S. 352), provides all and singular the powers, duties and liabilities of the executors are hereby extended to administrators with the will annexed. The Supreme Court in 

Kemerer admrx. v. Johnston, (318 Pa. 526-1935), has construed this provision to mean "whenever power is given to executors to sell real estate, with view to distribute the proceeds among legatees, the power belongs to them virtute officci, and may be exercised by an administrator c.t.a. This is so whether there be an absolute direction, so as to work a conversion or power be discretionary, and whether the distribution is to be immediate, or upon the expiration of a certain time or upon the uncertain contingency of life or lives." 

Trustees. With regard to trustees the rule is much the same. Provision is made by the Fiduciaries Act of 1917, §56 (a) (20 P.S. 971) and §56 (b), (c), (20 P.S. 972 and 973), to fill vacancies either in one of several trustees or all. These sections specifically provide that the trustee or trustees so appointed shall have the same power and interest over and in the property in trust as the trustee in whose stead he or they

§170-I 

419 

WILLS. 

shall have been appointed. While it may be regarded as settled, that in general the succeeding trustee has the right to exercise the powers given by the will to his predecessor, yet where the plain intent of the will is that the power granted to a named fiduciary was so far personal, as to make it clear that the testator was relying upon the peculiar ability and aptitude of the named fiduciary, then in such case the power has been held to be not exercisable by the successor in office. 

See for example Strite v. Wolfe, (268 Pa. 221—1920); Crozer v. Green, (298 Pa. 438-1938); Woodward's Estate (8 Phila. 

211-1871); Wilson v. Pennock, (27 Pa. 238—1856).

Surviving Executors and Trustees are by $28 (d) of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917 as amended by the Act of May 11, 1939, P.L. 120 (20 P.S. 714 anno.) vested with full authority to execute the powers and duties as fully and as amply as if all the executors or trustees who renounced, resigned or died, had joined therein, provided a testator has not otherwise directed.

171. Searches; Necessity for.

By searches we mean the examination of the title of vendor or prospective mortgagor in order to ascertain whether it is good, clear and free of encumbrance. The ability to make a satisfactory search and brief of title was formerly one of the most essential requirements of a good conveyancer. In 

Philadelphia and the larger cities of the State of Pennsylvania few conveyancers nowadays search the title themselves. Instead, it is done by the title insurance companies (See $200

§172  

infra.), who make a special business of searches which they insure or guarantee. In the smaller towns and rural regions of the State, however, considerable title searching is still done by the conveyancers, so that it is deemed well to devote a chapter to explaining the method of searching. 

172. How Records Are Indexed. 

First, a word as to the arrangement of the indexes which must be examined in searching title. The recorder of deeds' office is located at the county seat and contains, besides the deed books, mortgage books, etc., a series of books termed indexes. Deed indexes, mortgage indexes, miscellaneous indexes, charter indexes, etc. Some of the indexes vary in the different counties. Those mentioned in this chapter refer to 

Philadelphia County. If searching in another county the title searcher will do well to consult the Recorder or his deputy, who will be found courteous and willing to give full information as to what indexes are maintained, and where the matter searched for is likely to be found. 

Taking the deed index as an example, we find that deeds are indexed twice, once under the name of the grantor, called the "direct" or "grantor index", and once under the name of the grantee, called the "ad sectum," or "grantee" index. The indexing is ingenious and is done in this way. There is for the grantor's index one book for each letter of the alphabet, and each book is divided into twenty-six subdivisions, each subdivision lettered in alphabetical order, beginning with the letter A. The initial letter of the grantor's surname fixes the book in which it is to be found, and the initial letter of the Christian name fixes the subdivision of that book in which the name is to be found. Thus, in order to find the name 

Andrew Gallagher, you take down index book "G" and turn to the part under the letter "A". In that part you will find every person's name whose last name begins with "G" and first name with "A". Look through these names until you come to the name you seek. Having found the name you will see the following entry:

§423

Date. 

Book. 

Page. 

Grantor. Grantee. 

June 20 71 32 

Gallagher Andrew P. F. Smith

The first column is the date, being the year, month and day when the deed was recorded. Then follows the book, number and page. In Philadelphia, by custom, the recorder of deeds' books are designated by the intial letters of the recorder's name. Thus, all deeds recorded during the term of the recorder, Hon. Ernest L. Tustin, are recorded in books bearing the letters E. L. T. Next follows the name of the grantor, surname first, then the Christian name. Finally, the name of the grantee. The arrangement of the grantee index is practically the same, though, of course, the grantee's name would appear before the grantor's as follows:
