All of the modern indexes, both mortgagor and mortgagee as well as judgment indexes of the prothonotary's office follow this arrangement.

In making searches, care should be taken to note, not only the names searched against, but also any that might be re-

§173 

garded as reasonably similar thereto. Thus, where a tax was assessed and a lien was filed against John Maddox owner, although the owner held title under the name of Maddock, which was his correct name, the claim was held to be a valid one, even against an intervening grantee, the court saying, "No careful conveyancer could have been mislead by the slight difference in names. A reference to the claim would have disclosed the property and led to inquiry." (Lower 

Merion Twshp. v. Buckley, 21 D.R. 1029-1912). But in another case where a tax lien was improperly filed and indexed as 'Albert J. Foehl' instead of 'J. Albert Foehl', which was the name given in the deed by which he took title, it was stricken off on petition by an innocent purchaser for value without notice (Lancaster v. Foehl 21 D.R. 858-1905); and in Arch St. B. & L. Assn. v. Sook, (14 D. & C. 794-1931), omission of a middle initial in the record of a judgment was held to be fatal to the lien of such judgment on real estate, since an examination of the record would fail to disclose the identity of the judgment debtor with the owner of the land searched against. But the contrary was held where the name was uncommon (Coral Gables Inc. v. Kerl 334 Pa. 441-1939; 

See also Everett Bank v. Hall 138 Pa. Super. Ct. 79-1939).

What therefore, is a sufficient similarity in names to charge a person with notice is by no means clear, though it seems that where there is a record of an instrument, which if examined, would disclose the identity, omission of or perhaps a wrong middle initial, would not void the indexing. Title Companies customarily list all names found in the judgment index similar to that searched against and then take an affidavit from the party concerned that he is not any of the defendants in the judgment so certified. 

173. Kinds of Searches.

At the outset it should be remembered that a title may be bad because of its doubtful origin, as where a man purports to convey title to land which he never owned. On the other hand, while it may be without defect as far as derivation and

§425 

SEARCHES. 

origin is concerned, it may still be bad because it is so encumbered by mortgages and other liens as to be practically valueless. Thus searches are naturally divided into two kinds or classes. A conveyance search, which is a search to ascertain the sources from which a grantor derived his title, and an encumbrance search made to ascertain whether a title is subject to any mortgages, judgments or other liens. 

The word lien, says Judge Stewart, in Ziegler v. Weil, (21 D.R. 809, 810-1912), is a French word and originally signified a string, tie or bond, and in the metaphorical sense, in which the law uses it, it signifies such hold or claim on a thing for the satisfaction of a debt, duty or demand as that it cannot be taken away until the same be satisfied or paid. 

174. Conveyance Searches.

Conveyance searches are made at the recorder of deeds office by examination of the grantor and grantee index. In 

Pennsylvania the source of all title is a grant by William Penn, or, latterly, the State. Usually the recital in the deeds will provide a rapid method of reaching the source of title and making a rough brief without the aid of the index. 

Should a recital, however, be missing or incomplete, recourse must be had to the index to supply the missing link. 

After ascertaining the source of title to be proper, search for adverse conveyances against every person whose name appears in the chain of title from a time prior to his acquisition of title until six months after the recording of the deed, as the vendor may have conveyed to another purchaser by deed executed outside of this State. Search also for conveyances made by every one who has held title, because the conveyance of a parcel of a larger tract, of which the lot being searched was once a part, may have imposed restrictions or easements running with the land on the part retained (see 

Finley v. Glenn 303 Pa. 131-1931). Search against the present owner from the time he acquired title to date. The search should not only be made against the owners of the fee but against all having an interest therein in a representative

§175 

capacity, or by reason of having a power of sale, such as executors, administrators, trustees, assignees, receivers, guardians, committee of lunatics, etc.

Search now in the office of the courts of common pleas for possible sheriff's sales, by which the owner may have lost title. Since 1905 (Act of Apr. 22, 1905, P.L. 265 §6; 12 P.S. 

2548), however, sheriff's sales are now recorded in the recorder of deeds office, indexed both under name of grantee and the person whose title was divested by the sale. Search also at the office of the clerk of the United States Courts for sales by the United States marshal, and for possible bankruptcy of owner.

Searches of title to ground rents are made as in the case of other conveyance searches, and since they are real estate they must be searched also for encumbrances and liens. 

175. Search at Registry Bureau.

In Philadelphia, by Act of March 14, 1865 P.L. 320 $4 

(53 P.S. 4763), all deeds must be registered before being recorded. This is done at the registry bureau and forms an additional means of verifying the title of a vendor. Width of streets and how opened can be ascertained here. Search should, therefore, be made at the registry bureau which is established in Philadelphia, and since 1899, in all counties having a population over 500,000, and since 1901 in all cities of the third class. In Philadelphia, the registry bureau is a department of the city survey bureau. 

It seems that the duty of seeing that transfers of real estate are properly registered is imposed upon purchasers under the 

Act of March 29, 1867, P.L. 600 $1 (53 P.S. 4767). Thus notice of the filing of a municipal claim given to the registered owner, is sufficient notice, although the property had been conveyed to another, where such deed was not registered, and even though the mistake was that of the Registry Bureau itself (Phila. v. Sulger, 23 D.R. 321-1914). The Act of April 

22, 1915 P.L. 172 (53 P.S. 8721 et seq.), relates to registration in Cities of the second class, and the Act of May 14, 1915 P.L.

§427 

SEARCHES. 

489 now repealed but supplied by Act of May 22, 1933 P.L. 853 §408 (72 P.S. 5020-408), relates to registrations in townships of the first class. Under the Act of March 29, 1867 P.L. 600 

(53 P.S. 4767), relating to the registering of deeds in Philadelphia, it is the duty of a devisee under a will as well as an allottee in partition, to present his deed or title papers, and see that his title is properly registered. 

176. Encumbrance Search, (Mortgages).

Encumbrances are of two kinds: (1) such as affect the title, and (2) such as affect only the physical condition of the property. (Memmert v. McKeen 112 Pa. 315-1886). Every right or interest in the land which may subsist in third persons to the diminution of the value of the land, but consistent with the passing of the fee by the conveyance may be regarded as an encumbrance (Lafferty v. Milligan 165 Pa. 534–1895).

The most common encumbrances are the liens of mortgages, judgments, taxes and municipal assessments (Taylor v. Allen 

60 Pa. Super. Ct. 503-1915).

Having found the title to be without defect the next step is to see if it is encumbered. Search first for possible mortgages.

Search for mortgages is made at the recorder of deeds' office. The mortgages are indexed in a separate index called the mortgage index. Search should be made in this index as follows: 

Search in the mortgage index against every name in the chain of title back to the year of 1830 and back of that date until you meet with a sheriff's sale; this because prior to that date the Act of April 6, 1830 P.L. 293, a sheriff's sale discharged mortgages.

Most Title Companies in this State have agreed among themselves to practically ignore unsatisfied mortgages recorded prior to 1800 in Philadelphia, and prior to 1815 in the counties of Montgomery, Delaware, Buck and Chester.

The same course might well be pursued in every other county of the state where the prevalent practice is to insist on the

§176  

satisfaction of such ancient mortgages by court proceedings, before the conveyancer will approve the title. The risk of such a mortgage being still enforceable is after all negligible, the only question being whether it would make the title unmarketable. It seems strange that this doubt has not heretofore been settled by appropriate legislation, and the land owners all over the state thereby saved thousands of dollars in costs of court proceedings to satisfy these few old mortgages. 

After the Act of 1830, if there were no other liens ahead of the mortgage, except other mortgages, ground rents, or purchase money due the Commonwealth, the mortgage would not be discharged by any sheriff's sale made under a writ of vend. ex.

This was afterward extended to sheriff sales under any writ of execution by the Act of April 16, 1845 P.L. 488 (21 P.S. 653).

There was also special legislation applying only to Philadelphia County, by which mortgages on real estate situate in that County, were protected from discharge, even where there were tax liens duly registered ahead of the mortgage and still in force when the sheriff's sale took place. These local acts were held, in the case of Rhein Bldg. & Loan Assn. v. Lea, (100 Pa. 210-1882), to be still in force despite the general act of March 23, 1867 P.L. 43, which protected mortgages from discharge "by any judicial or other sale whatsoever whether decree of any

Orphans' Court or other Court, or of any writ of execution, or otherwise howsoever," whenever the mortgage had no liens ahead of it except "other mortgages, ground rents, purchase money due the Commonwealth, taxes ・・・ assessments and municipal claims whose lien though afterwards accruing has by law priority, etc." by virtue of any

This Act, by its express provisions, would not apply to mortgages on unseated lands,¹ or tax sales of such lands: and this exception to the immunity from discharge of mortgages still obtains. Mortgages on unseated lands are not protected from discharge by any judicial sale. 

1 See $100(a) page 259 for definition of "unseated" lands.

SEARCHES. 

The Act of 1867 was repealed by the Act of March 10, 1870 (P.L. 37) so far as it exempted mortgages from discharge by 

Orphans' Court sales; but even as to such sales the exemption from discharge was still kept in force as to Philadelphia, Venango and Perry Counties by express exception in the

Act of 1870. 

The Act of March 22, 1887 (P.L. 6), however, reenacted the provisions of the Act of 1867, thereby repealing the Act of 1870, and reinstating the exemption, all over the State, of mortgages from discharge by Orphans' Court sales, where there was no other lien ahead of the mortgage except the ones expressly designated as harmless by the said Act of 1867.

The result of this legislation, so far as Orphans' Court sales are concerned, is as follows: (1) Prior to 1867 Orphans' Court sales all over the State discharged any mortgage; (2) From 1867 to 1870, Orphans' Court sales all over the

State did not discharge any mortgage which had ahead of it no other liens excepting those expressly designated in the 

Act of 1867; (3) Between 1870 and 1887, all mortgages were discharged by such a sale, held anywhere in the State, except in Philadelphia, Perry and Venango Counties. (4) After March 22, 1887, the law became again the same as to such sales as it had been under the Act of 1867, as above indicated; and this still remains the law today, excepting where an Orphans' Court sale is made expressly clear of a mortgage, by consent of the mortgagee, as provided by §16 (0) 

of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917 (20 P.S. 574). 

After 1887 the following Acts were passed, dealing with the preservation of mortgages from discharge: 

The Act of May 19, 1893 (P.L. 110) which provided for a sale by the Orphans' Court clear of mortgages, when the mortgagee consents thereto in writing. 

The Act of May 8, 1901, (P.L. 141) which clarified and

§176  

amplified the prior Acts, by providing, in effect, that the only prior tax or municipal claim which would subject the mortgage on seated lands to discharge by any kind of a sale under legal process, was such as had, prior to the date of the mortgage, been duly entered as a lien in the local County Prothonotary's office. This Act was apparently never repealed or altered by any later Act until the passage of the Act of May 21, 1913 (P.L. 285), which provided for sales being made by County Treasurers of seated lands "in the same manner, and under the same conditions and with the same effect, as unseated lands are now sold by such Treasurer for unpaid County Taxes. 

This Act was amended in some minor detail by the Act of June 1, 1915 (P.L. 660); but the net result of this legislation was to permit County Treasurers to sell even seated lands for taxes, with the same effect as if the lands were unseated, which, of course, made the sale one which would discharge mortgages.

Then came the Municipal Claim Act of May 16, 1923 (P.L. 

207, 53 P.S. 2051), §31 of which exempted mortgages from discharge by any ordinary tax or municipal claim sale, if the mortgage was recorded before any tax had accrued, except for the current year, or before the actual doing of the work for which a municipal claim was filed, unless there was a lien, prior to the mortgage, which was also thereby discharged. 

The section then goes on to provide that, if any such sale would not produce enough to pay all taxes and municipal claims the sale might be postponed, and the plaintiff might file a petition, and produce a search showing all "the taxes, municipal claims, mortgages, ground rents, or other charges on" the land, and a rule would then be granted upon all of the interested parties to show why the property should not be sold clear of the said mortgages, etc. The Court, after proof of a lawful service of the rule (which a service, as provided for by the Act, does not need to be personal service), may then order a sale, clear of mortgages and other charges, etc.

$431 

SEARCHES. 

The result of these last three Acts was to take away completely the exemption of mortgages from discharge, in connection with tax sales, either conducted by a County Treasurer, or under the provisions of $31 of the Act of 1923, and to that extent the exemption provisions of the Act of 1901 were repealed. This would appear to have been the reason for the re-enactment, by the passage of the Act of April 30, 1929 (P.L. 874, 21 P.S. 651), of the provisions of the Act of 

1901, in identical language, with the addition of a proviso making clear that the law should still remain as theretofore, that a sale under a prior ground rent or mortgage should discharge a later mortgage; and that sales made by the Orphans' 

Court, with the consent of a mortgagee, clear of such mortgage, would discharge the same.

This Act of 1929 was generally supposed to have protected mortgages, which had no liens ahead of them excepting those expressly designated in the Act, from being discharged by any tax sale, including one made under the provisions of §31 of the Act of 1923, in view of the fact that §2 of the Act of 1929 expressly repealed all "Acts or parts of Acts . . . appertaining to the subject matter covered by this Act and inconsistent herewith." The Supreme Court, however, held otherwise in the case of Erie v. A Piece of Land, (339 Pa. 3211940), where it was definitely decided that $31 of the Act of 1923 was still fully in force, notwithstanding the Act of 1929, and that a sale for taxes made under §31 of the Act of 1923, discharged a prior mortgage, which was created before the Act of 1923 went into effect, and which was preceded by no tax liens whatever, nor by any other prior lien which would subject it to discharge under the provisions of the Act of 1929.

The result of this decision is that, no matter how clear the title is of taxes, municipal claims, or other liens, when a mortgage is recorded, it will nevertheless be susceptible to discharge by a sale for future tax and municipal claims if proceeded on under $31. 

Whether a mortgage on seated lands is protected from dis-

charge on a treasurer's tax sale, held under the Act of 1913 and its supplements, is rendered uncertain by the City of Erie case, as the Act of 1929 is given only a passing reference in the Court's opinion in that case. 

Of course, in searching for mortgages against persons in the chain of title you need only search against any one of them from the time he conveyed title back to the time he took title. Where the present owner against whom the search is being made took title within sixty days there is a possibility that a purchase money mortgage may be recorded later, for a purchase mortgage had sixty days, (now thirty days) to be recorded in $88 of this book. In such case the declaration of the present owner must be secured as well as of his immediate grantor that no purchase money mortgage formed part of the consideration.

The Act of April 27, 1927 P.L. 440 §1 (21 P.S. 622) ex pressly provides for a limit of thirty days from the date of a purchase money mortgage, within which it must be recorded in order that its lien may date back to its delivery; and it also defines a purchase money mortgage as one given by the purchaser to seller. When given to some person other than the seller, it is not a purchase money mortgage, even though the proceeds are paid over by the mortgagor to the seller as part of the purchase money due him (Martin's Estate 135 Pa.

Super. Ct. 136-1939; see $88 of this book where the Act of 

1927 and the Act of 1915 which it supplies are more fully discussed).

All assignments of mortgages and any "sci. fa." proceedings commenced thereon will be found noted on the margin of the mortgage record in the mortgage books as required by the Act of April 3, 1860 (P.L. 630, §1, 21 P.S. 796). 

176-A. Encumbrance Search, (Inheritance Taxes).

As hereinbefore indicated in $170-C (Supra.), inheritance taxes, both State and Federal, are liens, being so declared by Acts of Legislature and of Congress respectively.

§176A 

433 

SEARCHES. 

(a) Federal Inheritance Tax. 

(1) Lien of Federal Inheritance Tax. The Act of Congress (53 Stat. 128; 26 U. S. C. A., 1940 ed., §827) relating to 

Federal Inheritance Taxes, provides that the tax "shall be a lien for ten years upon the gross estate of the decedent; except that such part of the gross estate as is used for the payment of charges against the estate, and the expenses of administration", duly allowed by court, "shall be divested of such lien." The ten years runs from decedent's death.

Revised Statutes, §3186 (a) (26 U.S.C.A. 1940 ed. $3670) 

provides generally for a lien of "any tax" upon all the property, real and personal, of any person liable for the same. 

§3186 (b) (26 U.S.C.A. 1940 ed. §3672) however, expressly provides that the lien given by it "shall not be valid, as against any mortgagee purchaser or judgment creditor, until notice thereof has been filed .. in accordance with the law of the State . . . in which the property is situated" whenever there is a State law providing for such filing; and if there be no such State law then it should be filed with the Clerk of the United States District Court for the appropriate district. There is such a statute in Pennsylvania, to wit, the 

Act of May 1, 1929 P.L. 1215, 74 P.S. 141 et seq., which expressly provides for the filing of such liens in the office of the Prothonotary of the County where the real estate subject to the lien is situated, in a separate file headed "Federal Tax 

Lien Notices", and also for a Federal Tax Lien Index show ing the name and residence of the tax payer, date of filing, etc. 

§3186 would seem, from its broad general language, to apply to the lien of inheritance taxes, equally with that of any other tax, so that the lien would be invalid against mortgagee, purchaser, etc. unless notice of such lien had previously been filed in the proper county prothonotary's office. But according to a ruling of the General Counsel for the Treasury Department, 

(Internal Revenue Cumulative Bulletin VII-2, page 355, reg. 

70 art. 88, G.C.M. 2663 of 1928) the lien of an inheritance tax, imposed by the above cited Act of Congress, is "a lien entirely separate and distinct from that imposed by $3186,

Revised Statutes, as amended by the Revised Act of 1928 and is not subject to the provisions of the latter section relative to the filing of notice of the lien." (2) Method of Search for Same. There is no provision for the issuance by the Department of Internal Revenue of a search showing whether the inheritance tax has been paid on any item of decedent's real estate, and there are no records of same which are open to inspection. The Commissioner of 

Internal Revenue may however with approval of the Secretary of the Treasury, release any or all of decedent's estate from this lien (see this sec. subdiv. 3 infra.). 

Therefore, where the ten year limitation period has not expired since the death of any decedent, whose estate was large enough to be subject to a United States Inheritance Tax, if a release cannot be secured, the only safe method to pursue is as follows: 

(1) Search the records of the United States District Court for any such notices filed against such estate. (2) Search for same in Prothonotary's office of proper county. (3) Insist on production by the decedent's personal representatives of a copy of the return made by them to the Collector of the estate assets, showing the inclusion therein of the real estate in question, and the original receipt showing payment in full of the tax subsequently assessed thereon. (3) Release or Discharge of the Lien. There is one way in which an inheritance tax lien can be disposed of as to a piece of decedent's real estate, without actual payment of the same, and that is by means of a certificate of release, issued under the provisions of the above cited Federal Inheritance Tax Acts (26 U.S.C.A. 1940 ed. §827 (a)) and also provided for in the general revenue act (Rev. Stats. $3186 (c) 26 U.S.C.A. §§3673 and 3674) where the tax is sufficiently otherwise provided for. (See also 170-C, (b) of this book.)

There is also one way by which a federal inheritance tax

§176A 

435 

SEARCHES. 

lien (or any other federal tax lien) may be discharged, and that is by a judicial sale of the property under a lien which is prior to that of the United States, or, with the consent of the United States, even though the lien in suit be junior to that of the United States.

This is provided for by the Act of Congress, March 4, 1931, C. 515, 46 Stat. 1528 and supplements; (28 U.S.C.A. §901 etc.), which provides a procedure by which federal liens may be divested. In brief, the Act provides that the United States may be made a party to any suit which may be brought in a Federal Court, or "in any State Court having jurisdiction of the subject matter for the foreclosure of a mortgage or other lien upon real estate." $2 (28 U.S.C.A. §902), provides how service should be made and gives the United States 60 days to appear, answer, plead or demur. §4 (28 U.S.C.A. §904), provides "except as herein otherwise provided, a judicial sale made in pursuance of a judgment in such a suit shall have the same effect respecting the discharge of property from liens and encumbrances held by the United States, as may be provided with respect to such matters by the law of the state in which the land is situated, provided that a sale to satisfy a lien inferior to one of the United States shall be made subject to and without disturbing the lien of the United States, unless the United States by its attorney, consents that the property may be sold free of its mortgage or lien and the proceeds divided as the parties may be entitled; and provided further that where a sale is made to satisfy a lien prior to that of the United States, the United States shall have one year, from the date of the sale, within which to redeem.

This section also provides that in any case where the debt owing the United States is due, the United States may ask, by way of affirmative relief, for the foreclosure of its own lien or mortgage and in any case, where the property is sold to satisfy a first mortgage or first lien held by the United States, the United States may bid at the sale, such sum not exceeding the amount of its claim with expenses of sale, as may be directed by the Chief of the Department Bureau or other

Agency of the United States, which has charge of the administration of the law in respect of which the claim of the United 

States arises. 

§5 (28 U.S.C.A. §905), with respect to junior liens provides, "if any person shall have a lien upon any real or personal property, newly filed of record in the jurisdiction in which the property is located, and a junior lien (other than a lien for any tax) in favor of the United States, attaches to such property, such person may make a written request to the officer of the United States charged with the administration of laws in respect of which the lien of the United States arises, to have the same extinguished. If, after appropriate investigation, it appears that the proceeds from the sale of the property would be insufficient to satisfy, in whole or in part the lien of the United States, or the claim of the United States had been satisfied, or by lapse of time or otherwise has become unenforceable, such officer shall report to the Comptroller General, who thereupon may issue a certificate of release, which shall operate to release the property from such lien. The final section, §6, 28 U.S.C.A. §903, exempts the United States from any judgment for costs or other judgment for money which might be rendered in such proceeding. 

Prior to this Act such proceeding was impossible by reason of the well settled rule that no suit could ever be brought against the United States, or the United States named as a party without congressional consent, or except in accordance with governing Acts of Congress. If the United States is not made a party defendant, the federal lien would not be discharged even though the fund raised by the sale is sufficient to liquidate the federal lien. So also if the sale is made under another lien, junior in time of entry to the federal lien, the latter would not be disturbed, unless the United States consents to the property being sold free and clear of such federal lien. Where the sale is made on a prior lien, the junior federal lien will be paid out of the proceeds so far as they are able to respond, if the United States has been made a party defendant; and the United States has one year from

§176A 

437 

SEARCHES. 

the date of the sale to redeem the property if it so desires; but its lien is wholly discharged by the sale. (b). State Inheritance Tax. 

(1) Lien of Pennsylvania Inheritance Tax. The lien of this tax arises, as to real estate located in Pennsylvania, no matter where the decedent was domiciled or where his will was probated. It arises at the decedent's death and remains a lien until paid; but its lien is limited to the property chargeable therewith, and can therefore be separately assessed and paid on any particular piece of real estate. The Act of June 

20, 1919 (P.L. 521) §39 as amended by the Act of July 14, 1936, 1st Ex. sess. (P.L. 44 §3) expressly provides that suit must be brought by the State to recover the tax, within five years from the time it becomes due, or the tax will cease to be a lien as against any purchaser. The Act, however, expressly permits the Department of Revenue, within that five years, to file in the Office of the Prothonotary of the County where the real estate is located, a certificate of non-payment, which shall be indexed in the judgment index in the decedent's name, and shall keep the lien alive for five years from such filing; and within such additional five years another such certificate may be filed with like effect.

It has been held that even if the lien is not preserved by filing the certificate of non-payment within the 5 year periods the Commonwealth may file its certificate and re-establish its lien as against real estate still held by the heirs or devisees but not against such as has been bona fide conveyed away to third parties nor it would seem as against intervening encumbrancers. (Comm. v. Kirk, 39 D. & C., 276—1939). $1401 of the Fiscal Code (Act of April 9, 1929, P.L. 343 

72 P.S. 1401) originally provided that all State taxes shall be a first lien on the real estate of the person against whom they are charged, and should be first paid out of the proceeds of any judicial sale; but it was held that this would not give priority to an inheritance tax, as against a prior mortgage resting on the property when decedent died, and the mort-

gage was entitled to be first paid out of the proceeds of a foreclosure sale under such mortgage. (Scranton-Lackawanna Trust Company v. same Company, Guardian, 310 Pa. 

125, 1934). It seems implied from this case that a foreclosure sale of a decedent's real estate, under a mortgage given by a predecessor in title to decedent, will discharge the lien of an inheritance tax assessed against such real estate; as the opinion (p. 128) speaks of the tax as being "restricted to the owner's equity of redemption", and of the lien of the tax on this equity as ceasing when, by reason of the foreclosure, that equity "no longer exists." It had been held otherwise by the Common Pleas of Berks County in connection with a sale under an execution for a debt owing (apparently) by the decedent, which the court held did not discharge an inheritance tax lien, even though the sale produced a fund sufficient to pay the same. (Secretary of Rev. v. Goelz, 25 Berks 289, 1933). §1401 of the Fiscal Code was, however, amended by the Act of June 11, 1935 (P.L. 303 Act No. 138 §1; 72 P.S. 1401 ann.) 

so as to expressly provide for the discharge of any State tax or public account imposed or "settled against any corporation, association, or person", by any judicial sale "where the lien of a ground rent, mortgage or other lien created by or entered against a predecessor in title to such corporation, association or person is discharged" by such sale. The amending section further provides that such mortgage or other lien shall have priority of payment out of the proceeds of such sale.

The upshot of the above is that unless there be such a prior lien given by or entered against a "predecessor in title" to the devisee of the real estate, which is itself discharged by the judicial sale held after the decedent's death, the inheritance taxes will not be discharged thereby. 

(2) Method of Search for State Inheritance Tax. 

Payment of the tax on a Pennsylvania decedent's estate is made through the office of the Register of Wills of the

§439 

SEARCHES. 

County where the will is probated, and in case of a foreign decedent, settlement and payment of the tax is made directly to the Revenue Department at Harrisburg. In these two offices only can searches be made to ascertain payment of the tax; and of course a search of the judgment index for suits or judgments against the decedent will turn up any suit commenced, or certificate filed, by the Commonwealth for such taxes.

The production of an inheritance tax receipt will not necessarily prove payment of the tax on any particular piece of real estate, without additional proof that such real estate was included in the return made to the taxing authorities and also in the assessment of the tax itself for which the receipt was given. The receipt itself does not usually disclose the items covered by the payment. 

177. Encumbrance Search, (Judgment Liens). 

(a) Nature and Extent of Judgment Liens. 

Having ascertained the title to be good and marketable and free from any mortgage liens it is necessary to prosecute a further search in order to ascertain whether there are any judgment liens against the property. 

A judgment is a decree of a court of competent jurisdiction determining that the one person is indebted to another in the amount stated. The party in whose favor a judgment is rendered can, if it is not paid, proceed to sell the other's property. A judgment by law (Act of March 21, 1772, 1

Sm. L. 389, §2), is a lien against all of the real estate of the person against whom it is entered from the time of its entry. 

It is not a lien against personal property, but against real estate only. Its lien binds any freehold estate in land, whether a fee, life estate (Hoffman's Estate, 2 Pears. 3171878), or curtesy¹ (Beard v. Dietz, 1 Watts 309-1833), whether absolute or in common. It binds a ground rent but not a leasehold, which is a chattel (Krause's Appeal, 2 Whart. 

397-1837), nor a mortgage, which is also personal property. 

1 But not during the lifetime of wife since Act of 1863. See supra. $139 (a) page 353 of this book.

§177 (a)  

1 A judgment binds all of defendant's real property and interests therein unless it be restricted to a particular piece of real estate by agreement filed of record, signed by the party in whose favor it is rendered (Hendrick v. Thomas, 106 Pa. 

327-1884). A restricted judgment, when revived, becomes a lien on all the real estate of the defendant as of the date of the judgment of revival, notwithstanding the restriction of the original judgment (McMurray v. Hopper, 43 Pa. 468-1862). 

So, too, the lien of a judgment may be released as to a particular part of the defendant's real estate, without affecting its lien against the rest (Kirk's App., 87 Pa. 243-1878). It is only a lien upon the interest in real estate owned by the defendant at the time of its entry and does ot affect real estate conveyed before its entry (Bitting's App., 17 Pa. 211-1851), or acquired thereafter (Kemmerer v. Tool, 78 Pa. 147-1875). 

To make it a lien on after acquired real estate, a sci. fa. must be issued to revive it as of a later date; and under the Act of 

June 12, 1931, P.L. 506, 12 P.S. 876, the sci. fa. to revive it creates immediately a new lien on the after acquired real estate.

In Philadelphia County, by a local Act, a judgment may be made a lien on after acquired real estate by issuing execution against such after acquired real estate, and causing a levy thereon to be certified to the Prothonotary to index the same in the judgment index, whereupon it becomes "a lien like any other judgment" (Act of April 20, 1853, P.L. 610 §9, 12 P.S. 

$2293); and the levy itself must be so indexed (Ross & Co.'s 

App., 106 Pa. 82-1884, which case, however, was decided under a different Act, that of April 22, 1856, P.L. 532 §3, 17 

P.S. 1922).

Though a judgment is not a lien on after acquired real estate without the issuance of a sci. fa. to revive the same, it has been held, that, even without such a sci. fa., a sale under an execution levied on such real estate, will pass a good title, if the defendant does not raise objection until after the sale (Bryan v. Jones & L. Steel Co., 238 Pa. 191-1913).

§177(b) 441 

SEARCHES. 

(b) Duration and Revival of Judgment Liens. 

A judgment is a lien from the date of its entry. If entered on a money verdict, it relates back in lien to the date of the verdict. The verdict itself must be indexed in the judgment index (Act of March 23, 1877, P.L. 34, 12 P.S. 861); and its lien is limited to five years (Fuellhart v. Thompson, 11 Pa. 

Super. Ct. 273-1899). But the holder of a verdict is not within the protection of the recording acts as against an unrecorded deed until judgment is actually entered on the verdict (Irwin v. Zahniser, 21 Erie, 120-1940).

The Act of March 26, 1827, (supra.) provided that no judgments are the following: Act of April 4, 1798, 3 Sm. L. 331, 

§§2 and 3, (12 P.S. §§864 and 869); Act of March 26, 1827, 

P.L. 129, §1, as amended by the Act of June 1, 1887, P.L. 289, (12 P.S. 868); and Act of April 16, 1849, P.L. 663, 

§8, (12 P.S. 872). 

$2 of the Act of 1798 provided, in substance, that no judgment should continue a lien on the defendant's real estate for more than five years, unless the plaintiff should, within that period, issue a scire facias to revive the same. $3 of the 

Act required the sci. fa. to be served on "the terre-tenants or persons occupying the real estate", as well as on the defendant and his grantees, and for the entry of a judgment of revival which would continue the lien for another five years, and so on.

The Act of March 26, 1827, (supra.) provided that no judgment should continue a lien for more than five years from its entry or revival, unless revived within that period, by agreement of the parties and terre-tenants, or the issuance of a sci. fa. within that period, in either of which events the lien of the judgment would be revived for another five years therefrom. 

Let us consider first the effect of these two Acts in relation to the lien of a judgment as against the original defendant and his heirs or devisees. 

(1) Lien of Judgment Against the Original Defendant, and his Heirs or Devisees. Under the law as it stood prior to the 

Act of 1798, a judgment was a lien upon the defendant's land

§177(b)1 

for an indefinite period. "Thus stood the law in Pennsylvania until the Statute of 1798 restrained the lien of a judgment to a period of five years; but only in favor of purchasers from the debtor, and judgment creditors in his lifetime" (Aurand's App., 34 Pa. 151-1859).

As to the defendant himself, the lien of a judgment remains in force against lands still owned by him, without the necessity of issuing any sci. fa. to revive the same, for any period up to twenty years. After that period, the rebuttable presumption of payment arises (Brown's App., 91 Pa. 485-1879; McCahan v. Elliott, 103 Pa. 634-1883; Roberts v. Powell, 210 Pa. 5941905; and First Nat. Bank of Pittsburgh v. Bank of Pittsburgh et al., 99 Pa. Super. Ct. 600-1930).

It was also held that this was equally true as to the heirs or devisees of a deceased judgment debtor, and that they were not terre-tenants within the meaning of the above cited Acts (Shannon v. Newton, 132 Pa. 375-1890). In that case, a sci. fa. issued seventeen years after the judgment was entered, bringing in the devisee of the decedent, was held to be in good time. This has been changed by the Fiduciaries Act of 1917 

(P.L. 447, §15(f) and (g), 20 P.S. §§526 and 527). 

$15 (f) provides the "Judgments which were not liens on the real estate of the decedent, by entry or revival within five years prior to the death of the decedent ***** shall not be revived as liens of record against real estate by such death, but shall rank and be treated simply as ordinary debts not of record; and the lien thereof shall be continued only by writ of scire facias to revive, issued within one year" after decedent's death, and duly indexed and prosecuted to judgment. $15(g) provides in effect that judgments which are liens on the decedent's real estate at his death, by entry or revival within five years prior thereto, shall continue to bind such real estate for five years from such death; but to continue as a lien beyond that period, must be revived by sci. fa. issued within that period.

Under these sections of the Fiduciaries Act, if title is being

§177(b)443 

SEARCHES. 

made by heirs or devisees of a decedent, within the year following his death, a search for judgments must be made against the decedent for twenty years preceding his death, or for as long as decedent held title short of that period. All judgments entered or revived within the five years preceding his death are again revived by his death for another period of five years; and all judgments entered or revived prior to the five years, but within the twenty years, have the same lien during the year following decedent's death as ordinary unrecorded debts, and a sci. fa. to revive such judgments must be issued within the year, or their lien is wholly lost. 

(2) Lien of a Judgment as Against a Purchaser or Mort gagee. In considering how far back a search for judgments must be made, in connection with a proposed mortgage or conveyance, the vital question is, however, what is the effect of the above mentioned Acts, as they have been interpreted by the Courts, as affecting a purchaser or mortgagee? A review of the cases, including some of the early decisions, is necessary to determine this rather involved question. 

In 1843, in Armstrong's App., (5 W. & S. 352-1843), the 

Court held that even though a grantee of a judgment debtor fails to record his deed, and does not go into possession a judgment entered within five years before the deed, and revived within five years of its entry, by joinder of the judgment debtor only, loses its lien as against such grantee. This led to the passage of the Act of April 16, 1849 (supra.), which provided that "when a judgment shall be regularly revived between the original parties, the period of five years during which the lien ** ** continues, shall only commence to run in favor of the terre-tenant from the time the deed is recorded," unless the terre-tenant is in actual possession prior to the recording, when the period runs from the time when he took possession.

Two cases had already been decided by the Supreme Court, immediately prior to this Act, holding that the entry of a judgment of revival against the original judgment defendant, after deeds made by him, and without notice to the grantee, was

§177(b)2 

wholly ineffective to revive the old, or to create a new lien on such real estate, and that any new sci. fa. must issue on the original valid judgment, and not on the revival (Little v. 

Smyser, 10 Pa. 381-1849; Zerns v. Watson, 11 Pa. 260-1849).

In Armington v. Rau, (100 Pa. 165-1882) the Court held that where the judgment debtor had conveyed to his wife by deed duly recorded during the five year period from the entry of judgment, and the later revival by sci. fa. within that period was without notice to the wife, a sale under execution issued after the five years from the original judgment, but within five years of the recording of the deed, passed no title, as the original judgment had then ceased to be a lien on the premises by reason of the omission of the wife from the revival. The 

Court does not discuss the Act of 1849 at all. Within a few years after this decision, the above cited Act of June 1, 1887, was passed, reenacting the provisions of the Act of 1827, but adding the following clause: "No proceeding shall be available to continue the lien of said judgment against a terretenant, whose deed for the land bound by the judgment has been recorded, except by agreement in writing signed by said terre-tenant * or the terre-tenant or terre-tenants be named as such in the original scire facias.” 

In Uhler v. Moses, (200 Pa. 498-1901), the Court definitely ruled that, even though the deed to a terre-tenant is of record prior to the issuance of the sci. fa. to revive, and though the terre-tenant is not named as a party thereto, and even though the alias sci. fa., which brings in the terre-tenant, issues after the expiration of the five years from the original judgment, the lien of that original judgment is still valid and will support an execution at any time within five years from the recording of the deed to the terre-tenant. 

The Court did not discuss the meaning of the word "original" in the above cited provision of the Act of 1887, requiring the terre-tenant "to be named as such in the original scire facies", in order to continue the lien; nor does the Court refer to the case of Armington v. Rau. The Court, however, definitely ruled on the facts before it that it was not necessary

§177(b)445 

SEARCHES. 

to include the terre-tenant in the original scire facias in order to keep the lien alive; and that, under the Act of 1849, the lien of the original judgment remains alive for five years from the date of the recording of the terre-tenant's deed. 

In the case of Kefover v. Hustead, (294 Pa. 474—1928), the Court upheld the lien of a judgment as still in force, although no sci. fa. at all had been issued until after the expiration of five years from the entry of the original judgment. In that case the first sci. fa. which was issued upon the judgment was issued within five years from the recording of the deed to the terre-tenants, and the terre-tenants were included in the same. It is true that, in that case, the judgment defendant had died in 1918, after his deeds to the terre-tenants had been recorded, and the Court considered the question of whether, under §§15(f) and (g) of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917 (supra.) the death of the decendent had any effect in reviving the judgment in question as against the land which had been conveyed by the decedent by deeds recorded in his lifetime. The Court very clearly indicated that it did not think that the lien was revived by the decedent's death, in view of the language of $15(g) to the contrary. The Court, however, concluded that "The judgment was revived as to Husted's Estate for ***** five years when he died in 1918" and that it was therefore within the plaintiff's right to proceed against the land in question within five years from the recording of the deeds. 

In other words, the Court appears to hold that the death of the judgment debtor was the equivalent of a sci. fa. issued against him alone, and left the lien of the original judgment still good for five years from the recording of the decedent's deeds. The Court's language would seem to indicate that it still deemed it necessary for some revival "by sci. fa. or otherwise" to take place within the five years from the entry of the judgment, in order to entitle the plaintiff to the benefit of the further period of five years from the taking of possession by the terre-tenant, or the recording of the deed to him. 

This was the view taken of these precedents by the Superior 

Court in Everett Hardwood Lumber Co. v. Calhoun, (121 Pa.

§177 (b)2 

CONVEYANCES IN PENNSYLVANIA 

Super. Ct. 451-1936), where Judge James said, referring to the Kefover and Uhler cases: "From these cases the general rule may be found that where a judgment is revived within five years by means of the issuance of a writ of scire facias, or by an amicable agreement, such revival will bind the land that has been conveyed to a terre-tenant, if the judgment creditor revives the judgment" (evidently referring to the original judgment) "within five years of the recording of the deed, or within five years of the taking of actual possession by the terre-tenant." 

In Farmers Nat. Bank & Tr. Co. v. Barrett, (321 Pa. 2731936), however, the only sci. fa. which was issued to revive the judgment was issued within five years after judgment, and the grantee under a then recorded deed was not made a party thereto. It was held that, notwithstanding that no other sci. fa. had been issued to bring in the grantee, the lien of the original judgment was still good for five years from the recording of the grantee's deed, and justified an execution thereon to sell the land, the same being issued within the latter period.

This case was followed by that of First National Bank & Tr. Co. v. Miller, (322 Pa. 473-1936), where, after judgment taken on sci. fa. issued only against the judgment debtor, without bringing in the terre-tenant under a then recorded deed, the later sci. fa. which brought in the terre-tenant was not issued on the original judgment, but on the said judgment of revival, and it was held that such revival proceedings had no effect in reviving the old or in creating a new lien; but that the lien of the original judgment remained good until five years from the recording of the grantee's deed, despite the invalid intervening revivals. The Court uses the following significant language: "The judgment entered on the first sci. fa. neither continued nor preserved the lien of the judgment against the terre-tenant's land. ••••• That property was entirely unaffected by it. But the lien of the original judgment was not lost by that proceeding." 

The entire line of cases on this subject has been fully and

§177(b)447 

SEARCHES. 

excellently reviewed in the recent case of Klein v. Anderson, decided by Judge Wilson of Beaver County on May 14, 1940 (39 D. & C. 139-1940). In that case a sci. fa. was issued more than five years after judgment, which sci. fa. was a nullity, because it was returned unexecuted by the sheriff. 

Within five years after the recording of the deed from the judgment debtor, an alias sci. fa. was issued, bringing in a later title holder, and the Court held that this sci. fa. was issued in good time, and had it not been for certain procedural defects, would have continued the lien of the original judgment. The Court held that the recording of the terre-tenant's deed within five years of the judgment ipso facto extended the lien of that judgment for five years from such recording, notwithstanding the absence of any sci. fa. issued within five years of the entry of judgment. 

The upshot of these cases appears to be as follows: (I) Where a judgment is more than five years old at the date of record of a conveyance by the defendant, and no sci. fa. has then been issued to revive the same, the purchaser takes clear of the lien of the said judgment. (II) Where the judgment has been entered, or duly revived by sci. fa., within five years prior to the recording of the deed from the judgment debtor, the lien of the judgment is kept alive as against the grantee, as against the terre-tenant, and any subsequent grantee of his, for a further period of five years from the date of such recording, without any sci. fa. being issued during the five years from the entry of the judgment, or from the issuance of the previous sci. fa. (III) In such case, the issuance, after the recording of the deed, of a sci. fa. against the judgment debtor alone, with or without judment thereon, is wholly ineffective in reviving the lien of the original judgment, or in creating a new lien, as against the terre-tenant. (IV) The lien of the original judgment being still in existence for five years from the recording of the said deed, the land can be sold on execution under that lien, at any time dur-

§177 (c) 

ing the five year period, without the issuance of any sci. fa. at all, either against the judgment debtor or the terre-tenant. (V) Under such circumstances, in order to continue the lien of the judgment beyond the five years following the recording of the deed, a sci. fa. on the original judgment (being the judgment which was still a lien when the judgment debtor made his deed) must issue within that period, bringing in the terre-tenant.

Such being the state of the law, it is clear that a mere five year search for judgments, made against the persons holding title during that period, will not disclose all the possible judgment liens which may exist against the property. As to the persons whose record title commenced within the five years, the search will of course be made against each of them for the period running from the date of the deed into him down to the date of the recording of the deed from him. But as to the title holders who were the grantors in the earliest of the deeds for any of the land, which were recorded within those five years, and whose title commenced prior to that period, it would be necessary to search against them for the period of five years preceding the recording of the deeds from them, or at least for the full period during which they held title, if that be less than five years. Any judgments revealed by such a search as entered, or duly revived, against such persons beyond the five year period would appear to be still good liens, because they were still liens when the judgment debtors conveyed, and the five years would not yet have expired from the recording dates of the deeds out of them. 

(c) Discharge of Judgment Liens. 

Of course liens of judgments that are marked satisfied are discharged. So also a sheriff's sale will discharge or divest the lien not only of the judgment on which the sale was had but also of any judgment subsequent thereto as well as any prior thereto unless the land is sold expressly subject to such prior judgment. The governing rule has been well stated by 

Judge Parker in the recent case of Silverman v. Keal (135

§449 

SEARCHES. 

1 

Pa. Super. Ct. 568, 570—1939) as follows: "As a general rule a sheriff sale of real estate discharges all liens on the property sold unless the sale is expressly made subject to a prior lien or liens (Girard Life Ins. Co. v. Farmers & Mechanic's Na tional Bank, 57 Pa. 388, 394-1868; Olyphant Boro v. Egreski, 29 Pa. Super Ct. 116, 119-1905; Comm. for use Gurney's v. 

Alexander, Supra. [14 S. & R. 257-1826]), or unless it is otherwise provided by Statute as in the case of certain mortgages ¹ (Act of April 30, 1929 P.L. 874, 21 P.S. 651, a reenactment of many of the provisions of the original act of April 6, 1830, P.L. 293), and in case of tax and Municipal liens (Act of 

May 16, 1923 P. L. 207, 53 P.S. 2051). Prior to the Act of 

1830 the lien of a mortgage was divested by a sheriff sale on a junior judgment (Willard v. Morris 1 P. & W. 480-1830; 

Presbyterian Corp. v. Wallace, 3 Rawle 109-1831; Mode's 

Appeal 6 W. & S. 280-1843), and it required statutory authority to preserve municipal liens (Allegheny City's Appeal 41 Pa. 60-1861). The general rule applies and liens of judgment are divested by a sale even though they are prior and superior to the lien for the enforcement of which the sale is made or though the judgment was obtained against a former owner and the execution is against a subsequent owner (Comm. for use Gurney v. Alexander, Supra.), or even if proceedings are pending to revive the lien, (Foulke v. Millard, Supra. [108 

Pa. 230-1885] ).” 

178. Where to Search for Judgment Liens. 

Judgments are liens when entered by the following Penn sylvania Courts: Supreme Court, Courts of Quarter Sessions and Oyer and Terminer, Courts of Common Pleas, and in

Philadelphia County, the Municipal Court, and also when entered by the United States District Court for the particular district covering the county in which the real estate is situate. 

Judgments of the Superior Court become liens only when entered in the docket of the lower court. 

1 See $100(a) of this book for fuller discussion of discharge of Mortgages by judicial sale.

§179 

 Definitive orders or decrees by the Orphans' Courts upon parties other than fiduciaries, to pay sums of money do not become liens against the real estate of the party ordered to pay, until a transcript is filed in the Court of Common Pleas in conformity with §18(e) of the Orphans' Court Act of June 

7, 1917, P.L. 363, (20 P.S. 2461). From the time such transcript is filed and indexed, it becomes a lien with the same force and effect as in the case of other judgments. So also by the amendment of May 5, 1939, P.L. 94, §21(d) (20 P.S. 2585) of the same act, verdicts or judgments entered pursuant to a jury trial held in the Orphans' Court are required by the Clerk of that Court to be certified forthwith to the Prothonotary who files such certificate in his office, dockets such verdict or judgment, and indexes the same in the judgment index in the same manner as verdicts and judgments in the courts of 

Common Pleas.

Judgments of the Allegheny County Court are not liens until transcripts of the same are filed in the Prothonotary's office and indexed in the Judgment Index. 

Judgments of Magistrates' and Justice of Peace courts are not liens until transcripts of the same have been filed in the Common Pleas Courts, and duly indexed there. 

The various courts hereinbefore mentioned will be separately dealt with in the sections which follow. 

179. Appellate Court Judgments. (a) Supreme Court Judgments.

A judgment of the Supreme Court is only a lien on real estate situate in the county in which it is rendered. (Act of 

March 20, 1799, 3 Sm. L. 358, §1, 12 P.S. §865). It may also issue execution for costs. (Act of June 16, 1836, P.L. 784, §1, 17 P.S. §41). Though by $3 of Article V. of the Constitution of Pennsylvania the Supreme Court has original jurisdiction "in cases of injunction where a corporation is a party defendant, habeas corpus, mandamus to courts of inferior jurisdiction and Quo Warranto as to all officers of the Commonwealth

whose jurisdiction extends over the State". This jurisdiction is infrequently exercised so that it is not the usual practice to search for judgments in the office of the Prothonotary of that Court. 

(b) Superior Court Judgments 

Money judgments of the Superior Court are not liens until entered upon the docket of the lower Court. (Act of June 

24, 1895, P.L. 212, §8, 17 P.S. §192). Therefore, a separate search in the Superior Court is unnecessary.

(1) Common Pleas Judgments. By far the greatest number of judgments are entered in the courts of common pleas.

Both the Prothonotary and Recorder of Deeds of Philadelphia County will issue certificates of search if asked to, although they are not authorized or required to do so by any act of assembly. Outside of the City, it has been held a false search gives no right of action to the subsequent purchaser. The officer is liable only to the person who ordered the search (Commonwealth v. Harmer, 6 Phila. 90, Supreme Court, 1865, and

Sentences, decrees or judgments of those Courts may also be certified to the Common Pleas Court of the respective county, with the same effect as if they were originally entered by the latter court (Act May 8, 1901, P.L. 143 §1, 12 P.S. §1001). 

By the supplement to this Act, passed June 22, 1931 Act No.
