182. United States Court Judgments. 

Since 1911, there has been only one United States Court of original jurisdiction, whose judgments and decrees become liens on real estate, and that is the United States District Court. The jurisdiction of each of these Courts in Pennsylvania extends over a number of Counties. The clerks of these Courts are required by Act of Congress to "keep indices of all judgment debtors" under such decrees and judgments, which are open to the public (Act of Aug. 1, 1888, c. 729, §2, as amended, 28 U.S.C.A. §813). There is no question of the validity of the lien of such a judgment, when so indexed, upon land situate in the particular County where the court is lo cated. The Act of Assembly of May 17, 1929 (P.L. 1805, 17

§182 

P.S. §1932), after providing for the entry and indexing by the Prothonotary of the Common Pleas Courts of transcripts of judgments and decrees of the United States Courts "in the same manner" as transcripts of state court judgments are entered and indexed, to become liens, provides as follows: "and no judgment or decree entered in the **・・・ District or other Court of the United States shall be a lien on any real estate in any county of this Commonwealth, unless the same shall be so entered in the Court of Common Pleas of the county wherein such real estate is situate; provided that nothing herein contained shall be construed to required the docketing of a judgment or a decree of a United States Court, or the filing of a transcript thereof ***** within the same county in which the judgment or decree is rendered by such 

United States Court." (See Seventeenth St. Land Co. v.

Hustead, 263 Pa. 342, holding the same proviso in a prior Act of Assembly to be valid and binding). 

The existence of such a lien on land situate in any of the counties outside the county of rendition, over which the Federal Court's jurisdiction extends, without the filing of transcript of the judgment in the Common Pleas of such County, as required by the above quoted Act of 1929, is a more debatable question. Prior to the Act of Congress of Aug. 1, 1888 (28 U. S. C. A. §812), a judgment of a federal court was held to be a lien on all lands situate within its territorial jurisdiction, even in states where the judgment of a state court created a lien only within the county in which the judgment was entered (Massingil v. Downs, 7 How. 760-1849). By that Act, however, it was provided that: "Judgments and decrees rendered in a Circuit or District Court of the United States within any state shall be liens on property throughout that state, in the same manner and to the same extent and under the same conditions only as if such judgments and decrees had been entered by a Court of general jurisdiction of such State; provided that whenever the laws of any State require a judgment or decree of a State Court to be registered, recorded, docketed, indexed, or any other thing to be done, in

§457 

SEARCHES. 

a particular manner, or in a certain office or county before a lien shall attach, this Act shall be applicable therein whenever and only whenever the laws of such State shall authorize the United States judgments and decrees to be so registered, received, docketed, indexed or otherwise conformed to the rules relating to judgments of the state courts." 

One of the first cases in which the effect of this act in giving force to State laws requiring transcripts of both state and federal judgments to be filed in counties other than the county of rendition in order to secure a lien in such other counties, is the often cited case of Dartmouth Savings Bank v. Bates, 44

Fed. 546-(1890), where the point was squarely raised and the State laws, quite similar in effect to the Pennsylvania Acts relating to judgments, were held to be valid, and the filing of a transcript necessary to the acquisition of such a lien. 

This was a decision of the United States Circuit Court of 

Kansas. The Court said: 

"The first clause of the act (of 1888) places judgment liens in a federal court on the same footing in all respects, as a judgment in a state court of general jurisdiction. But the power of Congress was not adequate to the task of extending the territorial operation of a judgment lien in the mode provided by state laws for a judgment in the state court. **** There was no federal clerk's office * in each county of the state *. Congress could not make it obligatory on the state clerks to docket and enter a judgment of a federal court on their records. * • The proviso in §1 of the Act (of 1888) declares, in legal effect, that when the laws of a state provide for docketing in her clerk's offices or other offices, the judgments of federal courts, in the same manner that judgments in her own courts may be docketed, then, and not before, the territorial extent * of the lien of a judgment in a federal court in that state, shall be the same as that of a judgment in the state court." 

This case was cited with approval by the Supreme Court in 

Rhea v. Smith, 274 U.S. 434 (1927), where the Court said (p. 441):

§182 

"It is clear that Congress, by the first section of the Act of Aug. 1, 1888, intended to change and limit the existing rule ***** that federal court judgments were a lien upon lands throughout the territorial jurisdiction of the respective federal courts, but intended to do this only in those states which passed laws making the conditions of creation, scope and territorial application of the liens of federal court judgments the same as state court judgments." 

In that case the court held that the state laws of Missouri had not created a sufficient parity between the State and federal court judgments, in that the judgment of the State Court acquired a lien in the county of rendition, immediately upon its entry there, while the State law provided as to federal court judgments that "upon the filing of a transcript in the office of the clerk of any (state) circuit court, such judgments should be liens on the real estate situate in the county where the transcript was filed." (See Lineker v. Dillon, 275 

Fed. 460—1921, to the same effect.)

In Rathbone v. Kimball, 220 N.W. 244 (1928), the question before the court was stated to be whether, under the Act of Aug. 1, 1888, and the laws of Nebraska, a judgment of a federal court in Nebraska was a lien outside of the county where it was rendered, without the filing of a transcript with the local county court clerk, as required by the state laws; and the court held that it was not a lien, because those laws created "an exact conformity" between the two classes of judgments. 

The Supreme Court refused to grant a certiorari to this decision (278 U.S. 655).

It is difficult to see how, under the above cited Act of May 17, 1929, and the other Pennsylvania Acts relating to judgments, there is any lack of conformity between the lien of the judgment of any Pennsylvania Court of general jurisdiction (which, as was pointed out in Rhea v. Smith by Justice Taft, are the courts of first instance, like our Common Pleas) and the lien of a federal judgment. The non-conformity found in the case of Rhea v. Smith is expressly excluded by the proviso of the State Act of 1929, which makes no transcript

§459 

SEARCHES. 

necessary in the county of rendition. The Act also expressly assimilates the entry and indexing of transcripts of federal court judgments to what is required in connection with the transcripts of state court judgments. 

Until, however, the question has been judicially decided, as to the conformity of the Pennsylvania Acts with the requirements of the Act of Congress so as to make certain the validity of the provisions of the Act of 1929, calling for the filing of transcripts in counties outside the county of rendition, as a prerequisite to their lien in such counties, it will be the safer practice to always search for judgments in the office of the Clerk of the United States District Court, within whose territorial jurisdiction the land lies, whether within the county of rendition, or outside the same. 

183. Lien of Decedent's Debts. 

By the Act of 1917 (June 7, 1917 P.L. 447, §15 (a), 20 P.S. 

521) all debts of a decedent are a lien for one year after his death, on all real estate of which he died seised. After one year from the date of decedent's death the lien of debts other than judgments expires unless preserved by suit being commenced and indexed against the decedent in the judgment index of the Prothonotary (§15 (a) of the Act of 1917, supra.). 

If suit is commenced at any time before the expiration of the one year period, and is indexed as above stated and duly prosecuted to judgment, its lien is preserved for a further period of five years, and may be further revived by scire facias. In the case of debts not due within the one year period, a written statement of the debt must be filed and indexed in the judgment index of the Prothonotary within the year, in which event the lien is preserved until one year after the debt becomes due unless within such latter yearly period suit is commenced (§15 (b) of the Act of 1917, supra. 20 P.S. 

522). Unless the lien of a debt of a decedent is preserved by following the procedure provided in §15 of the Act of 1917, such lien is lost even if the land sought to be charged is in 1 Provided of course the heirs or devisees have been joined in the suit or brought in by sci. fa. within 6 years from decedent's death (Curtze v. Ostrow 22 Erie 256 -1941; Pyles v. Bosler 22 D. & C. 10—1934).

§184  

the hands of the heirs of the decedent or volunteers (Bindley's 

Appeal, 69 Pa. 295; Tourison's Estate, 321 Pa. 299).¹

Judgments which were liens against the real estate of a decedent at the time of his death continue to bind such real estate for a further term of five years after decedent's death without revival or further action ($15(g) of the Act of 1917 supra. 20 P.S. 527).

A positive direction in the will to convert real estate into cash works a conversion and will discharge the lien of decedent's debts on real estate sold under such direction (Mustin's Estate, 194 Pa. 437). Similarly the lien of such debts will be discharged where the will authorizes a sale and directs the payment of debts, and a sale takes place within one year after the decedent's death (Davidson v. Bright, 267 

Pa. 580-1920). Where a decedent's land is sold by Orphans'

Court sale for payment of debts the lien of all debts are immediately discharged and thrown upon the fund." 

184. Mechanics' Liens. 

Under the Mechanics' Lien Act of June 4, 1901, P.L. 431, as amended (Title 49 P.S.), mechanics' liens may become liens against property from the time of the commencement of the work if filed within three months from its completion for alteration and repairs and within six months from its completion for all other work (§10 of the Act of 1901, 49 P.S. 52). 

A writ of scire facias must issue on the claim within two years (unless waived for a further period not exceeding three years by writing signed by the owner of the property and filed prior to the expiration of the two year period) and prosecuted to judgment within five years, otherwise the lien will be lost. 

Mechanics' liens when filed are indexed in the judgment index at the prothonotary's office, but in addition to a search of the index, proof should be obtained by affidavit or otherwise that no work has been done in or about the premises in question 1 For further discussion of lien of decedent's debts see $170-A of this book. 

2 For further discussion of "conversion" and discharge of lien of decedent's debts thereby see $170-E(a).

§461 

SEARCHES. 

within a period of six months for which a mechanics' lien could be filed. If the right to file a lien be waived before the beginning of the work, by writing duly executed and filed in the prothonotary's office ($15 of the Act of 1901 as amended, 49 P.S. 72), no mechanics' lien can be filed either by the contractor, sub-contractor, or material man, and if filed will be stricken off. A mechanics' lien is divested by a sale under a prior lien and remitted to the fund. 

185. Locality Index. 

By virtue of §26 of the Municipal Lien Act of May 16, 1923, P.L. 207, (53 P.S. 2046), it is the duty of the prothonotary of every court of common pleas to keep a "locality index" in which shall be entered all tax or municipal claims filed. All such claims, in addition to being indexed in the name of the owner, are also indexed under the location or description of the property. Upon written order and for a small fee it is the duty of the prothonotary under the act to give a certificate of search showing all the claims filed against any property. 

Searching this index not only verifies the judgment index, but turns up liens against property where the name of the owner was either unknown or erroneously given. 

186. Taxes and Municipal Liens. 

(a) Under the Municipal Lien Act. 

Under the Municipal Lien Act of 1923 (Act of May 16, 1923, P.L. 207 as amended; 53 P.S. 2021) all taxes are a first lien on property even if unfiled until the last day of the third calendar year after that in which the taxes are first payable. To preserve the lien beyond this period it must be filed within such time. Municipal liens for improvements are likewise first liens subject only to taxes, but to retain their lien a municipal claim must be filed within six months from the completion of the improvement. Both tax and municipal liens, when filed, will appear in the locality index of the prothonotary's office, and must be revived as provided in the Act of 1923 every five

§186 

years. Claims for water rates, lighting and sewer rates, must also be filed in the prothonotary's offices within the time specified above for taxes or else they will not be liens. Upon the judicial sale of any property, taxes and municipal claims must be first paid out of the proceeds, and are only discharged by such sales to the extent that the fund is sufficient for their payment (§31 of the Act of 1923; 53 P.S. 2051). An ordinary sale of a property for unpaid taxes or municipal claims will not discharge a prior mortgage unless a lien prior to the mortgage is also discharged, but the municipality or lien claimant may, by following the provisions of §51 of the Act of 1923, obtain a sale by leave of court, which will discharge all claims, mortgages, charges and estates in the property. (See Erie v. Piece of Land, 339 Pa. 321, and §177-A of this book.)

To guard against the possibility of unfiled liens for taxes and municipal claims, see that all taxes and water rent receipts are produced for three years or a certificate of their payment obtained from the Receiver of Taxes. Require an affidavit from the owner also that no municipal improvements have been made within one year prior to the date of settlement. 

In Philadelphia unpaid charges for the use of waterpipe in any abutting street, are ascertained by securing an official water-pipe search from the Bureau of Water. 

(b) Tax Liens Under the Treasurer's Sales Act. 

The Act of May 9, 1929 (P.L. 1684, 72 P.S. §5951, et. seq.) 

which act supplied certain prior acts, and relates to taxes assessed by other than cities, provides for the filing by tax collectors "of any county, borough, town, township, school district or poor district," of returns of unpaid taxes on seated lands to the county commissioners of the county where the land lies, not later than the first Monday of May, in the year following that of their assessment. The returns are then certified to the county treasurer, who is authorized to sell the lands on the first Monday of August in the year succeeding the assessment year "or on any day to which such sale shall be adjourned."

§186A 

463 

SEARCHES. 

No court proceedings are necessary under this act, and there is no provision for official searches to be issued by any of the taxing authorities. The only means of protection is to search for treasurer's sales in the office of the county treasurer, and to search for unpaid taxes in the office of the county commissioners, from the year covered by the last treasurer's sale, down to the year covered by the last return of the tax collector; and in addition, the owner should be required to produce his tax receipts for those years down to and including the current year. 

186-A. Tax Searches by the Receiver of Taxes in Philadelphia.

The Receiver of Taxes of Philadelphia is required to furnish, upon request, a certificate of all taxes and claims which are a lien on real estate located in such City, and to receive therefor 50¢ for each certificate and 5¢ for each lien and claim certified (Act of February 2, 1854, P.L. 21, §11, 53 

P.S. 4831, and Act of May 20, 1921, P.L. 936, 53 P.S. 4942).

A clear certificate of search given by the Receiver estops the City from collecting taxes and the City cannot assert a lien or collect unpaid taxes from one who purchases a property on the faith of such a certificate (Philadelphia v. Anderson, 142 

Pa. 357-1891; Antonoff v. Zolyan, 104 Pa. Super. Ct. 1021931). In this respect the certificate of the Receiver of Taxes differs from a certificate given by the Prothonotary, liability for which is limited to damages recoverable from the Prothonotary by the person to whom the certificate is issued (House man v. Girard Mutual Building and Loan Association, 81 Pa. 

256-1876; Siewers v. Commonwealth, 87 Pa. 15-1878). In

Philadelphia, by the Act of April 13, 1872, P.L. 1140 (16 P.S. 

1186 and 17 P.S. 1542), liability to respond in damages for an erroneous certificate given by the Recorder of Deeds, the

Prothonotary or the Clerk of the Court, was extended to any person or persons claiming title through, from or under the person to whom the search was given or to anyone who may suffer loss by reason of the making or giving of a false or

§186B  

erroneous search, such liability continuing for a period of five years from the giving of the certificate. The Receiver of 

Taxes and his sureties are also liable in damages for the issuing of an erroneous certificate (Philadelphia to the use etc. v. Brenner, 138 Pa. Super. Ct. 454-1939). 

186-B. State Corporation Taxes. 

All State taxes imposed against a corporation are, by the 

Act of June 15, 1911, P.L. 955, as amended (72 P.S. 3342) as well as by the terms of the Fiscal Code (Act of April 9, 1929, P.L. 343, art. XIV, §1401, as amended; 72 P.S. 1401), made a first lien upon the franchise and property, real and personal, of the corporation from the date of settlement of the tax even though not certified to the county where the corporation land lies or indexed in the judgment index of such county. A search should be obtained as to corporate taxes from the 

Auditor General at Harrisburg (see Commonwealth v. Central 

Realty Company, 338 Pa. 172-1940). The lien of a mortgage executed by a predecessor in title to the corporation was held to be superior in lien to State corporation taxes assessed thereafter and a foreclosure sale on such mortgage divests the Commonwealth's lien (Davis v. Seltzer, 313 Pa. 3821934). This rule has been written into the Fiscal Code by amendment to art. XIV, $1401 (72 P.S. 1401). 

186-C. Federal Income Taxes. 

Income taxes as well as all other federal taxes are by statute made a lien upon all property, real or personal, of the taxpayer from the time the assessment list is received by the collector (53 Stat. 448, 449; 26 U.S.C.A. 3670, 3671). Such taxes are not a lien as against any mortgagee, pledgee, purchaser or judgment creditor until notice thereof has been filed by the collector at the place provided by the law of the State, or in the absence of such law in the office of the Clerk of the United States District Court for the judicial district in which the property is located (53 Stat. 449 as amended by 53 Stat.

§465 

SEARCHES. 

882; 26 U.S.C.A. 3672). In Pennsylvania the Act of May 1, 1929, P.L. 1215 (74 P.S. 141 et seq.), provides for the filing of such liens in the office of the Prothonotary of the County where the real estate is situated (see $176-A-(a)1 of this book). 

The protection afforded mortgagees and purchasers by these statutes has been extended to a mortgagee who knew at the time of the execution of the mortgage that the mortgagor owed taxes: United States v. Beaver Run Coal Co., 99 Fed. 

(2nd) 610 (C.C.A. 3rd-1938). No special priority is given by these acts to Federal tax liens and they are subject to liens existing at the time the Federal lien arises: (Exchange National Bank of Tulsa v. Davy, 13 Fed. Supp. 226-1936). 

187. Assignment of Mortgage Searches. 

When searching title in order to see whether a mortgage about to be assigned is good, search first against the title of the mortgagor, as if for a conveyance (§§174 to 186-C Supra.). 

Then search for possible prior assignments of the mortgage. 

Assignments of mortgages are indexed in a separate index, as well as noted on the margin of the mortgage book. Search should then be made for possible releases to see whether the mortgage still covers all the land described by it. In Philadelphia, releases of mortgages are also indexed in a separate index since 1880. Then search for bankruptcy against the mortgagee, and each subsequent holder of the mortgage in question. Having completed the search, demand as a final precaution a declaration of no set-off from the owner and ascertain if there are any outstanding unpaid municipal claims or taxes (See $186-Supra.) Above all insist on the production and delivery of the bond and mortgage with the assignment (see $101-A of this book). 

188. Examination of Property. 

After all searching is completed, personally view the property about to be conveyed. This will afford an opportunity of discovering any existing easement not disclosed in the

$189

chain of title. In Pennsylvania a person takes subject to any visible and notorious easement without express mention in the deed, the rule being, "Where an owner of land subjects part of it to an open, visible, permanent and continuous servitude or easement in favor of another part, and then aliens it the purchaser takes subject to the burden or benefit as the case may be" (Liquid Carbonic Co. v. Wallace, 219 Pa. 4571908). Ascertain also, if the owner is not in possession, whether the occupant is a tenant or claims to hold adversely to the owner. "It evinces as much carelessness to purchase property without having viewed the premises, as to purchase without having searched the register" (Woods v. Farmere 

7 Watts 382-1838). It is the duty of purchasers of real estate to make inquiry respecting the rights of the party in possession, and failing to do so they are affected with constructive notice of such facts as would have come to their knowledge in the proper discharge of their duty: (Lazarus v. 

Lehigh and Wilkes-Barre Coal Co., 246 Pa. 178-1914). "Nor does knowledge of the existence of a lease relieve one dealing with the lessor from the duty of inquiring from one in possession whether he claims otherwise than under the lease" (Anderson v. Brinser, 129 Pa. 376-1889). 

189. Synopsis of How to Search. 

(A) SEARCHES AGAINST A PROSPECTIVE GRANTOR OR MORTGAGOR. 

I. Conveyance Search. 

(1) Make a conveyance search by searching at the recorder of deeds' office as indicated in §§172-174 for flaws in the title. (2) Verify your search at the registry bureau as indicated in $175. 

II. Now make your encumbrance search. (1) For mortgages in the mortgage index at the recorder of deeds' office as outlined in §176.

$467 

SEARCHES. 

(2) Search for Supreme Court Judgments if deemed necessary (See §179). (3) Search for judgments at the office of the clerk of quarter sessions (§181). 

(4) Search for judgments and federal liens at the office of the clerk of United States courts (See §182). While at this office, make search for possible marshal's sales to complete your conveyance search (§174). (5) Search at the office of the prothonotary of the common pleas courts. a. Judgment index for judgments ($180). b. Judgment index for lien of decedent's debts, if any (§183). c. Locality index for municipal and mechanics' 

liens (§§184, 185 and 186). 

d. Ejectment Index for pending actions affecting the title ($180 (b)). 

e. Federal Tax Lien Index (§§176-A-(a) 1, and 

186-C). f. Search here also for sheriff's sales to complete conveyance search ($174). (6) Obtain certificates in Philadelphia as to unpaid taxes, water rent, and water-pipe charges; and outside of 

Philadelphia make searches in the offices of the county commissioners and the county treasurer (§186). (7) Wherever any corporation has been in the title, a search should be ordered from the Auditor General at Harrisburg to ascertain whether there were any taxes assessed against the corporation in the period during which such corporation held title. ($186-B.)

III. Personally examine property. 

(1) For easements not noted in chain of Title (§188). 

(2) As to occupation (§188).

$190 

Note protection against unfiled liens and taxes (§186).

(b) SEARCHES FOR GROUND RENT ASSIGNMENTS. 

Titles to ground rents should be searched the same as above.

(c) SEARCHES WHERE ASSIGNMENT OF MORTGAGE IS TO BE MADE. 

I. Search against the original mortgagor as fully as though he were a prospective mortgagor, or grantor, so as to establish the validity and nature of the lien about to be assigned. ($187). 

II. (1) Search against the original mortgagor and all subsequent assignees of the mortgage during the time they respectively held title, so as to turn up any adverse assignments. ($187.) (2) See that assignment is in proper form.

III. Search against all holders of mortgage for possible releases and for bankruptcy. (§187.)

IV. Demand declaration of no set-off. ($187 and $103) and insist that the bond and mortgage to be assigned are produced and delivered. ($187 and $101-A.)

All of the devisees named in said recited will are of full age except the said Mary Leath Courtney.

At an orphans' court for the city and county of 

Philadelphia, held at Philadelphia, upon the petition of the said Mary Leath Courtney, who was then above the age of fourteen years, The Fidelity 

Insurance, Trust and Safe Deposit Company was appointed guardian of her estate. 

At an orphans' court for the city and county of Philadelphia, held at Philadelphia, the petition of the said "The Fidelity Insurance, Trust and Safe 

Deposit Company," guardian as aforesaid, was presented, setting forth "That the said Mary

Leath Courtney is seised in her demesne as of fee

of and in an equal undivided fifth part or share of and in the real estate therein particularly described (being the premises conveyed by the next deed.) 

That all the other parties interested in said real estate being sui juris are anxious and desirous of disposing of the same. That Peter S. Dildine, of the city of Philadelphia, has offered to purchase the said real estate for the price or sum of $16,- 000.00, clear of all encumbrances, and all the other owners of said real estate have agreed to sell at said price and are anxious and desirous that the proper and necessary deeds and assurances for said real estate should be executed to the said Peter S. Dildine and a perfect title for the same made to him, but are prevented from so doing on account of the inability of the petitioners to join with them in the execution and delivery of said deeds as guardian aforesaid without the consent and order of the court. That the said price offered for said real estate is much greater than the assessed value of the same and that the said amount is, to the best of petitioner's knowledge and belief, as large a price as can now be obtained for said property. That is to the advantage of said minor's estate that said real estate should be sold, inasmuch as the same is in great need of repair and in a dilapidated condition." The petitioners therefore prayed the court to approve of the price offered for said real estate and authorize them to sell the said minor's undivided fifth interest therein for one-fifth of the said price offered as aforesaid, viz: $3,200.00, and that they be authorized, ordered and directed as guardian of said Mary Leath Courtney to join with the other owners of the said real estate in the execution and delivery of the proper and necessary deed or deeds and other assurances
